On Relevance: The Social Physics of Pluralism

A Cross-Platform Evaluation of the Structure and Function of Legitimacy and Standing

By Jonathan Rademacher

Dedication

To my wife and daughters, Kristi, Avalina, and Ellovee Rademacher, who have coupled me hopelessly to themselves and to the outcomes of their dispositions as women in a world that is predominantly shaped by male-driven outcomes:

May this work serve as an instrumental figure to increase the satisfaction of your experiences in the world and the collective of the human species on the whole. Without your help in coupling my understanding of autonomy to your own, this work would not have been possible.

To my foster parents, Gary and Debbie Forsman, who opened their home to me and coupled me with an understanding of humanity that was drastically divergent from what I had hitherto not been capable of comprehending:

May this work serve as a testimony to the payoff of your work in coupling my understanding to the benefits of human dignity, the countless times you endured my errors and failures solely for the hope that you inspired something nobler in the humanity you influenced, and as a validation that your efforts have not been in vain or ignored.

To my colleagues in the LGBTQIA+, Latin, African American, and other communities that established couplings for me to their perceptions and provided me with the means necessary to not only view the domains in this book as interconnected but gave the kindness and mercy to endure my ignorance in the hope that something less ignorant might emerge:

May this work serve as an instrumental piece to the goals of equity and fair treatment for all communities, confirm to your communities that this work is one which emerges as a culmination of your collective efforts and not as any variation of superiority. May it inspire hope that your efforts are not consolidated to works such as this but that they truly have a global impact that is radically shaping the world. Your efforts are likewise not in vain.

Special Acknowledgment

This work owes its deepest conceptual roots to my wife, Kristi Rademacher. Long before any formal structure, algebraic operator, or analytic engine emerged on these pages, there was her insight — her way of seeing autonomy, power, cognitive load, and unfairness from the inside. Through countless conversations, moments of shared frustration, and her generosity in letting me witness how asymmetries feel from her perspective, she gave me the phenomenological grounding that made all of this possible. The clarity with which this framework expresses asymmetry, coupling burdens, and nondomination is a direct inheritance from her lived experience, not merely my analysis of it.

Any conceptual rigor or structural articulation found here is built atop the reality she showed me — a reality that cannot be derived from theory alone. She did not merely inspire this work. She cooriginated it. Her brilliance in communicating her experiences, and in illuminating the many forms that autonomy can take — intellectual, bodily, emotional, and otherwise — is the core root of this framework. It is what allowed me to understand autonomy as a compositional variable that depends upon nonnegotiable structural criteria. In every meaningful sense, this work is as much hers as it is mine.

Foundational Axioms and Structural Laws

On the Generality of Structural Forms

The structural axioms developed in this book derive their force not from analogy but from the architecture of pluralist coordination. Systems that must coordinate without final authority exhibit a limited set of structural forms: equilibrium conditions, monotonic drifts, repair dynamics, and limiting behaviors. These same forms appear across many lawful systems.

Any crossdomain engine that claims structural portability must be capable of expressing these forms; one that cannot would violate regularities in at least one domain and thereby forfeit its claim to generality. The thermodynamic analogies developed later in the book are therefore not rhetorical devices. They show that the triad is not a constructed heuristic but an emergent structural profile of pluralist society itself.

A Structural Axiom on Interaction and Coordination

Where humanity exists as a pluralist society, it does so through partial and contested coordination.

Any final authority that does not interact with humanity cannot, by definition, coordinate it plurally.

Wherever a final authority does interact with humanity, pluralist coordination presumes accountability, exit, corrigibility, and nondomination.

Violating these conditions is necessarily structural domination and therefore structurally incompatible with pluralist society.

Domination is a way of coordinating behavior, not a way of coordinating a pluralist society.

The Axiom of Derivative Standing

To define the relationship between individuals and “the host” (corporations, governments, or publishers), we distinguish between two types of standing:

Primary Standing: Held only by the individual agents (A, B, C …) who possess Terminal Agency.

Derivative Standing: Held by collective institutions. This standing is “borrowed” from the primary agents to facilitate large-scale coordination.

The Subordination Principle: Since derivative standing is non-terminal, a collective can never legitimately claim standing over an individual’s level 1 or level 2 (life and sustenance) rights. The “organism” exists to serve the “cells,” not the other way around.

The Axiom of Pluralistic Inclusion (The Successor Axiom)

The Principle of Initial Nullity

Let U be the universal set of potential entities within a system. For any i ∈ U, let σi represent its standing (it’s weight or relevance within the system’s analytic engine).

If σi = 0, the entity exists in a state of nullity. In this state, the entity is invariant to all scaling transformations (T):

T (0) = к * 0 = 0

The structural insight:

No amount of systemic force, power, or “social physics” can act upon a null value. Multiplication (power) requires a non-zero base. Therefore, an actor with zero standing cannot be “empowered” before being “counted.”

The Successor Function (S)

The transition from Nullity to Relevance is governed strictly by the Successor Operator (S), defined as the primary additive act:

S (0) = 0+1

This “+1” represents the unit of standing. It is the atomic, indivisible act of recognition that brings an entity into the system’s calculable reality. The successor function represents the value of the additive property of frames to the perspective of an agent.

The Primacy of Addition (Perception Primacy)

Since all complex mathematics (multiplication, exponentiation, integration) is derived from the repeated application of the successor function, the additive property is the primary constraint. Likewise, since this is the analog for the concept of perception itself, the primary function of that property extends into this framework such that perception is also the primary function from which all complex variants arise.

Individuality: Each “+1” represents a discrete “law of standing” such that each frame is intrinsically valid unto itself as a non-null operator

Non-Dilution: In an additive framework, the arrival of a new actor (+1) increases the total system sum (∑σ) without inherently dividing or reducing the standing of existing actors.

The Law of the First Increment

A system’s structural integrity is measured by its “successor consistency.” A system is coercive if it possesses the power to perform the successor function for some entities while intentionally maintaining others at σ = 0.

A pluralist system is defined by the universal successor requirement:

Every potential actor must have a path from nullity to the first unit of standing before the system’s “social physics” (laws, ethics, coordination) can be considered legitimate. Consequently, to deprive this system of the successor function is not only domination but is structurally incompatible with pluralism.

Autonomy Singularities (Prime Standing Entities)

These are entities that satisfy:

Interpretation:
The entity is recognized (+1), has standing, but has no relational couplings or compositional dependencies.
It exists in a state of maximal autonomy, irreducible within the system.

Structural Composites (Composite Standing Entities or Compositional Couplings)

Entities satisfying:

σ(i)>1 ∨ deg(i)>0

Interpretation:
Their standing arises from:

multiple successor increments, or

relational couplings, or

frame composition, or

emergent structural relationships.

These represent social, political, identity, or institutional composites within the analytic engine.

The Axiom of Symmetry

In any coordination event between two or more agents, the stability of the system is governed by the Symmetry of Standing. Symmetry here refers to the symmetry of standing in rerunnable operations, not to equality of role, ability, or expertise. This is not a moral preference but a structural requirement for systemic equilibrium.

Systems that appear stable under asymmetry are stable only by suppressing rerunnability, not satisfying it. Rerunnability is the only known mechanism by which plural agents can contest, correct, or revise claims without appealing to final authority.  This axiom applies wherever agents share vulnerability to mutual impact and must coordinate without final authority.

The following section provides structural analogies grounded in feedback dynamics rather than thermodynamic solutions. Consequently, the term heat refers to resistance cost, and the term fragility will refer to sensitivity under perturbation. These terms are analogical labels for structural resistance and sensitivity, not physical claims; the argument does not depend on any thermodynamic model. We define this axiom through the following proof:

Coordination Equations

Let A represent the self (the observer/agent) and let B represent the other (the external agent). The state of their interaction can be expressed through three possible configurations of autonomy impact.

A>B (The state of domination): In this configuration, A expands their agency by consuming or suppressing the autonomy of B. This creates a “Systemic Heat” in the form of resistance, requiring A to expend energy on coercion. Since B is a “subjugated cell,” the system loses B’s capacity for independent sensor feedback, leading to eventual systemic blindness and collapse.

B>A (The state of Subjugation): In this configuration, the collective or the external agent suppresses the individual cell A. While this may appear stable in the short term, it creates Systemic Fragility. A system built on suppressed cells lacks the internal resilience to process novel information, resulting in stagnation and catastrophic failure under stress.

A=B (The state of Cooperation/Symmetry): This is the Steady State. When A and B have equal standing, the system achieves equilibrium. No energy is wasted on coercion or defense, allowing the total energy of the system to be directed toward complexity and endurance.

These configurations exhaust the possible autonomyimpact relationships between agents under coordination; mixture cases reduce to one of these when standing is evaluated under rerunnability. The decomposition into A>B, B>A, and A=B is complete under any monotonic autonomyimpact function. While overlapping cases may create an equality at a different scope, evaluating such larger scopes and attributing them to the individual parts that comprise them is fallacious.

Rerunnability in these cases collapses even when A>B arrangements maintain. A stable A > B or B > A configuration would disprove this axiom. No such system has ever maintained durable feedback fidelity under role reversal, correction pressure, or exposure equivalence, even in engineered cases.  The equations themselves, by definition, represent instability.

Structural instability is predicated on their destruction of error-correction fidelity and reduced environmental sensitivity. They force energy expenditure on coercion. Systems with asymmetric feedback cannot rerun roles without breakdown. Where there is rerunnability failure, structural illegitimacy follows.

The Law of Standing

Legitimacy is a procedural recognition of A = B. Traditional legitimacy theories presuppose standing symmetry; this law makes that presupposition explicit.  Any claim that seeks to break this equality establishes a structurally unsatisfiable burden for proof, as it introduces an inherent instability into the social fabric. This is in alignment with Fixed-Point Theory such that symmetric standing generates stable attractors and asymmetry causes divergence from the fixed point.  Repair is contraction mapping back toward equilibrium. Consequently, the only stable fixed point of coordination is equal standing.

Derived Structural Laws

The following structural laws are not axioms.
They are derivative consequences of the three foundational axioms.
Each law expresses a dynamic implication of the Axiom of Symmetry under conditions of asymmetry, transitivity, repair, or capacity. These laws are structurally analogous to the Zeroth, First, Second, and Third Laws of Thermodynamics, but the analogy is conceptual rather than physical. They formalize how pluralist systems behave under drift, correction, and limiting autonomy.

The Derivative Law of Asymmetric Fragility

When A > B, the system experiences a positive fragility gradient (dF/dt > 0).

As asymmetry increases, rerunnability decreases (d(Rerun)/dt < 0).

Instability accumulates under asymmetry (H > 0).

Symmetry (A = B) is the only stable fixed point.

Asymmetry generates structural “heat” (resistance cost), suppresses feedback, and increases fragility. Pluralist systems therefore drift toward collapse unless symmetry is restored.  This law is structurally analogous to the thermodynamic Second Law: both identify a monotonic drift toward instability unless corrective structure is applied. This law is likewise structurally analogous to classic Lyapunov instability. Systems drift away from unstable equilibria and toward stable equilibria. Symmetric standing is a stable attractor, and asymmetry is an unstable equilibrium.

The Derivative Zeroth Law of Transitive Symmetry

This law is derivative of the Axiom of Symmetry and specifies the transitive structure that must hold for symmetry to be preserved across multi-agent coordination. If and in standing symmetry, then the system requires .

Thus, symmetry of standing is not merely dyadic but transitive, ensuring that rerunnability extends through all connected coordination relations. Any break in transitivity generates local asymmetry, and thereby introduces fragility, heat accumulation, and loss of feedback fidelity in accordance with the Law of Asymmetric Fragility.

This law is structurally analogous to the Zeroth Law of Thermodynamics, which establishes the transitivity of equilibrium. In your framework, standing symmetry plays the structural role of equilibrium: transitivity is required for the system to maintain stable, rerunnable coordination across more than two agents. As in thermodynamics, the law is not fundamental in itself but derivative of deeper structural principles.

A=B, B=C⇒A=C (under symmetric standing)

The Derivative Law of Directed Repair

This law is derivative of the Axiom of Symmetry and describes the directed structural work required to restore symmetry once asymmetry has been introduced. In systems where , repair must actively reduce asymmetry rather than allowing correction to occur spontaneously. Formally, during a repair phase:

Repair continues until the asymmetry has been eliminated:

This constitutes the FirstLaw analogue within the structural framework. Just as the First Law of Thermodynamics characterizes how external work changes internal energy, the structural analogue identifies how directed corrective effort reduces asymmetry and restores the system to the symmetric fixed point required for rerunnability. Asymmetry cannot reduce itself; structural work must be applied.

The analogy is conceptual rather than physical: “work” here refers to directed corrective action necessary to restore symmetry of standing, not physical energy transfer. Both laws, however, share the same core functional insight: equilibrium does not spontaneously reestablish itself when the system has moved into a nonequilibrium configuration. Restoration requires deliberate intervention.

The Derivative Law of Capacity-Autonomy Gradient

This law characterizes the limiting behavior of coordination systems as agents approach full autonomy. As individual capacity approaches its maximum, the system’s ability to impose external asymmetry approaches zero. Let  denote an agent’s operative autonomy capacity and the structural asymmetry applied from outside the agent.

This is the ThirdLaw analogue. Just as the Third Law of Thermodynamics identifies a limiting approach to constant entropy as temperature approaches zero, the structural analogue identifies a limiting approach to zero externally imposed standing asymmetry as agents approach full autonomy. In this regime, no further coercive constraint is structurally possible: the system reaches a condition of “capacity minimum temperature,” where external asymmetry cannot be meaningfully applied without violating the Axiom of Symmetry and destabilizing the coordination environment.

The analogy is conceptual rather than physical. It marks a limiting principle on the structural side: as agents gain capacity, the system’s ability to impose unilateral constraint diminishes correspondingly. Fully capable agents inhabit a region of coordination in which external standing asymmetry is structurally unsustainable.

The Hierarchy of Impact

To maintain the symmetry of A = B in a world of scarce resources and conflicting claims, we apply the Hierarchy of Impact. This hierarchy tracks and maps structural collapse thresholds rather than moral importance or ethical priorities. These levels model failure modes, not value hierarchies; they reflect sensitivity to collapse. The protocol weights claims based on the dept of their threat to the agent’s Base Autonomy:

Level 1: Terminal Agency (Life/Death/Irreparable Trauma)

Level 2: Base Autonomy (Sustenance/Shelter/Health/Transportation/Communication/Clothing/Education/Etc)

Level 3: Derivative Agency (Expression/Movement/Association)

Level 4: Preference/Profit (Wealth/Comfort/Taste)

The Rule of Precedence

A claim at a higher level of impact (e.g. level 1 is higher than level 2 and so on) always holds more standing over claims at lower levels (e.g. level 4), regardless of the “authority” of the agents involved.

The Theorem of Restorative Standing

When the Axiom of Symmetry is violated (A > B), the resulting asymmetry creates systemic instability. Repair is structurally required because asymmetry corrupts error correction; restoration is therefore necessary for any future coordination to remain stable. Repair aims to restore rerunnability rather than to moralize harm. To resolve asymmetry without introducing new “heat” (retaliatory domination) we must apply the Protocol of repair:

Detection of Impact: Standing is granted to the impacted agent (B) to demand the cessation of the asymmetry.

Restorative Obligation: The dominating agent (A) incurs a “structural debt.” The goal of this debt is not retribution, but the restoration of B to their baseline level 2 (base autonomy) state.

Equilibrium Goal: A “repair” is only complete when the equation A=B is functionally restored. Any action taken beyond this equilibrium constitutes a new violation (B>A) and is therefore structurally illegitimate.

The Law of Cumulative Load

While the Hierarchy of Impact provides a universal ranking, the “mass” of an impact is relative to the agent’s existing systemic load. Cumulative load functions as an amplification factor on autonomyimpact, converting lowimpact acts into highimpact ones when baseline capacity is low. This is defined as the Contextual Relevance of Standing:

The Inverse Capacity Rule: The legitimacy of a claim is inversely proportional to the agent’s remaining autonomy

Load Aggregation: A level 4 impact (e.g., a financial penalty) can be mathematically transformed into a level 1 impact (terminal collapse) if the agent’s system is already strained at the edge of level 2 (sustenance).

Systemic Responsibility: Therefore, a “just” system must calculate standing based on the receiver’s capacity, not the sender’s intent.

Preface

Why This Work Exists

I hope this framework helps someone reason or act in ways that better preserve nondominant pluralist society. I cannot know whether it will, and I make no claim that it must. What I set out to do with this work was to find a way for pluralist societies to act together without turning disagreement into justification for harm. What emerged from the examination is something altogether different. There exists a class of structural constraints that philosophy encounters when philosophical claims are used as authority. These constraints do not depend on belief, endorsement, or metaphysical agreement.

Like gravity, they operate whether or not they are recognized, arising from the conditions under which claims coordinate action, allocate risk, and foreclose or preserve exit. This is not a rejection of belief or truth, but a refusal of absolutism as a coordination strategy under pluralism. What Nietzsche identified as the death of final authority is treated here not as a metaphysical event, but as a structural problem: the loss of any reliable basis for nondominating coordination under pluralism. Where Nietzsche diagnosed the collapse of ultimate authority, this framework analyzes coordination in its absence. What follows addresses a key structural problem left unresolved by nihilism: coordinating life after the collapse of final authority.

If we want to live together without harming each other, no authority gets to excuse that harm. Even if a will is ultimate, humans remain accountable for how they act in its name. If any authority can’t accept that, then it may act on its own terms, but then structurally excludes itself from serving as a basis for non-harmful coordination among others. Any system which outputs justified coercion as a positive claim has already replaced plural standing with procedural authority. Likewise, any text that claims perfection and authorizes coercive authority over nonconsenting others must satisfy pluralist nondomination constraints. This framework does not ask what God must do; it asks what humans may not justify doing to one another—even in God’s name.

Where it does not, the claim of authority is illegitimate under pluralism, since no appeal to perfection—divine or otherwise—can substitute for nondominating justification when binding others. Accordingly, the question this work asks is not “what must we do to get better?” but “what must we do to avoid becoming worse?” If there should ever arise a nondominating way to answer the former, this work becomes merely a mirror that directs toward it.

Everyday life is full of conflicting claims whether they are political demands, moral disagreements, rules for speech, or scientific debates. Across domains, there remains no stable, nondomainpreferential set of criteria for deciding which claims deserve authority. In concept, the presumption is that each domain itself would coordinate for the best interest of all parties involved. This is not always the case.

Many disagreements arise which do not apply simply to one domain. Philosophy on the whole has a coordination issue regarding disagreements that span cross-domain relevance.1 As conflicts emerge, they are commonly treated differently by their domain applications, and those treatments often do not align. This misalignment forces an evaluation of priority among domains where it is not inherently justified.

For example, a conflict of gender inequality could have an economical domain impact, political domain impact, moral domain impact, perception domain impact, and others. The outcomes of this inequality do not emerge in domain isolation. Historically, the autonomous impact to the female gender has not been given equivalent treatment to the political or moral domains. What this history demonstrates is not merely moral neglect, but the absence of a shared evaluative mechanism capable of recognizing autonomy collapse across domains simultaneously.

This is evident in historical women’s rights movements entering the political domain.  It demonstrates that conflict is not strictly limited to the moral domain of interpersonal autonomous impact. These observations expose the need for such cross-domain practice that philosophy has been incapable of answering because of its fragmented domain handling.

These inefficiencies emerge in both the structural systems that hold pluralist communities aloft and the mechanisms by which they attempt to ensure their own stability and endurance. Cross-Domain inefficiencies are hardly contained to these domains. In the religious domain, extremism has historically asserted to be in the best interest of plural communities while not holding itself to criteria which ensure it. Even the foundations of our knowledge come under assault as standards for authority when scientific and language domains interact.

This book is not a moral code or political ideology. It is not proposing to solve the metaphysical disputes or completely satisfying the demands of any single domain. The framework does not unify domains under a single logic; it constrains when domainspecific logics may override pluralist autonomy.

It approaches authority through the concept of standing: the conditional permission for claims to bind others under pluralist conditions. It offers a single structural method which can be used to evaluate authority, standing, and legitimacy across domains where existing philosophical tools fragment rather than coordinate judgment. Ordinary people, acting under normalized incentives, will sustain domination unless repair, exit, and contestation are structurally enforced rather than morally assumed.

This work does not attempt to resolve disagreements by ranking values, adjudicating truth claims, or appealing to shared moral foundations. It instead asks a prior question: under what structural conditions can any claim—moral, epistemic, political, or institutional—acquire standing to bind others at all? Many philosophical disputes persist not because of unresolved disagreement, but because this prior question is left unasked.

Author’s Coupling to the Subject Matter

Before explaining how this framework should be read and used, it may be helpful to briefly situate how I came to encounter the problem it addresses. Having been born and raised into Pentecostal Evangelical Christianity myself, atheism came to me only in adulthood. I was raised in groups where human action was commonly justified as being “god’s will” whether harmful or autonomy-impairing or not.

Something in this felt inherently contradictory to me, not because of claims about God’s perfection, but because human actions were being attributed standing by appeal to a final authority that was “good”, even where those actions were harmful or autonomyimpairing. This did not require concluding that God was unreal or imperfect; it revealed instead that attributing human actions to final authority had become the mechanism by which accountability was suspended. As this realization took hold, I was privileged to be in the company of many others who were unable to follow along that journey.

In my conversations with some of my colleagues I was initially a bit confounded at the idea that these rational leanings were rejected rather wholesale from people that I had until then understood to be quite logical and of sound mind myself. It was only after sitting with the thought of that exact sort of confoundedness that the realization occurred to me that this response then must not belong to that of their otherwise reasonable and sound faculties. This personal context helps illustrate why so many individuals attribute standing to divine claims even when public standing cannot be established procedurally by them.

Ironically, as I moved into other spaces searching for an answer which did not attempt to suspend accountability, I was profoundly dismayed. When I turned to politics, accountability was suspended in areas and justified by the authority of the domain. When I turned to morality, the same was true. In each of these domains, I again found myself among others who had not yet recognized how appeals to final authority functioned as a false validation of suspended accountability. It was this cross-domain problem that made me aware of the need for a cross-domain solution.

How could it be that completely different authorities smuggled across wildly variant domains can produce the same problem? It was when I read Nietzsche that I stumbled upon the truth. The god he declared dead is the final authority of every domain and not a metaphysical entity.

Humanity’s use of final authority claims reliably produces suspended accountability.   Constraints that preserve accountability and autonomy can then reliably offset that and do not make claims of final authority moot. Instead, they work to provide the only context where they may emerge as non-domination.

This book explores the consequences of these observations and builds a framework for how to proceed without domination - even without a final authority - until we find one that can work without suspending accountability for humanity. Ironically, the framework cannot “prove” itself without becoming authoritative. Consequently, this work does not claim its foundational axiom as a final truth. It offers it as a structural constraint whose relevance is demonstrated only where it proves usable for non-dominating coordination. Conceptualization, framework design, and methodology were developed solely by the author.

How to Read This Book

This book is not designed to be read quickly, nor is it designed to be read in only one way. It develops a single analytic framework and applies it across multiple domains—perception, morality, language, politics, economics, technology, identity, and culture. While the framework itself is stable, the domains differ significantly in their subject matter, scale, and intuitions. As a result, readers may encounter sections that feel immediately clarifying and others that feel demanding or unfamiliar.

That is expected. This section explains how the book is structured, what kinds of reading it supports, and how to navigate it without unnecessary strain.

Terminology Crosswalk: Orientation for Political Philosophy, Jurisprudence, and Social Theory

The following table provides approximate correspondences between the terms used in this framework and more familiar terms in political philosophy, jurisprudence, and social theory.

These correspondences are not equivalences. In most cases, the framework’s terms intentionally cut across or constrain standard usages rather than reproduce them.

Core Structural Terms

Coupling
→ Dependency relation; interactional relevance; mechanism of uptake; relation of determination

What others call causal dependence, social dependency, epistemic access, role relations, or institutional embedding are treated here as instances of coupling.

Unlike causal or relational accounts alone, coupling is standing-generative.

Relevance
→ Public salience under shared conditions; coordination-relevant impact

Not preference, attention, or importance.

Closer to “what enters public justification” than to subjective concern.

Relevance exists as a bimodal spectrum of urgency with the endpoints being “irrelevance” and “emergency.”

Coupling at all is the origin for urgency diverging from irrelevance to relevance.

Coupling to inevitability is what causes urgency to diverge from non-emergency to emergent levels of relevance.

Standing
→ Legitimacy to bind; right-to-rule conditions; public warrant

Not authority itself.

Not moral truth.

Standing is the permission threshold for binding others under pluralism.

Public Standing
→ Public justification; legitimacy under publicity conditions

Comparable to Rawlsian publicity or Habermasian answerability but procedurally grounded rather than discursively idealized.

Authority
→ Capacity to issue directives within a scope

Distinguished sharply from legitimacy.

Authority may exist without standing (paper authority, force-backed authority).

Legitimacy
→ Standing-sustained authority under plural conditions

Legitimacy is not moral correctness or democratic endorsement.

It is authority that survives coupling, autonomy, and risk tests.

Constraint & Autonomy Vocabulary

Autonomy (framework sense)
→ Non-domination condition; self-authorship capacity; viable agency

Not a moral right or metaphysical property.

A structural precondition for coordination.

Non-domination
→ Absence of arbitrary power; constraint without subjugation

Adjacent to Pettit but grounded structurally rather than morally.

Exit
→ Right of refusal; meaningful withdrawal; non-punitive dissent

Stronger than formal consent.

Exit collapse is a standing failure.

Corrigibility
→ Contestability; revisability; appealability

Oxford readers will often map this to “contestability” or “public reason responsiveness.”

Accountability
→ Answerability; duties of explanation; reviewability

Not blame.

Structural answerability under exposure.

Coercion & Risk

Coercion
→ Autonomy-reducing intervention

Includes non-violent and structural coercion (platforms, institutions).

Standing to Coerce (STC-5)
→ Legitimacy test for coercive authority

Analogous to proportionality + due process + necessity doctrines, but unified.

Risk Inheritance
→ Exposure without consent; burden-bearing asymmetry

Adjacent to environmental justice, minority rights, and fiduciary governance.

Validation
→ Authorization by risk-bearers

Not consent, not aggregation.

Closest analogue: “those subject to coercion must be justificatory participants.”

Institutional & Political Vocabulary

Agreed Operations
→ Public procedures; due process analogues; institutionalized justification

Calibration / replication / cross-check in epistemic domains.

Notice / hearing / review in political domains.

Procedural Capture
→ Sham procedures; hollow legality; rule-of-law failure

Comparable to “authoritarian legality” or “legal formalism without legitimacy.”

Paper Authority
→ Formal authority lacking legitimacy

Office without standing.

Derivative Authority
→ Delegated authority; borrowed legitimacy

Especially relevant for platforms and private governance.

Moral & Normative Vocabulary

Wrongness (structural)
→ Autonomy-impairing coupling

Distinct from blame or culpability.

Culpability
→ Responsibility plus attribution under capacity

Closely aligned with Hart / Fischer & Ravizza.

Independently Emergent Wrong (IEW)
→ Wrong without blame; structural injustice; faultless wrongdoing

Comparable to structural injustice, but with explicit standing consequences.

Repair
→ Restorative justice; agency restoration

Distinguished from punishment and compliance.

NRPP (Non-Retributive Proportionality Principle)
→ Least-restrictive means; proportionality doctrine

Narrower than utilitarian balancing.

Language & Communication

Speech Harm (SHT-3)
→ Autonomy-relevant communicative harm

Distinct from offense-based or content-based accounts.

Propaganda
→ Answerability-degrading communication

Closer to domination-through-communication than persuasion.

Epistemic Pollution
→ Capacity erosion; collective reasoning degradation

Adjacent to misinformation theory but structurally framed.

What This Book Is (and Is Not)

This is a frameworkdriven work of philosophy. It does not aim to provide a comprehensive moral theory, settle metaphysical disputes, adjudicate personal identity claims, or prescribe public policy. Instead, it specifies conditions under which claims, systems, or identities acquire standing to bind others, and conditions under which coercion becomes illegitimate, under pluralism.

This book does not claim that all domains reduce to one model, but rather that certain structural features recur across pluralist coordination systems. The engine constrains domains. It does not collapse them.

The arguments of this framework are structural, not exhortative. Readers should not expect conclusions that tell them what to believe, but tools that clarify when belief, authority, or enforcement may legitimately constrain others.

The Core Engine (What Persists Throughout)

Although the book spans many domains, it relies on a single analytic engine throughout. In simplified form:

Coupling → Relevance → Autonomy Impact → Standing Evaluation → Legitimate Constraint → Repair

This engine does not change from chapter to chapter.
What changes are the ways coupling occurs and the forms constraint takes in different domains. In practice, repair and correction overlap at the boundaries. Structural categories do not eliminate domain complexity; they provide clarity about when legitimacy is preserved and when a new standing relation must be established.

Readers may find it helpful to keep this sequence in mind while reading. When sections feel dense, the question is usually not what is being argued, but where in the engine the analysis currently is (e.g., relevance generation vs. exit collapse vs. repair).

Recommended Reading Paths

Readers are not expected to read this book strictly fronttoback on a first pass. The chapters are cumulative, but they are also designed to support selective entry.

How to Read Individual Chapters

Each major chapter follows a consistent internal structure:

Orientation — what the chapter does and does not do

Translation — how the framework appears in this domain

Domainspecific coupling channels

Standing and legitimacy analysis

Failure modes

Repair and limits

Readers encountering difficulty are encouraged to read the Orientation and Translation sections first, then return to the body of the chapter. The Translation Tables are designed to function as anchors, not glossaries to be memorized.

On Density and Pace

Some sections—particularly those dealing with perception, technology, and identity—are intentionally dense. They introduce distinctions that are necessary to prevent moralization, oversimplification, or category error.

Readers should feel free to:

pause and return later,

skim sections on a first pass,

reread Translation Tables after completing a chapter,

or move ahead and let later chapters clarify earlier ones.

Understanding in this book is cumulative and recursive, not linear.

On Discomfort and Disagreement

Some readers may experience discomfort, especially where moral language loses explanatory force, subjective experience is treated as evidence but not adjudication, or no party is identified as morally blameworthy despite real harm. Discomfort alone is not treated in this book as evidence of error or injustice. Readers are encouraged to distinguish between disagreement, distress, and legitimacy failure, as these are analytically separate.

What Success Looks Like for the Reader

A reader has not “failed” if they do not agree with the framework’s conclusions.

Success looks like:

being able to identify where standing is being claimed,

being able to distinguish coordination from coercion,

being able to ask who bears the risk of error,

and being able to see why some conflicts persist even when no one is acting in bad faith.

If the book equips the reader to make those distinctions more clearly, it has done its work.

A Final Note

This book is meant to be used, not mastered. Readers are encouraged to treat it as a reference framework—one that can be returned to when questions of legitimacy, authority, or coercion arise across different domains.

No single reading order is privileged. What matters is that the tools remain intact when they are applied.

Introduction

What This Book Is About

This book is not about an “ultimate truth” or an attempt to define reality. It is a structural analysis of coordination constraints that emerge with plurality itself rather than a political program, justice theory, or moral theory. When it speaks of relevance, it is speaking of why something matters for pluralist society.

It relies on a basis for how information or actions connect to us as coupling. As things connect to us and begin to matter, disagreements arise. If we want to have a community without domination, there needs to be a minimum amount of freedom from each individual to sustain that coordination. Without that freedom, the community itself collapses either wholly or into domination.

If freedom is a requirement for non-dominant society, then community also needs some limitations to this freedom as well. Otherwise, one person is free to do something that could be catastrophic to the whole group and poses a threat to all of us. While the book begins in the familiar language of fairness and coordination, it will progressively shift toward a structural account of autonomy, standing, and risk as the underlying conditions that make coordination possible at all.

When we speak of an action that impacts our freedom or autonomy, we call that coercive. Sometimes coercive acts are not unjustified. Across all domains, autonomy functions as a nonnegotiable structural precondition for pluralism. Where autonomy collapses, legitimacy questions precede all normative debate.

If there were someone threatening your family with a weapon, the coercive act of the police threatening this person with their own respective weapons may be justified. This book explores some of what creates that justification and, when it is granted, this is awarded as legitimacy. The difference between this person threatening your family and the police in this example is based on a different measure. That measure is of standing and it evaluates when a claim or rule gets to bind us or what makes it reasonable for that claim or rule to be followed. Standing is not a right to issue reasons, enforce rules, or command compliance; it is a conditional permission to constrain autonomy under publicly legible justification. [n.47] [n.185] [n.89]

Key Insight and Motivation

The book will take steps to show that the world only matters to us through our interactions. Interaction creates a test for uptake (whether we can perceive or test it), relevance (if we care because it affects us), and standing (whether it deserves public consideration). [n.1] [n.2] [n.26] These tests do not apply to personal beliefs. Those may matter to the individual, but they don’t bind others without evidence or consent. Why would they? Personal beliefs that do not interact to be perceived can’t be relevant to others. They haven’t been perceived. [n.47]

Anecdotally, you’ll find in some of the content that my personal motivations to evaluate these philosophies are rooted in the societal, political, and religious happenings of my time. While it is true that my personal interactions in these spaces have shown to be rather dramatic, there is nonetheless an underlying error in the understanding of how these domains gain relevance and standing at all which pokes at my conscience like a finger poking a bruise or lemon juice on a freshly opened cut.

Consequently, many societal structures rely on policies that violate their own premises. The recurring failure is not merely bad policy but a functional misunderstanding of how public claims acquire standing at all. [n.27] [n.205] To make the reader very aware, the motivations here are not of a personal retribution or vendetta which the writer has with any of these institutions or structures.

Instead, they are driven by a yearning to the entire opposite direction—one of optimism that the human species become capable of enduring and thriving while simultaneously sharing cultures, beliefs, and traditions. It is that optimism which exposes the root errors of the existing thoughts and so gently nudges me to pursue these ends.

This work does not offer internal critiques of existing theories of legitimacy, authority, or justification. Its aim is structural rather than doctrinal: to specify the conditions under which such theories can generate standing in the first place. Engagement with particular traditions is therefore illustrative rather than exhaustive. The framework does not advance moral doctrine or political ideology. Instead, it specifies a set of structural constraints under which claims—moral, political, epistemic, or institutional—can acquire public standing in pluralist contexts. It is concerned not with what ought to be believed or valued, but with what must be satisfied before beliefs or values may legitimately bind others. [n.47]

This work is best read as infrastructure rather than doctrine. It does not deliver verdicts about what ought to be valued, believed, or pursued. Instead, it specifies the structural conditions under which any such claims can acquire standing to bind others in shared space.

Some readers will approach this work as a political theory, moral philosophy, social theory, or institutional design. This work, however, is intended for readers concerned with legitimacy across domains under disagreement. Readers should therefore expect constraints rather than conclusions, diagnostics rather than doctrines, and repair pathways rather than final answers.

Structure as the Other Side of Pluralist Society

Pluralist society is not reducible to its members. Once plurality exists, certain coordination constraints arise necessarily. Standing, autonomy constraints, and legitimacy tests are structural reflections, not ethical recommendations. These constraints are not what society “ought to do” but what society already does if it is to persist as plural rather than collapse into domination.

This distinction establishes this framework not as a normative claim of what should be but as a structural framework of what emerges within pluralist collectives where domination and authoritarianism is not present. This structure and pluralist society are interdependent on one another that they are not collectively the sum of their parts but instead are two reflections of the same larger entity.

Society emerges as structure. By definition, it maintains structure whether it is authoritarian, egalitarian, or other forms of domination. Structure is not a normative constraint of these emergences but a property of them. What this work accounts for is the attributes of non-domination in pluralist society, how those attributes emerge, where they apply, how they remain intact, and what those who reject them stand to face. It is not a prescription of what is right or wrong, and it is not a definition of what will prevail.

Part I - Standing and Constraint: Clearing the Ground for Evaluation

I — Foundations

Purpose: This section sets out to establish the foundations for the work of this book. It will give the methods, means, and rules by which this structure operates as an introduction to the framework itself.

Orientation

What Foundations Mean in This Work

This work is not setting out to establish axioms, metaphysics, or ultimate truths. The foundations in this work are set as constraints, not grounds. They specifically regard how claims earn standing and not what ultimately exists. This work brackets metaphysics unless they change public practice. It is not vulnerable to global skepticism because it does not aim to secure certainty.

This framework is not universal in the sense of binding all agents regardless of aims. It applies conditionally to agents, institutions, or systems that seek durable plural coordination without domination. Within those conditions, however, the constraints articulated here are not optional; attempts to bypass them reintroduce coercion, hierarchy, or instability under different names.

This work aligns with pragmatist views in that it relies on public inquiry, corrigibility, and anti-foundationalism but departs when regarding pure instrumentalism or success-as-truth reasoning. [n.2] [n.14] Consequently, Dewey and Peirce are neighbors, but this is not epistemic laissez-faire. Instead, standing is the central bridge concept to this work. While this work shares Kant’s concern with the conditions under which claims may bind us, it rejects transcendental grounding in favor of publicly rerunnable operations. [n.67]

The framework does not remove the concept of power or claim that procedures have a defaulted value of fair or neutral. It recognizes that pluralist society itself exerts a form of power in numbers and that procedure is a descriptive accounting for how that power propagates. Violations of standing produce outcomes of coercion and domination.

In the sense of the pluralist collective society, we will see in About Morality that these are deemed as morally “wrong” from their perceptual frame agreement but, procedure itself is not a solution to power. It is a map to how power behaves under plural conditions and is interdependent with standing as a mechanism by which pluralist societies operate.

Standing is the operational imperative in this framework that licenses public warrant. [n.14] [n.15] [n.207] Any plural system that purports to coordinate action while bypassing standing does not eliminate authority; it merely obscures it. This is a departure from authority but establishes demands for licensing that warrant such as rerunnability and correction in pluralist spaces. Those constraints become the validation for those licenses in that space and are also why headcounts, sincerity, and office alone are not sufficient to render such license.

Structural Conditions

Within the structure of the group, there must be a method or mechanism by which the collective is capable of establishing agreed operations or the system itself is primed for self-destruction. So, in this sense, there is a legitimacy to epistemology in this framework, but it is not moral legitimacy — it’s structural legitimacy.

Hierarchical legitimacy requires stable A to B asymmetries. Feedback cannot be symmetric in these systems, forcing standing to become unidirectional. Rerunnability collapses when roles reverse. In such systems, A>B and B>A systems cannot produce stable, non-arbitrary constraint. Thus, hierarchal models cannot survive these pressure tests. A>B and B>A configurations introduce irreversible fragility because they break the reciprocity required for stable feedback, standing validation, and nonarbitrary coercion.

Pure consequentialism ties legitimacy to outcomes rather than couplings. Structurally, outcomes are not directly rerunnable. Exposure then cannot be equalized, and relevance becomes retrospective as a result. When risk bearers cannot validate future harm, standing for them evaporates. Consequently, such systems cannot maintain stability under interdependence.

Pure Proceduralism sets procedure as the source of legitimacy, but procedure presupposes a pre-validated group. Standing is assumed in these models, not generated. Procedural fairness does not equal symmetry of exposure. These systems can be structurally dominated while appearing procedurally valid and thus fail standing and autonomy-impact criteria.

Rawls/Habermas rationality models depend on discursive or justificatory preconditions tied to a shared domain. Their legitimacy tools are domain-bound, making rerunnability across plural global couplings impossible. Where there is no shared frame, no shared standing can emerge.

Their justificatory scaffolding presupposes shared standing conditions that cannot be guaranteed across heterogeneous or involuntary global couplings. The limitations of these models reveal why a domainportable structural constraint is required.

Symmetry is not a moral preference but a structural requirement of any system that must remain corrigible under changing couplings. If feedback is asymmetric, the system cannot be rerun without altering the autonomy conditions of the participating agents. This makes standing unstable and destroys the capacity for nonarbitrary constraint.

Symmetry is also necessary for sensor validity and feedback fidelity. A system cannot reliably adjust to harm, exposure, or error if the feedback channels themselves privilege one actor’s perception, options, or relevance over another’s. Without symmetry, systems drift because no correction loop is stable.

Finally, symmetry is required for nondomination. Arbitrary interference becomes structurally unavoidable when one side can impose relevance or autonomy-impact without being equally exposed to the same risk or feedback. Symmetry is therefore not a normative claim about equality; it is a structural constraint on any system attempting to maintain rerunnability, stability, and intentional pluralist coordination.

In any model, if the A>B or B>A arrangement could be shown to produce rerunnable, non-fragile feedback without arbitrary autonomy impact with reliable results, the axiom of symmetry would fail. To date, no such example has held under structural analysis.

Another constraint that emerges in this framework is that of restraint. This does not smuggle in any liberal moral realism or rights theory. Instead, autonomy is treated as a coordination precondition for non-domination. [n.25] [n.207] This doesn’t inherently make it a moral good intrinsically.

It does not have any sacred value or metaphysical property in this framework. Rather, autonomy is structurally necessary for pluralist coordination. Without it, the conditions that license warrant and establish standing lose their validity. A structural model cannot capture every domain-specific detail, but it identifies the boundary conditions any legitimate coordination system must satisfy.

Autonomy is one such condition in that sense, forming a causal chain so that it is not a moral absolute but a condition that enables the structure. As a result, nothing in this framework assumes moral equality between agents. It assumes only that asymmetric exposure erodes the system’s ability to correct itself.

Relations and Divergence

This framework can be related to moral theory based on constraint but does not carry with it inherent value for morals themselves. It does not treat endurance of the human race as morally “good” and does not suppose any metaphysical nature or origin for morality. Instead, it defines them as operational imperatives that emerge from a structure of plurality.

This framework implicitly rejects technocracy as expertise-over standing, pure constructivism without constraint, or authority by revelation, charisma, or force insofar as these bypass publicly answerable standing. [n.25] [n.185] These standpoints tend to produce domination-prone or unaccountable structures, impede the collected interests of plural spaces which are both inherently in conflict with a goal of the endurance of the human species and community. For those who do reject those goals, the off-ramps exist within this structure as well.

Given these constraints and neighbors, the rest of this book does not argue from foundations but operates within them. It is establishing a method by which these constraints building upon the work of many domains in philosophy share a common thread that can become operational across those domains in search of a method that ultimately serves those who choose to value the endurance of the species and our plural spaces.

Philosophical Commitments

This project is normatively aligned with relational ethics (in the broad sense of care, responsibility, and interdependenceoriented moral frameworks), postliberal political economy, and noninstrumental conceptions of value. [n.83] [n.84] It is written in critical dialogue with liberal individualism, market absolutism, and technocratic governance, while rejecting both moral realism and moral relativism as prerequisites for public coordination. Citations in this work function as orientation markers within broader philosophical traditions rather than as claims of exegetical authority or comprehensive interpretation.

The framework does not attempt to ground normativity in metaphysics, human nature, or objective moral facts. Nor does it treat values as purely subjective or arbitrary. Instead, it treats normativity as structurally constrained by the requirements of plural coordination, nondomination, and endurance under conditions of disagreement, asymmetry, and uncertainty.

Accordingly, this work does not ask readers to adopt a particular moral theory, economic ideology, or political doctrine. The neutrality of this framework is procedural rather than moral: it applies identical standing constraints to all claims, regardless of source or content. [n.47] It asks only that they consider whether shared life under pluralism requires publicly answerable constraints on how claims, actions, and institutions acquire authority to bind others.

Readers who reject the value of plural coordination or the endurance of shared social space will find that the framework provides explicit offramps rather than coercive moral demands. Agents or systems that reject plural coordination are not refuted by this framework, but they also do not receive justificatory protection.

As the reader will see in the “About Morality” section of this work, this does not reduce to “might makes right” but is an accounting of the risks which are inherited from both perspectives. It does not presume that other forms of legitimacy outside of the framework cannot exist. It asserts that failing the tests inherent to pluralist structures naturally declares a normatively oppositional stance and that the risks coupled to that stance are inherited.

Since this work rejects any metaphysical claims and does not assert any absolute moral truth, neither perspective is determined as “right” by it. It is an accounting of what becomes relevant for the pluralist perspective. Sartre’s characterization of consciousness as a structural nothingness underscores its nonsubstantial and nonselfgrounding nature, a feature this framework retains without adopting his ontological commitments. [n.126] Where Sartre diagnoses bad faith as an individual existential evasion, this framework treats analogous failures as structural collapses of exit, correction, or standing rather than as psychological fault.

In terms of ethics, the meta-ethical position of this work is that there is no non-authoritarian, non-metaphysical answer to “why be moral” that binds everyone. [n.11] Correspondingly, this work refuses to do certain kinds of normative work. That refusal itself is a normative position on the viability of the universal applicability of normative work itself and is justified in the later chapter “About Perception.”

These interrelated workings of normativity and evaluation across domains using the constraints and toolsets given demonstrate in this work the need for the cross-domain solution. Where cross-domain problems emerge, cross-domain solutions gain validity. Where those normative constraints apply, this framework applies them.

Readers seeking a theory of universal moral motivation or obligation should understand that this work does not attempt to supply one and that this limitation is not accidental—it is principled. It is a reflection of the insights earned in the earlier chapters of this work and supported by the same recognition of a lack of universality as the question itself crosses into other domains. One major contention of this work is that such a theory of universality is impossible to derive structurally in a way that would be relevant. This work endeavors to address what remains in the absence of that possibility.

Navigating the Framework

The Structural Engine of the framework

Coupling → Standing → Autonomy Constraint → Coercion Tests → Legitimacy → Revision/Repair

In this engine, interdependent or compositional coupling begets standing, which requires autonomy constraints. Those constraints are evaluated via coercion tests which afford them legitimacy or non-legitimacy and thus queue the need for revision or repair. We ask if the thing relates to us. If it does, then we want to know if it should have the right to guide our actions, if it respects our self-authorship, and if it limits freedom.

Unlike Sartre’s claim that freedom is inescapable even under constraint, this framework treats freedom as conditional on viable alternatives, reversibility, and nonpunitive exit. [n.126] If a thing or event does limit that freedom in this way, is justified and if so, what makes that justification legitimate? When those aims go awry, are there any ways to correct it?

The structural engine produces a framework that can be employed via the following steps:

Identify harm

Identify risk-bearers

Evaluate coupling

Apply autonomy constraints

Apply relevant tests as described later on (STC-5, SHT-3, NRPP, CPS-7)

Check scale and scope

Apply reversibility / off-ramps

Evaluate standing

Every game needs rules. Rules need referees and referees need oversight. This engine and framework provide a mechanism by which to provide that oversight.

Alternatives and Creativity

In this structural engine there are often demands for alternatives and off-ramps. It is inherent to this demand that creativity emerges. It may emerge through internal redesign, parallel institutions, or even entirely new systems. Thus, creativity stands at a place which enables both repair and exit, where exit can likewise become world-building.

The requirement of alternatives is the generative engine of pluralism itself, not merely a reactive standpoint. Alternatives are not purely mitigations but may likewise become sources of innovation. In some cases, they redesign within a society or system. In other cases, exterior creation provides a pathway for exit.

This synthesizes exit in this framework as not purely destructive (though it can take that form), but oftentimes constructive, creative, and historically common. Resistance to domination and refusal often take on creative forms not only as institutions but as expressions of dissent. It oftentimes exists to draw upon affective perceptions of the members of a society and inspire change.

The culmination of these creative expressions themselves lend to a history for pluralist societies to reference not only for historical landmarks, but as non-parochial evidence of the progression of that society itself. It lays the foundation for validation of archaeology and the pursuit of the arts and creative measures for the species. They establish this historical lineage of those progressions as evidence which may be evaluated even by this framework.

Why Does Any of This Matter?

In matters of public health, free speech, policing, parenting, online platforms, or even environmental policy, the community necessarily works together collaboratively. When these domains are given independent oversight the discrepancies between them muddy the water and make that oversight more difficult. As our societies become more and more advanced, this muddied water accumulates over time to the point where some fields like politics become densely saturated.

Those saturation points make a very difficult threshold for entry for many people, and we can see in our world that there are oftentimes people who disengage from them wholesale because of this threshold. The consequence of that disengagement is that the oversight in that domain is lacking or altogether collapses. As a matter of example, the emergence of crimes that the general public consider to be extremely severe among very influential, rich, and powerful people gives teeth to the collapse of that oversight.

We can see from the crossover of that crime between entertainment industries, politics, scientific monoliths, financial groups, and even educational systems that the problem itself with that oversight is a cross-domain issue. [n.97] Where there is a cross-domain issue, cross-domain solutions are required. If there is a fire in the living room and the kitchen, a stream of water that only goes into the living room isn’t going to fully solve the problem.

While this very macro-scoped example may be one that demonstrates the need and purpose for a cross-domain oversight tool such as this, the granularity of the tools arises from the simplest of places—the individual and their perceptions themselves. So then, even though this sort of book may appeal for many on the broad scale for those large macro-topics, the synthesis of these principles allows for the outcomes of these observations to sink down to the level even of the smallest plural communities, like a family.

Guides and Tools

Near the back of this book, you will find a Quick Reference guide for the reader. The structural framework established in this theory is operative of a set of portable tools across domains. These terms and tools will be introduced rigorously in later chapters; here they appear only as a preview.

A prototypical analysis will follow a chain of identifying candidate harm, performing assessment of risk-inheritance & validation, running a standing to coerce test, sizing reactions on a set of non-retributive principles, checking off ramps, checking for standing to harm in speech, and evaluating the sincerity of repair where it applies.

Where harm is potential, non-parochial evidence is considered and those who stand to face the consequences of such harm are evaluated. These considerations form the basis of what “validated harm” looks like in this book, as the reader will come to see operationalized in other domains.

Scope and Limits of the Project

What This Work Is Not

This work is not an attempt to determine what ultimately exists nor an attempt to resolve metaphysical disputes about reality in and of itself. It is important to know that this work is not maximization, social contract theory, metaphysical idealism, authoritarian technocracy, political moralism, constructivism, utilitarianism, deontology, discourse ethics, proceduralism, moral realism, or relativism.

This view shares constructivism’s rejection of mind-independent moral facts but differs in locating normative constraint in relevance-preserving structures rather than idealized rational procedures. [n.44] [n.46] Likewise, it does not ground normativity in hypothetical agreement, and it does not equate relevance to acceptability for all agents. While it does concern coordination, shared relevance, and justification, it outright rejects brute subjectivism. Contractualism is insufficient to sustain plurality in this sense.

What This Work Is

Where some tie perceptual authority to conceptual embedding alone, this framework additionally demands public rerun-ability by competent parties for shared standing. [L.13] It’s justified by its function: coordination without domination under uncertainty.

Standing is justified because coercion without publicly checkable warrant becomes domination. [n.185] In plural societies, public legitimacy requires corrigibility and shared correction pathways. Without them, the system inherently collapses either into authoritarianism or entirely. Therefore, standing is the minimal constraint that makes collective action legitimate under uncertainty.

Accordingly, claims about reality, deities, and morality do not acquire significance or standing merely by their assertion; they acquire standing only insofar as they enter into relation with our perceptual and social frames [n.2]. Likewise, descriptions of how facts are made do not by themselves say when claims earn public standing; for that, agreed, rerunnable operations and answerability are required. The term rerunnable regards the capacity for an operation to be re-initiated under the agreed terms in these cases.

As established earlier, private warrant alone does not bind others. Public standing regards that which is rerunnable, corrigible, and adheres to agreed operations. Private warrant regards individual meaning but is not action-binding so that public standing may be derivative of the collective of private warrants within a given perceptual frame but is not applicable individually to that scope.

This work is a structural-pragmatic theory of legitimacy and relevance. It features a unified procedural architecture with a non-metaphysical grounding of normativity. It includes a population-scale theory of legitimacy, a multi-domain theory of relevance, and a theory of constraint—not a theory of value. It is a structural framework for evaluating when claims, actions, and institutions acquire standing, legitimacy, and normative force under conditions of pluralism and examines how relevance, standing, and meaning arise for us through perception, interaction, and consequence. [n.1] [n.2] It is a framework that has capacity to unify disparate fields.

Constraints, Not Conclusions

This framework does not attempt to replace existing sciences, ethical theories, or political doctrines. It provides a set of constraints and evaluative tests applicable across domains, leaving substantive aims, values, and ends to be specified by the agents and collectives that adopt it.

Normative force in this framework is conditional: it binds only those agents and collectives who seek to coordinate, endure, and avoid domination under plural conditions. [n.88] It does not claim universal moral authority independent of those commitments.

This work is written for readers operating under conditions of deep pluralism—where shared metaphysical, religious, or moral foundations cannot be assumed, but coordination, accountability, and endurance remain necessary. It does not replace moral, political, or epistemic theories; it constrains the conditions under which their claims can acquire standing in shared space.

This framework is intentionally nonformal. Formalization would obscure rather than clarify the structural relations at issue by forcing premature precision across domains with incommensurate units. Rigor here is achieved through constraint articulation and failure diagnosis, not calculability. Some cases will remain indeterminate under this framework; such indeterminacy is not a defect but a signal that standing cannot be legitimately resolved without additional coordination, negotiation, or institutional development.

Original Contributions and Structural Innovations

What is Original

The originality of this work lies in structure and integration. It is not inventing new moral facts or metaphysics. Instead, the contribution here is architectural. Familiar components are re-specified under a unified constraint system. No single predecessor contains this framework or carries this level of portability across domains. This section is not exhaustive of all contributions in this work, however there is a section near the back for a more complete accounting. The major contributions follow here.

Coupling as a Single Cross-Domain Engine

In this framework, coupling is not just epistemic, moral, or linguistic. It is a single engine that governs relevance, standing, legitimacy and constraint. The nature of how this develops into a set of portable tools enables coupling to cross domains as the tools take on various iterations but carry the same core functions within each domain.

Since different philosophical traditions implicitly privilege different coupling mechanisms, debates about legitimacy, coercion, and authority often persist as intractable disagreements. What appear as disputes over values or principles are frequently disagreements between interdependent, relational, or teleological accounts of relevance that lack a shared diagnostic vocabulary.

This type of unification is not available from pragmatism, social epistemology, or political theory alone. Other frameworks fragment these domains whereas, for this work, the spine is that the same engine operates across domains without modification to its core constraints. [n.68] [n.69]

Coupling Typology

Coupling as an engine takes on more than one form. It represents when two entities whether objects, ideas, or otherwise interact in such a way that they are inherently impacted by one another as a matter of determination rather than optionally. These inherent couplings emerge in more than a singular sense necessarily because objects do not interact identically.

Methodologically, analysis should proceed by identifying all active coupling modes in a case. The coupling whose failure would collapse standing is the one that can ground legitimate constraint at the relevant scope. Consequently, this framework deploys several separate types of coupling. These typologies are not intended as an exhaustive metaphysical inventory, nor as mutually exclusive categories that must be applied in isolation.

Rather, they function as diagnostic lenses for identifying how relevance, standing, and constraint are generated in a given case. In most real-world situations, multiple coupling types may be present simultaneously; however, one form typically operates as dominant for the purposes of determining standing, legitimacy, or failure. We will call these the Coupling Typologies and they are as follows:

Interdependent Coupling: Interdependent coupling occurs when two entities are mutually defining such that neither can be specified without reference to the other. This form of coupling is symmetric and non-derivative. Examples include the relationship between the two sides of a coin or the directional opposition of north and south. Within this framework, interdependent coupling is central to concepts such as autonomy and standing, the autonomy-limiting reflex principle, and reciprocity-based constraints. These concepts do not merely interact; they are mutually constitutive.

Compositional Coupling: This type of coupling happens when the sum of a collection of items creates a necessary coupling by virtue of them comprising a new collected entity. This applies when bricks collect to become a wall, or where there are stacks of institutions, policies, or procedures that comprise a state.

Emergent Coupling: This form of coupling emerges intrinsically within a system as a phenomenon that is coupled directly to another entity such as an agent, object, or idea as a necessity which doesn’t have a direct object analogue. In this framework some examples are things like consciousness emerging from the brain while not belonging to the some of its parts or independently emerging wrongs belonging to the scope of morality while not inherently being comprised of morality themselves. [n.1]

Relational Identity-Defining Coupling: This form of coupling is established through agent-mediated identity assignment. When an agent or community confers an identity—such as teacher, doctor, or judge—that identity inherently couples the bearer to a corresponding role relation (students, patients, litigants).

Unlike interdependent coupling, which is ontological, relational identity-defining coupling is socially instituted. Its necessity arises not from metaphysical symmetry but from shared normative recognition.

Teleological Coupling: Teleological coupling arises when discrete actions or processes are coupled by virtue of their orientation toward a shared end, function, or practice. The coupling is not defined by material composition nor by emergent properties, but by purposive integration.

Individual heart contractions are coupled as a heartbeat; discrete rituals are coupled as a religious or cultural practice. The parts are intelligible as what they are only insofar as they participate in the larger end-directed structure.

These coupling types are not domain-derived but mechanism-derived. Each corresponds to a distinct way in which determination can arise: mutual definition, part–whole constitution, system-level emergence, normatively assigned role identity, and end-directed integration. Any proposed additional coupling either reduces to one of these or fails to generate standing independently.

Correctly identifying the dominant coupling type matters because different coupling mechanisms generate different kinds of relevance and impose different structural constraints. Dominant coupling emerges when one particular coupling type is doing the predominant volume of the standing-generating work. Whichever coupling mode corresponds to standing collapsing upon failure carries this burden.

Standing is scalar but thresholdsensitive. It admits of degrees, but legitimate constraint requires that a minimum threshold be met. Standing collapses when a claim, rule, or action can no longer plausibly bind others. Reliance on force, manipulation, asymmetric dependency, or procedural exclusion marks that collapse.

Collapse does not entail loss of influence or power; it marks the loss of justified authority. Disagreement about collapse is itself diagnostically tractable, often indicating decoupling or competing coupling claims rather than mere moral disagreement.

Many failures of standing, legitimacy, or justification arise not from disagreement over values, facts, or intentions, but from a misidentification of the operative coupling—treating a relational identity as interdependent, a compositional system as teleological, or an emergent phenomenon as if it were directly attributable to individual agency. These errors systematically distort relevance and standing.

The destabilizing types are:

Failed coupling (dynamic): These are coupling attempts which are made but are not successful. The explicit implication of this type is that there has not been an established prior coupling, and the attempt does not produce a successful result. For instance, when someone wants to couple their own identity as a teacher but lacks the community agreed operations to establish this coupling the community may reject that relational identity-defining coupling. This is a failed coupling.

Decoupling (dynamic): Decoupling is the form where a previously coupled set is separated from their coupled status to one another. Autonomy-infringement or evaluating a claim of another agent against your own criteria are both cases where an agent had decoupled. In the first example, the other agent or agents are being decoupled from their autonomy. In the latter, the agent is decoupling a claim from the original validating criteria and establishing another coupling to their own understanding instead.

Between these forms of coupling, there is no requirement that only one be present in a given case; however, in most situations a dominant coupling type governs how relevance and standing are generated. Coupling is not univocal, and different types produce different modes of relevance. Standing failures often arise from misidentifying the dominant coupling type, or from the presence of a failed coupling or decoupling that undermines the conditions required for legitimate constraint.

Any account of relevance or legitimacy that does not specify the mechanism by which determination arises—whether through mutual definition, constitution, emergence, role attribution, or end-directed integration—remains explanatorily incomplete, regardless of its normative appeal. Explanatory incompleteness here does not imply falsehood or irrelevance; it indicates that a framework leaves unspecified the mechanism by which claims acquire standing to bind others under plural conditions.
