Many longstanding disputes about authority, coercion, and legitimacy persist not because of unsolved moral disagreement but because competing positions implicitly track different coupling mechanisms.

What appear as normative disagreements are often disputes between interdependent, relational, or teleological accounts of relevance operating without mutual recognition. These coupling types exhaust the ways in which determination can generate standing: through mutual definition, constitution, emergence, normatively assigned role identity, or enddirected integration. Proposed alternatives—such as epistemic, causal, or powerbased couplings—either reduce to one of these mechanisms or fail to generate standing independently.

Like any framework, this one admits of failure modes: misidentification of coupling, improper scale selection, procedural capture, or strategic decoupling. The difference is not that this framework avoids failure, but that it renders failure diagnosable rather than implicit.

Standing as Distinct from Truth, Power, and Sincerity

The novelty in this framework as it regards standing is that standing is treated as operational, public, and constraint-bearing. It is not reducible by truth, belief, authority, consensus, or force. [L.13] [n.89] [n.90] Truth claims retain their full epistemic and practical importance within this framework; what they do not automatically confer is public standing to bind others under plural conditions.

The value of this to the structure is that it breaks the constraints that normally bind frameworks to a limited set of domains. Where other frameworks have been limited by binding standing directly to concepts like truth or belief, this framework instead treats truth and belief as terms that describe our interactions with things rather than the exact things themselves.

Risk-Inheritance as the Basis for Legitimate Authority

This structure rejects legitimate authority based on expertise, office, or majority alone. This does not mean those categories have no value but the origin or basis by which authority is built starts with a seed of evaluating the risk holders. This itself is an advance over standard democratic aggregation, technocratic governance, or moralized consent theories. [n.47] [n.13] [L.12]

Riskinheritance alone is not sufficient to determine authority. It functions as a diagnostic for legitimacy thresholds, not as a theory of responsibility or obligation. Riskinheritance is not a theory of responsibility, obligation, or moral repair; it is a diagnostic of when legitimacy thresholds are crossed, regardless of who ought to act.

The formulation of authority and legitimacy in this structure is a combination of usages of the toolset that will be evaluated on a case-by-case basis as the work tackles various domains and topics. While the tools themselves remain the same, their application takes on meaning as they interact with those topics and domains so that authority may ultimately be derived uniquely for each domain.

The Coercion Stack (STC-5, NRPP, Ceiling vs Prescription)

This stack establishes a procedural architecture for the framework. These tools are implicitly described both within the prose and in a section near the end of this work. They provide a portable decision discipline for coercion rather than a single principle.

By utilizing a stack, this work distinguishes itself from Mill and Rawls and proportionality doctrines used in isolation. [n.13] [n.47] It retains the capacity to set ceilings, narrow prescriptions, and enforce off-ramps. The major benefit of this formulation is that it becomes portable over domains because of the stacked nature of the architecture.

Independently Emergent Wrongs (IEW)

Independently Emergent Wrongs in this framework operate as an original concept that functions to designate wrongness without culpability. They are instances of emergent coupling, where wrongness arises from system structure without being reducible to individual agency or intent. The structure itself is not one that has the capacity to remove all harm and is not a fix-all to any wrong that could happen. Rather, structural failure from pluralist groups emerges without blame and repair is enabled without punishment.

As a consequence of this line of thought, the framework is capable of advancing moral theory without relying on moral realism. IEW is not a psychological or epistemic excuse category but a structural one. Where these IEW’s emerge, there is neither blame nor culpability to any individual agent within the group and yet recognizing that they emerge is foundational to pluralist systems as events are not completely capable of being controlled as if everything were operating in isolation. [n.4] [n.18] [n.19] [n.20] [n.59] [n.60]

Structural Treatment of Speech, Platforms, and Institutions

Within this framework, speech is treated as autonomy-relevant action via coupling. [L.6] [L.9] [L.10] Speech itself, being an act, then has capacity for impact on others and this takes on different forms via platforms and institutions. Platforms function as de facto coercive actors while lacking public standing. because of the nature of how they are formed via those autonomy-relevant speech actions. [L.12]

Institutions are diagnosed in this structure via operational capture so that we can unify speech ethics, platform governance, and political legitimacy. Operational capture is a structural diagnosis, not a genealogical or poweranalytic one. This innovation also deploys the existing toolset so that they are all subject to an identical framework and gain no level of exceptionalism that existing work may create by treating them separately.

Emergency Without Exception

Where many consider emergencies to warrant a lapse or reduction of the constraints that actors may have, this framework intensifies those constraints. It does not suspend legitimacy requirements. Provisional measures are permitted only where the criteria for full justification are specified in advance.

The constraints on agents with emergencies intensifying carries with it a challenge to state-of exception theories and security-first governance models. [n.91] [n.92] Where governments or states undergo more emergencies, the implication is that their roles are not effectively serving the purpose of avoiding those emergencies and as such, their legitimacy is called into question, and constraints escalate to empower their constituents but also as a natural product of their own action.

Why This Is Not a New Moral Theory

Moral theory tends to rank values, ground normativity in metaphysics, or supply a moral motivation. While the structure itself can give a reason for morality to persist and advance, it does not treat this as intrinsic to metaphysics or value. Instead, the moral motivation exists for those who already have agreed to the value for the persistence and endurance of pluralist space and the human race.

In this framework, moral theory does not supply motivation or ultimate justification; it supplies constraint—specifying when moral claims may legitimately bind others under plural conditions. Moral theory remains intact under this framework; what changes is when its claims may legitimately bind others under plural conditions.

Methodology

The Core Shift - Conditional Relevance

From this starting point, I intend to explore what follows when relevance is treated as conditional rather than intrinsic: how perceptual coupling grounds public standing, how claims that violate autonomy lose legitimacy, and how moral meaning emerges not from authority or revelation but from shared experiences and interaction. [n.1] [n.2]

What matters to us is not what is, but what we can meaningfully assert applies to us and the reasons why. (cf. Sellars’ rejection of the “Myth of the Given,” on which perceptual authority depends on inferential and social integration rather than raw experience.) [L.13] [n.66] Relevance here is not subjective salience but structural consequence—what enters shared coordination through coupling. [n.203]

Concepts

Key terms in this work are defined operationally and structurally, not essentially. Definitions are introduced as they become functionally necessary and remain open to revision where coupling and consequence demand it.

competence = training/skill + open reproducibility

operations = published protocol + known error bounds

auditability = independent access to methods + logs

corrigibility = recognized revision path

non-parochial = not controlled solely by the claimant

This is a normative decision discipline—a gatekeeping architecture for standing and legitimacy—not a positive theory of social causation. Formal names for these gates appear later; for now, I use their operational content. Where social-scientific accounts diverge, this framework functions as a referee for public warrant, not as an explanatory rival. Definitions and tests are reused across chapters without rederivation; later sections apply earlier constraints rather than reargue them.

Competence cannot be defined by incumbents alone. The criteria for competence in this framework are themselves subject to standing tests of being publicly contestable, auditable, and revisable so incumbents cannot unilaterally fix who counts as competent. Thus, the definition of competence here still adheres to the anti-gatekeeping structure of the framework.

Autonomy in this framework is a constraint on legitimate binding and not an account of good or morality. Autonomy constraints in this framework are applied relative to agents’ practical capacities within the conditions of endurance, a relationship that will be formalized later where authority and dependency make the issue unavoidable. The framework can host communities that rank values differently as long as they preserve non-denomination and correction pathways.

This is structurally established within the system as being coupled directly to the prospect of endurance for pluralist spaces. Still though, the framework recognizes that some failures are tragic, not unjustifiable. It does not offer salvation from these cases.

This book uses structural reasoning rather than empirical modeling. Empirical illustrations can validate but are not required for structural claims. The framework is compatible with empirical testing but is not dependent upon it. Empirical analogues such as feedback loops, runaway effects, and systemic fragility in ecology, markets, and technological systems illustrate the consequences of asymmetry.

While this work aligns with Philip Kitcher on well-ordered science, it aligns mostly in spirit and centers more tightly on risk-bearers. Likewise, among Dewey, Peirce, Longino, Hacking, and Latour, this framework keeps “agreed operations” stricter than their descriptive pluralism. [n.45] [n.2] [n.44] [n.46]

Agreed operations begin as provisional coordination conventions under minimal constraints of publicity, corrigibility, and exit. [n.14] [n.15] They gain standing by surviving repeated correction and contestation under plural pressure. They are not a “once-for-all” authorization but remain revisable so that the framework has reflective equilibrium and can retain stability under correction.

Procedural Capture and Standing Collapse
This framework does not assume that agreed operations remain functional or incorruptible. Where procedures become captured, insulated from correction, or systematically foreclose challenge, the result is not a failure of morality or coordination but a collapse of standing itself. [n.185] It establishes a decoupling between those procedures or operations and the pluralist collective of that society.

In such cases, legitimacy is not preserved by further procedural compliance. It is instead withdrawn. Exit, refusal, and resistance become structurally justified responses—not because procedures failed morally, but because they failed operationally. The framework does not guarantee justice under capture; it identifies when justice can no longer be claimed.

Said more plainly, when the framework recognizes that agreed operations and procedures are not serving the collective, they cease to have relevance to them. This does not mean they lose force, but it creates a justification for the agents within that collective to resist, refuse, and exit such systems where capable. It realigns justice to always side with those who are on the side of these constraints rather than simply to a majority or power structure. To analyze these structural failures across domains without importing contested moral or doctrinal assumptions, the framework requires a precise and neutral vocabulary.

Terminology and Necessity

Why New Terms Are Necessary

Many philosophical terms evolved to address domainspecific disputes and therefore carry historical, moral, and metaphysical assumptions this framework must bracket. Many terms such as “rights,” “agency,” “reasonableness,” “interests,” and “burdens” carry centuries of moral, cultural, or metaphysical correlations.

Using such terminology in the same respect that they have been used for tradition could smuggle in assumptions the framework rejects. Time has shown that they have been highly valuable in their domains, yet they carry too many presumptions into this framework to be of the type of use that is required across them. They embed often contested moral commitments and often undermine neutrality across traditions. This breaks domain-portability. Structural systems, however, require unambiguous vocabulary. This framework is structural, not metaphysical or moral.

It analyzes symmetry, rerunnability, feedback validity, autonomy-impact, standing, and legitimacy constraints. These all require clean, precise terms that function like tools – not inherited concepts distorted by prior philosophical debates. New terms help avoid moral loading.

The vocabulary in this framework is intentionally designed to avoid importing liberal rights frameworks or encoding cultural assumptions. It aims to prevent moral conclusions from being baked into definitions and to ensure that evaluations arise from structure rather than ideology. This framework identifies a structural problem in a lack of domain portability.

The same structural engine in this framework spans perception, morality, communication, institutions, politics, economics, culture, identity, psychology, and global coordination. Portability requires terms whose meanings remain invariant across domains. It cannot be tied to local norms but must operate across scales and contexts.

Mapping Terms to Concepts

Each term in this work maps to a specific structural role in the coordination engine. They are not stylistic inventions. They are operational definitions created to track exposure, measure constraint, identify standing, diagnose failures, and analyze legitimacy. A full glossary appears in the back matter for readers who want expanded definitions or domainspecific elaboration.

Micro-Glossary of Core Structural Terms

Symmetry
A structural condition in which agents share equivalent standing in rerunnable operations. Symmetry ensures reciprocal feedback, correction, and legitimacy.

Standing
The publicly valid capacity of an agent or institution to make claims that bind others without domination. Standing is generated structurally, not assumed.

AutonomyImpact
The degree to which an action or claim alters another agent’s baseline conditions for selfauthorship. Central to every legitimacy test.

IEW (Irreversible Exposure Window)
A structural harm pattern where consequences propagate beyond the authorized circle of risk bearers, indicating a standing failure.

Coupling
The structural linking of agents or operations into shared coordination. Proper coupling requires reciprocity, visibility, and rerunnability.

Risk Inheritance
The structural distribution of exposure across agents who bear the consequences of an action. Valid only when aligned with authorized standing.

This micro-glossary supports the reader with a short list of the core terms of the work to help the reader. It works to help understand how the system’s vocabulary is uses, to see how each term fits into the structural engine, and to avoid misinterpreting terms through prior philosophical frameworks. When engaging source materials, domainspecific terms should be read in line with the original authors’ intent but applied within this framework according to its structural constraints. This preserves the contributions of prior traditions while keeping their terminology properly scoped.

The Wager and What Follows

Across domains, the question is not ‘what is ultimately true’ but: what has standing for us as a species, why does it have such standing, and under what constraints? The questions apply similarly across domains by virtue of sharing the same structural error and thus inherit an opening to a structurally similar form of solution. When I speak of this error, I am speaking to the error of ignoring the mechanism which makes such frames relevant - their coupling.

As a preview and to again demonstrate portability, if the stimuli from a political act likewise does not couple to the perceptions of the constituents of said act, by what other mechanism does the act gain any relevance at all? Without any relevance to constituents, what standing could such a policy have?

So, it is with all of the things explored herein and consequently the mechanism which warrants usage across domains. Throughout this work, the same structural engine recurs across domains: coupling determines standing; autonomy constrains legitimacy; consequence sizes response. This framework does not imply global administration. Scale increases justification burden, not authority scope.

Differences among perception, morality, language, politics, resources or any other domain reflect scale and medium, not different foundations. The wager of this framework is that we can retain meaningful standards of legitimacy, responsibility, and constraint without appeal to metaphysical authority, while avoiding both moral relativism and authoritarian imposition.

This work does not aim to replace moral, political, or epistemic theories. It aims to constrain them—by specifying the structural conditions under which their claims can acquire standing. In this sense, it is not a competing doctrine but a framework of admissibility. Accounts of legitimacy that appeal to consent, procedure, expertise, public reason, or moral justification already rely—often implicitly—on determinations of relevance and standing. What this framework makes explicit is not a new source of legitimacy, but the structural conditions under which any such source can bind others at all. Coupling does not compete with these accounts; it explains the mechanism by which they succeed or fail.

What you gain from this book is a method—one that works the same way whether evaluating scientific claims, political policies, moral conflicts, speech harms, or even resource decisions. This framework does not claim that all people must adopt it, nor that coordination without domination is inevitable. Rather, it demonstrates that non-dominating coordination is structurally possible without relying on a final authority—a possibility that has not been clearly articulated in prior theory.

Whether the final version of authority comes from mathematics, science, a deity, metaphysics, philosophy, or otherwise, none can bypass the structural requirements for standing and legitimacy in pluralist contexts. Their claims acquire public legitimacy only when they satisfy the same structural constraints of coupling, answerability, and rerunnability that govern all other domains. Many academic practices already incorporate this value into their systems intrinsically.

To show what this method actually permits—and what it refuses to permit—we begin with a concrete case. This framework would be undermined if a stable plural system could be shown to generate legitimate, noncoercive constraint without reliance on standing, or if standing could be sustained where all coupling mechanisms fail.

Sample Case

Insider Trading by Elected Officials (Structural Legitimacy Case)

This case is not a moral argument or legal brief. It is introduced to demonstrate how questions of standing, legitimacy, and proportional constraint can be adjudicated under plural disagreement. The verdict is procedural, not punitive. It is intentionally resolved, not dramatized.

Scenario

Elected officials participate in financial markets regularly. In many jurisdictions, they are permitted to do so while in office subject to disclosure and existing insider-trading laws. At the same time, these officials often interact with non-public information through briefings, committee access, or advance knowledge of policy outcomes. In some cases, patterns emerge in which trades made by public officials appear to be suspiciously correlated with such access, even when no violation of existing law is established.

These activities are often considered legal under the current statutes. Many investigations fail to establish intent, misuse of classified information, or criminal wrongdoing. Nevertheless, public confidence in the integrity of governance and markets often erodes when those correlations become visible. The legitimacy problem arises prior to adjudication and, in many cases, persists even after legal exoneration.

Familiar Responses and Their Limits

A common response to this eroding of confidence in the integrity of governance and markets is the conclusion that legality is dispositive. If the conduct is permitted by law, no further action is warranted. This response treats legitimacy as exhausted by compliance. It fails to account for the structural harms that law may not have considered yet and does not offer remedy or remediation when public trust collapses despite the legality of action.

Another common response condemns the behavior as morally wrong and demands punishment. This approach collapses wrongs into culpability and escalates coercion without establishing standing or evidentiary sufficiency prior. It risks authorizing punitive actions where non-parochial evidence is absent and disagreement has not been resolved.

Yet another common response is to appeal to market dynamics. Some argue that information asymmetries are ubiquitous and already priced into the financial systems themselves. This view treats these cases as economically unexceptional and fails to account for the distinct standing of public office. The asymmetric risks borne by citizens who cannot meaningfully exit either governance or markets go unconsidered.

Still others respond by proposing transparency as a sufficient remedy, emphasizing disclosure and reporting. While transparency can reduce some of these informational asymmetries, it does not neutralize the timing advantages or address the downstream erosion of trust that these events create. Disclosure by itself does not serve to resolve conflicts of legitimacy.

Each of these responses works to capture a part of the problem but does not serve to resolve it.

Applying the Framework

This framework begins addressing the problem with the simple question of whether the conduct relationally (via public office) and emergently (via systemic trust) couples to others in a way that creates standing relevance. Trading by public officials is not merely private behavior. It shapes public trust, perceptions of fairness, and confidence in our democratic and market coordination systems. The effects are not confined to willing participants; they propagate to citizens and market actors who have no comparable access or influence through price changes and the like.

Having established that the conduct couples in a way that creates standing relevance, the next question concerns that standing itself. Public officials occupy roles that authorize them to bind others through law, regulation, and policy. It is given on the assumption that public power is not used to secure private advantage. When structural incentives permit otherwise, standing is called into question regardless of the intent. Thus, evaluation of that standing is in order.

Risk-inheritance clarifies asymmetry. If the trust in governance and markets collapses, the costs are borne diffusely by citizens and participants who cannot easily refuse exposure. Individuals cannot opt out of democratic systems or exit markets without significant personal cost. The downside risk is inherited by those without decision authority while the potential gains are highly concentrated.

Exit in this case is therefore not effective. Citizens cannot meaningfully withdraw from governance and market participation is often necessary for basic economic security. Where exit is non-viable, constraints that reduce autonomy trigger justification requirements rather than being dismissed as voluntary. [n.199]

Restricting trading by office holders does reduce individual autonomy. That reduction constitutes a form of coercion that must therefore be proportionate. Criminal punishment or retrospective sanction would require clear evidence of wrongdoing and intent. Absent such evidence, punitive measures lack standing.

Protective constraints, however, do not operate the same way. Measures such as blind trusts, trading prohibitions during tenure, or cooling-off periods do not assert guilt. Instead, they function to neutralize structural incentives and restore legitimacy going forward. These measures are reversible, role-specific, and limited in scope. They reduce autonomy only to the extent necessary to protect trust and coordination.

In this case, what is identified is structural wrongness. There is no established culpability as we have not concluded any non-parochial evidence of any crime or wrongdoing in this sample case. Consequently, the appropriate response is not punishment but repair of the structurally emergent wrong itself.

The Verdict

Under this framework, criminal sanctions or moral condemnation are not justified without proof of misuse of non-public information. Legal permissibility alone, however, is insufficient to confer legitimacy. Where public office creates unavoidable asymmetries of access and risk, prospective constraints on market participation are justified to preserve standing. This framework authorizes limits without blame, restraint without denial, and repair without moral theater. It refuses both permissiveness disguised as legality and coercion justified by outrage.

Policy makers using this framework might use it to attach trading prohibitions and blind trusts for asset management to all seats of public office, for instance. These constraints in such cases are coupled to the seats themselves, not to the individuals who temporarily occupy them. They apply uniformly and persist independently of electoral outcomes, ensuring that the structure of the system does not hinge on personal virtue or suspicion.

These constraints do not constitute punishment. The associated reduction in autonomy is prospective, transparent, bounded, and is incurred as a condition of assuming a position of public trust rather than as a response to alleged wrongdoing. The legitimacy of governance is protected not by asserting purity, but by designing institutions that do not require trust to be endlessly tested. Symmetric standing underlies the very possibility of stable coupling.

Notably, the legitimacy problem in this case emerges before proof and persists after adjudication. Public confidence erodes through perception, not verdicts. How beliefs, signals, and expectations become standingrelevant is not ancillary to governance; it is central.

Compact Summary

In the following framework, public standing arises only through coupling [n.1] [n.2]; autonomy governs legitimate constraint; moral practice is non-objective but non-arbitrary, constrained by consequence, autonomy, and shared capacities.

Punishment is a contingent social instrument with its ceiling set by a violation of principles while its prescription is narrowed by endurance, autonomy restoration/protection, consistency, and publicly cognizable moral debt. [n.8] [n.10]

Correction manages immediate risk through external constraint but does not restore moral agency. [n.13] Repair restores agency through internal coupling of culpability and will. [n.9] [n.8] Forgiveness releases a private moral claim without deciding public order or safety. [n.5] [n.2]

These moral dynamics are previewed here as a display of the portability of the structural engine. Understanding how perception itself couples to legitimacy is therefore essential. The next chapter begins there.

II — About Perception

Purpose: This section examines how the coupling-standing-legitimacy engine operates within the domain of perception and how misidentification of coupling produces characteristic failures of standing in this domain. Perception has many models. Though this section does call back to traditional philosophers and thoughts, it will derive a different function to those thoughts for the purpose of using those functions to support the established toolset. Thus, perception in this chapter is functional, not metaphysical. All that is required is that agents respond to stimuli using internal models. Coupling depends on mismatch between models.

Orientation

What This Chapter Is and Is Not

This chapter does not apply the framework to perception as a domain. It establishes why any public claim must pass through perceptual coupling in order to acquire relevance at all. [n.1] [n.2] The purpose here is not to settle disputes about realism, subjectivity, or truth but to show that standing cannot arise in the absence of shared, reproducible uptake. Later chapters will translate this constraint into domain-specific tools; here the work is structural. Readers should not expect prescriptions or evaluative verdicts in this chapter. Its role is to establish why perception is a necessary gate for standing across all domains that follow.

This chapter does not assert claims about metaphysics by means of perception. Instead, it interdependently couples the autonomy and agency of individuals to their perceptions and thereby establishes those perceptions and interactions as the basis for standing itself. This is realized as a structural emergence of pluralism rather than a metaphysical claim or value system. [n.2] [n.16] This chapter is not attempting to say what “is” but asserts what “matters.”

Future chapters will begin with a similar orientation section. Where tools or the engine of this framework have been demonstrated and apply, they will be iterated in this orientation section as they apply to that domain. These are not re-derivations of the tools themselves, and they do not take on new iterations intrinsically. Rather, each domain contains unique applications of the tools and engine due to their unique coupling arrangements so that the tools and engine are capable of considering them across many domains as a sort of proverbial “multi-tool” with many functions where the applications themselves may be limited in scope to their domain.

Perceptual Frames and Headcounts

Three-Room Thought Experiment

Consider how, without an agreed coupling protocol, no claim can achieve public standing. [n.2] There are three rooms and twenty people who are incapable of lying. The first two rooms each hold their own group of ten people and have a door by which you can call upon them. These two rooms are kept in such a way that no exchange is possible between either the rooms or the groups inside of them. You are unaware of what is in the third room (we will call this the “experiment room”). The rules for the experiment room are that only one group may be inside at a time and the information about what is inside is not able to be deduced or observed except from within it.

You want to know what is inside of the experiment room; however, whenever you approach the doorway, the doorway disappears, so you devise an experiment for the room. You invite each group from the first two rooms to independently enter the room at separate times so that they are still unable to interact with one another. After each exit from the experiment room, they give you their perceptions of the room and you write them down. When all groups are finished, you look at your writing to evaluate all of the perceptions.

In the first group, nine participants indicated that they could see, hear, taste, smell, and otherwise touch a glass of water. One indicated that the room was empty. When you review the second group of ten, the pattern is inverted, with only a single participant able to perceive a glass of water.

From the perspective of the first group, there is a glass of water, and one person has a malfunction of the senses. From the perspective of the second group, there is no glass of water and one of them experiences delusions. From your perspective, there are ten people who experience a glass of water and ten who do not. Which of these perspectives is the correct one and by what mechanism could you determine this? For that matter, how do you even know your experiment isn’t subject to coercion from whichever force causes the door to disappear for you? So what?

Headcounts and Manufactured Standing

There is no decidable correct perspective among these frames absent an interdependent coupling test between perceptual frames. [n.2] In kind, this experiment mirrors in structure the same principles for all cases where access is asymmetric, reports are private, and no shared protocol exists. For you, the question of the glass of water does not apply because you have not yet entered the room.

Those who argue that the majority having agreement determines the reality of the situation have committed argumentum ad populum (cf. Peirce’s account of inquiry, where truth is not determined by present consensus but by convergence under indefinitely extended, shared investigation) [n.14]. Headcounts are insufficient as a basis for standing—not just logically, but structurally. Structurally they do not correct for shared bias, shared malfunction, or shared isolation from the measured object.

While aggregation may be a part of agreed options (e.g., as one output) is never sufficient where exposure is asymmetric or where operations are controlled. After all, what if one group could control access to the room entirely? What if one group controlled which reports were recorded? What if one group were able to define what counted as “competent” perception? Would not standing in these cases be manufactured rather than predicated upon truth?

When agreed operations formally exist but are controlled, restricted, or designed such that correction is structurally foreclosed, this is the premise for “Operational Capture.” [n.205] It implies a decoupling between procedures and the pluralist collective where standing collapses not because claims are false but because the coupling that once licensed them has been severed. [n.185] [n.28] In the case of this room, the concept that the door disappears only for you when you approach is a form of operational capture where the agreed operations exist but the correction of your own perception of the room is structurally closed. We can recognize it by its two characteristics:

(1) formal procedures exist

(2) correction is structurally foreclosed (by access, design, or gatekeeping). Whether intentional or emergent, standing failure is structural for all forms of operational capture.

Although the three-room experiment frames the instability of standing under asymmetric operations, the same principle applies to how objects themselves become intelligible across agents. Before we can address how standing is generated through reproducibility, we must address how perceptual objects acquire continuity in the first place.

The stability of an object – its persistence as “the same” across observers and time – is not intrinsic to the object but is a coordinated achievement across perceptual frames. This becomes clear when considered through a well-known identity puzzle, which functions here not as a metaphysical dilemma, but as a demonstration of how shared perceptual coupling stabilizes an object for a pluralist group.

The Ship of Theseus as a Perceptual-Coupling Problem

Traditional presentations of the Ship of Theseus puzzle treat the question of whether the ship remains “the same” after replacement of its parts as a metaphysical dilemma about identity. Within this framework, however, the identity of the ship is not a metaphysical property. It is instead a structural output of perceptual coupling.

Each agent carries a perception that is indexed to their prior interactions with the ship. These histories stabilize how the ship appears to the agent and determines which features are relevant for recognition. When a group of agents shares sufficiently overlapping sets of operations and historical couplings, these individual frames may converge into a shared perceptual frame agreement, stabilizing a shared referent such that the “same ship” exists for that group.

From this perspective, the continuity of the ship is not inherent to the object but is maintained only through the stability of the shared perception that recognizes it. When that shared perception holds, the ship remains the same object despite material changes. When those perceptions diverge, multiple incompatibly “same” ships emerge, each anchored to different criteria of recognition. There is no “fact of the matter” about which interpretation is “correct” independent of the perceptual frame that stabilizes it.

This reframing dissolves the puzzle by relocating identity from the material sameness to the stability of collective relevance. The identity of the ship is an achievement of coordination, not an intrinsic property as the ship itself does not have internal agency to produce such intrinsic identity. It is the continued coherence of the shared perception – not the physical continuity of the object – that determines whether it is treated as the same ship across time.

Generating Standing

Reproducibility as a Basis for Public Standing

The three-room experiment shows that public standing rests on methodologically shared coupling tests (calibration, replication, cross-check), not headcounts. [n.2] The point of this thought experiment is to demonstrate that, absent a coupling test within the measurement protocol, results are not reproducible by multiple groups (cf. Longino’s account of objectivity as arising from critical interaction among perspectives rather than individual observation).

Furthermore, it is evidence of the consequences which arise when such methods for validating standing are absent from collected groups. Perception can generate relevance, but it cannot by itself generate standing; without publicly shared coupling mechanisms, perceptual authority collapses into either testimony or force. [n.185] [n.66] [n.164]

Private experience may matter to a subject, but it gains public standing only when its content is independently reproducible under agreed operations. [n.2] Public standing exists for the function of enabling coordination, correction, and shared action because standing’s function is shared action and correction. Claims that cannot be re-run by other competent parties cannot serve that function because shared rerun-ability translates private uptake into common action. This is why it grounds standing and not simply belief. This framework requires auditability and corrigibility, not Bayesian priors.

Reproducibility is a core structural element of all of those functions. Those goals are therefore dependent upon it. Similarly, measurement protocol among groups must employ some level of coupling in order to be reproducible to other groups. Where constructivist accounts describe how facts are made, the present framework specifies when fact-claims earn public standing: only when methods remain open, rerunnable, and non-captured. [n.44] [n.46] Where couplings fail, structural components of society and interpersonal interactions likewise fail, as they are dependent upon them. Where these failings occur, their consequences necessarily follow.

Standing Amid Proprietary Information and Privacy

So then, by what means can something obtain public standing? Public standing is obtained when a claim, action, or institution is coupled to shared perceptual frames through agreed operations such that it is answerable, corrigible, and usable for coordination by other competent parties. [n.2] [n.185]

What of proprietary data or patient privacy? Those cases are not exceptions to the rule. They merely present a contestation that is rooted in specificity rather than in structural concreteness. Where full public disclosure would introduce independent harm, tiered proxy validation (as discussed later) preserves non-parochial constraints without breaching privacy. [n.29] After all, even when data is proprietary or patient information is private, there must necessarily be a coupling between the owner of such data and the data itself but likewise these contestations only arise as the data couples to other parties. [n.30]

Could a claim of data being proprietary be validated without an intermediary likewise validating the claimant? Would the restriction of your information to privacy apply if there were no further parties to have interacted with it? The coupling of those claims, actions, and institutions still emerge through an agreed operation such that one cannot have a claim that privacy was infringed without both parties having already coupled through agreed operations. [n.185] [n.30] The accusation of infringement is for one party to assert that the agreed operations have been violated, not that the coupling was non-existent.

Caselet (medical privacy):

A hospital claims a new protocol reduces mortality, but patient data cannot be released.

Proxy standing: an independent review board (publicly authorized) audits de-identified outcomes using a pre-registered method.

Tiered disclosure: publish the protocol, statistical thresholds, and audit results; keep raw identifiers private.

Off-ramp: if independent auditors cannot reproduce the outcome pattern under agreed operations, the protocol loses public standing for coercive adoption.

Coupling, Failed Coupling, and Decoupling

Coupling, Relevance, and the Frame-Dependence of Reality Claims

Definitions: When speaking about our interaction with reality, we may speak of the causal, informational, or embodied uptake sufficient to change prediction, action, or shared measurement with the term “coupling.” [n.1] [n.16] [n.40] This account is compatible with enactive views: perception as skillful world-involving engagement rather than passive input.

Call the organized standpoint, whether physiological, practices, instruments, or concepts, from which uptake occurs as their “perceptual frame.” Whenever there are open, non-parochial procedures any competent party can in principle carry out (calibration disclosed, materials available, criteria pre-stated), call these “agreed operations.” [n.2]

Existence vs Relevance

While reality may exist independently of our perception, ultimately the value of reality claims is dependent upon their coupling and relevance to a perceptual frame. Causal effect without coupling has no relevance for a given perceptual frame. [n.1] [n.2] Objects and the perceptions of them may be related, but they are distinct.

Though an object may exist, it has no standing within a perceptual frame unless it can enter prediction, valuation, or action. [n.42] This became evident when René Descartes asserted cogito ergo sum. He rationalized that, where perceptions coalesce into thought, there then must be a perceiver which performs these perceptions. [n.95] So, Descartes does not deny metaphysical independence; however, he does draw a level of distinction between the perception, the perceiver, and the object being perceived.

So, while some have ventured to establish how coupling is established between a “real” object and the perception of this object, Descartes has keyed us in on an important distinction with his assertion: we only interact with the perceptions themselves. These perceptual uptakes form our perceptions and are composite of more than external stimuli so that when we speak to anything descriptively, what we are truly speaking to are those perceptions.

This is supported by Sartre. He agrees that consciousness is immediately self-aware and does not need inference, observation, or representation to know itself. It is pre-reflective. Consequently, self-awareness is structural. [n.126] It is by these assertions of Sartre and Descartes that this framework can likewise remain structural in asserting that perception is not mediated by representation, awareness is not produced by reflective access, and self-knowledge is not a special epistemic act.

In keeping with these assertions, Sartre supports the idea that perceptions are not discrete moral units or representational contents so that this framework does not assign any level of moral responsibilities or culpability to them later on. Instead, it agrees with Sartre that perceptions are how consciousness exists at all—not that they are the sum of its parts, but that they are a mode by which it emerges.

Where Sartre then presumes to tie the relation of consciousness directly to the world rather than that of the world formulating a representation which then imposes itself upon our consciousness, this present account rejects his furthest assumption of this but accepts what he has reasonably established: pluralism. This rejection is not a refutation of Sartre’s phenomenology, but a refusal to treat phenomenological structure as sufficient for ontological determination.

Where Sartre asserts that the consciousness necessarily requires otherness and implies plurality because it cannot be closed or self-sufficient [n.126], this is insufficient as proof that this plurality must be composed of independently existing objects. It does not presume that perception transparently reveals the structure of being as we will see shortly from variant perceptive capabilities.

Through logic alone could we not say that a singular object (call this Y) could function as a singular source of alterity whose outputs are encountered phenomenologically as plural without requiring ontological plurality. Could not Y simply be a singular “other” which we perceive as the sum total of the world and the independent separation of those perceptions? Are the bark and branches of a tree not the tree itself? Sartre provides no mechanism by which phenomenological plurality entails ontological plurality.

Sartre demonstrates that consciousness cannot be self-grounding and therefore requires alterity. This establishes pluralism as a structural condition of experience. [n.126] However, it does not determine the ontological form of that plurality. Phenomenological multiplicity does not entail a multiplicity of independent beings; the generative source of appearances may remain singular, opaque, or otherwise undetermined by perception alone.

If perception does not transparently reveal ontology, then neither individual nor collective perceptual uptake can function as a direct warrant for reality claims. Such claims collapse under the weight of their own demand. While this framework does not aim to establish any metaphysical claims, it operationally relies on these structural renderings of perception and recognizes them as non-ubiquitous. We do not all experience the same perceptions of objects or events. Even in eyewitness testimonies of events there are varying outcomes. [n.7] [n.42]

Testimony alone is insufficient for public standing unless its content is independently reproducible under agreed operations. [n.164] If it does not become reproducible to the public, how could the public even evaluate it for standing? When it becomes reproducible to the public, how can we know definitively that the consensus of that public is in accordance with reality?

A 2023 study in Nature Neuroscience (Rowland et al. 2023) [n.7] showed that variability in sensory cortex activity conditions whether a stimulus is perceived at all. What this means for public standing is that it cannot stand alone as a sole test of standing because variability of perceptual uptake inherently exists among the public. For this reason, testimony can trigger investigation when reliability networks and exposure are coupled to it but, without shared operations, it cannot by itself generate public warrant or constraint or bind action. [n.14] [n.15]

Testimony itself has provisional standing in ordinary life via trust networks and moral reliability, but it loses standing when it forecloses correction or becomes operational capture. In ordinary life, testimony carries practical warrant, but that does not carry coercive standing at all levels of epistemic risk as we will discuss further on. While this does not settle metaphysical questions, it demonstrates that perceptual uptake is not solely stimulus driven. [n.41]

Endogenous Valuation

Additionally, Nietzsche contends that the will to act is not so instant and voluntary as one might believe. Rather, he asserts that there is a sensation at present (what is being left), a sensation of a desired state (what is being approached or the motivation), bodily sensations of capacity to accomplish the motivation, a commanding thought (which many confuse to be the sum of all willpower), a feeling of superiority or mastery of the elements needed to accomplish the desired state, and that this culminates in an action.

Acknowledging Nietzsche’s insistence that drives can originate endogenously; external stimuli often trigger, shape, or redirect them rather than generate them. His structure shows that action presupposes an internal valuation prior to external fact, undermining the idea of value as discovered rather than enacted. [n.96]

Failed Coupling Illustrated (The Glass of Water Revisited)

So then, does it truly matter if the glass of water is there at all? One might say, “well if you were on the brink of death to dehydration, the reality of the glass of water is very important - even if you can’t sense it the water can still nourish you!” Can it?

If the whole of your being is the collection of your body and none of this body can sense the water by any form of biological coupling whether chemical, mechanical, or neural, then how could it know to absorb this water in the first place? What could signal to your cells to make use of it if they are incapable of receiving signal? If they too were stripped of these senses in all respects, truly the reality of the glass of water has no relevance for action or valuation within their frame. This is a case of failed coupling—not the loss of an existing relation, but the absence of any coupling capable of supporting relevance or standing. [n.195]

Failed coupling itself may happen by absence (no channel), distortion (misleading uptake), asymmetry (one-way access) or exclusion (procedural barriers). Each of these types of failure produces a different type of illegitimate standing necessarily as their causes of failure are also naturally different. Standing demands the requisite attributes of answerability, correction pathways, and shared uptake. Failed coupling, by definition, disables those conditions and results in illegitimate standing. Standing demands answerability and re-testability; failed coupling blocks both, so public standing is not obtained. [n.185]

The deeper instability described here is simply the perceptual expression of a more general structural rule: whenever standing becomes asymmetric, the same pattern of distortion recurs. Epistemic imbalance mirrors structural imbalance. The same structural logic helps illuminate the contrasting case, where coupling once enabled symmetric standing but later dissolves. This is the distinct phenomenon of decoupling.

Decoupling

Decoupling in this structure is distinct from a failed coupling. Decoupling occurs in concept where a coupling has already existed and no longer does. The causes of this are variant across domains. Though there are forms such as epistemic decoupling, communicative decoupling, logic decoupling, etc.—they are not exhaustive of the concept.

Modes of decoupling are not universal across domains but apply explicitly as they relate to the domain they apply in. For instance, when we speak of perceptual decoupling as being a failed uptake, we are speaking to the idea that there once was a coupled perception where the failure to uptake in reference causes that coupling to no longer exist. While this would be considered a failed coupling in that sense, the prior condition of this establishes that this is likewise a decoupling.

So, all decoupling is necessarily failed coupling because, by definition, the former has no basis without the latter. Not all failed couplings emerge as decoupling as there may not have been a prior coupling to decouple. Where decoupling does not break the parameters of the domain, it can be distinguished with a causal modifier. Where decoupling becomes destructive of the domain itself, domain modifiers carry more weight as the scope of the domain is naturally larger than that of its premises.

Portability of The Coupling Engine

This engine draws similarities outside of the field of philosophy as well. Special relativity denies any preferred inertial frame; analogously, no preferred perceptual frame is privileged for determining relevance. [n.43] Frame-relativity is not arbitrariness; in physics and here, structure is preserved across frames by relational constraints and invariance is found only via relations. Constraints such as invariance and relations survive across frames structurally. Only privileged access is rejected. In special relativity, measurements are frame-relative; analogously, meaning/relevance is perceptual-frame-relative (not whimsical), with relational constraints preserved across frames, matching the assertion that no perceptual frame is privileged for determining relevance.

If we speak of cosmology or metaphysical possibilities, when we speak of other universes, the question of their relevance to us is not resolved simply by their existence or non-existence. Rather, their relevance to us is resolved by their capacity to interact with us. [n.1] [n.2] Any claim about reality acquires standing only insofar as there exists some causal channel by which interaction and information transfer may occur. Where no such channel exists, no information can propagate, no coupling can take place, and no relevance can arise for our perceptual frame.

This limitation is not unique to hypothetical other universes but applies equally to vast regions of our own universe that are causally inaccessible to us. The consequences of any such reality only have value as they relate to us when the stimuli breach the realm of our perceptions. Even previous interactions among “real things” are inconsequential to the perceiver until the point that one stimulus from these interactions breaches the perception and carries with it the knowledge of those previous interactions or the information by which to infer them.

Consider star systems that are thousands of light-years away which we perceive currently. Finite signal speed and the structure of causality impose boundaries beyond which no influence, information, or interaction can reach us. The light which currently reaches our eyes delivers the breach of that perception and within that light is carried the information which we use to make inferences and yet, the current reality of that celestial body located an immense and causally inaccessible (for now) distance from us is yet unknown.

In this respect, the “reality” of distant or causally disconnected regions of our own universe is no different from that of other universes entirely. The current reality in the frame of that celestial body is irrelevant to our experience due to the entire lack of stimuli which can breach our perception. We must wait the appropriate time for such information to make the journey to interdependently couple to our perception and retroactively inform us of what reality once was for that body.

A Deeper Symmetry

The boundary that renders other universes irrelevant to us is the same boundary that mediates our relationship to our own universe. We do not encounter reality as it is, but only as it enters into relation with us through interaction (This parallels Kant’s distinction between phenomena and noumena, though without Kant’s transcendental commitments). [n.67] Meaning is not assigned independently to the thing itself but is dependent upon coupling to furnish this relation. [L.1] [L.4] [L.5]

For us, the universe is pragmatically the totality of what may enter into causal relation with our perceptual frames via that coupling. (cf. Kuhn on paradigm-relative salience and the framedependence of relevance and problemsolving.) [n.3] [n.203] What we engage with is never the thing in and of itself. We engage with the structure of its interaction with us.

It is this structure alone that grounds any claim to reality which can apply to us. This framework is agnostic about what exists independent of perception. It addresses only the conditions under which existence claims acquire epistemic and practical standing for agents and collectives. One should not construe this to reduce reality to opinion, deny causal independence, or collapse truth into consensus. Rather, it has rejected only the idea that claims acquire standing absent shared, reproducible interaction. Frame-dependence here constrains arbitrariness rather than awarding it license.

Consequences of Failed Coupling

Failed coupling within the structure does not inherently culminate in a loss of power or influence. Rather, failed coupling in group dynamics results in the emergence of systematic failure. [n.68] When the actions of the community do not couple to the members of that community, error arises.

When someone who can speak and who is heard is structurally gated, perceptual injustice is produced. [n.165] Those subjected to consequences lack meaningful correction channels. [n.49] Perceptual error becomes normatively significant when it cannot be corrected by those subjected to its consequences. It can lead to concepts like domination, coercion, and control. Where there is epistemic asymmetry, coercion is enabled.

In that same line of thought, perceptual control precedes most other forms of control in other domains and systematic failed coupling leads implicitly to domination. It should be noted that not every variant of failed coupling is directly correlated to intent or force, however it does leave those paths open where actors find that they have been enabled.

From Perceptual Error to Injustice

Error is not Injustice

Structurally, failed coupling is not implicitly injustice. Injustice is error that specifically forecloses correction for the exposed. [n.49] [n.166] [n.60] When failed coupling persists over time, scale, or institutions, those are the criteria where it ceases to be mere error and becomes injustice by virtue of foreclosed correction. Thus, the dividing line between error and injustice is structural itself and predicated upon that foreclosing rather than upon awareness or the action itself.

Where we find error, there are variant couplings within the group which define such error. Where those errors are persistent over time, scale, or institutions there is an implicit limitation to correction. After all, if the scope of an error is to never cease enacting itself, by what measure could you correct it? Would the error not consistently emerge after you had finished correction?

Likewise for scale. If an error were so massive in scale as to consume all possible perceptual frames, by what mechanism or measure could you correct such an error? Would it not be inherently carried into any solution which you might propose? The foreclosing of correction emerges as a phenomenon from those qualities so that the consequence of failed coupling inherently carries with it the need to evaluate their scopes as they regard those characteristics.

The Path to Injustice

All these elements are prey to perception in the sense that they depend upon channels of uptake to acquire relevance at all. Perception is primary. Subsequent domains all presuppose some channel of uptake by which claims can enter shared relevance at all, whether language, normativity, or institutions. [n.1] [n.2] [n.16]

This presupposed channel of uptake applies in scale just as it does to the individual so that failed coupling for the individual renders the stimulus irrelevant to them in the same way that it would for the group. Even in the presence of supposed infinite power, this power is still reliant upon coupling to perception because publicly checkable perception is what warrants standing and standing is the bridge concept that converts epistemic corrigibility into public legitimacy under pluralism. [n.185] [n.49] As a result, all public coercion requires publicly checkable perceptual uptake and warrant.

So, we evaluate the uptake and terminality of such errors and perceptions, to distinguish them plainly from injustice, not that remedy cannot happen in either case but that it be understood the exact nature of the problem itself and thus enable such correction to have relevance and standing by design. When we evaluate error and injustice the evaluations often include the topics of power and force as they frequently intermingle.

Power is the concept that an agent holds sufficient ability to modify outcomes, and force is the coupling of that concept to the infringement of autonomy. [n.118] [n.141] The dynamics of force and power, such as domination and coercion, are inherent to faulty couplings of error and injustice and may emerge whether intent is present or not. [n.25] [n.118] This is our justification to say that questions of perception are inseparable from those of force and power wherever pluralism emerges.

Collective Perceptions

Disagreement and Humility

Two agents within a pluralist community can be equally informed, competent, and reasoning correctly and arrive at opposing conclusions. When this framework addresses peer disagreement it is addressing disagreement between agents who meet the framework’s competence and access thresholds for the relevant domain. Historically these problems have been handled between the two avenues of conciliationism or steadfastness. [n.98] This framework does not demand that there automatically be declared a “winner.”

Instead, disagreement increases the epistemic burden, and action is gated by risk, reversibility, and autonomy impact. Testimony is an indispensable default for low-risk coordination; the framework tightens only as autonomy-impact and irreversibility rise. When two qualified peers disagree and no decisive evidence discriminates, this framework withholds permission to coerce, override, or force compliance.

This is neither skepticism nor quietism or authoritarian certainty because re-evaluations happen with further evidence, repeatable procedures, or when structural constraints break the symmetry. It is non-ideal by design. Its gates assume biased agents, incentive, and institutional capture. Those biases are what emerge in pluralist communities and have significant impact to the interactions in those spaces.

Collective Dynamics of Relevance

If we engage only with the structure of interactions and never with things in themselves, a natural question follows: how do groups arrive at anything they call “true”? Whatever “truth” means for a community cannot exceed the relevance a claim acquires through interdependent coupling with the perceptual frames of its members. [n.14] [n.2] In practice, collective truth is an emergent property of the stabilized overlap among individual frames under shared conditions so, by definition, they are inherently dependent upon them. This collective uptake does not reveal reality in itself; it furnishes the shared operational basis from which a group can act, coordinate, and correct itself. One recurrent pattern is what we may call Perceptual Frame Agreement (PFA). (cf. Peirce on convergence of inquiry and Dewey on experimental public practice.)

When many perceptual frames, under similar conditions, converge on the same uptake, the group treats this concordance as a stable basis for action. (cf. Peirce, convergence of inquiry) [n.14] [n.3] (cf. MerleauPonty’s account of perception as embodied engagement rather than passive reception.) [n.16] This is not a metaphysical guarantee of truth, nor is it simple headcount; it rests on the expectation that concordant frames under comparable circumstances are more reliable than isolated reports.

PFA is not a truth maker; it is the best publicly available warrant under corrigible access conditions. Practices such as measurement, observation, and peer review reflect this mode: they seek concordance of perceptual frames by opening procedures to multiple competent observers. (cf. Longino) [n.15] Claims that remain reproducible across frames under agreed operations come to function as the group’s practical “truths” until revised. [n.14] [n.15]

A second pattern arises when a group forms an understanding of what conditions would best sustain its existence over time, the Understood Conditions for Endurance (UCE) (This echoes Aristotle’s account of practices oriented toward sustaining forms of life, without presupposing a fixed human essence). [n.37] [n.82] Here, relevance is not grounded in immediate stimulus but in a shared sense of what is required for continued functioning or survival.

When these conditions are articulated and recognized by the group, they become an operative guide even in the absence of present perceptual confirmation. (cf. Hans Jonas on responsibility oriented toward the conditions of future endurance.) This mode underlies many collective orientations toward planning, resource use, cultivation, and longterm coordination. The “truth” in this sense is not about present perception but about a collectively understood orientation toward endurance.

A third pattern involves Rationalized Coherence (RC). Groups often subject their observations and expectations to internal tests of consistency, coherence, and inferential soundness. In these cases, a claim gains relevance not simply by being widely perceived or widely valued but by fitting within a structure of reasons the group accepts as binding for its inferences. (cf. Quine’s holism, where beliefs are evaluated within a web rather than in isolation.) [n.17] In traditions shaped by philosophical argument, formal reasoning, or scholarly debate, this coherence constraint becomes a central mode by which claims acquire standing within the group.

A fourth pattern is AffectiveVolitional Uptake. Sometimes the shared emotions, desires, or commitments of a group determine what counts as relevant for them, even when this does not align neatly with perception, planned endurance, or rational coherence. (cf. Hume on sentiment as a source of moral salience, though here constrained by coupling and consequence.) Artistic movements, ritual practices, festivals, and various forms of collective expression operate in this register. The group treats a claim or practice as significant because it resonates with shared feeling, identity, or aspiration.

What we call “truth” in collective life reflects not a revelation of things as they are in themselves but the stabilized points of relevance that emerge within these collective dynamics. Induction and Underdetermination remain but are managed by rerunnable operations, corrigibility, cross-checking, revision, and non-capture.

This framework accepts underdetermination in principle, but it constrains its political consequences by requiring corrigible, rerunnable coupling before coercive standing is granted. [n.167] While this doesn’t render those concerns moot, it functionally mitigates the problems as they apply to relevance, which is satisfactory for this framework.

These four modes—Perceptual Frame Agreement, Understood Conditions for Endurance, Rationalized Coherence, and AffectiveVolitional Uptake—do not exhaust every way a group may organize its sense of what matters, but they represent recurrent dynamics by which claims gain practical standing. Instead, this framework applies these modes in a hierarchal sequence to determine if relevance maintains itself. This hierarchy is emergent rather than determined perceptually so that relevance passes through these gates sequentially. While more gates may exist, none apply prior to the establishment of the gates which this framework asserts as primary.

The Hierarchy of Collective Relevance Dynamics

Across these modes a practical ordering emerges by function, not by fiat. Perceptual Frame Agreement is the default for empirical practice: concord under similar conditions provides the strongest basis for public uptake and revision. Rationalized Coherence supplies the testharness for those uptakes: claims that fit within a disciplined structure of reasons are easier to evaluate, challenge, and improve. Understood Conditions for Endurance furnishes longhorizon orientation when present stimuli are insufficient, provided the conditions are stated and revisable considering outcomes. Affective–Volitional uptake binds meaning and identity; it can energize collective life but does not, by itself, confer public standing. These modes differ in their capacity to support correction. Perceptual Frame Agreement offers the strongest basis for revision while Affective-Volitional Uptake is the least corrigible and therefore the weakest ground for public standing. Public standing is always provisional. (cf. Peirce) [n.14] It persists only so long as no better-coupled account displaces it through reproducible interaction and consequence. Salience and importance alone do not impart standing. Attention and intensity can amplify relevance by coupling to the group itself without providing the coupling to a claim or act, which is required for legitimacy. Thus, standing is scale-relative. A claim may acquire legitimacy via coupling within a smaller community while failing to meet the coupling requirements for broader public application.

None of these modes escapes the basic constraint already established: what gains relevance for a group does so only by coupling with the frames through which that group perceives, reasons, evaluates, or emotes. What a society calls “true” reflects stabilized points of relevance within these dynamics, held only until better coupling displaces them.

When asking what knowledge is, this framework does not make an analysis of knowledge itself but is an analysis of public warrant and standing. This work stands next to knowledge analysis rather than attempting to replace or contribute to it. Though later chapters will evaluate how coupling makes knowledge relevant to us and how it is gated, they will not address the formation of knowledge or how it emerges.

From the perspective of the reader, for the purposes of this framework, the nature of knowledge itself may be presumed so long as it can engage coupling conditions. Where knowledge couples, this framework engages in how that impacts warrant, legitimacy, and standing as it applies to pluralism.

Coupling conditions, however, are often controlled, restricted, or mediated by institutions and technologies. Consequently, questions of perception are inseparable from questions of power. With public standing grounded in shared, rerunnable coupling, we now test the hardest case—claims to final authority—and ask what, if anything, could confer public standing on them under plural conditions. [n.88] Questions of standing become most strained where perceptual access is asymmetric and agents differ in practical capacity, a problem that becomes unavoidable when authority is claimed under conditions of dependency, fear, or foreclosed correction.

What becomes visible at this point is not a conclusion about what is real, but a constraint on what can matter publicly at all. Claims may be meaningful, sincere, or deeply motivating, yet fail to acquire standing if they cannot enter shared, corrigible perceptual coupling. Perception does not privilege any frame, but it does impose a gate: without some rerunnable channel of uptake, claims remain private, insulated, or testimonial rather than publicly binding. This constraint applies prior to questions of truth, morality, or legitimacy, and it applies regardless of the domain in which a claim is made. With public standing grounded in shared perceptual access rather than authority or assertion, the next chapter turns to the hardest case—claims that present themselves as final, unquestionable, or exempt from such coupling—and asks what, if anything, could grant them standing under plural conditions.

III — About Deity

Purpose: This section examines how the coupling-standing-legitimacy engine operates within the domain of deity and how misidentification of coupling produces characteristic failures of standing in this domain. Having grounded our ideas of standing and coupling one of the primary arguments that arise against such standing comes from claims of final authority or theological correctness. This chapter does not set out to destroy belief sets but to derive what conditions such authorities or deities must meet in order to gain standing among pluralist groups themselves.

Orientation

What This Chapter Is and Is Not

This chapter establishes the structural conditions under which claims about deities and their authority can acquire public relevance and standing. It applies the already-built engine of coupling → standing → autonomy constraint without importing metaphysical commitments. This chapter treats deity claims as standing-candidates, not as truth claims to be settled. [n.47] [n.48] It likewise diagnoses why religious authority frequently collapses in pluralist space even when belief is sincere.

This chapter tests divine authority against the same public constraints as every other authority. This chapter is not a refutation of theism or atheism. It is not a metaphysical argument about whether a deity exists or doesn’t exist. There is not a theology, theodicy, or comparative religion study contained in it. Divine claims are evaluated under the same standing constraints as political, moral, or institutional authority, though standing here is grounded in publicly rerunnable coupling rather than in the content of reasons offered. [n.168]

It will outline specific applications where benefit to society may gain standing as completely separated from whether they contain standing to coerce publicly or not. Private warrant is explicitly preserved; public coercive standing is not presumed. This is the structural boundary for this chapter.

Expectations

The structural question that this chapter answer is: “by what mechanism could a divine claim acquire standing to bind others in pluralist space?” It will further ask: what fails when revelation, scripture, sincerity, or authority are asserted without coupling and why is translation into moral language alone insufficient for public standing? [n.47] [n.185]

This chapter builds directly on the concept of coupling as an engine of relevance, standing as distinct from truth and sincerity, and perception as a gate for public uptake. While there will be other tools introduced down the road that may be implicit to this framework, this chapter specifically belongs to engine validation rather than downstream prescription. Any of the tools that take implied form here will be further delineated by their function within the toolset in later chapters as well.

What readers can expect from this chapter is a structural analysis rather than a doctrinal resolution. This structural analysis will have symmetry with political and moral authority analysis later. Readers should not expect a position on whether deities exist, ranking of religions, or moral condemnation of belief.

Translations

This is the first chapter where translation becomes unavoidable. Religious claims already operate across domains of perception, morality, and politics (among others). A minimal translation table is therefore justified without presupposing later chapters.

Translation Table

Revelation: Private perceptual coupling that lacks public rerunnability or shared validation. Preserves personal meaning and conviction but does not, by itself, generate public standing or authority to bind others.

Faith: Voluntary internal coupling to a belief system or narrative framework. Preserves sincerity, identity, and existential orientation while not presuming epistemic priority or coercive authority.

Divine Command: A normative claim asserted without demonstrated public coupling. May function as moral motivation for adherents but does not establish standing to bind nonadherents under pluralist conditions.

Scripture: A textual artifact whose authority is mediated through interpretive coupling within a community. Preserves tradition, narrative continuity, and internal governance while not automatically acquiring public standing.

Sacred Authority: Relational identitydefining coupling operating within a voluntary group. Legitimate for internal coordination where exit remains real but does not confer jurisdiction over outsiders.

Miracle: Testimonial claim of causal significance lacking independent, reproducible coupling. Functions as a trigger for inquiry rather than as public warrant or standing.

Sin / Transgression: Internal moral accounting within a belief system that regulates group coherence and selfassessment. Does not, without further coupling, translate into publicly enforceable wrongdoing.

Blasphemy: An offense defined within an identitybound semantic frame. Preserves internal norms and symbolic boundaries but does not generate standing to coerce or punish in plural space.

Religious Law: An institutional ruleset derived from beliefbased authority. Legitimate where participation is voluntary and exit is preserved but not presumptively binding under pluralist coercion.

Divine Will: A claimed teleological coupling asserted without public validation. Preserves meaning attribution and orientation for believers while not establishing standing to override autonomy of others.

[n.47] [n.185] [n.50]

While these terms often may arise within specific religions, they should not be considered in this sense to be descriptive of only one value. Synonymous terms for these definitions which likewise carry the same definition then rationally carry the same translations. One example might be “religious law” versus “divine law.” While believers of a religion may draw distinctions on the origin of this law within the scope of their belief, the institutional rule-set is no less derived from belief-based authority in those contexts.

Deriving Necessity

Final Authority

Deities may exist and still lack standing for human coordination, absent public coupling. What follows in this section addresses any claims of final authority and public standing—not private faith, meaning-making, or personal spiritual practice. Theodicies—even if coherent—are explanatory, not standingconferring.
