[n.47] [n.185] This reflects the same structural principle introduced in the foundational axiom: when standing becomes infinitely asymmetric, the conditions for legitimacy cannot form, regardless of the intentions or capacities attributed to the agent in question.

Nothing can replace agreed, replicable operations when justifying coercive policies in the name of a final authority. Without such operations, standing cannot be generated. This isn’t a refutation of theism. Rather, it specifies why religious claims do not generate public coercive standing under pluralism absent reproducible standing.

Even scriptures of these belief sets are subject to these constraints when used to justify coercive policy. [n.170] Translation is not enough. Translation into public idioms does not replace validation by those exposed, publicly examinable evidence, or leastrestrictive design. [n.47] [n.185] [n.48] This is not a denial that scriptural discourse may function as authoritative within a faith community, as argued by Wolterstorff, but a claim about the conditions under which such authority can acquire public standing to bind nonadherents under pluralism. [n.170]

Private warrant may justify belief, but it does not, by itself, justify public constraint in plural spaces. [n.172] How could it? For public standing, final authority lies with agreed, replicable operations that make claims answerable and rerunnable by competent parties.

When we are first born, there is an obligation to become dependent upon a larger or superior entity for our endurance, or we do simply do not. [n.50] [n.65] We lack the capacity from the onset to ensure our own endurance. Consequently, we have a set of “custodians” or “proxies” which hold this capacity for us until we can establish this endurance ourselves.

These “managerial” roles may take on the form of a mother, father, brother, uncle, aunt, or any person who takes it upon themselves to aid in this endurance. As we grow older, the fallibility of these roles emerges to our consciousness via perception and likewise, we become aware of a dwindling capacity over time among them. We recognize that our parental figures are aging and cannot live forever.

Human beings are highly adaptable and have many forms of coping for change, but the coping mechanisms that emerge for this awareness typically emerge via two general categories - replacement and non-replacement (cf. Feuerbach’s analysis of divinity as the projection of human needs and dependencies). [n.65] This psychological response does not itself confer public standing but helps us identify why humans seek authority in the first place. Though this has application in psychology, psychological aspects of these differences are not something this framework sets out to resolve. The reason these coping mechanisms matter to this framework is not theological, but structural. [n.50]

They are emergent categories of actions within the framework that are then interdependently coupled by virtue of being actions themselves. They explain why agents try to locate an ‘ultimate authority’ even when public standing demands reproducible coupling. When these figures are replaced, historically, many replace the former figure with a deity or deities. Some even replace their highest authority figure pre-emptively with an authority which they give the attribute of being “indefinite” to avoid the need to replace them in the future.

Others follow a path that acknowledges, whether it takes the manifestation of a universe infinitely bouncing toward both the future and the past or one that collapses into nothingness, a void persists. There is no replacement for the final authority in this category. Rather, there simply is no replacement for a final authority at all.

Nonetheless, both categories fall under the same burden for granting public warrant in pluralism because it is a functional property to maintaining it. Consequently, neither the purely atheistic nor the theistic representations of these modes have a lower burden for public standing. [n.47] They are equivalent in structure.

Disagreements among exclusivist, inclusivist, and pluralist theologies do not alter the public rule: without public coupling, none acquires standing to coerce. What is left to consider on the matter except this: The fleeting moments we experience in life are among the rarest of commodities compared to the magnitude of time and space and the autonomy to utilize them is the minimal structural condition for coordinating finite lives without domination.

Social Actors of Faith

Standing via Consent & Coupling

Wherever these deities have actors in the form of religious institutions, socially they play the role of a social actor. The sum of authority given to those who purport to speak or act on behalf of deities is yet limited to those who consent and agree to the bounds of those practitioners and of the deity itself.

Private warrant (belief, meaning, personal conviction) is distinct from public standing (justified authority over others). This framework concerns both to some degree but this domain relies on relational identity-defining couplings of private warrant to establish public standing for social actors of faith.

Ideally, the supposition is that those who consent to the role of the leader socially in these settings do so from a teleological coupling between the practitioner and the ideological constructs of the faith system itself. [n.24] [n.22] It is this supposition of coupling by those who consent to such practitioners which furnishes for them authority by which those practitioners speak and act. Internal authority can be legitimate within a voluntary community while still failing to acquire public standing to bind non-members.

Consequently, practitioners and people of a given faith acquire standing where participation is voluntary. It is the coupling of the collected wills to that of the practitioner themselves under the agreed conditions that said practitioner is actively coupled to and engaged with the ideology which furnishes such standing. Consequently, speech and rituals from individuals who guide or provide these practices are not coercive so long as the autonomy is not infringed and correction is not foreclosed upon. Where exit is enabled, coercion may still exist in the form of social death, loss of family, or even violence in cases of extremism.

While the practitioners themselves are not held to account for this coercion unless they are themselves the actors which generate this coercion, many religious systems have historically entrenched the concept of loyalty so deeply that they become coercive as a consequence and not as a feature inherent to intent. That is, some faith systems lean so heavily on the concept of loyalty that the intrinsic consequence of no longer maintaining loyalty can become coercive, such as with social death. [n.24] [n.118]

Foreclosure of Exit and Loyalty Structures

Where religious upbringing permanently forecloses a child’s future autonomy (education, association, medical choice), standing collapses. [n.21] Under capacityindexed autonomy, such foreclosure represents the indefinite extension of PhaseA dependency, preventing transition toward independent coupling and thereby voiding any claim to legitimate standing. Children in this sense may be exposed to such foundational ideas without foreclosing on autonomy. It is not ideology per se but practices that foreclose exit, diminish agency, or remove future options (education, association, medical choice) that collapse a child’s autonomy.

Where some might find this fit for the group level of “family” or for the role of “parenting” this does not at all resolve issues of coercion or standing. Those are simply justifications for the presence of such coercion amid a lack of standing to do so. These justifications may likewise be evaluated from larger standpoints of community and found to have the same or even potentially different outcome based on scale itself.

Eschatological threats, when deployed to foreclose exit or limit practical refusal, satisfy the structure of autonomy-reducing speech that will be later on discussed and must conform to proportional sizing or forgo public standing. [L.9] [L.11] [L.12] Where practitioners knowingly enforce or reinforce coercive exit costs or loyalty structures, they re-enter culpability by coupling their own role to those outcomes.

Belief systems which foreclose correction and attempt to negate exit by virtue of threats are engaging in coercive tactics whether intent is present or not (this will be presented likewise structurally for political coercion where exit or dissent is foreclosed—as we will discuss later on). This corrects a persistent category error: private warrant for belief does not generate public standing for coercion. Absent agreed operations, riskbearer validation, and least restrictive and proportionate remedies, claims remain private commitments, not public mandates.

Exemptions of conscience are justified only where validated harms are non-inherited by others. In such cases, they still must be narrowed by a non-retributive principle, or they fall into the territory of punitive retribution. [n.5] In cases where these are absent, exemptions fail under the concept of risk-bearer evaluation and remain coercive and culpable. Conversely, proselytizing in public spaces remains permissible persuasion where refusal is real and deception or penalty are absent. [L.11] It crosses into coercion when exit is penalized or autonomy is foreseeably reduced and assigns responsibility to those who deploy it consistent with the foreseeability of its effects.

Wherever that coercion is coupled to intent, the concept of force emerges by definition. Whenever actors or a faith itself lobbies, legislates, or disciplines beyond voluntary leadership, they must pass the same standing gates introduced later as any other actor. Where those tests fail, likewise does the standing and legitimacy of the actor or even the faith system itself.

Religious arbitration retains legitimacy only with voluntariness, real exit, appeal, and a public-law floor. Private tribunals cannot bind non-participants; legitimacy collapses where real exit, appeal, or a public-law floor are absent. [n.185] [n.22] When participants are bound or exit is punitive, standing fails for lack of coupling. What right have these faith systems and practitioners to place upon the agent prescriptions for morality or normative behavior? In as much as there is voluntary consent to the faith system and practitioner itself.

Offense to the sacred, without autonomyreducing harm, cannot justify coercion. Standing tracks autonomy, not offense. [L.12] Offense alone never grounds standing to coerce in this framework; only autonomyrelevant harm does. Civil-religion symbolism must pass minority-exposure standing where symbolism imposes asymmetric burdens on non-adherents, legitimacy requires risk-bearer validation or narrowing based on non-retributive properties. State neutrality toward religion is not hostility but a standing rule: when public symbolism or accommodations impose asymmetric burdens on nonadherents, those exposed must be part of the validation and any measure must be narrowly tailored.

While historically some faiths have systematically broken this faith system, this does not impart further standing or authority to the faith systems themselves or their practitioners. Rather, events like the Spanish Inquisition, the Crusades, the Salem Witch Trials, and other such religious acts of force should not be seen as legitimate or to have standing. [n.85]

This does not strip those actions of power. Instead, it frames those particular actors and that particular faith system at the time as illegitimate to hold public standing. Likewise, authority laundering through corporate forms does not defeat actor-action coupling: institutional shields cannot convert private warrant into public standing nor erase culpability for coercive outcomes. Thus, these entities may retain force and power but likewise retain culpability for coercion where it applies.

Coercion & Force are Not Relevance & Standing

The level of coercive force by which any given group is enabled is not indicative of their relevance and standing for the whole. Standing tracks legitimacy, not magnitude of power. Where coercive authority persists after the conditions that justified constraint have lapsed, capacityindexed autonomy diagnoses this persistence as domination rather than governance. If those criteria were the mechanisms which impart relevance and standing to the whole, then logically the group with the most power would inevitably be the most influential.

If this were the case, would we ever see an exchange of power without one group first becoming more influential? If power and force were the mechanisms which couple these institutions and practitioners to relevance and standing, then it would hold that dictators and authoritarians are not particularly coercive at all. Instead, they would become relevant and gain standing. History shows this is not the case.

In principle, if this is not the case in the sense of state bodies then it is not the case at all, as the populations fall subject to the state by jurisdiction. Religious institutions and social actors who are practitioners of them then are subgroups within the larger group and are subject to the same set of governing dynamics by virtue of being nested inside the same set which is governed by those dynamics.

Some practitioners may suggest that the deity they consent to wields final authority. While the topic of final authority has been addressed, claims of their authority have not. These claims of final authority will be tested later on; however, it should be clearly understood first that actions of the social actor which can be attributed to them should not be conflated with the actions of any such final authority.

Attribution of Acts

Where the social actor acts, their motivation may be prescribed by the foundational values which they impart to their deity, but the act itself is coupled directly to their own selves. When their hand lifts the chalice of wine, it is their hand which lifts it. When they sip the wine, it is their lips which sip. Where there is an assertion of divine execution to describe the acts of a social actor, this is a manipulation of the understanding. [n.15]

The practitioner is creating a decoupling where the action of the practitioner is decoupled from themselves. They replace this coupling with a claim of emergent coupling of the deity as the actor. Such efforts may have the motivation of imparting the authority from that final authority to their own actions or to justify the concept that such deities act, however these explanations do not offer such coupling claims public standing absent non-parochial evidence and repeatable validation.

Likewise, this is true of acts which we observe of the actor in any capacity. Where there are emergent coupling claims to a final authority or deity, this does not pair the act or actor with that deity inherently. The act and actor are interdependently coupled to one another prior to the claim.

A further emergent coupling claim does not have standing to coerce publicly without validation and evidence. Likewise, to assert that the coupling was interdependent to a final authority or deity then demands evidence and validation of the interdependence itself to gain public standing.

Even in nature it is not the deities which pollinate the flowers but the bees and other pollinators. Where practitioners assert that the will of the bees and pollinators are given by a deity or final authority, this does nothing but demand repeatable testing and evidence of the actor. Claim of the act does not give evidence of the actor inherently.

For example, to claim that the light was left on in a room does not presume the particular individual who left them on or who was in the room when it was done. While we can establish that the light being on is a consequence of an action, it does not point directionally to a specific actor. This is likewise true of acts which many have described as “acts of god.” Where there are claims to such effect, the demand is to couple the act to the deity which asserted itself, whether interdependently or emergently. Absent this, it is a failed coupling of the understanding to an act. Acts must have actors. [n.157] [n.173]

Likewise, this failed coupling does not establish a truth claim of the non-existence of any deity. It only denies such claims public standing. Claims that such acts award standing via personal warrant or the private warrant of the institution or social actors agreeing to an emergent coupling in their perceptual frame agreement may have privatized standing within those frames. This does not, however, grant public standing outside of them.

By definition, it cannot rise to the level of public warrant absent public and replicable effects which can be directly coupled to the actor and is left at the level of institution and social actor. This corrects a recurrent category error: private warrant for belief does not produce public standing for coercion absent agreed operations and risk-bearer validation. That is the current public standing for practitioners of these faith systems, regardless of their appeals to authority.

Testing the Relevance of Deity

Autonomy Baseline

Where there is belief in deities there is commonly a belief in a final authority. This authority is often claimed to be situated beyond capacity for perception and deemed to be “above” it in the sense that it takes higher priority. In spite of these claims, the test for this authority stands readily available to any collective of humanity.

Whether norms are divinely commanded or humanly discovered, public coordination in plural space requires answerable, shared procedures. Command alone does not generate public standing. [n.185] [n.47] Again, this is not a claim about divine nonexistence but about structural requirements for public standing.

In the establishment of society, there is a structural necessity for a certain level of autonomy. The mutuality of autonomy of body and of the person is the very conceptual structure that precipitates society. Without this mutuality of autonomy, the individual is free to destroy any sort of component of society they will with no burden of consequence.

For example, say one person in a developed society takes it upon themselves to murder other people. If this agent murders everyone in society, there is demonstrably no society left. The thing that protects against this outcome is not personal value itself or society itself becomes reducible to “might makes right” mentality. In such a case, if the murderer values himself more than everyone in the community, he is right and society fails. It is the autonomy of each individual that sustains the development of society as it gives public warrant which serves to justify and enable it to endure. [n.25] [n.22]

Furthermore, if an agent has desires and if those desires are for themselves and they possess the freedom to exercise their will to this effect they are said to have agency. It follows from this that the agency of each individual is fully intended toward their own will, not that one is destined to achieve their desires but that the full exercise of their will is inclined to this.

If one is to assert their agency toward the will and their own desires, it is reasonable to presume that they do not desire to be stifled in their own ambitions but that they be free to assert their agency to full effect. Thus, it falls on each person to assess the measure of agency which they deem appropriate to achieve their desires and assert their will. If any authority—human or divine—is to bind agents publicly, its justification must satisfy the same structural constraints that preserve agency among plural agents for this reason. The implications of this capacityindexed structure extend beyond religious authority and will reappear wherever claims of protection, expertise, or necessity are used to justify constraint under conditions of asymmetry.

Considering agency from the inverse perspective, if an agent were to act in a way that infringes autonomy, this action concedes that a reduction of autonomy is allowed inherently. Presuming agency, the act itself is autonomy-reducing, and the consent of the actor is interdependently coupled to their action.

Furthermore, the degree to which they have reduced the autonomy of another is inherently the degree to which they have established with their actions that autonomy may be infringed. This is likewise emergent from an interdependent coupling of their action to their own autonomy such that the act itself. Since there is no objective perspective frame to view these autonomies from (as established in About Perspective), the default status is equivalency. Neither of them is “correct” but they both are validated by their own personal warrant as we will see later in About Identity & Psychology.

As this structural coupling applies to autonomy, let us call this reflexive principle the Autonomy-Limitation Reflex Principle (ALRP): Any agent who limits the autonomy of others thereby limits their own justificatory space by the same act. This is not a consequence but an emergent phenomenon of the interdependent coupling of action and agency.

If we align with the categorical imperative from Kant [n.64] and the concept of the ALRP were extended universally, the following maxim applies: “ANY willing violation of autonomy within the scope of culpability from another, whether by action or inaction, is a willing sacrifice of your own autonomy”. This concept preserves standing for any agent or group whose actions do not violate the autonomy of others.

This formulation is not adopted here as a moral law grounded in Kantian rational will, but as a structural analogue: the reflexive constraint that any authority capable of binding others must be capable of binding itself under the same autonomy conditions. Call this the “Maxim of Mutual Autonomy (MOMA)” (cf. Kant’s Humanity Formula).  Think of this as the inter-agent extension maxim of the ALRP.

This maxim applies to any agent or authority that would claim the right to bind others. It is in alignment with the Humanity Formula of Immanuel Kant in that it is consistent with treating each person as an end in themselves: a system that licenses violating other’s agency cannot rationally guarantee one’s own agency. This is likewise represented in Raz’s “autonomy requires adequate options.” 24 MOMA and ALRP demonstrate a mutuality of defining that establishes interdependent coupling, where neither can be specified without reference to the other.

By using this principle and maxim, it is the measure of autonomy which an agent endorses which becomes the measure for their own autonomy. For example, anyone seeking to violate the autonomy of someone’s protected beliefs would then be willingly sacrificing their own autonomy of belief to an equivalent extent for any case where correction or remediation apply.

As will be demonstrated see later in “About Morality” this has distinct implications for motivation to behave in ways which do not infringe autonomy. If one wishes to exert the maximum freedom of their own autonomy, this formulation resolves issues of self-interest by aligning it with non-autonomy reducing outputs, thus allowing self-interest to work for the agent while not collapsing the premises for collective pluralist society. Self-interest is not the problem; autonomy-reducing self-interest is.

Claims of divine authority most often arise precisely where human capacity is asymmetric—during childhood, dependency, fear, or epistemic foreclosure. To distinguish private warrant from public standing in these cases, we require a nonsubjective account of how autonomy scales with capacity. The following principle generalizes across domains but is introduced here because religious authority makes the problem unavoidable.

Capacity-Indexed Autonomy and Conditional Standing

Autonomy cannot be established on a fixed baseline. It is necessarily scalar. Treating autonomy as uniform breaks under dependency. Autonomy arises inherently from the execution of one’s agency. Agency is a compositional coupling of the emergent coupling of the phenomenon of abstraction and the emergent coupling of perception to the individual. It likewise cannot scale across domains when it has a fixed baseline. It forces moralization of incapacity and makes paternalism either over- or under-inclusive. Likewise, it fails in cases of incapacity, dependency, or transition as well as creating ambiguity around paternalism. A fixed autonomy baseline forces either unjustified coercion or unjustified non-intervention.

Understood conditions of endurance (UCE) which present to a group exist prior to preference, culture, or consent. These conditions must be non-normative and domain-general. Autonomy cannot meaningfully exceed or survive outside of the conditions of endurance because not enduring itself presumes a collapse of autonomy as the agent no longer survives. An agent that no longer continues themselves cannot reasonably be said to continue to have agency or autonomy.

Instead, capacity is a scaling variable within the understood conditions of that endurance. Capacity itself is an understanding coupled with a practical ability to maintain such conditions, which becomes publicly observable as a shared perceptual frame to the other individuals within that pluralist community. This makes capacity condition-specific, incremental, and revisable within the scope of those coupled within the same community. Capacity is then not subjective feelings of readiness, declarations of independence, or status-based assumptions but is directly coupled to the understood conditions of endurance where the known elements which are minimally required for survival among the perceptual frame agreement of a group are met by an agent or agents.

Standing in these cases exists only where capacity is insufficient. This is constrained by the ALRP in that any such standing must be conditionspecific, functionally minimal, and temporally bounded. Standing is not authority over persons in these cases. It is provisional authority over conditions.

An agent’s autonomy over a given condition is proportional to their demonstrated capacity to independently meet the understood conditions for endurance for that condition. This is the Capacity-Indexed Autonomy Principle (CIA). Where such capacity is absent, standing may arise for external authority to constrain autonomy only to the extent necessary to secure those conditions and such standing dissolves incrementally as capacity emerges. This is not moralized. It is capacity-indexed, publicly rerunnable, and scalar.

Standing in this light is conditional permission to constrain autonomy only where the agent lacks sufficient capacity to maintain their own conditions of endurance relevant to the condition at issue. The restraints of the ALRP apply conditionally just as well so that agents who infringe autonomy even in these cases are likewise restricted in their own autonomy for such authoritative action over them. Consequently, this standing is temporary, scoped, and self-liquidating. Where this authority is exceeded communities colloquially recognize these overreaches as “abusive” within their scope.

The Capacity-Autonomy Gradient

Autonomy and capacity are interdependently coupled in such a way that capacity is required for the execution and recognition of autonomy. This framework identifies three distinct phases in this gradient of transition. These are the Capacity-Autonomy Gradient Phases (CAGP), and the phases are as follows:

Phase A – Low Capacity / High Reliance

Agents are coupled to a system which manages understood conditions for endurance

Standing to constrain exists

Constraints must be:

Minimal

Protective

Non-Substitutive

Non-expansive

Phase B – Transitional Capacity

Capacity increasing

Standing begins to contract

System acquires positive obligations:

Provide Understanding

Transparency

Repair (as will be seen with the sincere repair checklist later on)

Failure to support transition is equal to structural illegitimacy – it is prima facie evidence of that illegitimacy

Phase C – Independent Coupling to the understood conditions of endurance for the pluralist society

Agent maintains conditions independently

Standing for external coercion collapses

Continued constraint becomes domination

The outcome of this gradient is that emancipation is a structurally necessary option which preserves alternatives and exit for those who are dominated before reaching what a society has set as legal ages for independent evaluation of these conditions. Transition to autonomy is done on a condition-by-condition basis in these cases and is a public operation. Subjectivity in these cases is insufficient to establish the criteria for these conditions.

Transition criteria must be non-parochial, evidence-based, and rerunnable. Autonomy is demonstrated, not asserted. It emerges structurally when these criteria emerge themselves within the PFA of a given pluralist society so that the PFA itself is what validates it rather than internalized versions or subjective viewpoints.

Any system that suppresses understanding or capacity in order to preserve its own standing to coerce in these cases is structurally illegitimate. This is a form of operational capture. This includes welfare traps, blocking skill acquisition, obscuring evidence, educational gatekeeping, platform dark patterns, carceral incapacitation, or epistemic opacity. No moral accusation is required in these cases. This is a structural diagnostic.

Freedom in this framework is not tantamount to a feeling or preference. It is not an asserted right or a declaration. It is publicly rerunnable independent coupling to the understood conditions of endurance so that freedom itself is not subjective. It is a demonstration of independence from coercive maintenance. This is in alignment with non-domination in pluralist society and public rerunnability.

Minimally autonomy reduction in these phases must be condition-specific, capacity-indexed, and self-liquidating. This is not only true in the case of children but of varying physical capabilities so that pluralist society not providing for the means for those with disabilities in public space becomes operational capture of their capacity to demonstrate such independence. This is diagnosed structurally rather than morally.

Who is Bound by Autonomy?

What we create with this system is a binding on that of the human race and not on that of any of their deities or final authorities. The result of this concept applied universally is that, should no actions of humanity be attributed to these deities, we are free to evaluate the hand of their gods and final authorities based solely on their own ability to act. For all which do not interface with this autonomy, the default state of maintaining universal autonomy is left intact and there is no discord between them and the pluralist collective.

Granting that some may not be ready to accept the coping mechanisms without a final authority, these final authorities may serve to assist them as a coping mechanism of replacement while not harming the whole of society. While we do not bind the divine causally, if a divine command cannot be interdependently or emergently coupled in such a way that it is capable of rendering itself relevant to the public, then such commands do not inherit standing for public coercion. Where such claims are made, non-parochial evidence is the minimum burden to gain public relevance.

Cause for Action

If they are capable of rendering those demands as relevant then I (and presumably others) willingly stand, ready to face them head-on and demand answers to their inattentiveness to human need and the structural demand for autonomy within society. Let them show themselves and, if they must punish anyone, let them punish those of us willing to force them into the light. If agreed operations exclude human intervention and still register a replicable effect, that effect enters ordinary causal adjudication. It stands or falls like any other cause. [n.2] [n.1]

Nietzsche may have cautioned against the dangers of nihilism but, unless these final authorities choose to interact with us on their own volition or we require the coping mechanism, there has yet to be reproducible non-parochial evidence of any coupling between agent and action on their behalf. These observations reduce the risks of nihilism present in a loss of authority, disorientation, or fear of consequence, as autonomy itself regards care, fairness, non-domination, and all individualized faculties which one might assert from their own perception.

Autonomy is defended structurally and pragmatically by pluralist groups in this framework. It minimizes domination across plural ends and enables error-correction via feedback, rather than by appealing to stance-independent moral facts. This autonomy furthermore scales to the collective, whereby another form of autonomy is formed among the collected and agreed perceptions of the group. While this logically is frail to argumentum ad populum, for the structure of that collective society, this is the operational imperative by which it sustains itself.

While the moral value of the endurance of society is not imposed here, this autonomy is structurally necessary to that endurance, whether moral or not. Those who do not believe in an obligation for society to endure place themselves in normative conflict with those who do. The latter are then committed by their own stance to favor and reinforce practices that sustain that endurance and to withhold cooperation or even resist practices that do not.

Authority, orientation, and value creation are rooted directly in the interdependent coupling of our perceptions to our experience and not to some unknown reality or final authority. Perception is constructed under constraint; stimuli are necessary but never sufficient explanations for all of perception. The cure for oppressive final authority is for a few brave human beings to challenge them solely on their own merits. Those with the will to stand against them find their drive embedded in the decoupling of their perceptions of that frame. There will be no challenge in return because there are no established instances of non-parochial evidence which are open to repeatable testing to validate any such actions or claims from them. This absence has rendered them irrelevant as well.

Call to Action

Miracles, Testimony & Divine Hiddenness

“You assume that divine action must be perceptible” some may say. “There are many testimonies where others have claimed to have perception of a deity acting!” To this I reply that any action uncoupled from perception is already irrelevant to that frame. If any final authority has made themselves objectively perceivable, then furnish such stimuli to our perception so it may be established as non-parochial evidence, test it, and establish its coupling among the public.

Until then, miracle claims are testimonial. They do not produce publicly rerunnable non-parochial evidence and thus do not override the prior established interdependent coupling of autonomy and agent. Consequently, testimony alone does not inherently trigger standing. It triggers investigation. [n.14] [n.15]

Some traditions centralize miracle evaluation to internal clerical processes. Such internal validation may guide adherents but does not substitute for public standing. Religious experience may ground private warrant, but it does not itself create public authority absent repeated and testable non-parochial evidence. [n.2]

Importantly, institutionally religious validation does not concede any interdependent or emergent coupling to the individuals who believe in this specific faith any more than they have coupled themselves as believers to those practitioners. In order for the miracle claims and testimony to interdependently couple with the group itself, the non-parochial evidence must be viewable to those who wish to couple to it.

Consequently, limiting of this evidence to the practitioners may interdependently couple it correspondingly to those clergy members, but the remaining coupling between them and the congregation is of a different type. Coupling between practitioners and the congregation is both teleological and relational identity-defining coupling. This does not speak to the acts of a final authority.

Even if their imperceivable acts were to form a chain or stack into recognizable outcomes of perception, are they not then limited by our capacity? What of our own capacity to manipulate the smaller values of our own perceptions? Divine hiddenness does not refute private belief, but it is intrinsically defeating of public standing. Absent public, repeatable, non-parochial evidence, claims to final authority cannot bind plural publics without passing a standing to coerce evaluation. [n.47]

Final Authority via Coupled Claims

Practically speaking, if God creates the cherry we create cherry pie. If God makes a poison in alcohol, we drink it for pleasure. If such claims are true, then God hides while we prepare an Old Fashioned from his cherries and alcohol. If God has been so careless and sheepish as to hide perception of himself from our capacities, then mankind waits, unchallenged, in refusal of those decoupled claims.

If any punishment occurs in a way that couples perceptually, it becomes repeatable non-parochial evidence which may serve to establish a proper coupling of the acts to the actor. If alleged non-public action yields public, replicable effects further on, it then gains standing as a cause to humanity. Likewise, should a deity ever couple publicly and reproducibly with human perception, such effects would engage ordinary causal adjudication like any other. Until then, it has no such standing.

What becomes visible here is not a conclusion about belief, but a boundary on authority. Claims of divine or final authority do not fail because they are false, insincere, or psychologically motivated; they fail when they seek to bind others while exempting themselves from the conditions of public coupling, correction, and accountability. This is not a restriction uniquely applied to religion, but the same structural constraint that governs every claim to rule or command under plural conditions. Where participation is voluntary and exit remains real, religious authority may legitimately organize meaning, practice, and internal life.

Where it asserts jurisdiction beyond that scope through threat, loyalty enforcement, or insulation from correction, it becomes a claim whose force depends on obedience rather than standing. Even if belief grants private warrant, public standing still requires non-parochial evidence and downstream reproducible effects; otherwise, it remains a private commitment. [n.2] [n.15] Insofar as public standing and authority are concerned, as Nietzsche declared, God is dead. [n.58] Peace exists only where dissent remains possible, safe, and nonpunitive — even if no one ultimately chooses it.

IV — About Morality

Purpose: This section examines how the coupling-standing-legitimacy engine operates within the domain of morality and how misidentification of coupling produces characteristic features of standing in this domain. This framework will not rely on metaphysics to derive a code of conduct. Rather, it sets out to define morality using the same engine and structural tools which apply across domains such that morality of the individual may take whichever form the agent aligns with while maintaining operational imperatives among their collective group to retain moral standing.

Orientation

What This Chapter Is and Is Not

This chapter is concerned with how moral claims operate. It addresses how they arise, how they are framed, and how they are interpreted. Rather than prescribing moral code, morality here is treated as a communicative and relevance-driven phenomenon. In this framework it does not assert universal truths. [n.174]

This chapter orients the reader to how morality functions within a relevancebased framework. It is a clarification of terms and not a defense of a moral system. It operates as an analytic lens for understanding how moral claims function, communicate, and gain authority. This chapter becomes a bridge between descriptive reality and normative language.

This is not a moral manifesto. The framework takes neither a theistic nor atheistic viewpoint as it is not a religious, ideological, or partisan doctrine. It is not a comprehensive survey of moral philosophy or an attempt to resolve moral disagreement.

Readers should not expect a final answer to what is right and wrong form this chapter. It does not attempt to solve the moral disputes themselves but makes clearer why such disputes persist and how moral language functions in pluralist societal structures.

Expectations

The topic of morality is oftentimes uncomfortable. Readers should be well prepared for precision over comfort in this chapter. Definitions may differ from common usage as they are, in this framework, tackled from the standpoint of structure rather than value systems.

Consequently, readers should expect moral language to be treated analytically, not reverently. As a result of this treatment, tension between institutions and the framework are likely to arise for many readers. Some definitions may feel unfamiliar or even counterintuitive. This is intentional. Familiar moral language often conceals unstated assumptions about authority, universality, and relevance.

The author here assumes that the reader is willing to temporarily suspend inherited moral frameworks. The framework presumes that readers are open to examining morality as a tool rather than merely belief. It should be understood that this framework stands as critique and not dismissal. To engage the chapter fully, the reader must be willing to treat morality not as a sacred inheritance but as a system that can be examined, translated, and understood in functional terms.

Translations

The function of translations in this chapter is to map common moral language into relevance-based terms. This serves to reduce ambiguity and emotional loading and front loading. It helps distinguish moral signal from moral content. Throughout this chapter, familiar moral terms will be translated into relevance-oriented descriptions. While these translations are not meant to strip morality of meaning, they strive to expose the mechanisms by which meaning is assigned.

Translations in this chapter are functional, not rhetorical. They describe what moral statements do, not what they claim. [n.66] Multiple translations may apply depending on context. A single moral statement may perform several functions simultaneously. It may signal group membership, enforce norms, express value, and assert authority all at the same time. Translation makes these functions visible.

Translation Table

Good: Constructive coupling that preserves or enhances autonomy, capacity, or collective endurance at the relevant scale.

Evil: Destructive or degenerative coupling that undermines autonomy, capacity, or collective endurance at the relevant scale.

Right: An action or omission that remains permissible under autonomy constraints and does not violate standing within shared social space.

Wrong: An action or omission that emergently or interdependently couples to an autonomyimpairing outcome under conditions of sufficient agency and capacity.

Moral Claim: A relevance assertion about how actions, omissions, or practices should be constrained or permitted within shared coordination.

Moral Authority: The structural constraint that arises from the requirements of sustained interaction among autonomous agents, not an externally imposed mandate.

Moral Community: The set of agents or entities susceptible to autonomyrelevant coupling and therefore relevant to standing evaluations, whether directly or indirectly.

Responsibility: The condition in which an agent’s capacities, agency, and cognitive reach are sufficiently engaged such that their actions couple to consequences.

Culpability: Responsibility plus attribution and viable alternatives; the condition under which an agent may be held answerable for a wrong.

Excuse: The absence or impairment of capacity, agency, or cognitive reach sufficient to decouple culpability from an agent while wrongness may persist.

Blame: The attribution of responsibility that carries standing to hold an agent to account, constrained by answerability and proportionality.

Forgiveness: The private release of moral claim by an offended party, without automatic public standing or cancellation of social consequences.

Punishment: A social instrument for maintaining order and safety, justified only within a ceiling set by the violation and narrowed by proportional prescription.

Repair: The restoration of moral agency through acknowledgment, concrete remediation, and futurefacing constraints (SRC3), distinct from mere compliance.

Correction: External constraint applied to neutralize immediate risk or harm, capable of restoring behavior but not moral agency.

Independently Emergent Wrong (IEW): A structurally produced autonomyimpairing outcome that persists without individual intent or blame and calls for repair rather than punishment.

SelfHarm: An action that diminishes the agent’s own autonomy and undermines the structural conditions of agency, wrong without necessarily licensing external coercion.

Sacrifice: A voluntary, scalepreserving action in which an agent knowingly accepts prudential cost to preserve or enhance collective autonomy.

Moral Luck: Outcome variation that alters repair or consequence prescription without altering the structural classification of wrongness or responsibility.

Standing: The legitimacy of a claim, judgment, or response to bind others, grounded in coupling, autonomy constraints, and public answerability.

Standing to Coerce (STC5): The fivegate test determining whether coercive response is legitimate: riskinheritance & validation, public coupling of evidence, NRPP fit, alternatives considered, and offramps.

NonRetributive Proportionality Principle (NRPP): The requirement that any response be the least autonomyreducing means sufficient to neutralize validated harm.

Ceiling vs. Prescription: The distinction between the maximum justified response set by a violation and the narrower action actually warranted under proportional constraint.

Moral Remainder: Residual obligation and justified regret that persists after all avoidable wrongs are avoided and culpable parties have acted.

Supererogatory: Actions that enhance autonomy or endurance beyond obligation and therefore warrant praise but not coercion.

SelfInterest: An agent’s pursuit of their own autonomy and flourishing, structurally aligned with collective endurance when not autonomyreducing to others.

Selfishness: Preference for prudential gain that foreseeably undermines collective autonomy or endurance.

Moral Reliability: Reproducible coupling between an agent’s behavior and shared moral expectations under agreed operations.

Moral Integrity: Consistent internal coupling of will and action to the structural conditions of moral good across contexts.

Plural Value Conflict: A situation in which multiple moral goods cannot be jointly satisfied due to incompatible or dependent couplings.

Plural Obligation Conflict: A situation in which multiple duties cannot be jointly fulfilled, making some wrongs unavoidable.

Scale Conflict: A conflict in which preservation of autonomy at one scale undermines autonomy at another.

Tragic Conflict: A condition of moral overdetermination under scarcity where every available option produces autonomyimpairing harm.

Overlapping Axes of Morality

Origins of Morality

If we have declared that God is dead, then what can be said about the state of good and evil? [n.58] Take a structural and metaethical accounting of this, not prescribing values but giving a description of how valuation operates under the conditions of pluralism (Like Blackburn’s quasirealism, this view preserves moral practice without metaphysical realism, but grounds constraint structurally rather than expressively). Like quasirealism, this framework preserves moral practice without metaphysical truth makers, but unlike it, standing is constrained structurally rather than expressively. [n.12]

Where some have held that they were objective standpoints, others have held that they are merely spooks, as Stirner argues. [n.57] With God dead, morality releases its grip on objectivity, but what remains are the practices that we have rooted in motivation, perception, and consequence. [n.11] [n.12]

Hume reduces this to an idea of vice and virtue as approval or denial and yet, is it not possible for the human mind to be mistaken or to have not taken full account of the vice or virtue values which might accompany another thing or event? Even Hume’s sentimentalist account implicitly presupposes this coupling [n.56] as sentiment points to coupling but is not sufficient to establish public standing. His ‘virtues’ are treated here as stable reliability couplings—patterns of integrity and repair—rather than metaphysical excellences. Correspondingly, mistakes may emerge.

As the outcome of a thing or event is yet unrealized to the perception, how is it possible that it be designated as “good?” It is precisely the uncoupled orientation to the perception of outcome while simultaneously being coupled to the values of the perceiver which affords such mistaken notions and unawareness.

Where the perceiver couples their perception of a thing or event to their values without coupling an outcome to it they may judge it as “good” or “bad” already. So, it is the coupling of the thing and event to the value system of the perceiver itself which furnishes this capacity and not the outcome of the thing or event itself.

What replaces objectivity in morality is not arbitrary designations of “good” or “evil” but constraint: moral judgments remain corrigible insofar as they are coupled to their consequences, autonomy, and shared human capacities. Where some theories aim to found morality in will, reasons, or fitness, this framework filters moral claims for public standing; it neither competes nor presupposes any such foundations.

While this author aligns with the Nietzschean formulation of will, that is not requisite for this framework. Comparisons align between his formulation and this framework containing layers, constraints, and the emergent accounts of agency. Where Nietzsche structures the will as emergent dependent on drives which are not chosen, a hierarchy which can be strengthened, weakened, or reordered, interpretation which has influence, and actions which are constrained - this framework aligns in structure.

Despite this similarity, this framework is compatible with multiple free-will positions because it grounds responsibility in capacities and coupling. It does not presuppose any formulation of will or freedom and it is not contra-causal freedom. This framework is then neither realism nor pure emotivism but is constraint-based normativity under pluralism. What remains is a need to distinguish the structural classification of actions from their evaluative classifications.

Good & Evil, Right & Wrong

This framework distinctly keeps two separate dimensions of evaluation as they regard actions. Right and Wrong operate on a constraint axis. They concern permissibility and standing. An act is wrong when it couples to an autonomyimpairing outcome under conditions where agency and capacity are sufficiently engaged. As formalized earlier under capacityindexed autonomy, the phrase “sufficiently engaged” is not rhetorical but structural.

Moral wrongness may arise whenever autonomyimpairing coupling occurs, but responsibility and culpability depend on the degree to which an agent possessed the capacity to understand, avoid, or remediate that coupling. [n.207] Wrongness does not scale with capacity; culpability does. This classification answers the question: May this act be permitted, excused, blamed, corrected, or constrained within shared social space? Right and wrong govern justification, responsibility, culpability, and standing to coerce.

Good and Evil operate on a value axis. They concern constructive or destructive contribution to flourishing and endurance. An act is good when its coupling is constructive—preserving or enhancing autonomy, capacity, or collective endurance at the relevant scale. An act is evil when its coupling is destructive or degenerative of those conditions. This classification answers the question: Is this act admirable, aspirational, corrosive, or worthy of reverence or condemnation?

These axes intersect but do not collapse into one another. Not all wrong acts are evil, and not all right acts are good. Tragic necessity, sacrifice, and moral remainder arise precisely where these axes diverge, while autonomy continues to function as the structural constraint constitutive of agency.

Euthyphro & Metaphysical Neutrality

How does this stance on morality apply to Euthyphro? [n.55] We have not asserted any state of morality having grounding or objectivity. This framework specifies a moral architecture that pluralist communities can treat as operationally necessary.

Whether these constraints merely structure our practices or also track some stanceindependent moral reality is a metaphysical question this framework does not need to settle. We encounter morality through practices, judgments, and their consequences; this framework specifies the constraints those practices must satisfy for public standing.

As stated in the Introduction, this framework does not aim to resolve metaphysical debates about moral realism. It brackets grounding questions unless they yield publicly answerable differences in practice.

Moral Authority as Structural Constraint

How Autonomy Binds

Moral authority in this framework is not imposed from outside but arises from the structural requirements of sustained interaction among autonomous agents. These constraints are not optional: they are the conditions for any agent to maintain standing within a shared world.

It is the minimal condition of mutual autonomy for coordination and non-domination across plural ends or groups and provides the structural basis for reciprocal justification, mutual answerability, and fair treatment. A simple structural argument links coordination to autonomy:

Coordination inherently demands agents and agency.

Agency is inherently bound to a minimal volume of autonomy.

Standing depends on preserving the conditions of agency.

Therefore, autonomy functions as the minimal non-domination constraint for any shared world.

Community Membership

What constitutes membership to these groups? Membership in the moral community corresponds to the capacity to be affected by autonomy-related couplings and to participate in standing relations including children, cognitively impaired adults, AI, animals, collectives, institutions, and peoples of all variant types. [n.61] [n.62] Participation may be direct (through reasoning or agency) or indirect (through being a bearer of autonomy-related effects).

Membership and standing are not equivalent in this framework. Moral community membership determines relevance via susceptibility to autonomy-impact. Standing regards the ability to impose claims on others. Community membership establishes relevance whereas standing scales with capacity, role, and exposure. Capacityindexed autonomy applies to individual agents, collectives, and institutions alike, with capacity assessed relative to role, scale, and control over relevant conditions.

Consequentially Constrained Social Normativity (CCSN)

From the frame of these constraints—consequence, autonomy, capacity, shared experience—judgments lose objectivity and gain constraints. [n.2] [n.5] For intersubjectively reproducible moral practices stabilized by their consequences for autonomy and group endurance, the term Consequentially Constrained Social Normativity (CCSN) applies. CCSN is not a source of standing but a downstream stabilization of judgments that have already passed coupling, autonomy, and consequence constraints. [n.5] [n.2]

That is—this framework yields outputs of standing constraints, not metaphysical primitives, despite what some may read as “rights-like protections.” They are the structural outputs of the framework itself—a stability pattern that emerges from autonomy constraints—rather than protections forcefully adhered to the system, consequentialism, or a maximizing calculus.

Good and Evil are then neither objective nor merely subject to the whims of the perceiver. Rather, they are judgments constrained in a causal, normative, and practical sense. The individual can make moral judgment based on the causal outcome for themselves just as the group can. As a matter of operational imperative, this perspective and coupling with stimuli take on new evaluations predicated on the establishment of newly understood social groups, however this does not necessarily reduce or modify any subgroups contained within the newly established groups.

Likewise, they may take a normative approach as they assert autonomy for a new and different endgame. In this frame, variation enters. If an agent who perceives does not hold the causal or normative value for society, practical moral judgments are bound differently than for those who do.

Those who don’t value society are not internally bound by its morality; however, the consequentially constrained social normativity of society is fixed by the commitments (and constrained by reciprocal justification, mutual recognition, and fairness) of those that favor the endurance of society. The internal endorsement of the individual is not an exemption from external constraint or consequence. Society’s commitment to favor and reinforce practices that sustain that endurance and to withhold cooperation and resist practices that do not is the social normativity of their stance.

Moral Wrongness

Autonomy-Impairing Coupling

What then constitutes something being morally ‘wrong’ within this framework? A moral wrong occurs when an action or omission emergently or interdependently couples to an autonomy-impairing outcome under conditions where agency and capacity were sufficiently engaged. Wrongness is not inherent to the act but emerges from autonomy-relevant coupling so that, in this framework, autonomy is a structural condition of agency rather than preference. Moral wrongness, particularly in emergent harms, arises most clearly when the symmetry condition between agents breaks down, even absent deliberate domination.

A collapse of standing is not identical to the presence of wrongdoing. Standing concerns legitimacy—who may bind, constrain, or enforce—not whether an outcome is morally bad, regrettable, or harmful. Wrongs may exist without standing failures, and standing may collapse in the absence of culpable wrongdoing.

This distinction matters because the framework does not treat moral judgment as sufficient to authorize coercion. Moral evaluation may explain why an outcome is tragic or unjust, but standing determines whether constraint, enforcement, or intervention is permissible without domination.

It applies reflexively to the agent as well. Thus, actions that undermine one’s own capacity, cognition, or agency (including self-harm) do not express autonomy but diminish it and therefore cannot be justified by autonomy-based reasoning. Such actions are morally wrong in the structural sense—they diminish the agent’s own autonomy and therefore undermine the very condition of agency. (cf. Feinberg, Harm to Self, on the contours of selfregarding harm and paternalism.) However, because they do not violate the autonomy of others, they do not generate the same standing to impose external correction. Rather, the tradition for evaluation of standing in this sense finds basis in the evaluation of the capacity of the agent themselves.

Terminal Illness & Self-Harm

In a practical sense, terminally ill patients who retain all of the conditions for agency may elect for their own controlled determination for their end of life. In terminal illness, the trajectory of decline is already coupled to the agent; the outcome is not a chosen harm but an inevitable one. To retain autonomy in those cases, such actions are considered justified when those rare conditions are met.

Thus, end-of-life autonomy is not “harm” but is instead a reorientation of agency within the trajectory of inevitable decline. (cf. Raz’s account of autonomy as dependent on adequate options and capacities.) Likewise, in cases where self-harm is present, but capacity is lacking, there is no coupling between the agent and the outcome. In both cases, agency for the individual existed in a stifled or altogether absent state.

These are often IEW cases: wrongness persists, blame does not. This provides for situational and conditional outcomes of morality such as accidents where the act itself is always structurally wrong but the conditions surrounding such acts inform of culpability. Consequently, the framework structurally defines true accidents as IEW cases.

Responsibility, Attribution & Culpability

Origins & Attribution of Responsibility and Culpability

Within this framework, standing, responsibility, and culpability are distinct. Standing concerns whether a claim or response may be publicly asserted. Responsibility concerns whether an agent’s capacities were engaged. Culpability concerns whether an agent’s action or omission is appropriately attributable given those capacities.

Responsibility itself requires capacity, agency, and cognitive reach. [n.4] [n.5] Within this framework, these requirements are governed by capacityindexed autonomy: responsibility arises only to the extent that an agent can independently sustain the relevant conditions of agency and endurance. Where capacity is partial, responsibility is partial; where capacity is absent, responsibility fails even though structural wrongness may persist.

Culpability requires responsibility, attribution, and viable alternatives. The latter term being dependent upon the former is structurally necessary both logically and for the maintenance of agency itself. Conflating these terms produces illegitimate coercion.

In our variant groups of society, individuals assert not only differing degrees of importance or rank but, along with them, levels of responsibility. While objectivists assert that responsibility is bound to an objective moral law as held by a final authority, with God dead, how can the distribution of responsibility be defined?

Responsibility does not arise from divine command, the metaphysics of free will, or from an objective moral law. (cf. Hart, Punishment and Responsibility, on capacity, knowledge, and excuse.) (cf. Fischer & Ravizza, Responsibility and Control, on reasonsresponsiveness.) Responsibility applies wherever there is an awareness of the concepts which generate it: capacity, agency, and cognitive ability. [n.4] [n.5]

Coupling Responsibility and Culpability

An agent is morally responsible to the extent that their action couples to consequences, the consequences were within their perceptual and cognitive reach, and their autonomy was engaged. The burden is upon the agent to willfully engage their faculties and consider moral responsibility. This is distinct from the inaction of the agent to engage in those considerations, as this inaction itself, where the criteria for responsibility apply and are fully enabled, is their burden.

An agent which rejects the consideration of the extents of their actions after the concepts have been made aware to them does nothing to reject their moral responsibility and where those conditions are fully enabled, their sustained coupling to this responsibility implies culpability. In this framework, Akrasia and compulsion are treated as capacity modulators: wrongness may persist while culpability scales down.

Where the concepts which create moral responsibility are externally stifled or are absent, we may rely back on our maxim, “ANY willing violation of autonomy within the scope of culpability from another, whether by action or inaction, is a willing sacrifice of your own autonomy.” Likewise, where these violations occur which infringe the capacity, agency, or cognitive ability, the culpability is then assumed by the offender.

Collective Responsibility & Culpability

When then are collectives actually responsible or blameworthy? Where the collective is presented with options to act as a collective there also emerges a collective criterion set by which this can be evaluated

Decision procedure(s) exist(s)

Role accountability exists

Foreseeability at the institutional level

Repair pathway exists

In order for the collective to reply, there must be a mechanism by which the collective can make such a decision to reply. Once this exists there must be a level of accountability for roles within the group. Whether the obligation is on the whole of the collective itself as a role of operationally imperative to its own survival may be sufficient. The role of the community itself plays a part.

Collective culpability is presumptively in-scope when (1) the collective has a decision procedure, (2) roles are accountable, (3) foreseeable harms are trackable at the institutional level, and (4) repair mechanisms exist and are ignored. Without this, how could repair pathways be known? Consequently, where communities meet these criteria and the collective itself refuses to act, this framework renders this as a failure of the collective itself and makes the community blameworthy.

Exceptions from Culpability

Absent Faculties & Intervention

Where capacity, agency, and cognitive ability to furnish consequence are absent, culpability for moral failure is absent; where they are present it remains. Where attribution cannot accompany culpability, it is the moral responsibility of the collective itself to engage remediation. (cf. Arendt on responsibility as a political and relational concept rather than a metaphysical one.)

Collective responsibility applies when the collective has control of the conditions, benefits from the structure, or can implement effective repair. [n.20] [n.60] This also applies to conditions of self-harm. When self-harm emerges within the group, it is the moral responsibility of the collective to engage in the assessment of culpability for this act and to engage in whatever remediation is justified within that evaluation. Intervention is then justified only when capacity/agency is impaired, and risk-bearers include the agent’s future self or dependents (or when immediate danger prevents autonomous choice). Such interventions are justified only under PhaseA conditions of capacityindexed autonomy and must contract as capacity is restored; otherwise, they constitute domination rather than care.

Moral Luck

Where some assert moral luck, this framework considers this to be only a manifestation of remediation prescription. [n.59] Should the outcome of a given action be given sole discretion as to the moral disposition of the act alone? No.

Responsibility has already arisen from the presence of the conditions which create it. Likewise, their burden to consider these conditions couples them to that responsibility. Inherently, these actions are attributable to them then as culpability. Luck in this capacity does not change agency, capacity, or reach.

Outcomes can change the repair or punishment prescription as we will see further on, but this is not a definite coupling to a ceiling. Luck is then only descriptive here of the chance that one may have taken actions which impede autonomy. The burden remained upon them to consider these outcomes from the onset of their actions.

The actions themselves, being no more or less morally good or bad intrinsically, do not yield any varying degree of morality. The wrongness classification remains fixed by autonomyimpairing coupling and foreseeability; what changes with luck is typically the downstream repair and riskmanagement prescription.

Independently Emergent Wrongs (IEW)

Diverging of the Moral Evaluation Axes

When the value axis and the constraint axis diverge upon an action rather than intersect, wrongness may persist even where culpability fails. Call this an Independently Emergent Wrong (IEW). An Independently Emergent Wrong (IEW) is a wrong that arises from autonomyimpairing coupling within a shared normative structure even when no agent is culpable, no intention is present, or attribution fails. IEWs are not failures of incentives, aggregation, or coordination efficiency; they are legitimacy failures that persist even when systems function as designed.

They overlap with what is often described as wrongdoing without blameworthiness (wrongness without fault) [n.59] and with faultless wrongdoing or moral remainder in tragic cases, but it is not restricted to epistemic excuse or exceptional dilemmas. Moral remainder and wrongness without fault being met with attributed blame or means of correction is, in this framework, definitively coercive as there is implicit in the description no coupling which justifies those ends.

IEW likewise resembles accounts of structural injustice and Arendtstyle responsibility for systemic conditions [n.60] [n.20], yet it is not limited to institutional injustice alone; it is defined by the structural wrongness classification itself—a publicly relevant autonomyimpairing failure that can persist without blameworthiness and without generating standing to coerce. In this framework, IEW marks a moral failure condition that calls for repair, redesign, or acknowledgment where possible, while keeping culpability, punishment, and public coercion as further questions subject to separate standing constraints.

Capacity, IEWs, and the Limits of Moral Attribution

IEWs arise independently of agent culpability. Capacity-Indexed Autonomy (CIA) provides the structural reason for this. It explains how harm can emerge where no agent had sufficient capacity. This does not mean that no harm has happened and is not a justification to remove repair or redesign.

It is instead a lack of justification for blame or culpability in these cases. Coercion fails standing without capacity because culpability cannot be structurally present in this case. This same principle will be repeated in later institutional repair and other domains so that IEWs are inevitable rather than simply stipulated.

Moral Goodness, Sacrifice, and Praise

Moral Goods

A morally good action is any positive, constructive action whose coupling preserves autonomy at relevant scale. While not an exhaustive accounting, two examples of constructive actions would be actions which enhance autonomy or actions which support endurance while preserving autonomy. This is what is structurally good within this framework.

Collective recognition of goodness occurs when constructive coupling is publicly assessable under agreed operations and aligns with UCE. In the personal sense, for those who have agency, the coupling of those same qualities to the individual constitutes a different scale of good so that there is what is good “for the individual” and what is good “for the group” and they necessarily diverge as these couplings diverge by the same pattern.

Scalar Variants of Moral Goods

With these distinctions there emerges two variants of what is morally good: Collective Good and Prudential Good. Prudential goods are not inherently selfishness and collective goods are not inherently moral realism—both are scale-relative classifications. Some collective goods may require sacrifice for the collective while prudential goods, by definition, enhance the individual’s autonomy overall and in the long-term do not require net sacrifice of individual flourishing or autonomy.

An individual may, in exchange for a long-term gain or upon realizing a net negative to themselves by use of their own autonomy, make a sacrifice of autonomy. An example of this would be an individual joining the military at the cost of their own autonomy. The individual exchanges the short-term autonomy for a long-term gain of benefits as a sacrifice to produce the positive and constructive outcome at the prudential level. The autonomy cost is voluntary, reversible over time, and offset by a long-term prudential gain, so the prudential good remains intact.

Likewise, this may also be seen as a collective good as the premise of military service is an implicit sacrifice for the collective to produce the positive and constructive outcome of security while preserving the autonomy of the citizenry. In this case, a single action is capable of taking on multiple frames while also being capable of sacrificing to achieve the end goals.

Nevertheless, the set of collective goods is larger than the set of prudential goods because the domain of potential benefit is broader at the collective scale than at the prudential scale, given the number of agents whose autonomy or endurance may be supported. Collective goods may exceed prudential goods because they may impose cost on the agent. Thus, all prudential goods are morally good, but not all collective moral goods are prudentially good. Nevertheless, collective good remains constrained by autonomy by virtue of also belonging to the structure.

Consequently, all morally good actions preserve autonomy overall relative to their scale, even if cost or sacrifice is involved for the agent. For example, a firefighter sacrificing their own life to save others is a collective moral good but a prudential moral wrong. In this case, there is no violation of autonomy as the firefighter chooses to use their personal autonomy and agency by voluntarily attributing more weight to the collective moral good of preserving autonomy at the group scale than the prudential moral cost of self-directed loss and so accepts this risk. In such a case, harm which comes to individuals who make these sacrifices as a cost is not attributed to them as “self-harm” or a moral wrong.

Self-Interest, Selfishness, and Moral Character

Distinguishing Self-Harm from Sacrifice

Self-harm requires autonomy-impairing coupling; sacrifice does not. Sacrifice bears a prudential cost; self-harm negates the agent’s structural conditions for agency. It is always voluntary, scale-preserving, and never licenses violating the autonomy of another.

As we have defined the collective moral good as belonging to a larger set which outweighs the prudential moral set, these acts which come at the cost of harm are re-labeled using this term within that collective and historically have held a place of reverence among people groups. This reverence emerges from the coupling of the recognition of the group to an understanding of the cost and the internalized will of those who endure those costs.

Selfishness

Where there is a collective moral good which abides the UCE and poses no risk to prudential good and the agent selects actions which prefer prudential good in an attempt to maximize personal net benefit to the detriment of others, the collective refers to such actions as “selfish.”

Self-interest which does not rise to the level of creating a moral wrong and is not “selfishness” because it does not carry culpability and it is not the obligation of the individual to actualize every collective good which presents to them. Where selfish acts do create a moral wrong, the collective casts judgment upon such acts and actors, with historically more condemnation coupling correspondingly to the level of harm which may have been avoided and the level of culpability of the agent who may have avoided it.

Moral Reliability and Integrity

The judgment of society upon selfish acts which carry no culpability may still give rise to condemnation predicated on the moral reliability and integrity of the agent which commits them. Moral reliability is the reproducible coupling between an agent’s outward behavior and the group’s moral expectations under agreed operations.

An agent is morally reliable when their actions consistently manifest patterns, whether aligned with the moral good or not, such that others can evaluate, predict, and hold them to account within shared normative structures. This reliability emerges as a value of trust which is generated from the repeated couplings of the actions of an agent to the perception of another.

This reliability is realized through colloquial group expressions like “good egg” referring to those who are morally reliable to moral goodness or the “bad seed” for the opposite. Trust, being a personal value of confidence, is not restricted to only that which is desired. While personal integrity may align to various moral standpoints, moral integrity remains aligned to that which is defined as morally good.

Moral integrity occurs with consistent internal coupling of an individual’s will and action to the structural conditions of moral good. It is a stability of internal alignment across contexts, such that the agent reliably enacts the moral good across contexts—those that preserve or enhance autonomy and support endurance. Individuals colloquialize this assertion with phrases such as “I am a good person.” It emerges among moral reliability and moral integrity that these may not always be aligned.

Perceptual Evaluations of Moral Reliability and Integrity

The group exposure to the moral acts of the individual may create, from the perceptual frame of the group, a moral reliability which does not match that of the moral integrity of the individual. Consequently, an individual who lacks moral integrity may be seen by the collective to be morally reliable to commit good acts, in spite of the sum of their acts not aligning with this value.

Inversely, those who maintain moral integrity are not determined to find themselves coupled to the group as morally reliable in a “good” sense. Various perceptions and perceptual frames still exist. Though trust and reputation as interpersonal concepts rely on judgments from society to some degree, they are not reserved solely to them either. There are, in fact, groups of individuals who infer trust based on a shared moral reliability of “wrong” actions and assign a reputation to those individuals within those separate values.

Reputation, in this collective sense, generally refers to the concept of moral reliability. The concepts of trust and reputation may also be predicated outside of morality entirely and be contrived by aesthetics, familiarity, or even blindly—that is, without structural coupling. Both concepts have capacity for evaluation from the individual standpoint of the agent and from that of the group, and culpability may apply in either case.

Attribution, Consequence, and Correction

Blame

Culpability entails attribution of responsibility and the standing to hold an agent to account, but it does not stand alone to justify autonomy-violating remediations since culpability itself does not identically associate to every modality of blame. Reactive attitudes are psychologically real but public standing of blame depends on answerability and proportionality.
