[n.174] Culpability itself is graded based on criteria of diminished or absent capacity.

Capacityindexed autonomy explains why graded culpability does not automatically confer standing to coerce. Where capacity deficits undermine agency, blame may remain expressive while coercive response fails the standing tests. While this doesn’t intrinsically absolve any wrongness of existing, culpability scales to capacity and standing to coerce may still fail if tests are not met.

In cases where remediations are not coupled with culpability, blame takes the mode of being “Expressive.” This might take the form of a conditional statement that the action was “wrong” (where there is a misalignment with stated goals and consequences) or that it “matters” (where there are implications for agency, repair, and future coupling). While these expressive forms of blame permit future coupling with an attributed form of blame or with an expectation of response, they do not intrinsically necessitate those burdens.

When culpability is coupled with an expectation of remediation, blame takes the “Attributed” mode. [n.6] While autonomy still is preserved in this directed attribution of blame, accountability and ownership of the consequences couple directly with the culpability and the burden of responsibility itself in this mode. (cf. Scanlon, blame as answerability rather than sanction.) Expectation of remediation is the result of the coupling of an undesired state, a level of culpable responsibility for this state to an agent or agents, and the will to reach a desired state. Attributed blame might take the form of an attributive statement such as, “This is your responsibility.”

Demand & Consequence Path Selector (CPS-7)

Where an affirmative coupling of the understanding of the violation, capacity for remediation, and the will to assert the desired state exists, demands for remediation are justified by the presence of those attributes. Demands where these attributes are uncoupled are not justified because it is the coupling of those attributes to the attributive statement which justifies them, not the expectation itself. It is neither justified nor reasonable to demand remediation when there is no desired state, no capacity for remediation, or where there is no understanding of the violation. [n.6]

Public standing arises when the wrong threatens or damages shared autonomy conditions such that third parties inherit risk. Though blame is capable of taking on a tertiary mode of being punitive, whereby one may assert that there is deserved “punishment or condemnation,” the concept of desert punishment functions as an upper-bound. Desert principles couple to the act in such a way that they justify these upper bounds while not justifying prescription.

Thus, justification for the upper bound of remediation and justification for the prescription of it are two facets of a single procedure. The sum of the procedure has both desert and proportional properties, where desert principles establish an upper-bound and the anti-retributive proportionality clauses offer constraints to prescription. Call this the Consequence Path Selector (CPS-7). CPS-7 regards the evaluation of remediation methods and aligns prescription with a set of constrained principles of prescription.

Defining Principles of Correction

Non-Retributive Proportionality Principle (NRPP) and Standing To Coerce (STC-5)

Blame alone does not determine consequence. It merely creates an opening for attributive statements which are justified and which couple with a level of culpable responsibility to the path of consequence. Along the path of consequence, we will call an agent, agents, or groups of any size who have committed these wrongs “offenders.” The external coupling of pressure, coercion, control or force with the offenders and the desired state is known as “correction.” [n.13]

In accordance with the Maxim of Mutual Autonomy, by the stripping of autonomy of others, offenders incur a sacrifice of the proportional level of their own autonomy. The scope and severity of autonomy sacrificed is designated by the coupling of the desired state and the level of autonomy which is required to achieve it. We will call this the “Non-Retributive Proportionality Principle” (NRPP) of the Maxim of Mutual Autonomy. [n.13] [n.21] [n.23]

Even translated moral claims such as “dignity” or “sanctity of life” must pass risk-inheritance & validation and be sized by NRPP to bind plural public groups. NRPP and standing constraints provide bounds, not a single metric; within bounds, plural agents negotiate. External correction as a mode of consequence is only justified where autonomy has already been compromised or where a validated, immediate threat outweighs the autonomy cost. This is the Standing to Coerce Test (STC-5) and it does not authorize action; it only determines whether action can be authorized without collapsing legitimacy. Correction authority, in this framework, is simply the operational expression of the symmetry constraint: coercion is legitimate only where autonomy loss has already broken the equivalence between agents.

Tiers of Foreseeability

In terms of harm, it is present where a non-trivial coupling between action, inaction, or idea and an outcome foreseeably or actually results in a reduction of autonomy or produces an outcome that the affected agent or group, under conditions of reasonable self-authorship, judges as incompatible with their interests or values. What then is foreseeable?

In such cases where the stimulus couples to the individual who has capacity, we call this level of foreseeability the “obvious.” Such stimulus may come from recalled experience, education, current experience, or otherwise. Nonetheless, where this extends further is when reach is combined with a role designation for this foreseeability.

As an agent inherits more couplings, they likewise inherit awareness of those couplings. This “reach” then implies an increased set of couplings by which to evaluate and becomes an information set by which foreseeability is also bound - so that they are likewise coupled. That is to say, that the collection of couplings an agent has becomes itself another coupling—one between the agent and their own understanding.

Where collectives of agents have shared perceptual frames of these standards, a new tier of foreseeability emerges in the form of a “professional standard.” This tier of foreseeability regards an expectation among individuals who have entered a similar field of perceptions such as a workplace. Where there is a largely shared expectation because of these perceptual frame agreements being so prolific, this standard emerges as expectations of those who enter this level of community as well.

It reflects with a given set of awarenesses of foreseeable action among peers in related fields. One example would be the understood foreseeability of the impact of tardiness one might have upon a workplace. This falls within the tier of “professional standard” to have a mutual understanding of the impact this has and is a distinct tier of foreseeability that is not wholly limited to the perceptual frame of the individual.

Where individuals within specific fields have a volume of couplings to individuals and data sets which far exceed the general grouping around them, the tier of “specialized expertise” arises as a level of foreseeability. As an agent or group couples correspondingly to more inclusive sets of data, actions, and exchanges among one particular group, the collected understanding of that particular group increases and formulates a reasonable expectation of outcomes of given events or actions.

We might take this type of specialized expertise when we choose a role such as a “doctor” or a “lawyer” and, in fact, this volume of couplings is a requirement to achieve those roles within society for the same purpose. That purpose is that they regard roles which operate functionally from a high level of foreseeability and a capacity for remediation.

To facilitate this function for those roles, the requisite to them is to have established those couplings to such an extent that the foreseeability rises to the level of specialized expertise. It is the volume of those couplings which itself validates such tiers.

Evaluating Risk-Inheritance

This accounting synthesizes and generalizes autonomy-based, agent-relative and structural conceptions of harm into a single coupling-based framework. Where threat of such harm exists, those to whom the harm is threatened, whether directly or indirectly of the action, experience a coupling of their autonomy with the outcome of the action, and so inherit risk.

Risk assessments made outside of those to whom the harm is threatened and which are not validated by those to whom it is threatened are not justified. Such unjustified assessments carry the potential for domination as the autonomy of those involved is not coupled to the outcome of the action. This absent coupling of autonomy to action removes the premise that a stripping of autonomy has occurred, which is the justification for corrective measure.

When justified, risk is assessed on a scale between the individual and varying sizes of groups to which the individual belongs, so justification scales correspondingly. What then is justified to the individual is predicated on the risk assessment of the individual and what is justified to the larger group is assessed by the larger group.

Correction, being coupled to the understanding of that assessment is then also coupled to that varying scale so that an individual’s assessment of correction is not sufficient to be coupled with that of a larger group and vice versa. Without these scales of assessment, we risk producing compliance without understanding and risking future resistance rather than repair. Consequently, correction can restore behavior without restoring moral agency.

While repair may attempt to restore such agency internally, remediation which is uncoupled from recognized culpable responsibility and the will to return to a desired state likewise only reforms behavior. Repair which truly restores moral agency is not without a form of pressure, however. Acknowledged culpable responsibility, when coupled with the will to return to a desired state forms an internalized pressure which is the drive that informs the will to act in these cases.

This is colloquially understood to give such remediation actions which belong to repair a “meaning” for other participants. This intuition is confirmed in the assertion that it is not the existence of the thing itself which provides the meaning but the interaction between perceptual frames and the stimulus which imparts meaning, standing, and relevance.

Repair, Forgiveness, and Excuse

Sincere Repair Checklist & Validation (SRC-3)

In this repair process, the coupling of the remediation actions with culpable responsibility and the will to return to the desired state of the agent or agents who were offended - that coupling itself is what separates performative repair from sincere repair which restores moral agency to the individual. This can be known as the Sincere Repair Checklist (SRC-3). Operationally, sincere repair exhibits transparent acknowledgment, concrete remediation steps, and future-facing constraints which the agent accepts without external compulsion. [n.8]

Absent these, repair is only capable of reforming behavior. Where this coupling is absent it is reparative of behavior but not of moral agency and where it is present, while it may be reparative of the moral agency of the offender, this does not presume absolution from punishment or forgiveness within social constructs as those concepts are not coupled to the will of the offender.

If they were, any criminal would be justified to say, “you must forgive me and not punish me” predicated solely upon their own will and the offended parties would be obliged to concede. We do not observe this. What mechanism could impose this obligation onto the offended parties? It is the will of the offended parties which gives forgiveness claims justification.

Forgiveness, Punishment & Moral Debt

Forgiveness is the coupling of a victims understanding of the culpability of an offender and a release from the moral debt which is created by it. It is, however, a private moral act with no automatic public standing. [n.5][n.2] It is the private release of moral claim. This does not guarantee absolution from punishment because punishment regards a restoration of coupling to a social construct of law and order, but moral debt is not necessarily coupled to that same construct.

Punishment is instead a social function designed to preserve the constructs of justice, safety, and social norms. [n.8] If justified, it addresses order and safety and therefore lies with those who bear the risk. While moral debt being satisfied in some of these instances is sufficient to restore coupling to those constructs, in other instances the satisfaction of moral debt is insufficient.

Whether punishment is necessary is predicated on the evaluated risk which the wrong posed to the parties involved and to society on the whole and its relevance and meaning as related to the restoration of the desired state for both the individuals and society. When the Maxim of Mutual Autonomy is applied, validated harm sets a ceiling of justified response, while the Non-Retributive Proportionality Principle (NRPP) governs prescription, requiring the least autonomyreducing means compatible with neutralizing that harm.

Ceiling vs Prescription

This justification is not imposed upon the offender externally but by their own actions establishing within themselves the very same ceiling. The offender has committed themselves to their own level of autonomy by virtue of their actions. The offender’s act sets the ceiling for what punishment could be justified but does not determine what should be prescribed.

Prescription is further narrowed by risk, necessity, consistency, and autonomy. Though this ceiling is justified, it implies no more satisfaction of moral debt or maintenance of social constructs. Call this “Ceiling vs Prescription.”

Likewise, systems within the social constructs even down to the individual find fit to couple this ceiling with their understandings of safety and reciprocity, which historically have not proven to be consistent to either the limit of this prescription or to the ceiling. Many deities have also found fit to execute the full prescription of the upper bound of punishment based on the commitment of the offender, yet this has not always been in alignment with the operational imperative that society casts upon itself to endure and thrive.

So, what normative constraints can be derived from this framework? In the normative sense, the level of punishment prescribed should be directly coupled to what ensures the endurance of society (as is their commitment), what satisfies the balance of moral debt (so far as can be determined by the coupling of the offender and their understanding of moral culpability), what ensures the restoration of stripped or violated autonomy, and what can be consistently applied for society. (cf. Aharon Barak, Proportionality, for the legal architecture of leastrestrictive means and necessity.) [n.23]

Systemic Harm and Excuse

This coupling works to avoid undeserved suffering, moral payback, and symmetry of harm as well as systemic harm. [n.10] This systemic harm is understood through colloquialisms such as “an eye for an eye leaves the whole world blind.” Functionally, since the taking of an eye is a permanent instance, the retribution of equal punishment in that case can result to the detriment of a whole society. If the whole of a society blinds themselves through justified punishment, they unjustly expose themselves to a new level of threat. [n.8] [n.10] [n.13]

Where capacity, cognitive reach, or autonomy is absent, the act may still occur, but responsibility does not couple to the agent. This is the condition for excuse. Excuse, in this sense, operates as the justification for the decoupling of moral responsibility from the agent or agents. Consequently, as culpability is coupled to moral responsibility, those who have the condition of excuse are not culpable for those acts despite that the acts themselves retain moral wrongness. While this is sufficient to describe how morality functions under stable conditions, what happens when morality is subject to pluralism, finitude, and scarcity?

Moral Conflict & Resolution

Moral Conflict and their Types

Must all groups and individuals necessarily come into agreement for cooperation then? If history of society is any indicator, this is surely not the case. What then is the cause of failure in moral systems if not conflict? Across scales, moral systems fail when they assume a single final authority, a single value ordering, unlimited resources, or non-conflicting obligations.

Where a single authority is presumed, those of the system who question or are uncoupled from it suffer. The lack of coupling causes detriment to their agency among the group. Where there is a single value ordering, those who stand in the same relevance likewise suffer.

Under finitude and plural frames, conflict is a structural feature, not a bug. Consequently, conflicting obligations do arise. Moral conflict arises when autonomy-preserving entities or goods compete under conditions with finite capacity, incomplete coupling, or incompatible scale demands. What sorts of conflict exist within this framework then? Among the types I have considered are Plural Value, Plural Obligation, Scale, Epistemic, and Tragic conflict.

Plural Value conflict exists where conditions provide that multiple moral goods cannot be equally satisfied. If I were to have told my daughters in their early years about the perils which women face as adults, I may have likewise subjected them to emotional and mental harm in the form of trauma. The plural values of honesty, truth-telling, and trauma prevention in this case are not all mutually capable of satisfaction.

As these values are coupled to the individual or to the group, a measurement between their scales, impact, cost, risk of harm, and outcomes for autonomy under agreed operations are assessed at their corresponding scale(s). Dissatisfaction of all of these moral goods is not an error or violation in these cases. Rather, they arise because the moral goods are not commensurable across frames. They are coupled dependently so that where one is satisfied, the other value may not be.

Some constructive acts are supererogatory: they enhance autonomy or endurance but are not owed. Failure to perform them is not culpable. This framework treats them as grounds for praise, not coercion. These acts are distinct from autonomy preserving acts which the collective itself is aware of and are a requirement for the maintenance of autonomy for the group. Conflict does not exist for supererogatory acts but may exist for acts that the collective recognizes are necessary where they conflict with others that are necessary.

Where there is conflict between multiple standing obligations or duties for an agent that cannot be jointly satisfied, Plural Obligation exists. So then, plural value conflict regards goods and plural obligation conflicts regard duties. As a working parent, the dual obligations of my professional duty and parental duties rest naturally opposed. Here, duties couple simultaneously in a juxtaposed nature so that they necessarily cannot be satisfied together.

The couplings of these duties are not dependent but opposed so that my actions may be, to some degree, modular between them and yet to fully satisfy one is to deny the other. In these cases, some moral wrongs may be unavoidable, and culpability is coupled directly to the capacity that those wrongs may be avoided. We recognize this colloquially with statements like, “it was an impossible situation.”

Scale conflict exists where good at one scale becomes detrimental to another scale, whether to another good or as a moral wrong as seen from the perceptual frame of the other scale. If I am the CEO of a company that produces harmful chemicals which spray into the community—leaving them sick—but this is required for my success, I stand to improve my personal flourishing and potentially that of those who work for and with me, but to the detriment of the whole community.

The scale of my personal actions for myself and the group of the company are thus pivoted against that of the community. Scale conflict is notoriously difficult to weigh among people groups. After all, are the beneficiaries of the product our company makes only me and the employees or shareholders? What if the product were a vaccine against cancer? Does this not present a new scale argument for the whole of humanity? Conversely, what if access to this vaccine is priced so aggressively that it exceeds the reach of the largest portion of that group?

Each of these changes in scope have realized impact to the scale conflict as it is predicated on the coupling of variant groups based on variant sets of agreed operations and variant implications to autonomy. The Scale-Relative Autonomy Preservation Principle applies directly to these conflicts.

When possible, each frame that evaluates these scenarios necessarily evaluate autonomy from their own scale, as they are coupled to it. Furthermore, another test is required: the Scale-Coherence Test. Scale-Coherence tests identify all affected scales, state the cost/benefit of each respective scale, and prefer options that preserve autonomy at the largest affected scales while not permanently destroying autonomy at smaller ones. Where there are temporary costs locally, off-ramps under agreed operations and constrained by NRPP and risk inheritance & validation principles apply.

Epistemic conflicts arise where agents disagree about the facts, risks, or outcomes by consequence of unequal coupling to them. Let us take again into consideration my two daughters. Say I baked some cookies. I set them out to cool and instruct them to not eat any until after we have eaten dinner. Upon returning to them later, I discover that the dog has eaten the cookies.

My daughters, having both witnessed the event, recall that it happened within different time frames. One presumes, from her frame, that the time must have been “about two or three minutes” and the other presumes “five to seven minutes” between the time I set the cookies out and the time of the thievery.

The conflict between their couplings to the time frame is an epistemic one. It is built upon their standing. It relates to their perceptual frames having variance between them and not directly of their beliefs regarding that alignment or their coupling to it alone. It is an epistemic conflict which could resolve to Perceptual Frame Agreement by means of a stopwatch.

This mode of resolution employs the ladder of evidence which begins first with testimony, then shared observation, then agreed operations, then instrumentation, and finally third-party replication. [n.14] [n.15] Agents progress up the ladder until Perceptual Frame Agreement is reached or the residual uncertainty is explicitly owned by an agent or agents.

Tragedy, however, is wholly without moral failure. It arises where there is moral over-determination under scarcity and consequently every available option results in some form of autonomy-impairing harm. Triage is one such situation. A bus full of people explodes. Not everyone can be saved due to scarcity of capacity.

The coupling here is determinate that autonomy-impairing harm, if by inaction for some victims, necessarily exists. This disparity is created by the limited volume of couplings between those who provide the moral good and those who stand the risk.

Moral Conflict Resolution Modes

Moral conflict types are not ubiquitous or unilateral. Consequently, neither may their resolutions be. This section will not be an exhaustive account for all modes of resolution but offers several of the primary ways by which the human species has been inventive of mediation to these conflicts. We will consider Negotiation, Compromise, Prioritization, Sacrifice and Tragic Acceptance.

Negotiation is the mutual alignment of couplings to interest so that moral conflict is minimized or removed altogether. It is achieved when the couplings of all involved parties have resolved to this mutual alignment in pursuit of Perceptual Frame Agreement (PFA). Negotiation exchanges reasons and evidence in a process of building PFA where none existed prior.

It relies upon an increased coupling, shared understanding, reframing of outcomes, and altering of constraints. It expands the option set that preserves autonomy at relevant scales. This is not to be confused with compromise, another mode of moral conflict resolution.

Compromise occurs when agents are coupled incompatible values, goals, or claims. While neither abandon their core position, each agent partially concedes their coupling to their perspective frame in order to resolve the incompatibility. Compromise is what occurs when Perceptual Frame Agreement is unachievable via negotiation due to that incompatibility.

It is not false agreement but is partial satisfaction under NRPP. It accepts the mutual disagreement of optimal conditions in favor of acceptable conditions that align with both NRPP and UCE but is constrained by ceiling-vs-prescription logic as well. One may say, “I agree to concede X, if you agree to concede Y.” Some conflicts are rooted in the whole or partial coupling of their temporal outcomes such as time-sensitive threats, emergency conditions or reversible harms.

Prioritization is the conflict resolution method which utilizes STC-5 logic by virtue of explicit off-ramps and sunset conditions to derive a temporary ordering by which to satisfy each moral claim. Prioritization still falls under the constraints of the risk inheritance & validation principles established earlier as such principles are coupled directly to the moral claims themselves and are used as the means by which to assign the temporary ordering.

The risk of one harm may be more emergent or severe than that of others. Correspondingly, prioritizations are time-bound, recorded, and reviewable for the purpose of not becoming normalized domination. We assign their order of resolution according to these conditions.

Another mode of resolution is Sacrifice. As we have already spoken of these conditions, I will simply reiterate that sacrifice is voluntary, scaled actions where the agent knowingly accepts prudential costs that collective autonomy is preserved or enhanced. It does not qualify as self-harm and requires both intact agency and consent to be present.

The last mode of resolution I will speak of is of Tragic Acceptance. Where all options will violate some level of autonomy, no further coupling can reduce harm, and there is no clean resolution, tragic acceptance remains as a default option. [n.53] This becomes the default because it is the condition whereby the naturally emergent conflicts simply play out. In cases where conflict is temporal, tragic acceptance may emerge as the default over time. The consequence or outcome has already happened and is not reversible.

In those cases, attributive blame may apply as the temporal factor is coupling inaction and the necessity of this resolution implicitly. Thus, the inaction couples to the agent to whom the responsibility was also coupled and attributive blame is enabled. Where there is not premise to attribute blame, tragic acceptance brings expressive blame, memorialization, and reparative practice into moral relevance as they are coupled as potential outcomes of tragic acceptance to the agent or agents which must enact it. Tragic acceptance shifts emphasis from justification to acknowledgment: moral remainder is owned, memorialized, and—where any capacity exists—addressed through repair (SRC3) rather than punitive blame.

Irreconcilable Pluralism and Structural Limits

This framework does not assume that all pluralist communities can or should converge on shared conditions of endurance. Where UCEs are incompatible, standing cannot be established and coercive coordination cannot be justified without domination. In such cases, the framework does not prescribe reconciliation but instead delineates the limits of legitimate authority. Separation, exit, and mutual noninterference are not moral failures here but structurally honest outcomes of pluralism under finitude.

Where there are no understood conditions of endurance and conflict threatens those conditions, endurance is threatened. Motivationally for individual agents, those who have capacity and agency to recognize this are afforded by this structure the justifications for leaving such situations. Where this is not the aim, the goal is then implicit. If agents wish to maintain that a pluralist collective endures, they must then consider what conditions create this endurance and abide them.

Principles of Constraint for Moral Conflict Resolution

Definitions

Decision making regarding moral conflict resolution is constrained within this framework. No resolution is legitimate under these concepts if it permanently removes self-authorship, forecloses dissent, or treats agents as mere instruments. Call this “Autonomy Non-Domination.” It may be tested by asking, “does this resolution permanently remove self-authorship or foreclose dissent?” If it does, the operational imperative is to reject or redesign the resolution.

Resolutions also must respect the agent or agents who bear the risk, who has standing to authorize harm, and who inherits the consequences as is a direct application of risk inheritance & validation. Call this “Standing Preservation.” To test this, ask yourself, “are risk-bearers the ones validating the harm and inheriting its consequences?” If they are not, pause and identify who the stakeholders are, since they are necessarily coupled to the resolution by definition of being stakeholders.

Harm that is produced by a resolution is only justified if it is no greater than required, targeted rather than diffuse, and revisable rather than entrenched as applies to NRPP and ceiling-vs-prescription ideals. Call this “Proportion & Need.” Addressing this can be accomplished with the question, “is this the least autonomy-reducing means among options that neutralize validated harm?”

Resolutions must prefer outcomes that preserve future agency, allow repair, and enable moral learning wherever possible. This is foundational to the concept of resolution itself so that we do not slip into institutional cruelty but have a method to handle tragic necessity. Refer to this as “Reversibility & Repairability” and you can test this by asking both if agents can recover standing and agency later and if the repair pathways are explicit.

Moral Remainder & Residue

The constraints that we have established are not free from moral residue. What remains after all attempts have been made to justify, remediate, or otherwise resolve conflict is moral remainder, justified regret, and obligation to repair. It consists of acknowledgement, transparency, compensatory repair where possible, and institutional redesign to prevent recurrence.

Moral remainder is justified regret and residual obligation after all avoidable wrongs have been avoided and all culpable parties have done what they can. It does not imply any new culpability. It is the portion of moral debt which is left after culpability has been coupled to its fullest extent and has no more couplings to be made.

Tragic cost is realized here as now unavoidable so that only those to whom culpability has been reasonably coupled hold blameworthiness. While justification exists in this state, so does absolution and forgiveness. For those who hold culpability, SRC-3 conditions become coupled to their efforts for repair. In more extreme cases of moral conflict, resolution may not be available. Where this occurs, refusal, dissent, and exit remain as options. (cf. Hirschman) [n.24]

Refusal, Dissent, & Exit

Refusal is the rejection of the conflict as imposed by another moral claimant. It is to decouple from the operational imperative in part or in whole. This is not to say refusal is without consequence as the actions of another agent may retaliate by force to an agent’s refusal to accept moral conflict and pursue resolution—as is an all-too-common outcome that has produced many wars over the span of human civilization. In short, refusal is justified when compliance would destroy agency, enforce domination, or require self-betrayal.

Dissent, however, does not share a decoupling from the operational imperative. It is the decoupling of justification of the moral claim while remaining coupled to the operational imperative of the group and involves appeals to standards, values, and reasons. Dissent exists to preserve coupling integrity to morals, prevent false consensus, and sustain moral reliability. Justification for dissent emerges when standing is contestable and institutional channels exist.

Exit is among the most extreme of outcomes. Exit is to decouple entirely from the group both in terms of moral claim and operational imperative. The agent ceases engagement, ceases appeals, and removes themselves as a moral interlocutor to the group at all. This is not a moral collapse. It is structural decoupling. Exit is justified when participation sustains domination and no repair pathway exists.

Civil Disobedience

Civil Disobedience triggers and becomes salient when institutional standing collapses (i.e., when legitimacy no longer supplies defensible reasons for compliance in the relevant domain). [n.99] Disobedience is treated in this case as relevance-preserving response and not a rejection of normativity or coordination in these circumstances. After all, if the standing has collapsed there is a decoupling between the collective and the institutions which only hold their position predicated on that coupling.

Acts of resistance however must be no more disruptive or harmful than necessary to contest the specific constraint at issue. For instance, a curfew being met with setting government buildings on fire is not justified. The principle of NRPP applies unilaterally in this sense and not purely to those of the institutions so that there isn’t justification for riots and looting absent them being the only reasonable methods to contest constraint. Such actions themselves establish an extremely high demand for justification just as well.

Resistance should aim at the norm, rule, or practice causing domination and not at unrelated agents or background coordination systems. Justified resistance seeks to reduce arbitrary power, not substitute one unchecked authority with another. If it did, what progress would have been made? It is a means to an end and not a means to engage more authority itself.

As with remedies, these means escalate only as less disruptive channels close or fail. Civil disobedience likewise remains compatible with exit and refusal strategies. It is one mode of contestation and not a mandatory endpoint. Some actions of this type may not be entirely public either. Public, reason-giving action strengthens legitimacy claims and enables social evaluation, but secrecy may be permissible under domination.

An illustrative limit case is the hiding of Anne Frank during the Holocaust. Under conditions of total domination—where public standing, appeal, and exit have already collapsed—ordinary expectations of public reasongiving are no longer available. In such circumstances, secrecy does not constitute domination; it functions as an autonomypreserving response to an already dominating structure.

Motivation, Containment, and Ascension

Moral Motivation

Moral conflict is structural, not pathological. While some harms are unavoidable, cruelty is not. What matters is not the achievement of perfect outcome but preserved agency, minimized domination, honest acknowledgment of loss, and openness to repair. Why would anyone choose to be moral when doing so can be costly? This account does not aim to explain why agents come to care about morality in the psychological sense, but why agents who already care about preserving their own freedom, standing, and exit have structural reasons to restrain autonomyreducing behavior.

Morality exists as a standing filter that doesn’t promise motivation within itself in this framework. The same constraints on this framework establish a network of constraints which inherently serves the self-interest of the individual and the group at the same time so that, what is in the best interest of the individual most commonly aligns with that of the group.

Can a purely self-interested agent understand why violating autonomy routinely undermines their own ability to act freely and bind others? This framework does not depend on moral motivation in the traditional sense. It requires only that agents prefer to preserve their own capacity to act, exit, and bind others in plural conditions. The reflexive properties of the ALRP and MOMA imply that education for agents of the structural coupling of their own best interest to that outcome is required to generate capacity for this motivation and nothing more.

Actions in this framework operate under the Maxim of Mutual Autonomy, NRPP, Ceiling vs Prescription, STC-5, and every other constraint in this system. They subject agents to a reciprocal volume of correction and/or punishment. Minimally there is a preservationist motivator. There is no objective demand for motivation to be generated from morality itself or from an altruistic final authority. Rather, self-interest itself becomes a prime motivator for preserving autonomy as well.

Non-Cooperators and Containment

Likewise, for those agents who do not concede to the moral community or to the group on the whole, was there ever any reason to validate their desire to behave morally to the community? Have they not, by virtue of their adversarial normative stance to the community self-attested to their exit and dissent simultaneously to those benefits?

If they do not desire the benefits of the group, do not reject the consequences of exit, and dissent from the group then the logical consequence is to simply enable their exit as a matter of operational imperative. Non-cooperators are handled via standing-to-coerce constraints; the framework doesn’t promise persuasion, only legitimate containment and off-ramps.

This is not a structurally maximizing stance. Rather, it is a minimal accounting of moral motivations and alignment to their coupling structure. Since those who choose avenues of refusal, dissent, and exit have avenues for correction and redress or the option to exit the onus of aggregate welfare is no longer upon the framework but upon the individual agents within the framework itself. Agents are directly coupled to their own welfare within the structural framework and the guidelines built uphold that as a minimal condition—hence autonomy. Accordingly, outcomes matter only insofar as they couple to autonomy and standing constraints, so that obligations are not derived purely from outcome.

Though morality in this sense is not objective, the ascension into improved morality comes via expansion of who counts as a risk-bearer, increased inclusion in validation, reduced foreclosure of correction, and better alignment between consequence visibility and autonomy constraints. Foreclosure of correction can occur not only by silencing speakers but by depriving groups of shared interpretive resources (hermeneutical injustice). As those conditions improve, so does the morality of outcomes among groups that employ these conditions and constraints.

Moral Ascension

Coordination failures are not reduced by appeals to final authority alone. Instead, it is within the best interests of the group to adopt individuals who are morally inclined toward the “goodness” of the group and, as they pursue these goals, the framework is self-reinforcing. It expands inclusion, reduces foreclosure of consent, improves alignment between consequences and standing, and narrows coercion incrementally as the system builds so that the internalized “draw” and the “indicators of improvement” are likewise aligned in coupling.

At this point, morality no longer appears as a source of final authority, but as a constraint on how claims, actions, and responses may legitimately bind others under plural conditions. Moral language persists without metaphysical grounding not by asserting objectivity, but by remaining answerable to autonomy, consequence, and shared human capacities. Wrongness, responsibility, culpability, and blame no longer collapse into a single verdict, and conflict—sometimes tragic and irresolvable—registers as a structural feature of finite, plural life rather than a failure of moral reasoning.

The significance of this shift is not that moral disputes can now be settled, but that many cannot be settled without domination, and that repair, restraint, refusal, and exit remain morally intelligible even where consensus fails. Having established how coupling yields standing, how autonomy constrains legitimate response, and how correction/repair/forgiveness/punishment are selected and limited, we can now turn to language, the primary medium through which social couplings are created, amplified, or dissolved.

The tests introduced here—harm thresholds, risk-inheritance and validation, NRPP, and ceiling versus prescription—will be applied to communicative acts: persuasion versus coercion, slogans versus propaganda, sincere versus performative apology, and decoupled speech. What remains unresolved is not what outcomes should be chosen, but how any outcome may legitimately bind others once final authority has been set aside.

A Measure Under Its Own Constraints

Pluralist societies cannot be coordinated by final authority, because final authority resolves disagreement through domination. The absence of final authority does not eliminate the need for coordination, but it does remove any shared external standard by which outcomes can be declared binding. This framework proposes a structural measure for evaluating when interactions preserve nondomination and when they collapse into domination. If adopted, this measure does not become a final authority: it does not determine outcomes or adjudicate values. Questions of right and wrong, good and bad, best and worst remain open to other philosophies and traditions.

What follows does not extend this framework by introducing new principles, tests, or authorities. The analytic engine is complete. The chapters that follow apply it across domains whose differences lie not in logic, but in pressure—scale, urgency, reversibility, and lived consequence.

“Domain enrichment” names this increase in diagnostic resolution. As the same constraints are traced through concrete forms of coordination—institutions, roles, norms, and infrastructures, the framework does not adapt to the domain. The domain is measured against the framework. Where outcomes diverge, the divergence reflects intensified coordination, not relaxed constraint.

Interpersonal Misalignment

Two individuals share a public space when one abruptly steps sideways, colliding with the other. Each modeled the approaching figure differently: one perceived a jogger changing lanes; the other perceived a potential threat and moved to block it. These internal models generated incompatible relevance—each agent acted under their own frame, but neither validated the other’s exposure. When one agent’s movement constrained the other’s autonomy without standing, the result was a structural wrong without blame: a misidentified coupling produced an A > B impact pattern. The conflict does not arise from intent or moral failing but from perceptual frames that failed to synchronize. This illustrates how standing collapses interpersonally when relevance is mis-coupled and correction cannot occur in real time.

Part II - Domain Enrichment: Scale, Time, and Coordination

V — About Language and Communication

Purpose: This section examines how the coupling-standing-legitimacy engine operates within the domain of language and communication and how misidentification of coupling produces characteristic failures of standing in this domain. This section sets out to determine how language and communication become relevant to groups, how meaning is attached to those forms, and what constitutes harm in these cases while maintaining the engine and toolset.

Orientation

What This Chapter Is and Is Not

This chapter examines language and communication as coupling mechanisms, the primary means by which relevance, standing, coordination, and coercion are created, amplified, and dissolved in pluralist society. Language in this framework is not merely a neutral carrier of meaning.

Instead, it is action, capable of producing obligations, foreclosing autonomy, redistributing power, and altering standing. This chapter treats language as a domain of action rather than description. Words do not merely represent the world; they alter relevance, redistribute autonomy, and create or resolve standing. Language is one of the most powerful coordination technologies available to pluralist societies.

This chapter will apply the already established structural engine to communicative acts. It shows how speech acquires force, how meaning stabilizes or drifts, and how communicative practices generate moral, political, and institutional consequences.

This chapter is not a theory of semantics, syntax, or linguistics in the technical sense. It does not create a defense of free speech absolutism or speech restriction. There is no moral ranking of words, intentions, or expressions and it does not create an account of meaning that is grounded in metaphysics or mental representation.

This framework does not attempt to settle debates about truth, reference, or meaning as such. Instead, it asks a prior procedural question: When does language acquire standing to bind, obligate, or constrain others? This chapter does not adjudicate which speech is “good” or “bad” in isolation. Rather, it evaluates when communicative acts become autonomy-relevant actions within shared space and what constraints follow when they do.

Expectations

Readers can expect from this chapter that language will be analyzed functionally rather than sentimentally. Familiar concepts like truth, persuasion, offense, and harm will be structurally redefined. Speech is not merely expression but treated as potentially coercive action in this chapter.

Discomfort may arise for readers where common intuitions about intent, offense, and neutrality are challenged. Many readers are accustomed to treating language as either harmless or intrinsically dangerous content. This chapter rejects simplification on both accounts. Language is evaluated here by what it does: how it couples to autonomy, standing, and consequence.

The author assumes that readers are willing to suspend the idea that speech is normatively special or categorically exempt in this chapter. Readers will need to be willing to accept that intent is not sufficient to determine communicative legitimacy and to treat silence, omission, and framing as inherently communicative acts. This chapter will examine how power, reach and amplification alters responsibility.

To engage this chapter fully, the reader must be willing to treat communication as a form of social infrastructure. They will be exposed to the idea of it as one that can fail, be captured, or become coercive without ever raising its voice. While this may run counter to intuitive stances on language, taking these steps to suspend prior conceptions of language can help readers with the range of concepts in this chapter.

Translations

Translations in this chapter are functional, not rhetorical. They describe the effects of couplings, not speaker psychology. Multiple translations may apply simultaneously depending on scope and reach and a single utterance may operate across several coupling modes at once.

A sentence can inform, persuade, threaten, bind, and signal identity at the same time. Translation makes these layered functions visible so that standing can be evaluated without mystification. Language already operates across every other domain in this framework. As a result, translation is unavoidable.

The purpose of translation in this chapter is to expose how linguistic concepts function structurally. It separates semantic meaning form normative force and clarifies when communication gains standing to obligate or constrain. This chapter levies translation to distinguish persuasion from coercion without relying on intent alone. The translations in this chapter do not redefine language arbitrarily. They make explicit the structural work that communication already performs within pluralist coordination, whether visible or not.

Translation Table

Language: A coordination medium that couples understanding, perception, identity, and obligation across agents and groups.

Communication: The act of attempting to establish coupling between agents via a shared or interpretable medium.

Meaning: Stabilized coupling between an expression and shared understanding within a perceptual frame agreement.

Reference: The aspect of a perceptual frame around which action is coordinated through linguistic coupling.

Speech Act: A communicative action that attempts to create, modify, or dissolve couplings, not merely convey information.

Locutionary Act: The production of an utterance that presents content without directly creating obligation or constraint.

Illocutionary Act: A communicative act that performs an action (e.g., promising, ordering, declaring) by virtue of its utterance.

Perlocutionary Effect: The downstream outcome of a communicative act, such as belief change, fear, trust, or compliance.

Semantic Meaning: Relatively stable coupling between expressions and shared understanding that enables baseline coordination.

Pragmatic Meaning: Contextdependent modulation of meaning produced by implication, emphasis, omission, or framing.

Interpretation: The process of resolving an utterance into a candidate coupling capable of supporting coordination or evaluation.

Misinterpretation: A failed or mismatched coupling that does not support coherent uptake or coordination.

Charity (Interpretive): An operational discipline of selecting interpretations that preserve coherence, minimize unnecessary conflict, and maintain corrigibility.

Drift: Gradual change in stabilized coupling between expressions and meaning due to repeated use over time.

Private Language: A communicative system that lacks shared coupling and therefore cannot generate public standing.

Influence: Noncoercive coupling that alters preferences or beliefs while preserving refusal and selfauthorship.

Persuasion: Influence that preserves epistemic freedom and practical alternatives for the receiver.

Coercive Speech: Communication that foreseeably reduces autonomy or removes reasonable alternatives through coupling.

Threat: A communicative act that couples compliance to the avoidance of harm, directly reducing autonomy.

Deception: Intentional miscoupling that forecloses informed selfauthorship by withholding or distorting relevant information.

Propaganda: Structured communicative coupling designed to shortcircuit deliberation, degrade answerability, or normalize domination.

Dogwhistle: Splitcoupling communication that coordinates ingroup uptake while preserving plausible deniability externally.

Silence / Omission: Communicative inaction that can constitute action when role, reach, and foreseeability couple it to harm.

Standing (Speech): The legitimacy of a communicative act to bind, obligate, or constrain others.

Speech Harm (SHT3): Autonomyrelevant harm arising from communicative coupling, evaluated independently of offense.

Epistemic Risk Ladder (ERL): The escalation framework that increases evidentiary and accountability requirements as autonomyimpact rises.

Normative Linguistic Coupling: Language that directly creates or modifies obligations, permissions, or prohibitions.

Affective Linguistic Coupling: Communication that directly alters perception or emotional attunement without propositional uptake.

Social Linguistic Coupling: Language that signals identity, belonging, status, or exclusion within a group.

Semantic Capture: When control over meaning stabilization forecloses correction and manufactures standing.

Decoupled Speech: Language that retains form but lacks consequencerelevant or autonomyrelevant coupling.

Relevance and Meaning

Language as Coupling & Relevance

As in other domains, standing to constrain or guide speech is indexed to capacity: where an agent lacks the ability to interpret, contest, or refuse communicative uptake, limited intervention may be justified, but such standing must contract as communicative capacity emerges (CIA). Systems that manipulate language to prevent capacity development become structurally illegitimate in this framework rather than merely deceptive. In order for the language to be relevant to individuals in a non-dominant way, this is a precursor condition for any language coupling and gaining validity and relevance. This will become demonstrable in this chapter via propaganda and epistemic pollution later on.

Language acquires relevance and meaning through linguistic relational identity-defining coupling between understanding and a communicative medium. [L.1] [L.13] This next section will treat the linguistic modes of coupling specifically as they play an integral part in many other domains. In language, to couple is to let a signal seize what we can know, feel, belong to, or be bound by. This framework will handle those couplings independently over the span of this chapter.

Systematic forms of communication among people groups that rely on a coupling to the understanding of the group form the basis of shared language. [L.2] This is not to say that individualistic forms of language cannot and do not exist. We have seen in authors such as Tolkien that whole systems of language may be synthesized purely from the individual coupling their own understanding of relevance and meaning to a given medium of communication. [L.17]

These media are not limited to the written word or characters implicitly. Various forms of sign language by gestures, Morse code via timed tones or signals, and other variants of language have emerged, making visible that language is not limited in form to that of written characters. In coupling the understanding to the corresponding medium, those who have the understanding of that medium are capable of the exchange, interplay, and collaboration of thoughts and ideas.

These systems of communication do not exist in isolation, however. They are fluid and experience changes over time based on colloquial usage, inventive additions, modifications of assigned meaning, or other changes in the utilization of the system. [L.3] Utilization at all demands stabilized coordination in order to function across time and groups. Questions of reference, naming, and objecthood arise immediately.

Stability and Action

Reference, Names, and Objects

With regard to reference, the primary function of terms in this framework is for their instrumental function or to the operational imperative of the agent or agents. They serve the function of cooperative and collective action and reaction. [L.23] While an individual agent may assign their own labels as reference to any particular thing, idea, concept, or otherwise, the function of the label itself is to establish an internal ordering of perceptions within their frame.

As this function is inherited by the group via coupling of the individuals of the group, these labels themselves undertake a further evaluation to likewise establish ordering of perceptions within the PFA of the group. While descriptive features of terms hold utility in the value of separating elements of a particular perceptual frame, they are not in this framework tied to any metaphysical claim in itself.

Instead, they become organizational tools by which to separate elements within the perceptual frame being evaluated. [L.20] [L.21] Within this framework, reference stabilizes through three primary mechanisms that account for most ordinary linguistic practice. Call this the “Reference Stability Triad” (RST).

Referential Stability: One of the prevalent methods for extending these references is to rely upon the previously made references and adopt them into new formations as they align with the PFA of the group. For example, where there is an object which has been related to the term “desk” and this object performs the action that has been related to the descriptive term of “rising” a very common formulation is to create an implicit reference to this particular subtype of object as a “rising desk.” This example shows how the reliance on previously established references can inherently formulate new references as they emerge. [L.23]

Origination Stability: Another method of reference creation occurs when originating figures of an idea, object, or concept make a concerted effort to assign the reference label to those entities themselves. Colloquially we refer to this as “coining” the term—an homage to the act of imprinting an image upon a coin just as a creator may imprint themselves upon their creation in this same fashion. It serves a function of attribution between the creator and the creation and helps established a coupled bond between them. [L.22] [L.23]

Frame Agreement Stability: A third method for reference to gain meaning is through PFA itself. As agents collectivize within a group, their collected PFA sometimes causes references to arise organically whereby one agent of the group may assign a label intuitively and the label is accepted among the PFA without being specifically attributed to the agent. This is not definitively limited to a single agent but can emerge from several at once. Where there is no attribution of the reference to a claimant, these give rise to “trends” and “colloquialisms” within the group. It is also the genesis for uncoupled or incoherent slang which fails to stabilize across uptake or scope and can apply to the repurposing of existing references as well.

Insofar as anything has a proper name, whether a person, idea, object, concept, or anything else, the function here applies similarly in that of designation. While descriptive efforts give the function of separation of entities within a frame, proper names and even names at all serve the function of implicit identification within those efforts and supplies the function of recall and mutual understanding. While names then are not pure descriptions, they are not mutually exclusive by definition either.

Some expressions stabilize in practice without a referent (fiction, empty descriptions). They can still coordinate imagination, identity, and social play, but their standing is domain-limited and does not automatically license coercive prescriptions. Reference then is the successful coupling within a scope, and names are stabilized reference handles. [L.22] [L.23] The functional definition of objects in this sense is not a metaphysical term either but regard whatever a coupling successfully coordinates action around so that their implicit metaphysical status is untouched.

This is not claiming metaphysical anti-realism but is establishing linguistic coordination. What we call “object” in this framework refers to the aspect or element of a PFA around which action is coordinated. It regards the standing of that aspect or element as a reflection of PFA itself rather than any sort of metaphysical claim. Reference establishes what language coordinates action around, so the next question is: what does speech do?

Speech Acts and Private Language

Within the domain of language speech acts have previously been given several core distinctions already. Acts may be broken into Locutionary acts (saying something) and illocutionary acts (doing something in saying it). [L.6] [L.7] Examples of locutionary acts include statements of fact (declaratives), interrogatives (questions), Imperatives (requests), exclamatives (expressions), performative-form utterances, reverences, predictions, and negations. Examples of illocutionary acts include assertations, promises, orders, or declarations. [L.6] [L.7]

In this framework, locutionary acts rise to the level of attempted coupling of rhetoric to an evaluation. For instance, a claim of truth is an attempted coupling of the rhetoric of that claim to an evaluation (seen later). Locutionary statements in this framework are not inherently bound to the normative situation itself but stand alone for independent evaluation. These statements create candidates for relevance by inherently prompting evaluation of their coupling.

Illocutionary acts then rise to the level of an action itself within the framework. [L.13] These acts couple intent and context to the speech and result in couplings themselves. These couplings differ from perlocutionary effects, which are outcomes rather than commitments. Where illocutionary acts are asserted, there is an action taken within the structure itself, and consequently couplings to those actions have capacity to create obligation or burden.

For instance, by definition, making a promise as an illocutionary act and is a form of teleological coupling, where present action is intelligible only in light of a future-directed end. When promises are issued from a role (e.g., judge, employer), the teleological coupling is mediated through relational identity-defining coupling.” These illocutionary acts couple to the current status of an agent to an intended future outcome. Where locutionary acts do not couple directly in this sense, illocutionary ones do. Whether they have authority to bind others or create obligations for others rests with a STC-5 test, as creating such obligations or bindings are inherently coercive. In classical speech-act terms, STC-5 functions as the felicity/authority gate for obligation-creating acts under pluralism.

Perlocutionary effects may arise from either of these types of speech acts as outcomes of them. Obligation, Trust, affective changes, binding are examples of perlocutionary effects. They emerge as phenomenon of the couplings themselves. Trust in terms of trusting someone’s words is then a coupling of the moral reliability of the individual and the claim which the individual makes.

Performativeform statements are always locutionary, but only rise to illocutionary force when intent, authority, and standing are coupled. Intent coupling for illocutionary acts is inherent but performative-form statements may be made without any such intent. Colloquially we describe these statements as “flippant, empty, or careless” as is intended to reflect the absence of coupled intent.

Performative form in this framework is an act of utterance. Illocution depends on intent, authority, and standing. Without those, the performative-form statements are empty, not because authority is present but because it’s absent. STC-5 tests establish the justification to obligate or bind others while not providing a level of authority or force by which to ensure satisfaction of those obligations or bindings.

The authority itself in this framework may arise from roles that are attributed authority and earned by a volume of autonomous consent. Though coercive, authority may also arise from force where performative-form statements such as threats are granted illegitimate standing but also carry authority from that force. The coupling of coercive authority to invalid standing by STC5 explains how force can be effective without being legitimate.

For example, a threat at gunpoint. The threat of force coupled to the gun and subsequently to the potential victim establishes a level of risk. This event passed through STC-5 fails for standing and falls into strict authoritarianism. In this example we can see that the action has invalid standing, but this does not strip it of all authority.

Validity of all of these acts is still dependent upon standing, scope, and risk inheritance. While private language may exist and have standing or value to the agent themselves, in the context of pluralism, the utility of any of these languages is constrained minimally to stabilization via shared coupling. [L.1] Institutional speech acts are role-mediated: the ‘speaker’ is the office/role whose standing is delegated by consent and bounded by scope. Collective speech inherits standing only through those delegated role couplings. [L.6] [L.7] [L.9]

Though the validity of these acts at variant scopes takes on different methods of evaluation, this does not immediately grant them understanding, meaning, or authority. When speech acts generate claims, the question follows: what is being communicated?

Meaning, Interpretation, and Evaluation

Pragmatics vs Semantics

Classic distinctions between semantics and pragmatics regard concepts of encoding by convention or regard what speakers do with the expressions in context. These distinctions are analytic and operate simultaneously in real communication. [L.24] [L.25]

In this framework, semantic content corresponds to stabilized coupling that occurs between expressions and shared understanding within a PFA. Semantic meaning is invariant across ordinary contexts and enables baseline coordination in this sense. Some examples of this would be Dictionaries, protocols, and formal language as they regularly stabilize the language by coupling the expressions to the understanding of a given group.

The autonomous uptake of participants in the group to this semantic content is what grants it validity within that scope. Context-shift in indirect speech and quotation raises additional complications for semantic evaluation. This framework treats those as specialized cases of scope and uptake relevant to the regarded PFA.

Pragmatic meaning, however, arises where contextual factors modulate or extend coupling beyond the encoded content in this framework. For instance, in this framework Deixis (‘I’, ‘here’, ‘now’) is a paradigmatic context-dependent coupling. [L.24] Implication, emphasis, irony, and omission operate by coupling relevance, expectation, background norms, moral reliability, reputation, and other contextual factors to the value of the expression itself. [L.4] [L.5] [L.25]

Pragmatics in this sense explains how speakers routinely mean more—or something different—than what is strictly said. [L.26] [L.24] It couples contextual stimuli to the expression and any available semantic meaning to derive itself. Metaphor functions in this framework as pragmatic modulation: it reshapes coupling by importing a frame rather than asserting a proposition. It can function as a method of “meaning making” and can become a tool for deception. Accordingly, pragmatics are central—not peripheral—to speech harm analysis, which will be discussed later.

The boundary here is not fixed. Rather, it shifts as pragmatic usages stabilize into semantic content over time as a consequence of repeated coupling to the understanding of the collective over that time. This isn’t limited strictly to terms which have previously held semantic meaning. Slang, technical jargon, and legal terms often migrate from pragmatic inference to semantic coding which can constitute linguistic drift. [L.25] [L.26]

Drift and Collective Usage

The changing of an assigned meaning becomes evident when we evaluate words in the U.S. English language like “swagger.” [L.3] The root etymology of the word lies in the 1500s and was derived from roots of Old Norse and Proto-Germanic language as a derivative of the word “swag” - which meant to sway or move unsteadily. [L.19] Over time, additional use for this word has emerged so that it can be used to describe a bold self-assurance and style.

Slang and drift prove meaning’s dependence on practice. [L.3] Dictionaries chase usage rather than fixing it. Drift matters when it moves belonging or power, not when it simply mints novelty. The shifting of this coupling between the word and the former meaning to the latter does not strip the word of meaning or function.

It is evidence that the coupling of the word to a given meaning is also dependent upon the collective of people and the pervasive culture of the time. [L.3] It is, among other mechanisms, capable of inducing coupling among contemporaries via admiration, inspiration, love, or otherwise. Such changes can contribute to changes in interpretation, misinterpretation, and charity.

Interpretation, Misinterpretation, Charity, and Authority

How can meaning be evaluated before it has been settled? It cannot. Interpretation is the process by which an audience attempts to resolve utterances into a candidate coupling within a perceptual frame. It succeeds when it enables coherent uptake that supports coordination or evaluation. It is not a subjective relation but regards coupling alignment. Interpretation is not free invention; it is constrained by semantic stabilization, pragmatic context, shared norms, and scope-relevant expectation. [L.27]

Interpretation may vary across scopes due to different risk inheritance, different background norms, or different pragmatic salience. There is no single interpretation which automatically dominates across scopes just as there is no “correct” PFA as we established. Interpretation authority instead tracks who bears the risk of acting on the interpretation and prepares the receivers for scope-sensitive evaluation.

Where collectives have PFA agreement, the normative case is to designate these agreements as “correct” and where they diverge, evaluation happens. When a divergence has taken place and evaluation then centralizes a group to a PFA, within the context of that particular scope-sensitive evaluation, those with the perceptual frame diverging from the PFA are given the “incorrect” designation. Thus, interpretation itself is a process of evaluation and not implicit instrumentalism.

When interpretation fails to enable coherent uptake to support coordination or evaluation it is known as misinterpretation. It occurs when semantic content is insufficient, pragmatic context is mismatched, or when audience background diverges across scopes. It does not inherently imply fault. Many disagreements arise from scope drift rather than factual disagreement.

It functions to separate innocent errors from intentional misdirection which may couple with moralized blame. In this framework, charity operates as an operational discipline, not just moral generosity. Charity requires selecting interpretations that preserve coherence, minimize unnecessary conflict, and maintain possibility for future correction. [L.27]

It is bound in this structure by scope, prior uptake, shared linguistic norms, and reasonable expectations of the audience. Charity is treated here as both (i) a practical interpretive discipline and (ii) a constitutive constraint for stable coupling across agents. Its withdrawal conditions mark the boundary where interpretation becomes domination aware.

It is not without limit, however. Charity may be reduced or withdrawn when ambiguity is repeatedly coupled and exploited, correction is refused, or pragmatic mechanisms are used strategically to evade accountability. For instance, patterns of mis-coupling shift interpretation from error to deception and thus charity may come under re-evaluation. Charity, in this sense, functions to create a principled exit from a perpetual “benefit of the doubt.” [L.27]

As the consequences of acting on a claim become more coercive, the claim must become less dependent upon any single interpreter’s judgment and more open to independent verification, audit, and challenge. Since interpretive uncertainty can scale into coercive outcomes, epistemic requirements must scale with autonomy-impact. The Epistemic Risk Ladder (ERL) is the bridge rule linking interpretation to standing-to-coerce thresholds. The ladder is as follows:

ordinary reliance (low risk scope)

corroboration required (moderate risk)

independent operationalization (high risk)

audit / transparency requirements (institutional risk)

ERL Example (public-health rumor):

Level 1 (ordinary reliance): A friend claims “the water is unsafe.”

Level 2 (corroboration): Check multiple independent reports; ask for source and date.

Level 3 (independent operationalization): Consult a published test protocol or verified lab report; reproduce sampling steps if feasible.

Level 4 (audit/transparency): Require public posting of sampling locations, timestamps, thresholds, and an appeal pathway for disputes.

As autonomy-impact rises (closures, mandates), evidentiary standards must climb the ladder before coercive standing can be claimed.

Level one of the ERL corresponds to Nietzschean execution-level freedom and is self-regarding only. Level two is where epistemic humility becomes ethical responsibility and creates soft influence. Level three is where the hand-off from disguised will to these framework constraints happens via standing to coerce tests as limited coercion emerges. Level four is where coercion becomes systemic and epistemic authority becomes answerable structurally via legitimate authority.

Where claims are received, evaluation is enabled. Evaluation of claims presupposes that a claim has been identified, scope has been clarified, and it’s meaning has been stabilized enough for comparison to a PFA. Since disputes over truth often mask unresolved interpretive disagreement, interpretation of claims causally must be addressed prior to evaluations of truth claims.

Truth Claim Evaluation (TCE)

One of the most persistent questions in philosophy concerns truth. As this work is not a metaphysical theory of truth, we do not treat this term as objective in the sense of objective truths pertaining directly to reality. Rather, truth in this framework applies to Perceptual Frame Agreement as distinct coupling. Truth claims are then attempts at coupling a claim to the relevant scope of the perceptual frame being addressed.

The result of this configuration is that truth undergoes evaluations based on the relevance of the claim to scopes of community, the agreement of perceptual frames from the standpoint of that scope, a comparison between the PFA of the scope and the claim, and the moral reliability and integrity of the agents making the claim. Where truth claims are called into question the operational imperative in this structure is ordered. The process by which a group evaluates truth claims in this framework is known as a Truth Claim Evaluation (TCE), and the process is as follows:

Scope Evaluation: The claim is evaluated for scope to determine who inherits risk by the claim itself as compliant with Risk-Inheritance & Validation. The scope of community which inherits the validated risk becomes the scope of community which has standing to make the evaluation of truth because the validated risk inheritance is what couples them to the claim itself. While smaller communities may additionally couple, this is an important step to maintain as it is an explicit step to invalidating speech domination over truth claims.

PFA Alignment: The community at this given scope must first undertake the efforts to achieve a perceptual frame agreement to establish a base-level of understanding for what the truth is as it relates to the perception. Importantly, this is not deciding of an implicit or objective truth, and it is not purely based on the rhetoric or speech of participants. Perceptions do differ. Where claims concern empirical systems, PFA is constrained by interaction with those systems and their consequences, not by consensus alone. In the section regarding methods for mitigating this, there are listed methods for aligning to perceptual frame agreement in order to avoid rule by consensus. It is the burden of such communities that have determined truth claims to be relevant to them to engage in these processes.

Comparison: Once the community has reached a PFA regarding what the operational imperative is for the claim, the consideration of the claim is compared against that PFA. Where the PFA is in alignment with the claim of truth, the presumptive operational imperative is to determine that the statement was “True” or “honest”. After this, the group can evaluate impact. Where there is disagreement between the PFA and the claim, a further test is made.

Agent Consideration: If there is disagreement between the PFA and the claim, there is no inherent way to directly couple the claim to that agreement by definition. In some communities this is given a designation of being a “lie” or “dishonest”, but this isn’t strictly an objective claim in this framework. Those terms simply apply to claims which cannot be reconciled to the PFA of the group at that scope. In such cases, the moral reliability and moral integrity of the individual become tools for the group to evaluate the agent who made the claim. Moral reliability and integrity do not convert false claims into true ones; they guide how groups interact with unresolved or irreconcilable claims.

It is important to remember a few key distinctions here. The PFA of the group does not define a truth objectively in this framework. Truth is not defined by consensus but is instead an outcome of a corrigible evaluation procedure constrained by interaction, consequence, and risk-inheritance. The capacity for the group to be incorrect still exists. It is not immutable but becomes an operational imperative.

As new perceptions emerge from more information becoming available or new insights being reached, it becomes justified to perform new iterations of the TCE based on the new criteria. This aligns with appeals processes for court systems and with analogues to due process. It is an important distinction which affords pathways to remedy IEW’s that emerge due to insufficient information or poorly aligned PFA.

It is also important to note that this does not imply that all truth claims are equally valid across scopes, but that their authority is bounded by the risks they impose and the communities they implicate. Correspondingly, a truth claim at the scope of a family may take a more valid stance as it regards the family, but this does not absolve the claim of evaluation at the scope of extended family or even local community.

One claim may be evaluated from several scopes wherever they apply, and they may not apply equally across those scopes. Scopes bind them via risk, and this risk inherently imposes ceilings for remediation and impacts the prescription constraints as well so that each scope may also have variant justifications for remediation limits and prescription. Thus, we have demonstrated that NRPP applies to truth claims as well as to potentially coercive speech.

Persuasive and Coercive Speech

Influence, Deception, and Coercive Communication

As interpersonal couplings network together over various groupings, patterns emerge among them and those who find themselves coupled to more individuals gain a form of influence among them. [L.14] Influence, though not always meeting these criteria, can become coercive when it becomes exclusive of reasonable alternative action under conditions of self-authorship through deceptive or autonomy-reducing coupling. [L.11] [L.12]
