[n.130] [n.140] [n.91] While this model does handle prediction well, it commonly fails at legitimacy under uncertainty and accountability across time. It fundamentally struggles with pluralist agreement.

While the features of its accuracy and predictability are necessities to successful ecological governance models, they are insufficient to address the full scope of considerations which are structurally necessary for pluralist society. Without standing validation and NRPP constraints, technocratic management produces domination under the guise of expertise.

Consent-Based Environmental Legitimacy

Consent frameworks for environmental governance assume legitimacy if affected parties consent and democratic procedures are followed. These assumptions are outflows of earlier presumptions of contemporaneous stakeholders, reversible outcomes, and bounded participation sets. These assumptions are often not in alignment with non-parochial evidence and are subject to a fallacy of appeal to majority.

Consent based models are absent of stakeholder and risk bearer consideration. Future generations cannot consent and ecosystems cannot self-advocate. While inherited risk persists due to the interdependent coupling of environment to future agents, consent cannot be meaningfully given for irreversible inheritance. Non-participants remain exposed regardless of refusal.

Unanimous consent in the present moment does not afford legitimacy for binding future risk bearers. Even though democratic legitimacy may become procedurally valid in these cases, it is structurally illegitimate and fails STC-5 evaluations that are structurally bounded to pluralist society. Consequently, consent-based environmental governance alone is insufficient to satisfy the structural needs of society.

Consent is necessary where available but cannot ground legitimacy alone. It cannot rescue standing under irreversibility. Environmental legitimacy cannot be procedurally derived where coupling precedes participation. Consent that does not consider future risk bearers is functionally incomplete and subject to “might makes right” mentality.

Non-Accidental Failure

These failures across these models are not accidental. There are common structural assumptions across all of these models. They all lack reversibility and substitutability to some degree. They stifle voluntary exit and do not consider contemporaneity.

Environmental domains break these assumptions because they impose proxy necessity, temporal asymmetry, and the concept of irreversibility. [n.129] Environmental domains are particularly sensitive to exit collapse and give rise to a variant form of autonomy in formal autonomy. Where legitimacy cannot be preserved under any dominant model, what remains is not optimization or agreement but the management of unavoidable loss, remainder, and tragedy.

Scale, Tragedy, and Remainder

Failure, Tragedy, Irreversibility, and Moral Remainder

The diagnostic signals of failures in standing for resource governance then structurally implicit. Decisions made without future representation, permanent licenses under irreversible depletion, ‘consultation’ without veto or revision power, or emergency extraction normalizes as a baseline are all key signals of failure. Where they are present, a decoupling between some level of the community and the ecosystem has occurred.

Consequently, unjustified coercion takes place and standing is not validated. This does not imply that institutions, agents, states, or other actors within the community are regulated in power or capacity. Instead, it implies that they have decoupled themselves in a way that recognizes failed standing as it relates to the environment and resources themselves. Colloquially we have referred to this condition as being ‘unsustainable.’

Some losses simply cannot be repaired. Some thresholds will inevitably be crossed. Extinction is a reality that has already manifested for some species. Ecosystems have already collapsed to some degree. Losses as they regard climate change have some aspects that cannot be simply repaired at this point.

Sometimes these wrongs are intentional and sometimes they rise to the level of IEWs. While some generations and agents assert that they are not to be the subject of attributive blame on account of this, the moral remainder remains. Moral remainder reflects emergent coupling between irreducible loss and interdependent obligations that cannot be jointly satisfied. [n.52] [n.53] [n.59] With that remainder comes the obligation for plural communities to address these concerns or concede that their own endurance is up for debate.

Sometimes repair isn’t possible within these systems. The responsibility to attempt those repairs or create alternative systems which perpetuates that endurance remains structural to UCE. While this can be something that is denied, the denial of those responsibilities is coupled directly with the PFA that does not value human endurance and is a declarative normative stance for those agents.

Considering the finite resources available from the planet and the ever-expanding human population, unsustainable practices create irreversible risk inheritance for future stakeholders. [n.35] This irreversible risk inheritance creates a coupling between our current generation, whichever that may be, and that of their successors and it becomes structurally necessary within the framework to take these considerations with deep sincerity.

As in moral injury, ecological destruction leaves a remainder. Some losses cannot be compensated, restored, or offset. With cases of extinction, for example, these losses have those ends foreclosed upon. This is the justification for heightened restraint regarding those resources prior to collapse, rather than relying on tragic acceptance and regret afterward. Relevance accounts not only for action guidance but also what is lost beyond repair. As resources become scarce and coordination is required catastrophic cases may emerge.

Catastrophic Edge Cases

Total Refusal

When all or most relevant agents refuse participation, reject constraints, or deny standing claims, this can be seen as total refusal. In this case there is no consensus, no buy-in, and no procedural legitimacy is established. It is characterized not by structural failure inherently but by a failed coupling between the ecological model and public society.

Where society fails to couple to these constraints, exit collapse and IEWs emerge. Refusal does not inherently eliminate exposure. Systems that govern the well-being of the plural community and are required for their UCE still persist even when constraints are refused. Harm can likewise continue without intentional coordination.

Coupling persists regardless of refusal and standing arises from impact, not assent. Legitimacy therefore cannot be grounded in consent. Standing is a structural diagnostic, not an elective to optimize societal conditions. Refusal does not remove responsibility once autonomy is impacted. ALRP structurally couples this inherently to those who are members of the community.

Constraints to responses and the prevention of punitive domination are mitigated by the NRPP principle even in these cases. Ceilings may still apply even when prescriptions are rejected. Refusal does not nullify legitimacy constraints; it raises evidentiary and proportionality burdens structurally.

When total refusal emerges, legitimate action becomes narrower, more defeasible, and more heavily constrained. These are not prescriptive measures but structurally interdependent coupling results. Refusal removes procedural legitimacy but does not change structural standing within systems.

Ignorance and refusal to do what is necessary to maintain the structural requirements of society, if unaltered and unchanged, culminates in the structural collapse of the coupling of that society to those requirements. Where no alternatives are available or considered, ultimately such societal structures collapse either into domination systems which are self-preservationist or completely.

Asymmetric Power

Asymmetric power emerges where one or more actors possess disproportionate economic power. This can take the form of military force or other control of critical resources by other means. When this form of catastrophic case takes shape, other agents lack exit, enforcement ability, and bargaining capacity.

This catastrophic case causes structural coercion and a collapsing of alternatives. In these events, coupling is imposed rather than negotiated. Legitimacy cannot be inferred from capacity or dominance. Consequently, in these cases, standing is intensified for those with no exit. Power to act does not imply standing to act. [n.118]

Asymmetric power shifts STC-5 toward protecting the weakest risk bearers where proxy standing becomes necessary for those who are structurally silenced. In such cases, NRPP remains to limit scope even when enforcement is possible.

Asymmetrical power increases legitimacy burdens on the powerful and escalates constraint requirements. This framework explicitly rejects might-makes-right mentality. Power amplifies responsibility rather than erasing constraint.

Coordination Failure

Coordination failure emerges when agents prefer mutual restraint and long-term preservation but simultaneously exhibit mistrust, collective action problems, and prisoner-dilemma dynamics. [n.36] [n.145] This failure often comes about due to time-binding and extraction logic. Where those concepts are present, the pathway to failure is enabled.

Regardless of coordination efficacy, coupling persists in amid failures of this kind. Legitimacy is not dependent on mutual agreement. As coordination begins to fail and thresholds approach for irreversibility, standing escalates.

As standing escalates, ceilings emerge sooner and are justified to prevent forced emergency coercion. Precaution becomes structurally warranted rather than fear-based. NRPP constraints favor early and light constraints to later and harsh ones in this case. Coordination failure is not morally neutral once irreversibility looms.

Failure to coordinate itself does not justify inaction. Instead, it justifies earlier intervention, narrower options, and stricter ceilings. Where coordination fails, constraint replaces negotiation. This does not remove consent in such situations but narrows the field of negotiation to impress the urgency for those who coordinate. The structure itself becomes more inherently coercive to prompt coordination where it has not emerged as a property of negotiation.

Worst Case Scenario

In the worst sense, compound collapse emerges ecologically simultaneously. Where failures like refusal, asymmetry, coordination breakdown and irreversible harm stack, real crises take shape. [n.175] This is not hypothetical.

We have seen crises like these emerge with the mass bleaching of the Great Barrier Reef, coinciding with sharp coral declines after extreme marine heatwaves. Peer-reviewed work documenting high bleaching and high mortality underscores AIMS reports that this stress event is not reversible in many areas and may be approaching a point of irreversibility altogether. [n.178] [n.180] It is a demonstration of asymmetry of power, coordination breakdown, and irreversible loss.

Another example is the degradation of the Amazon and drought/fire feedback. [n.179] It illustrates a contemporary refusal and under-enforcement regime under asymmetric incentives. Cross-jurisdictional coordination breakdown and repeated shocks already produce irreversible losses in parts of this system. Assessments and research summaries describe these intensifying pressures from deforestation, droughts, fires, and illegal activities. They likewise have given warnings regarding destabilization and localized harm.

Cases like these examples imply maximum stress on the framework of pluralist society. Coupling becomes total and unavoidable and standing becomes universal among risk bearers. In these cases, legitimacy must be structural rather than procedural as a reflection of the structural emergence of the crisis.

The toolset likewise maximizes constraint at crisis level. NRPP becomes the dominant limiter while ceilings remain strict, and prescriptions become narrow and time-bound. Audits become essential to prevent the normalization of emergency practices. [n.92] Though proxy standing is unavoidable during crises, it become heavily constrained.

When crises emerge, no solution preserves full autonomy. Instead, the framework works to minimize domination, allocate loss transparently, and prevent unlimited coercion. When loss is unavoidable or inevitable, legitimacy governs how loss is borne.

Legitimacy Amid Guaranteed Loss

Some ecological failures cannot be repaired. Some cannot be reversed and oftentimes they cannot be equitably distributed. Even when these cases do not culminate in total UCE collapse, moral remainder persists. As noted in previous chapters, tragic acceptance remains where the structure of society itself is not compromised to a total failure point.

While power structures tend to assert force more brazenly and superfluously during times of crises and domination may emerge, this does not inherently grant legitimacy to those structures. Even when outcomes are tragic, proportionality, transparency, accountability, and defeasibility constraints still apply.

When loss is guaranteed structural resolution no longer presents legitimacy in terms of consent, success, or benefit. Instead, it means constraint without domination, loss without exploitation, and endurance without denial. When legitimacy must operate under guaranteed loss locally, the necessity of non-local and global constraint becomes unavoidable.

Global Commons and Non-Local Coupling

Ecosystems themselves regard the concept of a system that is self-contained to a degree. Regardless of this perspective, ecosystems themselves also engage with interaction of a kind. Where some ecosystems produce or have an output, the outputs they create have capacity to become inputs for other ecosystems.

Consider the interaction of these systems on our planet. Rainforests generate massive atmospheric nutrients and moisture flows. These rainforests are major engines of evapotranspiration and release mineral-rich dust and volatile organic compounds which seed clouds and influence nutrient deposits over the ocean. [n.76] [n.77] [n.78]

Atmospheric transport delivers nutrients to the ocean surface and Atlantic trade winds, and large-scale atmospheric circulation carry these nutrients away from Africa and into the Atlantic Ocean, acting as fertilizers for marine ecosystems. [n.73] They provide iron and phosphorus that stimulates phytoplankton growth.

Phytoplankton depends on nitrogen, phosphorus, iron, and sunlight. These nutrients are foundational to photosynthetic organisms that are responsible for at least 50 percent of the earth’s oxygen. [n.72] [n.75] Likewise, these phytoplankton supply nearly all marine food webs.

As zooplankton like krill and larval fish eat this phytoplankton they transfer the energy from the microscopic level to mobile marine animals. Small fishlike anchovies, sardines, herring, and mackerel directly feed on those zooplankton, and they are major food sources for larger fish species, sea birds, and whales.

What we can see from this example is that the solitary ecosystem of the rainforest does not exist in isolation. Proxy standing, tiered validation of the constituents, and non-parochial evidence constraints apply to the beneficiaries of these systems as well. Jurisdiction, though a system of administration for pluralist collectives, does not override this coupling.

No volume of policy or administration from a state has the capacity to render these interdependent systems moot. National sovereignty does not defeat standing for these dependents. While their influence and force are not stripped by this invalidation, structurally, the choices of those entities necessarily cause outcomes in spite of that influence and power. Where resources apply to global commons and non-local groups, exchange and economics become structurally necessary to those larger entities.

VII — About Economics

Purpose: This section examines how the coupling-standing-legitimacy engine operates within the domain of economics and how misinterpretation of coupling produces characteristic failures of standing in this domain. It sets out to evaluate economics in a light different from growth orientation where coordination and endurance become the primary values instead. It advances the toolset into a domain with high volumes of conflict as a test to its durability across domains.

Orientation

What This Chapter Is and Is Not

This chapter treats economics as coordination under scarcity rather than value maximization, efficiency, optimization, or welfare aggregation. It applies the same standing-based engine developed in prior chapters to economic institutions, markets, property, labor, money, and debt. It provides a legitimacy framework for economic coordination, diagnosing when markets coordinate and when they dominate, without presupposing any particular economic ideology or institutional form.

This chapter is not a defense of capitalism, socialism, or any fixed economic system. While there may be commonalities within those systems to this framework, this framework itself is neither endorsing nor rejecting whole established models of economics. The framework here exists as an evaluative tool for those other models such that the principles and tools may be used to evaluate their efficacy toward plural ends.

As a result, this chapter is not a theory of value or utility itself. Value and utility for the economic means within a structure are defined by those structures. While those means should rightfully be coupled to the tools which this framework sets out in the case that the economy in question is pursuing the endurance of plurality, it does not presuppose what those values or utilities are in and of themselves. Instead, it is for each pluralist community to establish those themselves predicated upon this framework.

This is neither welfare economics nor moralized redistribution either. While there may be an element which considers the autonomy of the collective to be coupled to the welfare of the economic plural community itself, welfare economics as a concept of people getting what they want via utility and opportunities is not inherently a part of that coupling. Consequently, the coupling of a community to an economic system does not directly imply a redistribution based on moral standing and does not inherently suppose that every member is ultimately coupled to their desired end state economically.

This chapter sets out to demonstrate the cross-domain portability of the tools and framework that has been previously established by extending it into the economic domain. This is realized as a legitimacy framework for economic institutions and policies. It follows with a set of constraints and validations as have other domains previously in this text.

Economically speaking, this framework applies as a constraint-based account of when markets coordinate and when they dominate. [n.81] [n.118] Unlike accounts that treat spontaneous order, efficiency, or equilibrium as legitimacyconferring, this framework treats markets strictly as coordination instruments whose outputs require independent standing justification.

Economic efficiency becomes normatively relevant only after standing is established; absent standing, efficiency merely optimizes coercion. This framework does not suppose any metaphysical values for that domination or coordination but evaluates them based on their relation to pluralist spaces and, once relevant, efficiency may enter. The goal of this framework applied here is the same goal as it is with any domain—to establish what conditions are necessary for the endurance of that pluralism. Markets, by definition, are a form of pluralism. [n.107] [n.137]

Within this scope of the cross-domain engine the necessity to evaluate the justification of intervention remains identical, while the nature of those outcomes are coupled to the domain itself so that the actions which are taken are unique to the domain while the scope of justification is not. Those couplings are unique in nature and shape how standing takes place within each domain. One such factor in this case is that of scarcity.

As the economic abundance, opportunity, and resources become scarcer, the Risk-Inheritance valuation for the community necessarily changes. These changes imply that the abundance or lack thereof itself is what is coupled to the community so that, where it begins to impact the autonomy of the collective itself, the criteria for evaluation of that coercion enter.

This framework sets out to establish how such changes reshape standing economically. It analyzes economics as a standing-relevant domain where coordination mechanisms can become autonomy-constraining without force, intent, or illegality. It is not an argument that markets are inherently just or unjust or a claim that inequality is inherently illegitimate. It does not rank economic outcomes in isolation. It evaluates when economic arrangements acquire standing to bind, exclude, or foreclose autonomy.

Function

This chapter serves multiple functions as it takes on the toolset and engine which this framework endorses. In this framework, economics is recast as coordination under scarcity rather than value maximization. [n.35] [n.93] [n.107] We have denied any necessary coupling of the resources or outputs themselves as we recognize them to any implicit value or metaphysical entity or concept thus far, granting us this capacity.

Within this system, what some have conjectured to be authorities morally or otherwise become standing-governed tools of coordination. Tools like markets, prices, labor, money, debt, growth, and redistribution all serve the need of coordination in this sense. True to the claim at the outset, these tools serve the function of endorsing cooperation in pluralist spaces and economics are, by definition, a pluralist space.

As with any other domain which enters pluralist space in this framework, the same conditions bind the couplings which occur within the domain. Economic coercion is no different than other forms of coercion in that when the resources and needs of a society are coupled to the economic factors of that society and the agents within it are coupled to the resources, this creates a dependency chain that implicitly gives economics coercive capacity. [n.25] [n.118]

Since economic coercion exists in a very real sense for constituents within pluralist communities this coercion then must pass the same constraints as any law or force otherwise in this structure. To gain standing, economic coercion must pass the same STC-5 standards as morality, language, or politics. The actions are likewise scaled by NRPP both in action and in remediations so that economically an agent is not justified to simply retaliate via economic devastation without sufficient publicly available non-parochial evidence. [n.23]

This is not to imply that economic coercion outside of these parameters happens or is not possible by force. Again, this framework does not speak to those elements as something that cannot happen but labels those efforts as structurally authoritarian and unjustified coercion. Power and force remain economically regardless of those labels in those cases, however as a framework this structure gives them a defined standpoint as to their benefit or detriment for pluralist space.

As with other domains, off-ramps and correction exist for the function of the collectives within those pluralist spaces to stand upon the operational imperative to act in the best interest of their survival. Where moral, linguistic, or political coercion is often episodic, economic coercion is often ambient, cumulative, and time-binding.

Scope and Domain Applicability

While this framework does not presume market economies, formal institutions, or state enforcement, it does utilize them. The concept of the engine applies wherever coordination under scarcity exists and access to survival or future agency can be conditioned. This might be markets, kinship systems, customary obligation, informal exchange, policy regimes, or force. [n.136] [n.81]

Markets, subsistence systems, informal economies, and state-mediated economies differ in their coordination mechanisms, not their susceptibility to coercion or standing failure. The framework therefore is evaluative of economic arrangements by their coupling to autonomy, exit and risk inheritance.

Where institutional form takes shape, the content is intended to speak to them, but this work does not presume all systems naturally integrate institutional systems. Where they do not, the toolset and engine still couple to the economic system by definition. Economic standing applies even where no formal institutions exist because dependency alone can generate coercive relevance.

Expectations

In this chapter, readers should expect familiar economic justifications like efficiency, growth, consent, and price to fail as legitimacy substitutes. Markets will be treated as conditional coordination tools and not as inherently autonomous or metaphysical entities. Readers accustomed to treating markets as normatively neutral should expect that assumption to be withdrawn wherever exit collapses or survival is gated.

This section may cause readers discomfort where voluntary exchange can be diagnosed as coercive, price is rejected as legitimacy, and inequality is treated as conditionally relevant rather than morally decisive. Readers accustomed to appeals to an “invisible hand” of the market will encounter no acceptance of mystic or metaphysical claims in this chapter.

The author expects that readers will be willing to separate coordination success from legitimacy and evaluate economic systems structurally rather than ideologically. The chapter assumes the reader is willing to evaluate economic systems without appealing to virtue, ideological identity, or aggregate welfare alone. The reader should be willing to accept that economic coercion can exist without force and to accept repair and constraint without moral blame.

Translations

The translations of this chapter remain structural rather than ideological. They are standing-oriented rather than outcome-oriented and compatible with pluralist disagreement. They are time-sensitive and scale-sensitive while showing how economic power becomes coercive without intent.

The purpose of these translations is to expose how economic structures condition autonomy and distinguish pricing signals from standing. They translate economic terms into coupling, exit, risk, and time-binding. Where any of these terms do not conform to other economic models, they strictly adhere to the structural framework that pluralist society is comprised of and which those models rest upon.

Translation Table

Economics: Coordination of scarce resources under conditions where not all preferences can be simultaneously satisfied.

Scarcity: A structural condition of finite resources amid competing claims; not a moral failure.

Economic Coordination: Allocation of access, production, and distribution under scarcity without implying legitimacy.

Economic Coercion: Autonomylimiting dependency created by survival gating, exit collapse, or timebinding—independent of force.

Standing (Economic): The legitimacy of an economic arrangement or intervention to bind, exclude, or constrain autonomy.

Market: A coordination mechanism for decentralized information and exchange; not a source of legitimacy.

Price: A signal of relative scarcity and demand; not permission, entitlement, or standing.

Price ≠ Standing: The principle that willingness or ability to pay does not justify exclusion or coercion.

Efficiency: An outcome metric relevant only after standing is established.

Utility: A preference measure insufficient to establish legitimacy or autonomy relevance.

Exit (Economic): The practical ability to refuse participation without catastrophic loss of survival or future agency.

Exit Failure: A condition where refusal is nominal, punitive, or nonviable.

RiskInheritance (Economic): The distribution of downside exposure across agents, including future agents.

Option Loss: The narrowing of future choices over time due to economic structures.

TimeBinding: Economic commitments that bind future agency to past conditions.

Debt: A temporal obligation that constrains future autonomy and exit.

Inescapable Debt: Debt that forecloses exit, discharge, or renegotiation; structurally coercive.

Labor: The coupling of human agency to economic coordination; not a commodity.

Labor Market Failure Boundary (LMFB): The threshold where labor exchange becomes coercive due to exit failure.

Livelihood Gating: Conditioning access to survival resources on economic participation.

Structural Coercion: Constraint arising from system design rather than intentional enforcement.

Property: Delegated control subject to standing constraints, not absolute dominion.

Property as Conditional Standing: Property rights are legitimate only insofar as they preserve autonomy and correction.

Capital: Property extended through time and accumulation.

Capital Accumulation: Scaleamplifying control that escalates standing burdens.

Capital Concentration: Accumulation that forecloses exit, concentrates risk, or binds future agents.

Money: An abstraction layer for coordination; not a source of value or legitimacy.

PolicyBased Mutual Provision (PMP): Coordination without currency via shared obligation and guaranteed access.

Institution (Economic): A coordination technology that allocates risk and enforces rules.

Firm: A hierarchical coordination institution with coercive capacity over labor and access.

State (Economic Role): An institution with nonoptional jurisdiction over taxation, contracts, and public goods.

Market Failure Escalation Ladder (MFEL): Market → Firm → State → Legitimacy crisis escalation pattern.

Inequality: A descriptive distributional condition; not inherently unjust.

Economic Wrong: An autonomyimpairing structural outcome, with or without culpable agents.

Independently Emergent Wrong (IEW): Systemlevel economic harm without a responsible actor.

Public Good: A nonexitable, nonsubstitutable, autonomyconditioning good.

Externality: Risk imposed on nonconsenting, nonexiting agents.

Standing for Intervention: The legitimacy to impose constraints when coordination fails under shared risk.

Growth: An increase in throughput; not a legitimacy warrant.

Endurance: The preservation of autonomy thresholds over time.

PostGrowth: A legitimacy standard that rejects growth as a universal telos.

Economic Emergency: Widespread exit collapse combined with irreversibility and escalating risk.

Provisional Justification (Economic): Timebound permission to deviate from normal coordination under emergency.

AntiPrecedent (Economic): Emergency measures cannot justify normal governance.

Repair (Economic): Restoration of exit, autonomy, and correction capacity.

Market as Informational Tool: Markets coordinate signals, not legitimacy.

Structural Domination: When economic coordination hardens into unavoidable constraint.

Economics As a Coordination Domain

Scarcity as the Defining Condition

Economics is the study of how societies coordinate scarce resources under conditions where not all preferences can be satisfied simultaneously. [n.107] It is important to understand that when the word scarcity is used, it is being used to mean finite resources amid competing claims and non-simultaneous satisfaction. This is a structural inevitability in pluralist communities. [n.35] Economic asymmetries reproduce the A > B structure directly: resource flows amplify or mute standing depending on whether the system preserves or violates the symmetry condition.

Sources and resources within an ecological system are not infinite. Likewise, where a population within a particular ecosystem is expanding, the affordable resources within that ecosystem are diluted necessarily. In the most literal sense, one could distribute them exactly equally as a reflection of the population growth to see this taking place. Where more human beings endure there is an implied consumption of resources at least to the minimum extent that those resources are needed for that endurance.

Scarcity, in this framework, is then structural, not moral. [n.35] [n.36] There isn’t a “right or wrong” element to the idea that these claims are in competition itself—it is an emergent property of finite systems and collaboration. Where the coordination within those systems fails under scarcity it can lead to domination rather than inefficiency. The structural nature of scarcity is itself the inefficiency. The failure of the coordination and collaboration creates the opportunity for coercion and domination.

Economic Coordination vs Moral Evaluation

When considering economics, it becomes necessary to distinguish distinctly between economic coordination and moral evaluation. Moral evaluation of these properties would be to assert that something was “good/bad” or “right/wrong” in this domain. It might assert what is “just” or “unjust” for the agents involved. Economic coordination on the other hand is concerned with who gets what, when, and how.

Economics itself does not generate standing. It does not stand independently to coerce and does not dictate any outcomes implicitly for autonomy. Instead, economic outcomes must pass standing constraints. Utility aggregation is insufficient to create these standings because utility itself is not coupled to autonomy-impairing outcomes necessarily. [n.36] [n.123] [n.145] While someone may find a better economic situation for themselves to aggregate utility to them, this does not presume that it has standing for them because of this, for example.

Why would it? The claim to standing is predicated upon the risk-inheritance, impact to autonomy, capacity and agency of the individual, and how those relate to STC-5 standards. They are limited likewise by NRPP constraints. When these measures are applied to such utility aggregation there is no inherent risk or impact to autonomy by not coupling to all forms of utility.

Translating the Toolset

Coupling in Economics

Economically speaking, coupling emerges as structural dependence rather than mere interaction. It is not correlation, market anticipation, or voluntary exchange. Instead, couplings themselves are evaluated on their structural dependency to one another. These dependencies are not always symmetrical, and some agents necessarily bear more constraint than others as a consequence.

Production values, for instance, shape consumption options. Consumption is not a free choice if alternatives are structurally absent. This results in production itself being a normative issue rather than simply a market outcome. When survival goods, cultural goods, or information are structure by production bottlenecks, autonomy collapses into dependency. [n.123] [n.100] [n.202] This fundamentally undermines the idea that consumer sovereignty dissolves responsibility. [n.81] [n.136]

As it regards that production, labor is coupled to income. Labor markets themselves generate standing, not just contracts, because income itself is required for survival. Income itself within economic structures is the means to healthcare, housing, and participation. When refusal to work entails loss of basic agency, consent is constrained. [n.116] [n.117] [n.146] How can someone be said to have the “option” to work if not working is to strip them of their agency at all? This dependency creates relevance even without coercion and this coupling grounds later discussions of domination, refusal, and resistance.

When laborers enter into markets, prices do not just regulate information but also access. High prices function as exclusion mechanisms. [n.123] [n.100] Consequently, price signals are also not normatively thin. Instead, when prices gate essentials or civic participation, they act as de facto constraints on agency. This is not to say that all pricing is unjust—only that pricing can acquire standing when coupled to necessity.

Where pricing establishes gates, these gates are not isolated cases of pure exclusivity. Instead, the capacity to borrow exists in the form of debt, or an obligation to pay as a temporal function. Debt is not only an intertemporal exchange; however, it limits exit, refusal, and renegotiation by determining future requirements. Debt binds future choices to past conditions and is a clear demonstration of irreversibility without physical force. [n.102] [n.108] Long-horizon constraint on agency generates relevance even when initially “voluntary.”

The infrastructure of these settings determines who can participate in the economy at all. Non-participants are not choosing exclusion; they are structurally excluded. For this reason, infrastructure decisions are normatively prior to markets. [n.81] [n.51] Control over infrastructure generates standing because it conditions agency within the scope of the plural community that relies on economics.

Economic relevance arises when economic structures couple directly to autonomy, survival, or future options. It regards production, consumption, labor, livelihood, prices, access, debt, future agency, infrastructure, and participation. Relevance in this framework remains structural. Standing arises without intent and harm/offense language is insufficient to establish relevance to economic standing. [n.118] [n.136]

This is not a rejection of markets themselves, and not all couplings justify intervention. Relevance triggers burden-shifting, not automatic prohibition. ERL, NRPP, and remedy ladders still govern responses so along with Ceiling vs Prescription models and standing to coerce conditions. Once economic coupling is made explicit, questions of welfare, efficiency, and growth can no longer be treated as normatively self-contained; they must be evaluated against the autonomy-relevant structures they presuppose. [n.104]

Standing in Economic Claims

Standing arises economically only when economic arrangements allocate risk, foreclose options, or eliminate exit, thereby coupling economic outcomes to autonomy. The economic facts of price, contracts, and policies do not themselves automatically generate normative authority. [n.31] [n.60]

Standing in the economy authorizes whoever already has legitimate coercive ability. This framework does not generate new sovereigns. Economic failures where no legitimate actor exist take on the form of IEWs rather than policy failures themselves. These considerations allow the framework to scale to transnational or fragmented economies where economic outcomes may vary.

Within an economy, prices, contracts, and policies describe the outcomes. Standing itself concerns who may legitimately impose or enforce those outcomes. This is then definitively separating standing from separate normative claims of legality, efficiency, or equilibrium. Those claims regard coupling to the system of economics itself rather than to the agent or agents who impose or enforce the outcomes of such systems.

When concerning who may legitimately impose or enforce the outcomes, standing depends on who bears the risk, who loses options, and who cannot exit. Risk allocation within the system of economy is not neutral. Standing inherently increases when downside risk is concentrated rather than shared. [n.118] [n.133] This becomes particularly salient when risk involves survival, health, or long-term agency. Those who stand a concentrated risk to economically lose their lives for being priced out of healthcare have much more standing than those with no risk at all, for instance.

Within these frames of risk it is important to recognize as well that voluntarily assumed risk and structurally imposed risk are not the same. Where one asserts a voluntary risk in attempt to gain economically, they are not predisposed to the risk by the system itself. While agents may create such risks voluntarily that jeopardize their economic sustainability within the system (e.g., gambling addiction, etc.), those behaviors to not impose internal standing or any culpability externally as the structural system did not predispose them to these risks.

Exit, Risk, and Option Loss

So, when does standing arise then? Standing arises when economic arrangements narrow future choices, lock agents into paths, or foreclose refusal without severe costs. [n. 60] Option loss over time in this sense matters more than momentary disadvantage because it is the ultimate outcomes as they apply to the plural community that these arrangements are coupled to. Since not all outcomes have an immediately terminal outcome, it is the longer-term view of option loss that gains relevance.

Standing in this framework is evaluated on a scalar basis predicated on the varying nested levels of pluralism. For instance, the standing may be established from the PFA of a family but that family belonging to a town means there is a new evaluation economically for that town as well. Neither invalidate one another but the standing is relative to that PFA evaluation itself.

At the cultural scale, exit collapse functions as the baseline standing failure because membership is relational rather than contractual. When refusal becomes nonsurvivable, consent collapses structurally even without enforcement. Exit must be effective, not merely formal. [n.24] [n.36] [n.141] Exit failure can persist even when there are multiple nominal alternatives.

Autonomy in this framework is not a value to be balanced against others, nor a moral preference among competing goods. It is the structural condition under which pluralism is possible at all. Where agents retain viable exit, revisability of commitment, and nonpunitive refusal, disagreement can persist without domination. Where these conditions collapse, coordination ceases to be pluralist regardless of intention, efficiency, or consensus.

For this reason, autonomy functions here as a baseline rather than an outcome. It is not something this framework aims to maximize, distribute, or perfect. It is the precondition that determines whether standing, justification, and legitimacy questions can meaningfully arise in the first place. Any structure that forecloses autonomy collapses the possibility of plural coordination before any further normative evaluation can begin.

Exit failure here does not concern comparative attractiveness of alternatives, but the loss of refusal as a viable option consistent with survival or future agency. These partial-exit collapse cases are still structurally coercive without being a total exit collapse. When exit is blocked, costly, or illusory, economic claims gain normative weight. [n.24] When rendered impossible, it converts market outcomes into constraint-bearing structures because they are now definitively coupled to any agents seeking exit. [n.136]

Standing in economics then can shift the burden of justification, trigger ERL escalation, and requires publicly legible reasons. It does not automatically invalidate pricing or contracts. I cannot mandate a specific policy response or collapse into welfare maximization. It serves as a mechanism to mitigate the outputs of economy for the best interest of pluralist group endurance.

Take the housing market, for instance. High exit costs are typically predicated on geography, jobs, and schools. [n.117] Risk is concentrated on tenants and option loss enters through displacement. Prices in this case carry standing because shelter couples directly to survival and participation within the community.

In labor markets, income becomes coupled to livelihood and creates limited exit due to healthcare, visas, or debt. There is a risk asymmetry between firms and workers so voluntary contracts can still generate standing when refusal is not meaningfully available. Consequently, the emergence of economic outcomes from a market are not what produce standing but the constraint to agency itself.

Examples like this demonstrate how pricing and labor within a community gain standing to coerce that community itself. When pushed to the furthest degree, if all housing were to be priced outside of the range of affordability within an area, this standing to coerce would fail based on the risk evaluation and, via NRPP, the community in the area gains standing to coerce via remediation. This demonstrates how economic claims acquire standing when they allocate risk, foreclose options, or eliminate exit in ways that materially constrain autonomy or future agency.

Autonomy Constraints in Economic Systems

Within economic structures autonomy is built upon the availability of alternatives, non-coerced participation, and reversible commitments. Where those elements are missing or are infringed, so is autonomy, as the concept is inherently coupled to those specific outcomes. Economic constraint is legitimate only where agents lack the capacity to secure the conditions of their own endurance; as such capacity develops, standing for economic control must contract accordingly (CIA).

Where the structure of the economy itself has shown us how constraints arise and where they matter, it further has the capacity to explain how autonomy is structurally limited. Choice within these systems are necessary but not enough to stand alone as sufficient for autonomy. Economic systems can preserve choice while undermining agency. Like with the housing example, if all of the housing in an economy were priced so that you must take out a loan for them and you were foreclosed on leaving because the cost of leaving is also higher, your choice remains while your agency has been undermined.

The presence of the formal choice between moving at a cost you cannot afford and taking a loan you cannot afford to stay is ultimately not indicative of effective agency. Where the choice is present, there is truly no other option outside of the coercive ends of having no shelter or taking on debt. One of those choices constituting a sacrifice of your own safety and autonomy itself by being unsheltered imposes an inherent limitation on agency. This is an example of how markets themselves and voluntariness are not the same.

Economic autonomy minimally requires meaningful alternatives. For the alternatives to become viable to the agents of a community they must be accessible, substitutable, and non-punitive. Where alternatives exist that are unable to be accessed, it is also reasonable to say they do not exist as relevant to that PFA. They do not reasonably couple in the economic domain. While they may couple in other domains using these same tools, they ultimately have no PFA relevance economically when evaluated from that standpoint.

Likewise, when alternatives are not substitutable it can hardly be retained that they are alternatives. The term alternative carries, by definition, the idea of being capable of substitution, whether punitive or not. Where those substitutions imply a level of punitive damage, they cannot be seen as economic alternatives but as coercive punitive actions. “Take-it-or-leave-it” options do not ground autonomy because the scarcity of alternatives converts choice into dependency.

In order for a system to not be one which creates dependency, participation needs to be non-coerced. Where refusal entails a loss of basic survival, social exclusion, disproportionate penalty, or other societal harm there is structural coercion. [n.36][n.24] Economic systems become structurally coercive when participation conditions collapse meaningful refusal, exit, or future agency—though this does not foreclose on interpersonal economic coercion.

If autonomous economic commitments are not bounded by a duration, exit, or renegotiation, this cannot be seen as economic autonomy either. A home loan in perpetuity which is never satisfied is not truly a loan but an obligation to pay or face punitive consequences. We have already discussed how that creates dependency. Where you are unable to negotiate your payments or leave the home, this is essentially then tantamount to ransom for a home and is overtly coercive.

Structural Coercion Without Direct Agency

How can this happen outside of an agent taking action? Structural coercion exists where exit is nominal but infeasible, time binds future autonomy, or survival goods are market based. [n.24] [n.25] [n.118] [n.136] [n.139] Unlike genealogical accounts that suspend questions of legitimacy in favor of description, this framework retains explicit criteria for justification and standing even where coercion arises without identifiable intent. When access to essentials like housing, healthcare, food, and energy are conditional upon market success, the system itself is coercive. When survival depends on market position, refusal ceases to be meaningful. When NRPP is applied, the reflexive aspect of a market position dictating survival is a loss of autonomy over that position as it relates to the agent.

Though legal exit may exist, when costs are prohibitive, alternatives are unavailable and penalties are cascading, nominal exit does not negate constraint. As those risks escalate along ERL, the evaluation of STC-5 for agents increases in standing. Likewise, present consent locking future exit or other actions have a similar effect. When debt, penalties, and compounding obligations narrow future choice, amplify asymmetry, and reduce exit, coercion is operative without presenting force.

Not all markets here are coercive and not all constraints negate autonomy. Temporary, reversible, low-stakes dependence is compatible with agency. This framework diagnoses when thresholds are crossed, not when inequality merely exists. Economic autonomy exists only where participation is meaningfully optional, commitments are reversible, and access to survival and future agency is not conditioned on submission to a single structure. Where economic systems systematically defeat these conditions, questions of efficiency give way to questions of legitimacy, standing, and justified intervention.

Power, Standing, and Manufactured Legitimacy

Power can shape perceptions, procedures, and institutions, but power alone does not generate standing. Where power manufactures apparent legitimacy by foreclosing correction, silencing dissent, or blocking exit, standing collapses rather than transfers. The framework treats such cases not as morally ambiguous but as structurally illegitimate, regardless of stability, compliance, or duration. Power explains how domination persists; standing explains why it cannot justify itself.

Power is a dynamic that is still inherent to systems and yet does not inherently carry normative authority. Instead, it carries a capacity for coercion and dominance. Where economies are concerned with this coercive capacity regards where the capacity for coordination is converted into a form of that structural coercion.

STC-5 for Economic Coercion

Economic policies can move from coordination into coercion then and this coercion must be justified. To demonstrate this in the same sense as law or force, we can apply the Standing to Coerce Test (STC-5) to evaluate their legitimacy to bind agents or foreclose autonomy. This is not only another demonstration of the cross-domain property of the tools but a necessary one within each domain as well.

While economic coercion is real, it often goes unnamed. Economic actions or policies can remove options, bind future agency, and impose non-consensual costs without imposing force. This places them squarely in the domain of autonomy-impacting coercion. Economic necessity isn’t given a special exemption here because scarcity itself does not grant automatic standing. Efficiency, legality or macroeconomic necessity do not substitute for justification. Economic coercion must meet the same legitimacy criteria as political coercion or any other domain. Consequently, we do not modify the rules of STC-5. We simply apply the tool where it is applicable within the domain.

Within the domain, economic coercion is legitimate only if all five gates are satisfied: Risk-Inheritance & Validation, Non-parochial Evidence, NRPP fit, Alternatives considered, and Off-Ramps and Exit identified. The process looks identical for applications within the domain as well:

Identify the coercive mechanism

Identify the risk-bearers

Indicate typical failure modes

State what STC-5 requires for legitimacy

Let’s take on a few examples. Start with taxation. The coercive mechanism is a compulsory extraction of resources backed by enforcement and penalties. Those whose basic autonomy and survival is impacted by the tax are the risk-bearers, as evidenced by public accounting of necessity, scope and burden distribution. NRPP requirements indicate progressive scaling to avoid pushing agents below autonomy thresholds. Alternatives exist as non-tax revenue, narrower bases, and timing adjustments. Off-ramps exist as hardship relief, exemptions, credits, or deferrals. In this evaluation, the standing for failure signal would be flat or regressive taxes that ignore asymmetric exposure.

For another example, let’s look at debt enforcement. The coercive mechanism is a legal compulsion to repay or face asset seizure wage garnishment, or exclusion. Risk bearers are the debtors whose future agency is bound by the debt. Evidence exists as a distinction between strategic default and structural incapacity. NRPP suggests proportional recovery and protection of survival baselines. Alternatives exist as restructuring, forgiveness, or collective risk-sharing. Off ramps include bankruptcy, discharge, and statutes of limitation. The standing failure signal in this case would be perpetual or inescapable debt regimes.

General failure modes of economic coercion likewise exist. Aggregation without exposure weighting, efficiency claims replacing justification, irreversible commitments without exit, absence of review or appeal mechanisms, and temporal displacement of harm are all diagnostics of standing collapse. They are not simply bad economic policies within the system.

Economic instruments themselves acquire standing to coerce only when they satisfy STC-5. When those who bear the risk validate that necessity, evidence is public and non-parochial, the measure is the least autonomy-reducing option, alternatives have been seriously considered, and real off ramps remain available, they retain such standing.

Failure modes are indicative of economic coercion. They lose standing structurally via STC-5 evaluation and cause standing for the agents or institutions that enact them to collapse and opens them to remediation. Passing STC-5 establishes standing to intervene, not discretion over our lives. Without proportional prescription, economic coercion predictably hardens into domination.

NRPP in Economic Prescription

Even by passing STC-5, economic remedies are not universally legitimate even when remedy is justified. Standing itself is not a license to overreach. The act of passing the test of STC-5 establishes the permission to intervene, not permission to maximize impact, punish, or restructure lives indefinitely. Economic coercion is especially prone to over-prescription because the harms it creates are delayed, diffuse, and often framed as “necessary.”

To that effect, economic remedies likewise have a capacity to become punitive without intent. Where economic measures scale automatically, compound over time, and bind future agency, NRPP exists to prevent structural punishment masquerading as policy. One coercion has been justified by STC-5, NRPP determines how it may be applied.

Remedies in the economic domain must satisfy all three of these conditions simultaneously. They must be the least autonomy-reducing means, targeted rather than diffuse, and reversible or reviewable. The non-reflexive part of the principle ensures that agents which are subject to this coercion are not summarily forced into detrimental situations by a single agent or institution. Doing so creates a gateway to authoritarianism from such agents or institutions.

When evaluating the least autonomy-reducing means, economic translations mean finding remedies that neutralized validated harm without collapsing agency. This means economic remediation will prefer partial relief over total withdrawal, graduated obligations over cliffs and income- or capacity-sensitive measures over flat penalties. This can be evaluated by asking “does this remedy preserve the maximum feasible self-authorship consistent with harm prevention?”

When the framework dictates that remedies must be targeted rather than diffuse, it means in principle that burdens must fall on causal sources, not on convenience populations. In terms of economics, this means avoiding population-wide deprivation for localized problems, collective punishment for macro levers, and generalized scarcity responses to specific failures. The question to evaluate this becomes, “are those bearing the burden also those causally coupled to the harm?”

As with other domains, remedies in economics need to be reversible and reviewable. They must allow for exit, renegotiation, and rollback. This takes on the form of sunset clauses, review triggers, and appeal or relief mechanisms. A way to diagnose if this is happening is to check if autonomy can be realistically restored if conditions change. If they cannot, then this is not reversible or reviewable.

What NRPP Does Not Authorize

NRPP in economics does not authorize blanket austerity. Blanket austerity enacts weak causal targeting, diffuse harm, and concentrated autonomy collapse. [n.121] [n.122] This does not preemptively determine that governments may not use spending cuts, tax increases, or a combination of them. It means that they are not a reasonable remedy for economic standing to coerce. The fiscal balance is not enough to justify this action. It treats fiscal balance as sufficient justification and converts coordination failure into mass deprivation.

This framework also does not endorse permanent exclusion such as lifetime bans from markets, blacklisting without appeal, or irrevocable loss of participation. Though this may seem controversial, when considering especially heinous financial crimes or extremely pervasive criminals in that space, that controversy is bleed over from the morality domain where general groups have determined the moral reliability of those individuals to be aligned with moral wrongs in the financial domain.

That is not to say that such actions cannot also weigh in to the risk of those who evaluate such punishments. That said, even in those cases, the prescription limit is not that they should be disabled from participation at all but that their autonomy within the space is constrained to the degree that they have imposed that upon others with their actions, as it would be in any other domain. Permanent exclusion fails because it is irreversible, offers no repair pathway, and forecloses on future agency. This is a proportionality failure, not a denial of wrongdoing or responsibility.

In the same spirit, this framework does not support debt peonage like inescapable compounding debt, wage garnishment without discharge, or intergenerational debt transfer. [n.112] [n.113] These methods bind future autonomy indefinitely. They convert obligations into domination and eliminate exit as a meaningful option and have systematically been used in former systems to justify acts such as slavery. [n.109]

When considering safeguards that comply with NRPP, efficiency is not a proportionality standard. Efficiency has the capacity to justify mass harm, asymmetrical burdens, and irreversible outcomes. [n.123] NRPP instead constrains efficiency whenever it collapses autonomy. While it may be a considering factor it does not become the standard for proportional prescription within the framework.

Likewise, deterrence is not punishment by proxy. Economic deterrence that destroys livelihoods, forecloses participation or binds future agency becomes punitive itself. When prescriptions claim to be deterrents but satisfy any of these criteria, they are no longer simply deterring. NRPP allows constraint to neutralize harm, not suffering to “send a message.”

Within the scope of NRPP and economic repair, the preference is always for repair over retaliation. Whenever possible remedies should restore participation, rebuild options, and re-enable exit. Where structural failures exist and economic IEWs emerge such as housing crises or debt traps, wrongs can emerge without a culpable agent. [n.103] [n.106] In those cases, NRPP prevents scapegoating, moralized punishment, and irreversible harm in response to IEWs.

Even when economic coercion is justified, NRPP requires that remedies be the least autonomy-reducing. Causally targeted and reversible measures capable of neutralizing the harm become the standard for prescription. Economic prescriptions that impose irreversible loss, collective punishment, or permanent exclusion exceed standing and form the basis for domination.

With the limits of economic prescription established and justified coercion afforded for, the markets themselves become the next natural point of focus. Markets in this framework do not operate as moral authorities and price signals cannot justify autonomy-reducing outcomes alone in this framework. Instead, markets are a coordination instrument structurally.

Markets as Informational Tools, Not Moral Authorities

What Markets Do Well

Markets themselves perform coordination functions when autonomy constraints are low. When they persist, they can become signaling mechanisms that become actionable non-parochial evidence to pluralist collective groups. This evidence, being necessary to the framework, couples directly as a mechanism for collective health within the structure.

Prices within markets function as compressed signals of relative scarcity and demand. [n.93] They do not encode moral worth, entitlement, or legitimacy. They do not directly impart a value to the thing itself. Instead, they are domain-local and context-dependent so that scarcity signaling is not justification for exclusion.

Particularly, in complex systems, centralized calculation fails. [n.93] Markets allow agents to adjust their behavior, reallocate resources, and anticipate constraints. These are generally desirable for pluralist ends as systems of finite natures often have shifts which alter the requirements of the collective as well. Likewise, from an economic standpoint, they help establish reasonable off-ramps and exits.

The constraints to markets are that they function as a signaling role that presumes meaningful alternatives, non-coerced participation, and reversible commitments. When those constraints fail, the signal persists but loses normative relevance. Where markets force participation, have no way to pivot, and have locked in commitments, the market itself is coercive to the participants.

Markets also operate well as information-coordination systems. Where knowledge is dispersed, markets have the capacity to coordinate that information without requiring shared values. Information about preferences, local conditions, and opportunity costs that would normally be fragmented across agents can be consolidated and operationalized for the collective. In this capacity, markets answer what is happening and not what should be imposed. They coordinate the information, not reasons themselves. [n.93] [n.100]

Coordinating the information itself works well and markets perform well when participants can enter and exit, risks are not asymmetrically imposed, errors are correctable, and feedback loops remain intact. When markets have compulsory participation, errors compound, and feedback is delayed or blocked, they degrade. [n.103] [n.106] It is evident from the outputs of how markets function that the principles of NRPP and STC-5 play a direct role in the success of those markets as tools.

Constraints to markets emerge where markets enable voluntary exchange. In such cases, voluntariness is a threshold condition. When refusal is not meaningful, market exchange is no longer autonomy-preserving and does not actively signal the outputs that are helpful to the collective that make it beneficial. Consequently, voluntariness requires real exit, tolerable cost of refusal, and absence of survival gating so that formal consent and autonomous consent are not equal.

However, when the stakes are low and exchange is reversible, markets excel at allocating non-essential goods, coordinating preference-sensitive trade, and enabling experimentation and diversity. These domains themselves are characterized by low irreversibility, bounded downside, and symmetric exposure—aligning with the UCE of the group itself.

Markets perform well as signaling and coordination mechanisms under conditions of low coercion, meaningful exit, and reversible exchange. Their outputs describe coordination states, not moral authority or standing to impose outcomes. Understanding what they do well clarifies their limits. When they are treated not as tools but as moral authorities, price signals are misread as justifications and coordination can harden into domination.

What Markets Do Not Do

Markets compress information; they do not generate legitimacy. [n.93] [n.100] [n.123] Price signals summarize relative scarcity and demand, but they do not determine who may be coerced, who must bear harm, or which outcomes are normatively permissible. [n.81] They are not the arbiters of moral or ethical decision making either.

Identifying the normative tasks of markets and what they are incapable of performing even when performing efficiently helps prevent misinterpretation of price signals as sources of that legitimacy or authority. When markets are treated as normative verdicts instead of the outputs they are, the road is paved for domination and oppression.

Markets themselves are not capable of generating standing because standing itself is not an emergent property of exchange. While the members engaging in such exchanges may have standing themselves, the act of exchange conceptually itself does not hold this standing because it is not particularly coupled to the outcomes of the act itself.

Standing concerns who may legitimately bind or constrain others, so market participation alone does not establish authority, entitlement to impose costs, or permission to exclude. Even universally accepted prices do not create standing. Standing requires autonomy-relevant coupling as established previously. Treating prices themselves as standing collapses power into legitimacy, erases risk asymmetries, and disguises domination as coordination.

Markets also do not justify coercion itself. Efficiency within them is not a license to bind. While they can recommend allocations they cannot justify enforcement, penalties, exclusion, or compulsory compliance. Any coercion itself still becomes subject to STC-5 regardless of the level of market efficiency. Claims of market demand is not a justification. It’s a description of pressures—not permission.

Since they cannot give such permission, they cannot validate harm either. Aggregation masks exposure and as market outcomes aggregate things like willingness to pay, purchasing power, and ability to absorb loss there are losses. [n.123] They do not track who bears harm, who loses options, and who falls below autonomy thresholds. [n.100] Harm does not become acceptable simply because it is priced into the structure.

Markets themselves do not contain internal mechanisms for detecting domination, dependency, or irreversible loss. Those require standing analysis, not pricing analysis. They are not concepts that are coupled directly to the exchanges or pricing themselves so what mechanism could impart these conditions for cooperation to them?

Environmental, Social, Governance (ESG) scoring models claim to measure responsibility, sustainability, and ethical risk but they do not measure whether a firm’s profits depend on non-exitable labor conditions. They do not assess whether communities are locked into economic dependency or whether harms are reversible versus “offset.” A company can score highly on ESG while actively suppressing wages via monopsony, engaging in financialized housing extraction, or externalizing long-term community harm—because ESG evaluates disclosure and correlation, not exit, dependency, or reversibility. [n.136]

Welfare and Cost-Benefit Optimization algorithms claim to measure aggregate welfare gains, net social benefit, and efficiency improvements but do not measure even the irreversibility of their harm. They do not address the distribution of autonomy loss, if some losses are non-compensable, or even if those harmed consented or could exit. Aggregation itself is insufficient to satisfy the conditions to gain standing.

Financial algorithms fail here not because they are inaccurate, but because they are answering the wrong class of questions. They optimize outcomes without evaluating standing. These algorithms and ones like them are outcome-oriented rather than standing-oriented. [n.136]

They ask what will happen, how likely is default, and what maximizes return or stability. They do not even pretend to ask who is bound by the outcome, could they refuse reasonably, or if it forecloses future agency. Standing precedes outcome evaluation but algorithms substitute outcomes for legitimacy.

Algorithms encode preferences, not constraints. They infer a willingness to pay, behavioral compliance, and revealed preferences but they do not distinguish freedom of choice or choices made under survival pressure. Consequently, constraint can present as preference, dependency as reliability, and irreversibility as stability.

These formulations cannot represent asymmetry without explicit standing rules. They have the capacity to optimize bias reduction, fairness metrics and risk parity but cannot determine when risk shifting is unjustified, coercion is legitimate, or who is entitled to impose costs. Those require normative constraints, not prediction.

Asymmetric exposure is not resolved by markets either. Symmetry assumptions fail. Markets assume that agents can exit, diversify risk, and wait out losses but market outputs misrepresent legitimacy. Where exit is costly of the entire livelihood of the constituents, exit is not without coercion. Risk diversified doesn’t mitigate the asymmetry as was displayed in the market crashes of the great depression. Since it is not possible to directly predict such downturns as a comparison of the capacity or lifetime of an agent the symmetry assumption inherently is flawed.

Asymmetry as a concept in the market matters because when exposure is unequal pricing doesn’t reflect consent but power. The outcomes then reflect constraint rather than choice and this applies across several areas of the markets including housing, labor, healthcare, and debt markets. This particular weak point of the markets becomes detrimental over time as well.

When those asymmetries lead to irreversibility, markets do not price that irreversibility. Irreversibility exceeds market time horizons. Markets discount the future and systematically underweight extinction, lock-in, and loss of future agency. [n.104] [n.108] [n.114] [n.115] Once harm is irreversible though, no price can compensate and no ex-post adjustment can restore autonomy. Thus, irreversibility requires precaution and proportionality, not optimization.

Since markets cannot generate standing, justify, coercion, validate harm, resolve asymmetric exposure, or account for irreversibility, price cannot be treated as a proxy for legitimacy. It is not bound to the same qualifiers that standing presupposes and loses its claim to be that proxy by that same principle. This brings us to the next explicit point: price is not equal to standing.

Price is Not Equal to Standing

Price within markets expresses willingness to pay under constraint whereas standing concerns who may legitimately impose or enforce those constraints. Where one regards the participant the other regards the enforcement of constraint. Therefore, price cannot be equal to permission, entitlement, or justice itself.

As a general rule prices fail when they gate survival, participation, or future agency. In this capacity market coordination then collapses into domination. If price cannot equal standing in any capacity, one of the most visible demonstrations of that is within labor markets.

For instance, wages gate livelihood rather than preference. They do not merely allocate discretionary goods. Wages determine the access of an agent, agents, or institutions to food, housing, healthcare, legal status and future agency. Labor effectively forces the issues here because exit is structurally compromised.

Claims that someone “can quit” or a platform can do the same presumes viable alternatives and tolerable refusal costs. Instead, in labor markets, exit often entails homelessness, debt, deportation, or medical loss. Where refusal is not survivable, price no longer coordinates—it coerces. [n.116] [n.117] [n.118]

Wage pressure reflects a bargaining asymmetry. It is an indicator of dependency and scarcity of alternatives. It does not validate deprivation, exposure, or future binding. Because of this standing no longer resides in market rates or what employers are willing to pay. Instead, it shifts to workers whose agency is foreclosed and institutions that maintain survival-gating conditions.

If price cannot generate standing where it gates autonomy, then labor markets—where livelihood itself is priced—require a direct standing analysis. The claims of that livelihood are normative claims of the structure itself while the pricing claims themselves are not. The next section takes labor as the clearest case of market coordination crossing into structural coercion.

Labor, Livelihood, and Structural Coercion

Labor as Coupling, Not Commodity

Structurally this framework defines labor as being a coupling of economic coordination and human agency itself. When this coupling is made so directly to the agency of human beings, failures of exit, consent, and bargaining become structurally coercive inherently. They are not merely inefficiencies. Any economic system that stabilizes itself by suppressing capacity rather than enabling transition fails standing structurally.

Labor presumes a commitment of irreplaceable time, not fungible units. The time which is taken is not capable of being refunded in kind. Likewise, it makes use of the physical and cognitive capacities of human existence that degrade, exhaust, and age. Individual labor history shapes skills, health, debt, mobility and even exit capacity. With it being so dependent on human qualities to function, how could it be considered to be coupled to anything less than human agency? It can’t. Labor binds present coordination to future agency.

Where some might contend that these features of human agency are the goods which the agent is effectively selling, goods are alienable and labor is not. Goods can be transferred without ongoing agency—labor cannot. [n.86] [n.116] Goods do not carry forward dependency in most cases; labor does. Treating labor as a commodity or good itself hides the autonomy costs embedded in the exchange. It denies an irreversible human cost in favor of a non-human view. [n.109]

Since labor is inseparable from agency, labor markets generate relevance and standing far earlier than markets in ordinary goods because those goods are the outputs of that labor. This is a structural normative consequence of the system and not a preference of markets themselves. Labor markets imply a volume of human agency and necessarily carry with them the constraints related to them and gain relevance and standing on the same premises. [n.116][n.132]

Exit, Consent, and Labor Coercion

Just as in other aspects of the economy, voluntary employment becomes coercive even without threats, force or illegality. Consent to employment itself requires real exit. Consent is meaningful only when refusal is not risking survival. [n.24] [n.116] Absent those meaningful methods of exit, this presents only as ultimatum. Formal “freedom to quit” does not establish this exit without the ultimatum. [n.142]

This is not a moralized claim because this framework does not assert bad motives. It diagnoses constraint on agency, not blame. Coercion is identified by exit failure, not employer psychology.

For instance, wage labor becomes coercive when alternatives collapse, survival is at stake, or bargaining power asymmetry is extreme. This is structural coercion even if intent isn’t present. Where there is no viable substitute employment, geographic immobility, lock-in, loss of survival resources, one-sided contract terms, replaceability without reciprocity, or information asymmetry the agents do not have a true freedom to consent.

Minimum Conditions for Legitimate Labor Markets

Consequently, a theory of failure-boundary emerges: the Labor Market Failure-Boundary Theory (LMFB). The theory asserts that exit conditions are only legitimate if they are real, survivable, and non-punitive where real alternatives exist not just as theory, exit does not entail loss of basic needs, and there are no cascading penalties for refusal or departure. If exit fails, consent collapses.

It additionally applies that standing failures happen when survival goods are conditional on participation, collective bargaining is foreclosed, or monopsony/near-monopsony exists (a condition where one buyer significantly influences the market for a good or service). If employment is the gatekeeper for healthcare, housing, or legal status, the conditions convert coordination into domination. [n.134] [n.132] The same is true when legal, structural or economic suppression of coordination among workers emerges—such as the breaking of workers unions. When workers face a single or dominant employer or buyer of labor and when exit becomes nominal, the same consequences follow structurally.

These failures have normative consequences, but they do not implicitly prescribe outcomes. The standing failure itself does not mandate a specific policy. It shifts the burden of justification, triggers ERL escalation, and constrains permissible remedies via NRPP.

Labor coupling economic coordination directly to human agency enables constraints to set the legitimacy boundaries for property claims, capital accumulation, and the control of productive assets. This is an instance of interdependent coupling between economic coordination and human agency—neither can be specified independently without collapsing autonomy. The resources needed to provide for the UCE of the community from the PFA of the pluralist space they occupy, and the labor required to meet the same demand both belong to the human agency by virtue of that coupling.

Capitalism which capitalizes this human agency is not only unjustified to be structurally coercive but has historical ties and analogues to slavery. [n.109] [n.110] [ n.111] This criticism is not of exchange, ownership, or profit as such but of systems that convert human need and survival dependence into capitalizable inputs. Human agency cannot be capitalized while abiding the UCE of any pluralist PFA because human agency is not capital.
