It is only after these limits are established that ownership and accumulation can be evaluated without collapsing autonomy into abstraction.

Property, Capital, and Accumulation

What is Property?

Property as a concept exists for the purposes of coordinating use, preventing conflict, and enabling planning. It does not exist to foreclose on the survival of others, bind future agents, or monopolized shared necessity. Property as a designation is a tool which helps coordination and doesn’t carry inherent absolute authority. [n.138] This account explicitly rejects labormixing or natural entitlement as sufficient grounds for property legitimacy, treating exclusion as a standingbounded delegation rather than a prepolitical right.

Property allocates control over scarce resources. These arrangements can scale from individual use to collective exposure so that some levels of property can take any of the scales of agents and institutions between the individual and the state. At scale, property decisions allocate risks, determine access, and condition survival. These are the basic premises of what it means by definition to be an “owner.”

Since property allocates control over these resources, it implies a volume of coercion. Control is a form of coercion and thus is coupled directly to STC-5 tests. It must abide standing constraints.

Property as Conditional Standing

Property as a term imparts delegated control under constraint to the owner. [n.70] An owner in this case is the agent or agents which are coupled to the item or idea itself. Property is the designation for that coupling itself within our economic system. It is a socially recognized delegation and is bounded by autonomy preservation, reversibility, and collective correction.

Due to the structure of how this coupling emerges and the constraints applied, no absolute dominion of any idea or resource is valid. There is no inherent right to exclude beyond legitimacy conditions. Property itself is standing-dependent.

Property grants exclusion power, enforcement power, and temporal control of the thing or idea itself. These are intrinsically coercive properties. Consequently, property is coupled to standing tests because it is coupled to coercive warrants that it implies.

Standing for property collapses when property forecloses correction. If there are no appeals, review, collective override, or locks in harmful arrangements, correction has been foreclosed upon. Likewise, property that destroys autonomy thresholds converts survival into permissioned access.

As mentioned, this is a nod to historical slavery when property itself prices others out of housing, food, healthcare, or energy. It presumes that a quid pro quo can be established for access to the owned idea or resource as a coercive measure of survival. This permissioned access has historically not only been used to control groups but was a core harm embedded in the horrific American slave trade where many slaves only had such permissioned access because they were also designated as property. [n.109]

As was custom with those terrible moments in history and among many other areas, property has an intergenerational binding via the concept of passing property down. To pass property down is to establish a new coupling label of property between a successor to replace your own. Property can likewise bind future agents irreversibly. [n.109] [n.111]

Intergenerational exclusion, ecological depletion, and long-horizon lock-in without consent are some examples of such irreversible future agent binding. The default state of the property designation, depending on use by the owner, can eliminate correction, survival access or future agency. When it does, it loses legitimacy. [n.136][n.81]

This does not establish property as an expression of entitlement. It does not generate justice of validate harm. Moral relevance arises in some of these cases from impact, risk distribution, and autonomy loss. This is evidence of the cross-domain application of this structure but beyond that also the very validation of the necessity to have such a framework. This outcome impacts morality, ecology, economy, politics, and language simultaneously so that individual uses of the tools in those domains are justified.

So, while property is not moral authority, the applications of these tools cross into those scopes. Consequently, the accumulation and scale of these concepts can scale proportionately across those domains when the common thread among them is that agency or autonomy. Capital accumulation is one such category which does so.

Capital Accumulation and Scale

Capital is the concept of property that has been extended through time, accumulation, and reinvestment. It amplifies effects beyond local coordination structurally because the temporal characteristic of capital itself carries an inherent property of the pluralist community that originally coordinated changing. The effect necessarily must be amplified by the definition of what capital is.

When this accumulation scales it creates effects that increase reach, risk-inheritance, and responsibility. Correspondingly, because decisions affect distant people and non-participants are impacted control extends beyond the consent boundaries. Losses are externalized while gains are privatized and vulnerable populations absorb the downsides. Consequently, as impact of capital increases, more burden for standing emerges. [n.101] [n.118] The scale escalates justification requirements.

This concept can be illustrated through a plethora of video and social media posts that evaluate the disparity between the effective value that an individual can provide and the volume of value representative of the world’s richest billionaires. The common thread many of them assert is a mathematical impossibility of meeting the burden of justifying the claim to that much of a resource that is intended to impart value.

The bulk of their worth comes from drastic increases in capital however the flaw that many already recognize is that they are not meeting the burden for standing in that sense—that is, they haven’t justified the capitalization of that much of the resource. This is a demonstration that scale itself changes legitimacy as it regards property. Small property errors are correctible but large-scale accumulation blocks exit, resists correction, and hardens dependency. The consequence of this is that scale converts coordination into domination when left unchecked. [n.118] [n.81] [n.101]

Autonomy and Capital Concentration

Autonomy is also not individual. It likewise accumulates among the collective so that the collective develops a volume of autonomy itself. Collective autonomy includes shared access to necessities, resilience, and capacity to adapt. Capital concentration can undermine this, and this is the exact problem those videos and social media posts expose.

The crux of the problem lies in the fact that capital draws from finite shared pools that collective groups enter a PFA with the ecosystem to couple with. Accumulation reallocates resources like labor, land, energy, attention, and ecological capacity away from others. This is not an anti-capitalist sentiment of morality or political affiliation but a structural reality of the framework.

The consequences in this framework of capital accumulation include the raising of prices. Prices can gate shelter, mobility, and participation. This is not neutral coordination. It is exclusion through scale. Pricing-out of autonomy thresholds constitutes a failure of STC-5. Such pricing has no standing so whichever cause is coupled to this outcome fails the same standing test by virtue of producing the pricing as an outcome that is known and therefore foreseeable.

These are not moral or absolutist claims because there is no claim that accumulation is evil or that ownership is wrong. The claim is structural. Autonomy loss triggers relevance. Moral domains are triggered by harm, not ownership. This is cross-domain consistency, not moralization. When property and capital foreclose agency, impose irreversible loss, and extract from survival, moral evaluation becomes relevant by virtue of their coupling to harm.

The same is true of the impacts of capital consolidation regarding the ecosystem and resources. Ecological systems have some resources that cannot be replaced or priced meaningfully. These systems also bind future agency. Meanwhile capital accumulation and ecological lock-in extract today and remove options tomorrow. Future agents cannot consent.

Where depletion is irreversible, standing collapses because future agents bear the risk, loss, and constraint. Standing must account for non-present agents and non-consenting populations who are subject to it. The rules of this framework as they apply to property, capital, and accumulation are clear:

Property is legitimate only as conditional standing, not absolute dominion. [n.70][n.136]

Capital accumulation escalates standing obligations as scale increases.

Where property or capital forecloses autonomy thresholds, standing collapses.

Collective and ecological autonomy constrain accumulation just as individual autonomy does.

Irreversible extraction invalidates consent and requires precaution, not optimization.

Property and capital are standing-bounded delegations of control whose legitimacy collapses when accumulation forecloses autonomy, correction, or future agency—individually, collectively, or ecologically. Having established legitimacy limits of property and accumulation over time, the next section will push into the aspects of money, debt, and time-binding which also have temporal values.

Money, Debt, and Time-Binding

Why Money Emerges

Money, whether existing as paper currency, gold, or other mediums arises to abstract value, enable indirect exchange, and coordinate across distance and time. It simplifies accounting, transfer, and comparability. In this sense, money is an abstraction layer to economic systems. What it coordinates is claims on future resources, priority of access, and enforceable expectations.

Consequently, these attributes establish money as a coordination medium and not a value source in itself. Since the money is not a source of value itself in this case it does not stand validity tests when considered as fiat currency because there is no commodity or thing which is behind the actual value either. Having no coupling to any of the items which can stand risk, the money itself fails standing tests.

Debt introduces temporal standing requirements that are absent from simple exchanges with money. Debt binds future agency in that it converts present need into future obligation. [n.102] [n.108] It narrows exit, refusal, and negotiation. Consent failure across time can still apply here where consent is evaluated at the initial time variable but obligation constraints at subsequent time variables so that futures selves cannot meaningfully refuse.

While the emergence of money and debt within economies is prolific among many societies, it is a category error to treat money as if it were inevitable. Other systems of exchange such as barter have existed and are yet known. Trade without currency is also an option which exists. [n.80]

The Category Error: Treating Money as Necessary

Money is often in economies mistaken for the economy itself. It’s a common assumption among many people that “without money, there is no economy.” This simply is not true. Coordination is not the same as currency. Whole groups can coordinate exchanges without any sort of tertiary medium of value imparted. [n.80] Direct exchange is one such case.

While money is a solution to solve problems of scalability, enforceability, and compatibility with accumulations, it is not the only solution even historically. Coordination itself does not require a hard object. This can be illustrated by digital pay solutions where no actual hard object is facilitating the exchange itself in the traditional sense.

Like with those systems, economic coordination can be mediated by rules, policies, commitments, and shared obligations. No physical token is required. A coordination medium is anything that reliably aligns contribution, access, and expectation, such as the shared blockchain ledgers of a crypto currency. The physical coinage of such crypto coins is immaterial to their value in actual practice.

Policy-Based Mutual Provision (PMP)

Insofar as no hard object or coinage is required to be the medium, the medium may likewise be something which is conceptual, like a policy. The requirements of the medium are not that they have some metaphysical or object which mediates the transaction but that they enable coordination of economic systems.

Policy-Based Mutual Provision (PMP) is the concept where members of a community engaging an economy agree to provide labor, create goods, or offer services. In return, the community guarantees access and removes survival gating. No exchange token changes hands. This is conceptually mirroring of the gift economy that Kimmerer mentions but also stands structurally sound within this framework. [n.34]

Such a provision establishes coordination through obligation rather than debt. [n.74] The obligations are contemporaneous, role-based, and revisable instead of time-compounding, transferrable, or enforceable against future selves. Mutual autonomy in these provisions is the governing principle just as it is within this framework.

Obligations to the collective are not the same here as debt to a creditor. Such systems operate under mutual provision, shared responsibility, and non-punitive participation. Contributions are bounded, renegotiable, and exit compatible. As a result, the criteria of these systems then are subject to similar constraints as any other domain in this framework.

Without currency as a token one of the primary concerns is that of fairness. In PMP economies fairness is maintained through transparent rules, contribution norms, review, and correction. This then avoids accumulation, interest, and scarcity pricing but still triggers standing and NRPP evaluations.

These policies within PMP economies still require justification, off-ramps, and proportionality. An absence of money is not equal to an absence of constraints and analysis. As has been established in the several domains prior to this one, the constraints derived here have likewise operated independently and if attributed to the economy itself supply fairness.

PMP’s likewise have limits and failure modes just as well as many other alternative media to money. Scale and complexity constraints with policy-based systems become more difficult to enforce at very large scale. While they do not definitively require high trust, where they do not, policies must have an extraordinarily high volume of exacting language. Across cultures, systems like this likewise become a challenge.

This is concept is not a utopian claim from this framework because the framework does not assert universal applicability or moral superiority. It asserts availability and legitimacy while satisfying many conditions of the traditional media of money as a reflection of the potency of the portability of this engine and toolset but also as a demonstration of concept of the crossing into moral considerations of economic systems themselves.

PMP systems are notoriously difficult to establish, require much more granularity in their oversight, have higher standards for the exactness of their language, and struggle to gain high adoption rates because of these challenges. Coupled with a lack of awareness of their fundamental operation, they cast money and debt systems as the much simpler and straightforward approach to economic systems, though not without its own drawbacks. The differences between the two may seem minor, but the impact of their direct coupling to autonomy can carry large sweeping consequences.

Where money & debt systems have high values for time-binding, PMP’s are low. Likewise, where the former often has extremely prohibitive exit costs, PMP’s are typically designed to be survivable at minimum. Accumulation is not a consideration of PMP’s while money & debt systems are structurally attuned to it. Money and debt impose high standing escalation and are commonly intergenerationally binding where PMP’s avoid such binding and contains escalation via established principles.

Money and debt systems that enable debt without exist violate both NRPP and ALRP principles. [n.102] [n.113] This justifies the establishment of bankruptcy, forgiveness, restructuring and jubilees as procedural rather than moral.

When debt binds future agency, it becomes coercive as it becomes non-dischargeable, survival-linked, inherited, or opaque. Insomuch as these systems can become coercive over those principles or over time, they may likewise become coercive based on scale of coordination. [n.114]

Institutions of Economic Coordination

What Do Institutions Do?

As with politics, economics has variant institutions which are non-neutral containers of exchange. They are coordination technologies whose legitimacy depends on how they allocate risk, enforce compliance, and preserve exit. [n.119] Each particular coordination level, or institution, introduces distinct coercive capacities, standing burdens, and failure modes. As with other domains, this structure reflects one of scale as well as variant levels of justification.

In economic systems institutions operate as coordination mechanisms. They exist to reduce transaction costs, stabilize expectations, enforce commitments, and coordinate large-scale cooperation. Regardless of whether this is realized via tokenized currency like money or a PMP, they emerge wherever informal coordination fails, scale exceeds trust, or time-binding becomes necessary.

Institutions themselves are inherently structurally coercive. [n.140] All economic institutions condition access, enforce rules, and impose penalties. Consequently, they all carry coercive capacity and require justification for their standing. While different institutions coordinate differently and fail differently, they are all subject to the same set of rigorous evaluations at their respective scales.

States

States as economic coordination institutions serve the primary functions of coordinating taxation, public goods, redistribution, money authority, and legal enforcement of contracts. They solve coordination problems that markets and firms cannot such as non-excludable goods, large-scale risk pooling, or systemic stability. They are uniquely placed to service these problems by virtue of their jurisdiction, just as with other domains that couple to jurisdiction.

States, being institutions, have an inherent coercive capacity. Among these are compulsory taxation, regulatory enforcement, legal penalties, and a monopoly on legitimate force whether at a city level, state level, federal level, or otherwise. These capacities for them bypass voluntary consent, operate territorially by jurisdiction, and bind future agents through law and debt.

They typically exhibit unique standing characteristics to their scale. Standing for them escalates because participation is non-optional, exit costs are typically high or infeasible, and risk is imposed collectively. [n.31] [n.121] As a result, state economic actions must therefore satisfy a high evidentiary burden, public justification, and robust off-ramps and correction mechanisms in compliance with STC-5, NRPP, ALRP, and CPS-7 standards.

The diagnostic signals of their failure modes become readily apparent as they emerge. Treating legality as sufficient standing, collapsing efficiency into legitimacy, permanent emergency measures, or irreversible fiscal or ecological commitments are all examples of these diagnostic signals. [n.121] [n.122] These failure signals are suggestive of unjustified coercion or authoritarianism and do not reflect a loss of force or power to the state, as an important distinction.

Firms

Firms as coordination institutions serve primary functions of production, labor, capital allocation and internal risk management. They replace market transactions with hierarchy, internal rules, and managerial authority. [n.119] Colloquially some English-speaking nations may call these “companies”, but this is not particularly limited to for-profit style institutions.

Firms have coercive capacities in that they have control over livelihoods, enable contractual enforcement, may subject employees to workplace surveillance, and may impose exit penalties such as non-competes, visas, or debt. [n.120] Their coercion measures are formally voluntary, structurally binding, and often survival gated. These coercion methods may be intentional or not from the PFA of the institution itself.

Standing for firms is called into question when they gate survival resources, foreclose meaningful exit, impose asymmetric risk, or bind future agency. Within the scale of institutions, firms likewise scale within their relative frame. Standing requirements for firms increase with firm size, market dominance, labor monopsony, or control over essential goods or infrastructure. Housing equity firms would be an example of an extremely high requirement for STC-5 for a firm because they have market dominance, their firm size is large, and they have a large volume of control over essential goods (shelter).

Failure for firms likewise has some very clear diagnostic signals. When they treat consent as sufficient justification for their actions, treat wages as giving them legitimacy to act, externalize risk while internalizing profit, or engage in lock-in via debt, credentials, or dependency—they are engaging in coercion. The coercion of firms arises from the formal consent, but this does not imply autonomous consent. [n.202]

Typically, it is the role of state institutions to likewise curb the unjustified coercive behaviors of firms. Firms as institutions still fall within the jurisdictions of states and are subject to the monopoly of coercive measures that states are coupled to. Where these diagnostic failures emerge, it is the obligation of states to address these failures via the means available to them. In this framework, those obligations are still constrained by NRPP, STC-5, CPS-7, SHT-3, Ceiling vs Prescription, and Risk-Inheritance & Validation principles so that states do not simply consume firms at will.

Markets as Institutions (Not Just Mechanisms)

Markets do not exist only as exchanges or coordination mediums. Markets likewise exist as institutionalized rulesets. [n.81] They can take institutional form by the inclusion of rule-governed systems, when they are structured by law, norms, or infrastructure, or when they are dependent on enforcement. This is not a unique stance among all domains but is a variation of institution that not ubiquitous to all domains either.

Markets require property rules, contract enforcement, currency or coordination medium, and exclusion mechanisms. These requirements position them well to coordinate decentralized information, preference-sensitive allocation, innovation under low coercion, and low-stakes and reversible exchange. It is their scale as independent of firms and states while also not constituting a solo actor that places them in this position.

The coercive capacities of markets emerge when participation is compulsory, prices gate survival, alternatives collapse, or exit is illusory. Their coercion is indirect, impersonal, and often misread as neutrality even when it has personal impact. The indirect nature of their coercion is not neutrality because neutrality implies a lack of coercion.

Markets do not generate standing themselves. They do, however create standing failures and pricing outcomes can trigger standing escalation. Standing for them shifts when markets foreclose autonomy thresholds, market design allocates risk asymmetrically, or time-binding in the form of debt replaces exit.

The modes of failure for market emerge when they treat price as legitimacy, treat demand as justification, ignore asymmetry and irreversibility, or assume exit where none exist. Where states have strength in coordinating public goods and stability and firms have strength with production efficiency, markets primary coordination strength is in information signaling.

Institutional Interactions and Escalation

No institution is normatively primary in this framework. None of them are inherently legitimate or coercive. Legitimacy for them is situational, scale-dependent, and autonomy-bounded. One of these levels does not have more priority than another but are independent as coupled correspondingly to their relative scale.

Accordingly, hybrid coordination emerges among them. States regulate markets, firms operate within those markets, and markets can influence state policy. Standing failures can emerge at those intersections as well and are not isolated exclusively within the institutions themselves. These failures have an escalation logic that operates with the toolset where each escalation increases coercive capacity, justification burden, and irreversibility risk. This escalation logic is the Market Failure Escalation Ladder (MFEL) and operates as follows:

Market failure → Firm dominance

Firm failure → State intervention

State failure → legitimacy crisis

The primary failure in this ladder escalates up to the next level of institution within the economy. At the top end, when legitimacy crisis exists, it becomes the burden of the collective itself which generates the economy to evaluate the legitimacy of the coupling of the state to the economy and the practices in. Those evaluations are still subject to the toolset this framework sets out so that states are also not subject to undue punishment or cruelty from the remediation methods of civilians.

The application of MFEL works across pluralist groups and within them as long as a larger group contains recognizable institutions at these levels. At larger levels, these institutions have a level of power and force that start to dilute, such as organizations like WHO or NATO. The power itself of those institutions at those levels are a manifestation of the options for remediation of this ladder and not indicative of the capacity for this ladder to operate itself. As a pluralist group escalates to the global scale, the capacity to meet the conditions to be considered a “State” become increasingly difficult as the burden increases.

States, firms, and markets are distinct coordination institutions with different coercive capacities and standing burdens. [n.144] None is self-legitimating. Each must be evaluated by how it allocates risk, preserves exit, and respects autonomy thresholds at scale. having identified how economic coordination is institutionally structured, the analysis can now turn to how these institutions distribute risk, generate inequality, and condition who bears the costs of coordination.

Distribution, Inequality, and Risk-Inheritance

Inequality is Not Automatically Injustice

Inequality is a descriptive economic condition rather than a moral verdict. [n.36] [n.107] While moral verdicts about the outcomes of this inequality can be evaluated by the principles found in the “About Morality” chapter, this concept itself is descriptive in nature for the economic domain. Inequality within this structure becomes relevant only when it alters who bears risk, who loses exit, or whose autonomy becomes structurally constrained.

Consequently, inequality in this domain is not automatically injustice. It does not exist as only unequal outcomes, opportunity, exposure, or risk alone. It is the culmination of an economic condition. Outcomes are not standing. Price is not legitimacy. Distribution is not authority.

Inequality emerges from voluntary specialization, risk seeking vs risk-averse choices, temporary asymmetries that arise from innovation, scarcity, or timing, or even differential contribution under reversible conditions. These are legitimate only where exit remains meaningful, risk is voluntarily assumed, and losses are bounded. Thus, the framework itself is not egalitarian by default.

For example, this framework does not presume that being a billionaire itself is inherently coercive, subject to standing tests, authoritarian, or even morally wrong. The inequality itself only interfaces with those tests when the inequality itself emerges in a way that being a billionaire begins to have outputs for pluralist collectives where the very act of this aggregation itself has outputs that necessarily impact autonomy. The aggregation outside of any of those impacting outcomes does not hold relevance to the PFA of those collective groups by definition if they do not interact with the PFA.

Structurally, inequality can be potentially illegitimate when it concentrates downside risk, forecloses exit, converts survival into permissioned access, or binds future agency. There is no moral blame, intent, or violation of law required for this to emerge. What matters in this sense is not how unequal the outcomes themselves are but how risk and constraint are distributed across agents as a result of the inequality itself.

Risk-Inheritance and Distribution

Riskinheritance is defined not by blame or desert, but by who bears downside exposure, who absorbs system failure, and who experiences severe exit costs. Some risks are voluntarily assumed through autonomous choice. Their consequences couple directly to the stance that generated them.

Structurally imposed risks differ. They arise from participation in systems whose conditions agents cannot meaningfully refuse. Examples include housing insecurity, labor dependency, environmental exposure, and infrastructure failure—domains where downside risk attaches independently of intention.

Housing displacement illustrates cumulative load and structural asymmetry. When rising rents force relocation, the autonomyimpact does not remain at preferencelevel disruption; it cascades into access loss, transportation strain, and income instability, pushing already strained households toward collapse. The asymmetry reproduces the A > B structure, as the risks fall on agents with no leverage while advantages accrue to actors insulated from comparable exposure. In such cases, standing becomes structurally relevant because nonrerunnable impacts are imposed on agents who cannot exit, triggering legitimacy constraints independent of intent.

As risk concentrates, the need to evaluate standingtocoerce (STC5) intensifies, since concentrated asymmetry increases autonomyimpact and reduces rerunnability. Likewise, NRPP becomes necessary to prevent IEWs and exit collapse. These dynamics are not limited to a single generation: future workers, residents, ecosystems, and taxpayers inherit exposure through debt, ecological depletion, and infrastructure decay. Distribution across time is still distribution, and thus risk still applies.

Distribution Without Redistribution (Yet)

This framework diagnoses when justification is required, not when policy must follow. It rejects equality as intrinsic good. It does not endorse welfare maximization or automatic redistribution. This framework is not built as a redistribution argument but has capacity to address distribution and redistribution alike.

This operates in this fashion because when risk-inheritance becomes asymmetric, standing shifts along with the burden of justification. Consequently, standing escalates and coercive tools enter the scope. This does not presume that there will be policy mandates over taxation, price controls, expropriation, or even universal provision.

Instead, because risks can become shared or imposed collectively, individual coordination breaks down in those spaces. Market signals in those cases are insufficient to address those needs. Distribution in such spaces becomes a precondition for the analysis of public goods because, when risk is collectively inherited, coordination must also become collective.

Some private risks themselves become distributional problems before any market failure is realized. Pollution, climate risk, public health, or even infrastructure failure can be examples of private risk translating to shared exposure. While markets may sometimes signal such risks, price does not compensate irreversibility. Furthermore, markets may not offer exit or voluntary opt-out for non-participants in cases that translate to shared exposure.

Collective action is not about free riders primarily. It is about who may impose constraints when coordination fails. It regards legitimacy and is thus coupled to standing tests and evaluations of retributive reciprocity. When viewing distribution in this framework and under these constraints it becomes evident that public goods are not a state ideology but a coordination necessity.

Public Goods, Externalities, and Collective Action

Public Goods as Coordination Problems

If public goods are a coordination, then what makes a good public to this framework in the first place? Textbook definitions are not primarily attached to this framework for public goods. Instead, the framework structurally sees them as goods which are non-exitable, non-substitutable, collectively risk-bearing, and autonomy-conditioning.

The “publicness” of the goods emerges from coordination conditions, not from inherent properties of the goods themselves. Any good becomes “public” from the PFA of a pluralist collective when individual coordination fails under shared risk and exit collapse. Where those consequences present to the PFA of the collective, they are naturally considered “public” already. Having been coupled to the goods themselves, those consequences then carry this public designation with them to the goods that create them.

Markets alone do not have the capacity to resolve public goods because they presume voluntary participation, individual exit, and price-mediated consent. Public goods violate those assumptions because non-participants are affected, refusal is non-viable, and harm is non-compensable or irreversible. This further reiterates that prices are not legitimacy, consent is not autonomy, and exit is a baseline condition.

The characteristics of public goods are different than those of private goods. They both give structural indicators of their type. Private goods have bounded downsides, individual refusal is possible, and participation is reversible. Public goods share collective downside, have irreversible failure modes and diffuse exposure.

Externalities and Distributed Risk Failures

Externalities exist when costs are imposed on agents who neither consented nor could reasonably exit. They are risk misallocations not as a side effect but as risk that is imposed without standing. Externalities become in this structure a distribution problem before they become an efficiency problem. [n.100]

Where externalities can become negative and exit collapses, risk inheritance increases and inequality emerges as a concept (as shown before). For example, pollution, public health, or other negative externalities can cause non-participants to inherit risk. For example, consider a company that produces steel but creates pollution.

The factory produces voluntary exchange. Buyers and sellers benefit. Pollution harms nearby residents who were not definitively parties to the transaction. The harm here is presumably incidental to the productive activity under the premise that the pollution itself is an unavoidable outcome of the steel production. The system itself can function normally here while costs spill over as a negative externality.

Standard remedies fail when the harms like these are irreversible, exposure is existential, and future agents are affected. Pricing, offsetting, and compensation do not inherently return consent or create it retroactively. Compensation does not imply legitimacy to groups. These failures have true capacity to impact both pluralist groups and the individuals that comprise them.

Collective Action Beyond the Free-Rider Frame

Free-rider models are inadequate. [n.36] [n.51] They assume voluntary cooperation, low stakes, and reversible harm but public goods failures occur even without strategic free riding. The problem is not non-cooperation; it is who may impose constraints when coordination fails.

All systems historically have had demographics which could be seen as free riding. In feudalist systems this could have been considered the feudal lords themselves on occasion. In capitalist systems, this can be considered of some of the top 1% of the wealthy on occasion. In socialist systems, this could be considered leaders that have historically distributed more for themselves than for others without justification.

Not all forms of non-contribution should be considered free riding either. Where capacity is lacking, this cannot be reasonably labeled as a free rider. Instead, the free rider problem only exists when all of the following are true:

A good is non-excludable

The good is necessary for collective survival or autonomy

Voluntary provision is insufficient or unstable

Failure to provide the good harms non-consenting parties

Exit from the system is not meaningfully available

When this coordination failure emerges from these criteria, the question becomes “Does this coordination failure generate standing?”

Collective action itself is a question of standing. It reframes regulation, taxation, mandates, and restrictions as legitimacy questions rather than policy preferences. Risk concentration structurally triggers standing reviews. As the risk becomes collective, non-voluntary, or non-exitable, standing escalates and the toolset of this framework is engaged.

Standing for Intervention

Intervention is not a default. It is conditional. This framework outright rejects automatic state action, technocratic authority, and moralized necessity. Intervention is justified only when standing conditions are met.

Standing emerges when ALL are present: Risk is collectively inherited, exit is unavailable or punitive, non-intervention perpetuates autonomy collapse, and harm is irreversible or compounding. This is the same coercion logic that runs throughout this framework and applies the same STC-5 and NRPP constraints while upholding the ALRP and MOMA values.

This standing does not imply who can intervene, but that intervention itself becomes legitimate. Who can intervene has been established by the institutional analysis prior. It operates as a scalar value and relates directly to the functions of those institutions. Once coordination becomes collective and standing to intervene emerges, the central economic question is no longer allocation but endurance: how a system sustains itself over time without compounding risk or collapsing autonomy.

Growth, Endurance, and Economic Technology

Growth is Not the Goal

When speaking of economic stability and endurance, growth itself is not compatible with the function of a goal. Growth itself via GDP, output expansion, and accumulation are treated normatively. It is not itself inherently a moral good.

Growth itself is not legitimacy and doesn’t inherently become endurance. [n.35] [n.104] It likewise does not coordinate success by default. Cancer grows. This is not evidence of it aligning with legitimacy, success, or endurance. This is not to say that the framework is anti-growth but that it is against treating growth as self-justifying.

As it concerns economics in this framework, growth is an increase in measurable throughput, output, or market activity within a coordination regime. While this is scoped to the community, institutions, agents, and PFA of the group, it can also be autonomy-expanding, neutral, or collapsing. In this sense, growth is similar in concept to pricing as an outcome metric.

Growth itself reflects coercive labor, debt expansion, ecological depletion, monopoly rents, and externalized risk. Growth in this framework is a signal rather than a warrant. It doesn’t confer standing or legitimacy because it is structurally non-authoritative.

The goal is instead for endurance as it relates to the PFA of pluralist groups. The UCE of that PFA become the pillars which uphold this goal. Endurance in this sense is the ability for a pluralist economy to maintain autonomy thresholds over time without compounding risk.

Growth is not eliminated from this goal but becomes acceptable when it passes certain gates. It must increase resilience, preserve exit, remain reversible, not collapse shared thresholds and not bind future agents unjustifiably. So, the question in the long-term horizon is not “how do we grow?” but “what growth modes preserve endurance for the group?”

Long-Term Temporal Economics

When considering the concept of long-term temporal dynamics, it is important to recognize that time itself is not neutral. [n.114] [n.115] Economic decisions bind future options necessarily. The outcomes of one choice by definition become onset conditions of the next choice or they simply do not interact with that PFA.

To discount this value and focus only on short horizon is to fail STC-5 evaluation by virtue of ignoring several of the stakeholders who stand to face the risks. This is a failure of the risk validation steps. Some harms created by choice now become irreversible and demand consideration in these evaluations.

What breaks endurance over time are patterns that cause compounding risk. They are the temporal failure modes for economics. Examples of these failure modes include debt spirals, where obligations compounding narrows exit over time and ecological depletion where extraction today removes options tomorrow. These present threats to endurance itself.

Other examples include infrastructure lock-in, institutional entrenchment, and path dependency. This is not an exhaustive list but failure modes that align with these outcomes of threat to endurance are triggers for standing escalation. They likewise are often generators of systemic IEWs. [n.206]

Temporal economics exposes hidden coercion in this way. Present decisions often impose future constraint without future validation. [n.37] [n.115] Who bears the costs of the decisions being made and who can consent? Temporal distribution is still a method of distribution when the answers to those questions lie downstream.

These temporal distributions do not invalidate the existing toolsets. STC-5 still governs interventions with long-horizon impacts. The scope simply is ramped up as the steps which identify risk inheritance gain a temporal value as well. Likewise, NRPP constrains those choices as the retributive property inherits a temporal value and factors into those considerations.

When future agent exposure emerges, such temporal values coupled to the processes of evaluation gain standing intrinsically as representative of those groups within the toolset itself so that these proxies do not need to be “considered” externally from the system but are inherently structured. Thus, when the outcomes of these evaluations are considering off-ramps, they too must be temporal when those values are necessarily coupled to the risk inheritance.

These considerations are inherent to the framework and to the nature of PFAs necessarily having time vectors inherently coupled to them. The differences in these time vectors impose a need for evaluation of those vectors. From this structure, we frame the argument as being “post-growth” not in an anti-growth sentiment that would mean to “stop doing things” but in a temporally bound way to say, “stop binding the future without granting them standing.”

Post-Growth without Anti-Progress

Post-growth is not a policy of reduction; it is a legitimacy standard for expansion. Post-growth here means rejecting growth as a universal telos, allowing domain-specific growth where justified, and prioritizing endurance, resilience, and autonomy thresholds. This does not imply austerity or stagnation.

Austerity is a coercive prescription where post-growth is a constraint on unjustified expansion. Austerity imposes diffuse harm and weak targeting. [n.121] [n.122] It is often survival gating and irreversible from human outcomes. Post-growth in this framework imposes selective expansion, targeted constraint, resilience building, and future preserving.

When considering those expansions, constraints, resilience, and future, progress becomes a primary concern. Progress is not constrained to the concept of gross domestic product (GDP). Instead, progress is an indicator of improvements to autonomy preservation, exit viability, resilience, reversibility, risk distribution, ecological stability, and repair capacity. Progress itself relates to a coordination design.

Conceptually, progress from this standpoint can be measured by metrics of autonomy thresholds where housing, food, health, education, transportation, communication, and participation access stability is evaluated. It could take on the form of irreversibility exposure metrics by evaluating permanent ecological, financial, and institutional outcomes. It could evaluate risk distribution both short-term and long-term with minority exposure safeguards.

Within this framework and armed with methods to track progress, progress itself becomes an endurance-compatible innovation itself. As we push our economies further into the future new technologies can emerge and enter the economy in the form of growth. What emerges, how it emerges, the impacts to those communities, and the progress it couples to are all likewise subject to evaluations of the toolset.

Emergent Technology in Post-Growth Economics

Emerging technologies within the post-growth economic PFA become effectively coordination tools and not implicit output multipliers. While they may carry the added benefit of output multiplication, they are not engines that increase throughput by default. Instead, technology in post-growth economics is evaluated by how it redistributes coordination burdens and risks.

Some technologies emerge which help redistribute risk. Automation, for instance, can concentrate risk so that there are less opportunities for failure along the innovation of progress. Technology emerging is inherently tied to risk-inheritance, exit collapse, and standing escalation where the impact of that technology likewise has autonomy-impacting outcomes.

When considering economic technology, exit viability becomes a primary evaluative criterion. Where they foreclose exit via dependency, lock-in, and opacity, the burdens on them for justification rise significantly. Where they enable decentralization or modularity with minimal downsides, the justification requirements inherently become looser.

While they exist and emerge in their own temporal spaces, they also bind the future via debt systems, infrastructure, data systems, and ecological extraction. Time-binding increases the burden for standing and where technology becomes irreversible the justification standards are high. Regardless of the class of technology in this framework, it is never neutral. [n.130]

Classes of Economic Technology in a Post-Growth Context

Within the framework, technology that has impact on the economy, but which serves a post-growth PFA can take on several classes. Some serve the purpose of allocation while others regard information and decision or enforcement and constraint. While they may all work together in this economic system, they do not serve identical functions. They are all, however, evaluated by reversibility, transparency, risk distribution, and autonomy impact.

Allocation technologies serve the purpose of allocating economic resources. They might take the form of markets, planning systems, rationing or quotas, or even policy-based allocations (including PMP). Many of these tools help with the innovation of progress and serve to support PMP economies as they pursue larger scales.

Information and decision technologies provide necessary input which may have been unknown or illusive before. Computers fall into this category as the computational power of them yields new actionable economic information. Aside from computers, measurement systems, forecasting tools like business intelligence (BI), modeling and simulation tools, or even decision-support systems qualify as this type of tool. This class of tools are vital for endurance as the information they yield becomes pivotal knowledge to avoid foreclosure and irreversibility.

Enforcement and constraint technologies provide capacities to structure the systems themselves. They tie back to standing to coerce constraints, NRPP, and pose a risk of domination via automation. These technologies hold both immense potential for scaling PMP economies but, left unchecked, can quickly devolve into domination and coercion. They take the form of contracts, automated enforcement, surveillance systems, and access or credential systems.

AI in a Post-Growth Economy

AI as a technology that emerges is both ecologically and economically relevant in terms of post-growth context. There are ecological costs to the expansion of this technology while it also serves as a coordination accelerator, decision-compression tool, and pattern-recognition infrastructure.

While it is not inherently labor-saving, growth-producing or efficiency-optimizing, the outputs from it can be used for those purposes and ends. They likewise present a risk in the centralization of decision authority, obscured accountability, and can scale errors rapidly. Accordingly, those properties likewise escalate the standing requirements from STC-5, auditability demands, and exit safeguards.

The risks of opaque decision systems, non-contestable outputs, and dependency on proprietary models with AI are real. In this framework, they are evaluated by whether agents can refuse, override, or appeal those outcomes. AI itself in this framework does not get exceptional authority. It is subject to satisfying the same reversibility, proportionality, transparency, and least autonomy-reducing means as any other agent in the framework.

Adoption of these new economic technologies redistributes power, allocates risk, and binds future agents. Technology selection itself therefore triggers standing reviews because it is not neutral. [n.130] [n.131] The choice of these selections themselves at various levels within the PFA of pluralist collectives is scope sensitive but likewise inherent.

Whether AI or not, all technology design criteria in a post-growth economy should consider preserving exit, distributing risk, reversibility, contestability, and autonomy preservation at scale. This applies to the whole of technologies that interface with the economy so that public goods lead to collective risk, collective risk leads to standing, standing leads to choices about technology and how we mitigate those risks, and impacts how we handle economic emergencies.

Where constraints and technologies are unable to mitigate these problems pre-emptively, emergencies may emerge. The core question at hand with technology is not about whether it’s good or bad but whether it preserves the correction capacity that has been established as necessary. The next section therefore examines crises at the point where economic coordination most readily becomes coercion and where the framework’s gates must necessarily tighten rather than relax or pivot them to technology.

Economic Emergencies

What are Economic Emergencies?

Emergency as a concept is predicated on conditions which cause a domain to potentially inherit undesirable outcomes. An economic emergency, in this framework, is a condition in which widespread exit failure combined with escalating riskinheritance and irreversibility threatens the nearterm autonomy or future agency of a pluralist community. Emergency itself has both a long-term and short-term temporal condition so that it is not equivalent to urgency but emerges as an emphasis of degree of impact of the outcomes. Short-term temporality is a common cause of this degree of emphasis but is not exclusive.

As it relates to economics, economic conditions qualify as an emergency only if it simultaneously satisfies all of the Conditions for Economic Emergency (CEE):

Widespread exit failure

Irreversibility if no action is taken

Non-parochial exposure (not limited to isolated agents)

Extreme escalation of risk-inheritance

Economic emergencies collapse exit. They are not volatility in markets or systems. Economic downturns and cyclical recessions are not equivalent to emergencies where exit becomes non-viable for large portions of the population. Emergencies are diagnosed by a loss of refusal, not price movement. Consequently, functioning markets can generate emergencies.

Though these emergencies alter standing conditions, they do not suspend them. Emergencies do not justify coercion by necessity intrinsically. They do not stand alone to grant authority or bypass evaluations of standing to coerce. Standing itself still depends on risk-inheritance, exit collapse, and proportionality (NRPP).

The standing conditions that emergencies alter include compressing time horizons, raising irreversibility stakes, and increasing the cost of inaction. These can justify temporary deviations from normal economic coordination but only as provisional measures. Where provisional measures collapse into normativity for the system without justification, coercion emerges inherently.

Crises and Provisional Justification

The purpose of these provisional justifications is to prevent emergency economics from becoming permanent economics. An example of this principle being violated in state budget systems is the perpetual use of continuing resolutions (CRs) as a normalized output rather than balancing the budget itself. Cases where this happens are examples of provisional justifications becoming permanent economics.

Provisional justification is time-bounded, purpose specific, non-generalizable, and justified by the emergency condition itself. It is not permanent authority and does not create new entitlement. Provisional deviations from existing economic coordination may be justified by crisis conditions alone, but only within the limits imposed by standing, proportionality (NRPP), and explicit termination criteria. The conditions for provisional economic measures are that they must be the least autonomy-reducing option (NRPP), preserve future exit where possible, include explicit sunset conditions, and include criteria for termination.

Pivoting back to the perpetual CR example, the lack of sunset conditions or termination criteria implied by that perpetuality are the measures which fail in such provisions. The lack of those conditions carries with it uncertainty that autonomy-reducing options (NRPP) has been considered. Some other examples include capital controls, price freezes, debt moratoria, or temporary nationalizations. Each of these should be evaluated by exit restoration capacity, reversibility, risk redistribution, and repair compatibility.

Anti-Precedent in Economics

Economic emergencies should not set precedent. Historically, provisional authority has hardened into normal governance and emergency measures have persisted beyond emergencies. [n.91] [n.92] These are common failure modes of crisis economics.

Emergencies structurally distort justification thresholds. Using them as a precedent invalidates standing analysis as a result. When emergency measures are later cited to justify similar actions in nonemergency conditions, the justificatory threshold collapses, and standing is retroactively conferred where it was never earned.

Anti-precedent here means that emergency actions cannot be cited as normal-case justification. It likewise means that no policy, institution has a valid claim of legitimacy simply because it once addressed an emergency. This is the economic analogue to constitutional emergency limits. It is a structural feature inherent to the framework and not a legal claim.

Anti-precedent methods preserve pluralism, prevent ratchet effects, and protect against emergency normalization. They are a standing safeguard where anti-precedent methods directly couple to exit restoration and future agency. The outcomes of these protective methods are inherently coupled to their imposition. They function as the structural bridge between emergency response and transition, ensuring that provisional authority dissolves rather than ossifies.

If emergencies justify only provisional measures and explicitly prohibit precedent, then emergency action alone cannot resolve economic failure. The task becomes not merely stabilizing the system but restoring conditions under which ordinary coordination regains legitimacy. Since emergency measures operate by suspending or bypassing normal coordination constraints, legitimacy cannot be restored merely by stabilization; it must be actively reestablished through transition paths that restore exit, reduce inherited risk, and unwind provisional authority.

Transition Paths and Economic Repair

Economic Harm and Wrongs

As established in “About Morality,” harms and wrongs are not equivalent. This remains true in the economic space. Economic harms are a negative outcome such as loss, deprivation, instability, or displacement. Economic wrongs are autonomy-impairing couplings where the structure, an institution, or agent’s role made the outcome foreseeable or enforceable. Not all harms in this domain are wrongs and, likewise, not all wrongs require culpability.

Harm becomes standing-relevant when coupled to autonomy thresholds, exit collapse, and future agency binding. Economic wrongs in the framework are often structural rather than interpersonal. They can emerge without intent, illegal acts, or identifiable perpetrators. [n.199] It is possible for economic wrongs to exist without culpability.

When wrongness is detected economically, standing escalates, justification burden shifts, and remedy options become constrained by NRPP—as with any other domain. They are standing triggers and not moral verdicts in themselves. When economic wrongs persist without an attributable wrongdoer the correct classification is not moral exoneration but Independently Emergent Wrongs (IEW).

Economic IEWs

Economic IEWs are a special case of IEWs. They imply system-level autonomy collapse that arises from structural design, incentives, scarcity pressures, time-binding, locked infrastructure, or market architecture even where no agent is culpable. They are structural and not partisan themselves. Cumulative load explains why identical impacts produce different autonomy outcomes: resource scarcity amplifies low-level impacts into structural collapse for agents near baseline.

Some examples of them would be housing traps where displacement cascades, infrastructure collapse where dependence is non-substitutable, or public health spillovers where exposure is non-exitable. These are all examples where system-level autonomy collapses for variant reasons. They emerge from structural stresses.

Classifying these cases as IEWs creates presumptive duties of redesign or repair where possible. It constrains scapegoating and shifts attention to structural coupling. It focuses the attention back to the core objective of structural integrity itself which is inherent to the UCE of pluralist communities.

Economic IEWs likewise trigger repair priority over retaliation, audit and correction capacity requirements, and transition planning rather than emergency permanence. They do not authorize punishment, assign blame, or justify coercion automatically. They are wrongs without culpable agents so legitimate response cannot be punitive; it must be repair that restores agency and exit. [n.60] [n.37]

Repair without Collapse

Repair in the economy is not the same thing as recovery or growth. [n.143] Growth may accompany repair, but it cannot substitute for it where exit, autonomy, or correction capacity remain collapsed. Economic repair is restoration. It restores exit viability, autonomy thresholds, correction capacity, reversibility (where possible), and risk distribution that does not concentrate downsides. Repair is not returning to the pre-crisis status quo, maximizing output, or punishing perceived enemies.

The onset of repair presumes that emergency provisional actions have already been deployed or are actively being unwound. The implication from this is a failure of the non-emergency baseline conditions for survival. Consequently, the first step of any repair ladder for economic crisis needs to be to stabilize the baselines for survival. Without this first step, survival itself collapses.

Ideally, these baselines are the basis of temporary provisions from the onset but, where they are not, they become the immediate need and are constrained by the same STC-5 gates and NRPP sizing as any other policies. They likewise require off-ramps and anti-precedent constraints.

Once survival is stabilized, the first barrier to autonomy maintains the same as it has in this framework—consent. Without real exit, consent does not exist more than formally. Restoring exit channels through mobility, discharge, portability, or alternatives is the second step in this repair ladder. It ensures autonomy that has collapsed is reintroduced to the system if not fully then at least in the minimum sense.

When autonomy is reestablished in minimal terms for the immediate pluralist community, the next consideration is for the temporal impact on autonomy. Where the problematic element of the economic system is compounding or is not-negotiable, this time-binding being reduced increases the value of autonomy for future agents. Failing to address this leaves room for domination of future agency.

Once present and future autonomy is secured the specific IEW that led to the failure itself can be addressed from the standpoint of establishing correction capacities. Where audits, review, appeals, or reversal pathways were closed, opening them strips the IEW itself of a level of capacity for coercion while simultaneously increasing autonomy for agents bound to the economy.

After these grounds are established, it becomes the obligation of the collective, by virtue of standing escalation, to redesign the coupling itself by changing the mechanism within the economy which produces the IEW itself. Each of these steps is constrained by STC-5, NRPP, off-ramps, ceiling vs prescription principles, ALRP, and MOMA principles.

Consequently, repair must avoid collective punishment, permanent exclusion, irreversible deprivation or foreclosure of exit. Repair should be targeted, reversible, reviewable, and exit preserving. Emergency measures must be time-bound, sunset-governed, and replaced by ordinary coordination modes only once exit is restored. Repair is the structural means by which emergency legitimacy returns to ordinary legitimacy without importing emergency authority into normal economic life.

Economics Without Domination

The central error in economic reasoning is to mistake outcomes for permission. Exchange being voluntary, a price being paid, or a system being efficient says nothing about who lost exit, who inherited risk, or whose future agency was foreclosed in order to secure those outcomes. Markets can function perfectly while converting survival into an obligation that no one was free to refuse. Once economic arrangements are seen as binding structures rather than neutral processes, legitimacy can no longer be inferred from consent, growth, or equilibrium. Economics in this framework retains its power to coordinate—and is stripped bare of authority it has systematically smuggled but never structurally earned.

The economic domain forces explicit interaction between language, politics, morality, ecology, and time. The fact that the same standing constraints, autonomy thresholds, and proportionality limits remain operative across these interactions demonstrates that the framework is not domainlocal. Chapters that follow do not re-derive these tools. Instead, they will show how the same evaluative engine manifests differently across domains with distinct failure modes.

Since economic coordination is implemented through technologies that structure access, enforce constraints, automate exclusion, and determine exit viability, technology itself demonstrates an inherent capacity for scalable coercion. The next chapter examines technology as more than a neutral instrument. Technology stands as its own standing-relevant domain rather than simply an efficiency multiplier because it structures exit, enforcement, and correction at scale. Consequently, it warrants evaluation in its own right.

IX — About Technology

Purpose: This section examines how the coupling-standing-legitimacy engine operates within the domain of technology and how misidentification of coupling produces characteristic failures of standing in this domain. This section sets out to establish technology as a medium which can amplify other domains and potential risk but likewise stands in its own right as a domain unto itself. It will additionally introduce coercion without command as a distinctive coercive form.

Orientation

What This Chapter Is and Is Not

Technology as a domain is not a “topic” but exists as a medium of coordination and constraint. Technology is the point where coordination becomes scalable and therefore where coercion becomes automatable. It is not merely “tools” or “innovation” but mediation that can shape access, visibility, enforcement, and exit. It matters because it can reallocate autonomy without issuing commands and can do so silently. [n.130] [n.131] [n.28] [n.140] [n.118]

The engine and toolset in this framework are already established. This chapter applies it by identifying how technology uniquely couples to design, mediation, automation, opacity, lock-in, and time-binding. In technology the “act” is often design and the “enforcement” is often automatic meaning standing failures can occur even when no agent is visibly commanding anything.

This is a unique aspect of technology as an implementation substrate. [n.28] [n.46] [n.69] It is often without jurisdiction, often non-transparent, and frequently self-executing. [n.31] This chapter continues as a domain translation for the toolset and engine within this scope. It identifies when technology is mere coordination support versus when it becomes autonomy-limiting structurally.

This chapter treats technology as a standing-relevant mediation. It is not a celebration of innovation or a blanket anti-technology critique. It will not claim that technology is either “evil” or “destiny.”

It is not a comprehensive or exhaustive political program or regulatory blueprint for technology, and it will not re-derive the core toolset or engine itself. This framework does not moralize technology. This chapter will not include a theory of technological determinism, claims that designers are always culpable, or claims that technology itself is an agent. There is no moral theory of good or bad technology within it. It evaluates when technological mediation acquires coercive capacity and therefore requires legitimacy constraints.

If we wish to speak to technology as a domain, we must first define technology as a domain. This chapter establishes technology as the domain where coordination is converted into system behavior and where coercion can occur without law, orders, or identifiable commanding agents. It does not assign moral intent or blame to technology. It evaluates when technological mediation acquires coercive standing regardless of intent, legality, or innovation value.

Function

This chapter translates standing analysis into design-level constraints. It explains why technological systems often acquire de facto authority before legitimacy. It will identify technology-specific coupling channels such as automation, opacity, lock-in, and persistence. Where politics governs by declaration and economics by scarcity, technology governs by system behavior.

This chapter functions to show how coercion can emerge in technology without commands. It provides a diagnostic typology for technological failure modes and establishes when repair or redesign becomes obligatory. The technology domain explains how coordination is executed at scale, not why coordination pressures exist.

In this chapter, technology is not sovereign, but neutral. It operates without jurisdiction and often enforces without visibility. Technology adds unique failure modes of it own since it can outpace institutional correction and consequently can inherit coercive effects from other domains.

Expectations

When reading this chapter, readers should expect technology to be evaluated by effects and not intentions. Design choices are treated as standing-relevant acts and automation is analyzed as coercion-capable. Readers accustomed to evaluating technology by usefulness or innovation should expect those standards to fail wherever exit collapses or correction is foreclosed.

Discomfort may arise as technological efficiency is rejected as legitimacy. Innovation in this chapter does not excuse autonomy loss. Consequently, “neutral” infrastructure can still be diagnosed in some cases as domination.

This chapter assumes the reader is willing to treat design as action and mediation as constraint, even when no command is issued. The author expects the reader to be willing to treat systems, not just actors, as legitimacy-relevant. Readers should evaluate technology structurally rather than morally when reading this chapter.

To get the most from this section, readers must accept that coercion can be automated and that, while technology is a domain unto itself, it is also an amplification substrate for other domains which make it especially potent and potentially coercive as a result. Consequently, in this chapter readers will benefit from being accepting of redesign as a legitimacy obligation and not overreaction.

Translations

The purpose of translation in this chapter is to make technological coercion legible. It translates standing into design, audit, and exit constraints. This helps distinguish coordination support from autonomy-limiting mediation and exposes how automation substitutes for authority in some technological systems.

These translations are structural rather than moral. They are system-oriented instead of actor-oriented and are compatible with pluralist disagreements. They are scale-sensitive and time-sensitive.

In this domain, the engine does not change; what changes are the channels through which it couples. With technology, standing is triggered not only by direct coercion, but by the design choices that structure access, enforcement, and correction capacity. [n.130] [n.131] [n.185] Consequently, technology introduces unique coupling channels such as opacity, automation, lock-in, and time-binding that take on forms unique to this domain.

Translation Table

Technology: A standingrelevant medium of mediation through which coordination, enforcement, and constraint are executed at scale.

Technological Mediation: The structuring of what is visible, accessible, actionable, or allowable through system design rather than explicit command.

Technology as a Domain: The domain in which coordination becomes scalable, coercion becomes automatable, and legitimacy can fail without identifiable authorities.

Design (Technological): A form of action that structures outcomes, defaults, and constraints prior to deliberation or consent.

Automation: The transfer of enforcement or decision from agents to systems, where penalties or exclusions occur without casebycase judgment.

Automated Coercion: Autonomylimiting constraint imposed by system behavior rather than explicit intent or instruction.

Standing (Technological): The legitimacy of a technological system to bind, constrain, or exclude agents through its mediated effects.

De Facto Authority: Effective power exercised by technological systems prior to or without legitimacy evaluation.

BlackBox Authority: A standing failure where system outputs are treated as binding despite being noncontestable or nonexplainable.

Coupling (Technological): The interdependent linkage between agents and system behavior that conditions access, participation, or future agency.

Technological Relevance: The condition in which a system’s mediation has autonomyimpacting consequences for agents or populations.

Autonomy Constraint (Technology): Reduction of viable selfauthorship caused by dependency, default enforcement, lockin, or loss of refusal.

Formal Choice (Technological): Apparent choice that exists only procedurally, where refusal or exit is functionally nonviable.

RiskInheritance (Technological): The allocation of downstream error, exclusion, surveillance, or future harm to agents who did not control design or validation.

Asymmetric Exposure (Technology): Unequal distribution of technological risk, where harms concentrate on users or nonusers while benefits accrue upstream.

Exit (Effective, Technological): The practical ability to disengage from a technological system without catastrophic loss of function, livelihood, or participation.

Exit Collapse (Technology): A condition where leaving a system is nominal but infeasible due to dependency, interoperability denial, or switching costs.

LockIn: Structural dependency created by design that makes exit costly, impractical, or irreversible.

Interoperability Denial: Design choice that prevents migration or substitution, foreclosing effective exit.

TimeBinding (Technological): The persistence of data, infrastructure, or models that bind future agency to past system decisions.

FutureAgent Binding: Constraint imposed on agents who cannot meaningfully consent due to temporal distance or system persistence.

Persistence: The tendency of technological systems to endure by default once deployed, even after provisional justification expires.

NRPP (Technological): The requirement that technological enforcement be the least autonomyreducing means sufficient to neutralize validated harm.

Automation Cliff: A proportionality failure where minor triggers produce maximal or irreversible penalties.

Graduated Response: A design principle that scales intervention incrementally rather than through binary enforcement.

OffRamps (Technology): Explicit design pathways for rollback, sunset, migration, or disengagement from a system.

PermanencebyDefault: A failure mode where provisional or emergency technological measures become normalized infrastructure.

Correction Capacity (Technology): The ability of a system to detect, contest, override, and repair its own errors.

Contestability: The availability of intelligible challenge, appeal, or review of system outputs.

Auditability: The capacity for independent evaluation of system behavior, error rates, and impacts.

Override: A human or institutional mechanism to suspend or reverse automated outcomes.

NonParochial Evidence (Technology): Publicly checkable, reproducible evidence about system behavior, effects, and error bounds.

Opacity: Design or institutional conditions that prevent affected agents from understanding or contesting system behavior.

Tiered Disclosure: Graduated transparency that preserves security or privacy while enabling public validation of effects.

Scale (Technological): The amplification of impact whereby small design decisions produce large, populationlevel consequences.

Error Propagation: The rapid spread of mistakes or bias through automated or scaled systems.

Technological Emergency: A condition where rapid, largescale, autonomyrelevant risk converges with exit collapse and irreversible harm.

Provisional Justification (Technology): Temporary legitimacy for emergency technological measures, strictly timebound and nonprecedential.

AntiPrecedent (Technology): The rule that emergency or provisional technological measures may not justify normal operation.

Procedural Capture (Technology): A standing failure where systems appear procedurally valid while foreclosing correction or accountability.

Technological IEW (Independently Emergent Wrong): Autonomyimpairing outcomes produced by system interaction or scale without identifiable culpable agents.

Repair (Technology): Restoration of exit, correction capacity, contestability, and autonomy within an existing system.

Redesign: Structural replacement of a technological system when repair cannot restore legitimacy.

AntiLockIn Design: Design principle that preserves modularity, migration paths, and reversibility.

HumanOverride Requirement: The obligation to retain accountable human intervention for autonomyimpacting outcomes.

Technological Domination: A condition where system mediation forecloses autonomy, exit, and correction while continuing to operate.

Technology as Coupling Accelerator: The property by which technology increases the speed, scale, and opacity of standingrelevant effects relative to governance capacity.

Technology Without SelfLegitimation: The principle that innovation, efficiency, adoption, or necessity cannot substitute for standing.

What Counts as Technology

Technology as Mediation, Not Artifact

Technology as a domain is not equivalent to tools, machines, or software objects. [n.130] [n.131] The artifacts themselves matter only insofar as they mediate action, perception, access, or enforcement. Technology enters this framework when it structures how coordination occurs, not when the object exists. [n.28]

Someone inventing a new machine with no purpose in their basement, for instance, would not particularly be an entry point for technology in this framework. A hammer in a drawer is not technologically relevant, but a hammer embedded in a production system, safety regime, or enforcement pipeline is. Technology in this framework is defined by its role as an intermediary layer between agents and outcomes.

Technology can mediate what can be seen or known, what actions are possible or impossible, how decisions are made or enforced, how errors are detected or ignored, and even how exit is enabled or foreclosed. [n.40] [n.41] [n.16] This mediation can occur without explicit commands, visible authorities, or internal coercion. Consequently, design choices in the technological domain function as action.

Technology can redistribute autonomy without issuing directives through defaults, interfaces, protocols, thresholds, and automation rules. They act prior to and often instead of deliberation. This is a characteristic that distinguishes technology as a unique domain from others. Technological authority is legitimate only where users lack the capacity to oversee, contest, or exit its effects, and must be designed to dissolve as that capacity is built (CIA). Systems that obscure understanding, foreclose exit, or prevent users from gaining operational competence intentionally arrest the autonomy gradient and are therefore structurally illegitimate.

Domain Boundary

Technology as a domain interacts with several others. Consequently, it is necessary that we identify the boundary where technology crosses over into other domains and where it does not. For instance, when technology interfaces with economics, the economic domain explains why coordination pressures exist, and the technology domain explains how they are enforced at scale. [n.93] [n.81] [n.28]

Likewise, where politics binds through declared authority, technology binds through operational necessity.
