[n.31] It coordinates through system behavior rather than through jurisdiction or exchange and scarcity. These operational mechanisms serve as signals to the boundaries for domain considerations.

Technology as a domain is the substrate through which coordination is realized for many other domains. As such, technology inherits coercive effects from those other domains. [n.118] [n.136] It can add its own unique failure modes and can outpace institutional correction mechanisms. Consequently, technology is neither neutral nor sovereign but is standing-relevant when it structures autonomy, exit, or correction. [n.130] [n.24] [n.185]

Since technology mediates coordination without always appearing as an authority, traditional legitimacy criteria often fail to detect when it becomes coercive. This domain therefore requires translation of standing into design constraints, attention to mediation rather than intention, and evaluation of systems rather than only actors. While technology itself is not an agent within the framework, its operation as a substrate that can amplify or act on behalf of agents demands this evaluation.

Three-Class Typology

As we saw in previous chapters, technology is not strictly limited to its own domain and yet the typology of it is not classificatory for its own sake. It identifies where couplings arise.

The following Technology Coupling Variants (TCV) identify the specific ways in which the stable tools of the framework attach to the technological domain. These are not new principles or tests; they are the domainspecific channels through which standing, exit, proportionality, and correction capacity become relevant in technological systems. The Three-Class Typology of Technology is as follows:

Allocation Technologies allocate resources, access, visibility, and opportunity. [n.125] [n.100] They can include ranking and recommendation systems, eligibility and scoring systems, access gates and credential systems, or pricing, prioritization and queueing mechanisms. Allocation technologies introduce primarily couplings to asymmetric exposure, exclusion risk, exit collapse through dependency, and automation of scarcity.

Information and Decision Technologies produce, compress, or operate information for decision making. [n.100] [n.15] They can include measurement systems, predictive models, optimization and forecasting tools, and dashboards, metrics, or indicators. They are primarily coupled to epistemic authority without contestability, opacity and nonparochial evidence failure, amplification of error through scale, and substitution of prediction for justification.

Enforcement and Constraint Technologies impose, automate, or scale compliance and penalties. [n.140] [n.131] [n.130] They can include surveillance systems, automated sanctions, access revocation, algorithmic moderation or policing, or technical lockouts and throttling. They are coupled primarily to coercion without visible agents, proportionality collapse via automation, irreversibility of penalties, or loss of appeal and correction capacity.

This typology helps diagnose which kind of coupling is responsible when legitimacy collapses. Standing failures often emerge at the intersection of these classes or types. A single technological system can span all three classes as they are not mutually exclusive.

Technology Coupling Variants (TCV) take the following forms:

Technological Mediation Coupling

Tech which couples to mediation operates as a mediator for what counts as:

visible

accessible

actionable

allowable

Automation Coupling

Tech which couples to automation shifts enforcement from decisions to systems via:

default rules

algorithmic penalties

automatic exclusion

Technological Opacity Coupling

Tech which couples to opacity makes non-parochial evidence harder to achieve through:

black boxes

trade secrets

complex models

non-disclosure agreements [n.28] [n.185] [n.30]

Technological Lock-In or Exit Coupling

Tech that couples to exit or lock-in makes exit costly or illusory via

interoperability denial

switching costs

path dependency

Technological Persistence Coupling (Time-Binding)

Tech that couples to persistence forms data, models, and infrastructure that bind future agency by creating:

irreversible records

permanent reputational effects

infrastructure that cannot be rolled back [n.37] [n.38] [n.129]

Technological Scale Coupling

Tech that couples to scale applies small design choices that have large impact through:

amplified consequences

asymmetric exposure

rapid propagation of error [n.129] [n.68]

Technology as a system becomes standing-relevant when it:

Conditions access to essentials or civic participation

Makes refusal non-viable (effective exit collapses)

Automates penalties or exclusion

Forecloses contestation or appeal

Binds future agency through persistence or lock-in

Scales error or harm propagation non-parochially [n.24] [n.185] [n.23]

Domain-Specific Properties of Technology

Technology as a Coupling Accelerator

Technology is not a peer domain. It is a force multiplier on coupling that inherently increases the demands of those coupling outputs as a result. As a default, coercion emerges because governance coupling lags as a default of the disparity in capacity for uptake. Technology such as computers are far faster at uptake and coupling output to the public than governance models that rely on human uptake.

The result of this is that technology increases the speed, scale, and opacity of coupling simultaneously. Adjudication of standing is inherently slower than technological deployment for the same reasons that governance models are slower. Technological mediation often imposes influence without restoring the agenttoagent symmetry required for stability, producing systemic fragility across the network. Consequently, technology routinely creates de facto authority prior to legitimacy. This is not an accidental outcome of technology but is structurally inherent to the domain. [n.185] [n.28]

Algorithmic ranking systems produce asymmetries by amplifying visibility for some agents while suppressing it for others without restoring agenttoagent symmetry. A misranking error can propagate rapidly, altering reputational perception or economic opportunity at a scale no individual actor could match. Because the coupling is technologically accelerated, the autonomyimpact becomes nonrerunnable and cannot be corrected by ordinary feedback loops. Structural legitimacy therefore requires constraints that neutralize these acceleration asymmetries, preserving standing before downstream harms accumulate into IEWs.

When uptake and coupling accelerate, autonomyimpact accelerates with them, and acts that alter standing arise faster than governance can correct. Since the causal chain compresses, technologically mediated domains become structurally prone to coercion and domination in ways slower domains do not. For this reason, many canonical standpoints on technology are insufficient for addressing the structural properties of technologically accelerated coupling. With the domain delimited, classified, and translated, the next task is not to derive new tools but to situate the framework relative to major philosophical standpoints on technology.

Coercion Without Command

Coercion in technological systems does not require intention, orders, threats, or identifiable authorities. This claim is not based in metaphysics but is structurally grounded in autonomy, exit, and coupling. Consequently, technology emerges as a coercive substrate itself and not only a tool. [n.195] [n.203] [n.206]

Coercion is traditionally understood as commands, threats, and punishments but technology makes a fourth mode of coercion visible: control. [n.191] Absence of command is not equivalent to absence of coercion because even where algorithms or code compilation of tools generate unanticipated levels of control, coercion emerges. As a result, coercion within the technology domain can present both with and without intent.

Intent alone is not sufficient or necessary in the defining of coercion. As the previous chapters on economics and ecology showed, coercion may develop structurally so that intent is absent and yet the outcome to agents is still coercive. Systems that constrain without addressing anyone create constraint without any interlocutor. Consequently, autonomy loss an occur in these cases even without speech acts.

In technological spaces, algorithms and general usage rules like terms of service operate these constraints independent of speech acts and default rules operate as pre-decision enforcement. [n.190] Penalties can happen simply because “the system says so” as a defaulted force multiplier.

These attributes that are unique to the technology domain present automation as a silent form of enforcement. It can enable opt-out instead of real exit and automate the outcomes of those multipliers of force. This is why traditional legitimacy checks fail in this domain.

Where there is no issuer of the policy there can be no appeal target and where there is no moment of enforcement there is no review trigger. In this particular domain, coercion and influence are distinct just as constraint and persuasion or structural force and interpersonal force are. Technological systems having these unique values warrants consideration of design as an action which pre-emptively can relay these outputs both with and without intent where capacity and awareness are interdependently coupled to the designers.

Design as Action

Design choices in systems are normatively equivalent to actions because they structure outcomes prior to choice. They therefore must be evaluated under standing and legitimacy constraints. Design itself is not preparation for action. It is action itself. [n.189] It operates upstream from consent and often have greater reach than execution.

Design as opposed to use is a false distinction because design already encodes and presupposes use conditions. This is commonly delineated to users as terms of service in a legal sense but likewise has a practical sense in the execution of that design itself. [n.197] These directly inside the boundaries of design itself rather than outwardly towards users or in the user interface.

Likewise, design choices are actions whose effects occur later than their action. This creates a temporal displacement of responsibility in many cases from the PFA of users, but this does not erase the standing constraints which are present in the development stages to begin with. Actions of designers, being actions themselves, are likewise subject to STC-5 constraints as well as NRPP and ALRP principles. The temporal and scale factors of technological adoption over time are what structurally are interdependently coupled to the domain, and which furnish the capacity for accelerated coercion and forms it as a substrate for that coercion.

Design choices such as defaults, thresholds, friction, and visibility shape agency before deliberation. Though moderation actions sometimes retroactively work to resolve these disputes, they serve as a remediation tactic and not as a mechanism for avoiding domination or coerciveness in the first place. Design itself is choice architecture for usership and the agency of those who adopt technology, oftentimes in spaces where opt-out or exit can have steep costs.

When there is no decision point to contest and systems foreclose reflection entirely, the systems themselves are technologically coercive. It is design without deliberative movement and creates standing implications. Where this is a direct result of design choice by agents, those acts may rise to the level of attributive blame and culpability, but where it does not, IEWs may emerge.

When standing burdens arise within design itself whether either of these cases, standing tests apply to the technology and to the designers and developers of those tools. This is not a prescription of the system, but what is structurally interdependent of the system. Where general public finds these actions unjustified and opt-out is low, userbases often reflect this interdependent coupling as a disengagement from the technology.

Many canonical standpoints each describe genuine aspects of technological mediation and coercion. What they lack individually is a shared criterion for when technology and technological systems may legitimately bind others. The following section maps these standpoints as partial descriptions and uses the translation table to show where each succeeds or fails and where standing collapses.

Canonical Standpoints

SECTION PREAMBLE

What follows is not a history of philosophy of technology. Each standpoint that follows is treated as a descriptive lens. They capture something real about technological mediation but are insufficient on their own to answer questions of legitimacy and standing. What distinguishes these positions is not whether they are “right” or “wrong,” but what they are capable of describing and what they systematically leave unresolved. This section does not ask whether the standpoint explains technology but whether it offers criteria for when technological systems may legitimately bind others.

Each standpoint in this section will follow the same sort of diagnostic pattern:

Core claim of the standpoint

What it explains well

Where it fails standing analysis

Why that failure matters

Where these failures emerge, repair becomes necessary whether corrective or not. This will be addressed later in the chapter.

Instrumentalism / Neutral Tool View

The core claim of instrumentalism as it relates to technology is that technology is a neutral means. [n.130] The moral responsibility lies entirely with users and intentions in this canonical standpoint. It works really well for differentiating tools from ends and accounting for misuse and proper use. It also avoids determinism, which is a structural strong point.

Where it fails for standing-relevance lies in what it cannot account for. It has no mechanism to account for design-level coercion or default-driven outcomes. It does not speak to automation without intent or exit collapse that is created by the infrastructure itself. Instrumentalism assumes voluntariness where effective exit may not exist.

Instrumentalism fails regarding technology when systems constrain autonomy prior to use or when refusal is non-viable. It cannot diagnose standing collapse in the technology domain caused by mediation itself, because it lacks criteria for evaluating autonomy loss, exit failure, or correction capacity prior to use.

Technological Determinism (Hard & Soft)

The core claim of technological determinism is that technology drives social structure and outcomes. It asserts that human agency is secondary or adaptive. [n.151] This works well to explain path dependency. It also explains lock-in and irreversible infrastructure as well as the scale amplification of effects.

Standing-relevant failure emerges when it treats inevitability as explanatory and justificatory. When it collapses legitimacy into necessity or constraint into fate, this likewise collapses standing. Determinism in this domain removes the space for standing evaluation entirely.

Technological determinism explains why exit collapses but not whether coercion is justified. It disables proportionality, correction, and off ramps. By describing exit collapse without supplying constraints on justification or repair, determinism risks treating necessity as legitimacy rather than as a condition requiring evaluation.

Social Constructivism of Technology (SCOT)

Social Constructivism of Technology (SCOT) primarily claims that technology is socially negotiated. [n.149] It asserts that design reflects interest, values, and institutions. [n.28] [n.44] [n.46] This is very effective to explain cultural and institutional shaping, contingency of design, and embedded power relations.

Where it fails is in an overemphasis of origin over operation. It underplays persistence, automation, non-intentional coercion, and future-agent binding. Once systems stabilize, Social Constructivism of Technology no longer guarantees contestability.

SCOT explains how systems come to be but does not explain how they legitimately continue to bind. It does not speak to the temporal effects of these emergent technologies. It likewise does not acknowledge long-term coercive effects of those emergences.

Substantive & Autonomy-Eroding Views

This canonical standpoint centers on the claims that technology is not neutral and that it reshapes ends, values, and forms of life. [n.147] It asserts that efficiency and control effectively become dominant norms. It works to explain value drift, autonomy erosion, and technological rationality as domination very well.

Substantive & Autonomy-Eroding Views often treat autonomy loss as inevitable, totalizing, or morally catastrophic though. This can collapse diagnostic evaluation into pessimism or legitimacy into rejection. These both represent standing-relevant failure modes.

Where substantive critiques identify real harms, they lack the criteria for proportional intervention, selective constraint, or repair without wholesale rejection. When agents wish to engage a technology, but the standpoint itself cannot constrain or repair without rejection, coercion which is not justified gets enabled.

Phenomenology & Post-Phenomenology

Phenomenology & Post-Phenomenology assert the core claim that technology mediates experience, perception and embodiment. [n.16] [n.40] [n.148] [n.150] Its core claim is that human-technology relations reshape subjectivity. This accounts for lived experience, attention, affordances, perception, and micro-level mediation very nicely.

Standing-relevant failure emerges because it remains largely individual, experiential, and pre-institutional. It struggles to scale to infrastructure or automated enforcement. It has a hard time accounting for population-level coercion.

Phenomenology explains how technology feels but not how it binds. Standing requires moving from experience to constraint and this standpoint inherently struggles to make this move. It lacks the resources to constrain technological systems as they scale beyond individual experience into infrastructure and automated enforcement.

Critical Theory of Technology

Critical Theory in the technology domain claims technology embeds power. It asserts that design choices have politics and that domination can be engineered. [n.130] [n.131] [n.140] This works very well to explain structural power and hidden coercion. It is a sound accounting of technological governance without democracy.

Where it fails for standing relevance is that it often suspends legitimacy, proportionality, or corrective pathways. Critique can diagnose domination without offering non-authoritarian constraints in response. It is fatalist to a degree in this respect.

Critical Theory identifies standing collapse in the technology domain. It does not, however, constrain coercive remedies. This creates a pathway toward authoritarian responses and domination by leaving coercive remedies unconstrained.

Systems, Cybernetics, and Control Views

From the standpoint of systems, cybernetics, and control views, the core claim is that the technology domain has primary goals of stability and optimization. [n.152] It claims that technology is feedback, regulation, and control. [n.68] [n.69] [n.153] This serves as a reliable accounting for automation, self-regulation, and large-scale coordination.

Standing-relevant failures arise where it optimizes stability over autonomy, efficiency over exit, or prediction over contestation. This standpoint often places control above legitimacy. Legitimacy, having lower priority in some cases, can give way to coercion that isn’t justified.

Systems views explain how control works but not when it is justified. It works well to point to the signals themselves but prioritizes elements that do not inherently serve to constrain coercion in all cases. It often fails to address exit requirements.

Why These Standpoints Are Insufficient

Each of these canonical standpoints does capture a real coupling. Instrumentalism couples usage. Determinism couples lock-in. Constructivism couples design politics. Substantive critique couples autonomy erosion. Phenomenology couples mediation of experience. Critical theory couples power. Systems theory couples control.

Where these standpoints fail is their ability to establish a shared criterion for legitimacy. They do not establish a way to distinguish coordination from coercion or constraints on intervention that preserve autonomy. In order to accomplish those goals, the primary concern as established and derived earlier in the engine and framework is to establish legitimacy and standing. The framework introduced here does not replace these standpoints; it supplies the standingbased adjudicative discipline they individually lack, starting with gates for standing.

Standing Gates for Technology

Gate 1 — Risk-Inheritance & Validation

When considering risk-inheritance and validation within the scope of the technology domain, the framework applies the rules in the same way. What changes is how technological systems trigger it. Consequently, for this consideration we need to ask who inherits the risks of the technological system and are those risks: immediate or delayed, visible or opaque, and reversible or time-binding. [n.129] [n.37]

Risk can take on many specific forms with technology. Misclassification via eligibility, ranking, or scoring or even surveillance exposure can emerge as risks. Likewise, technology may impose risks of exclusion from participation or livelihood, cascading downstream harms, or even future agent binding via infrastructure and records. Data persistence and reputational lock-in are very common risks in this domain.

Technology also exhibits unique validation problems. Risk bearers are often diffuse, unaware, unable to attribute the harm to design, or structurally excluded from validation itself. Many times, risk is inherited by users or non-users without validation channels while design authority remains upstream.

Where these technologies fail to sufficiently evaluate risk, they likewise fail STC-5 based on this initial evaluation. Technology within this framework does not have the standing to coerce where it has not sufficiently been designed to consider stakeholders. It creates opportunities for coercive ends whether intent is present or not in these cases.

Gate 2 — Public Coupling of Evidence

Once technology can be said to be considering risk inheritance properly and has validated it, the next core question is that of non-parochial evidence as is maintained in the toolset. The framework requires us to know if the systems outputs and effects can be publicly examined, contested, and evaluated. [n.15] [n.30] [n.185] While proprietary algorithms and institutional privacy exist, the impacts they have or the outputs they have on the public do not belong to that category as public effect is, by definition, coupled to the public and not private warrant.

Challenges arise in the technology domain not just for proprietary constraints or trade secrets but also among black-box models, non-disclosure regimes, complex or non-interpretable systems, or asymmetric access to system internals. These challenges do not inherently apply a failure itself so long as the outputs and effects remain capable of being evaluated and potentially contested by the public.

Within this domain, transparency may be seen as auditability. Privacy and security constraints may be translated as tiered disclosure. [n.30] [n.28] The domain of technology is inherently subject to reproducible evaluation of outcomes and established error bounds and documented failure modes. When the system outputs bind agents, but no non-parochial pathway exists to justify those bindings, the system itself has failed STC-5.

Gate 3 — Proportionality (NRPP)

NRPP in the technology space prompts the question, “is the technological intervention the least autonomy-reducing means available?” [n.23] The risks involved that are specific to this domain are automation cliffs, over-scaling minor violations, irreversible penalties, and one-size-fits-all enforcement. These are notably common in the technology domain.

In this space, NRPP translates to graduated responses and reversible enforcements. It takes the shape of design that imposes minimal intrusion and pathways for human-override capability. It prefers localized rather than global penalties.

Where automation substitutes efficiency for proportionality or collapses remedies into punishment, STC-5 fails for technology. These are intrinsic gateways to coercion and without the justification builds a path to authoritarianism and domination. These failure signals are not exhaustive but are demonstrations of violations of NRPP in this domain.

Gate 4 — Alternatives

Where technology is seen to be intrusive or coercive the primary concern arises to ask whether less intrusive or non-coercive designs were genuinely considered. [n.79] Alternatives can take the form here of changes in design. It prompts consideration for non-automation or semi-automated processes. Opt-out or parallel systems become options for consideration. Decentralized or modular architectures offer avenues which are less intrusive and less coercive.

Failure for standing emerges at this gate when the technology treats current implementation as inevitable or uses “the system requires it” reasoning. Post-hoc justification via performance metrics are a common mode of failure in this domain. One of the key signals for STC-5 failure is when design choices are treated as necessities rather than contestable decisions.

Gate 5 — Off-Ramps, Exit, and Correction

Technology that does not offer off-ramps, exit, or correction cannot be said to continue to offer autonomy. Consequently, where technology emerges the primary consideration is whether it offers realistic paths to exit, appeal, correction, and the recovery of agency. [n.24] [n.30] [n.185] Intent is not requisite for this to violate these standards.

Technology specifically can create exit problems of interoperability denial, data immobility, switching costs, credential dependency, or network effects. Corrective capacities require audit logs and appeal processes. Minimally, emergency tech needs sunset clauses and override mechanisms. Error correction pathways must always be available to preserve autonomy. Participation that is formally voluntary but functionally non-exitable are autonomy-reducing and signals of failure for STC-5. Where errors are permanent, exit is not possible.

Cross-Gate Failure Patterns in Technology

While each of these gates has some specific challenges and can have unique translations of what failure looks like, those failures often do not happen in isolation. Oftentimes, multiple or several gates may collapse at once. This is indicative of structural standing collapse, not isolated defects.

For instance, efficiency with a lack of alternatives often creates coercion by optimization. Opacity that has been automated can lead to domination by error. Lock-in that is coupled to time-binding creates future-agent coercion. Scaling concerns when paired with non-parochial evidence failure can lead to the masking of legitimacy.

Despite these cross-gate failure patterns, the threshold for determining domination among them remains as it does with all STC-5 evaluations. Technology must pass all five gates or the system loses legitimacy. A technological system acquires standing -relevant coercive force when it does any of the following:

Structures access to essentials or civic participation

Collapses effective exit

Automates penalties or exclusion

Forecloses contestation

Binds future agency irreversibly

Scales harm asymmetrically

These standing gates do not prohibit technological coordination; they constrain it. Where the gates fail, repair, redesign, or de-escalation becomes necessary. This is not because technology is harmful itself but because its mediation has crossed into unjustified coercion. Technology being a substrate that mediates establishes a coupling to both its creators and users.

Resolving Technology Neutrality

Technology is neither neutral nor destiny. It is a structural substrate that is evaluated via standing-based neutrality. Neutrality itself cannot be defined by intention, capability, or general-purpose use. It is defined by autonomy impact.

Many claims of neutrality in the technology domain persist because of institutional convenience and moral outsourcing. Still others insist it is neutral with innovation shielding. Nevertheless, technology exhibits design-level bias and default coercion factors that can result in exit foreclosure.

In order to address this structurally, it must be evaluated as standing-based neutrality where a system is only neutral if exit is viable, refusal is survivable, and correction is accessible. This neutrality is not static either. It may be lost over time as standing tests fail over time. They may likewise pass those tests in one scale and fail at another, making them neutral to one scale and coercive to others.

Neutrality, which is not standing-based collapses under scale where automation, opacity, and persistence obstruct it. When these factors fail standing tests, neutrality becomes domination. Lack of intent, market adoption, and general-purpose does not presuppose neutrality.

Though these STC-5 failures expose when failures and coercion happen, technology is susceptible to temporal status changes and extreme risk escalations which can constitute technological emergencies also. One such example was the Y2K emergency in 1999. [n.154] When these emergencies appear, constraints on technology engage faster just as they would in any other domain.

Technological Emergency

What Constitutes a Technological Emergency

Technological systems are uniquely susceptible to emergency conditions because they operate at scale, bind future agencies, and often fail silently until thresholds are crossed. Failure within a technological system is not constitutive of a technology emergency in this framework. A technological emergency exists when all of the following are present:

Rapid escalation of autonomyrelevant risk

Imminent or irreversible harm if no action is taken

Collapse or nearcollapse of effective exit

Nonparochial exposure (systemic, not isolated)

Timebinding consequences for future agents

Emergencies in this domain are not defined by severity alone but by the convergence of scale, irreversibility, and loss of correction capacity under time pressure. [n.68] [n.69] Bugs, outages, and performance failures do not default as emergencies in this structure. In the case of Y2K, there was global infrastructure dependency, time-binding risk, near-simultaneous failure potential, and emergency coordination without permanent authority expansion. [n.129] [n.34] [n.154]

No Exceptional Authority

Emergency status never creates new standing. [n.31] [n.24] [n.185] No new actors gain coercive authority simply because time is short, harm is large, or coordination is urgent. Emergency conditions affect urgency, not legitimacy.

The conditions of emergencies compress time horizons and increase irreversibility risks. They raise evidentiary urgency and narrow acceptable error margins. They do not change standing requirements, risk-bearer validation, NRPP, exit and off-ramp requirements, or correction capacity expectations.

The technology domain has several fallacies that serve as signals of collapse of standing because they do not offer justification:

“We don’t have time for review.”

“The system must act automatically.”

“Manual override is too slow.”

“Transparency would worsen the crisis.”

“Temporary measures can be normalized.” [n.130] [n.131] [n.140]

This is the opposite of how this framework handles emergency. Emergencies accelerate the standing gates and heighten their duties rather than altering them. These fallacies fall in direct contradiction of these principles of the framework and can become the groundwork for normalization of emergency solutions.

Anti-Precedent for Technology Emergencies

As with any other domain, emergency measures in technology may not migrate into normal operation without renewed standing evaluation. [n.28] [n.118] [n.136] Emergency justification is time-bounded, purpose-specific, and non-generalizable. Sneaking precedent into normal operation by way of emergency does not justify it or grant it standing, though this framework does not speak to the power or force of agents in this regard.

Technology as a mediation tool is particularly susceptible to precedent laundering. [n.129] [n.81] It tends to persist by default and embed emergency logic into infrastructure. This makes it easier for systems to erase the memory of its emergency origin and normalize provisional settings. Consequently, anti-precedent safeguards are essential to the domain.

When speaking of these safeguards, the requirements must always include explicit sunset clauses and termination triggers. Public documentation of user impact and emergency scope become essential. Post-emergency review, restoration of exit, and correction pathways are mandatory to these emergency cases. Absence of them is a standing failure and cause for repair or redesign.

Procedural Capture in Technical Systems

Where procedures exist but correction is foreclosed, procedural capture emerges. In terms of technology, this can take on the forms of protocol capture, interface capture, metric capture, or opacity-as-capture. These forms may emerge without bad intent while still persisting through scale. Capture on the whole creates standing without accountability, which fails STC-5 evaluation, showing it to be coercive.

In technology, capture does not occur after authority is established; it occurs as the mechanism by which authority appears. Technological authority emerges inherently from the procedural capture that is derivative of the pace of its uptake and output compared to the pace of adjudication of its own output. [n.130] [n.131]

Though many of these forms are reliant upon a designer in an earlier phase of development, oftentimes the capacity to anticipate these outcomes cannot be reasonably said to be contained within the scope of awareness of a single developer or team. Many of these technologies emerge as a product of collected efforts where no single agent is wholly aware of the system itself, such as with AI models and their training data. Consequently, technology frequently emerges with authority prior to a standing test being conducted.

Technological Repair and Redesign

Repair Versus Redesign

When technological systems fail standing—whether gradually or under emergency conditions—the legitimacy question does not end with containment. Repair and redesign become standing obligations rather than discretionary improvements. [n.24] [n.185] [n.118] Technology repair and redesign differ from emergency response, and the governing objective is always the restoration of autonomy, exit, and correction capacity rather than performance or efficiency.

Repair differs from redesign in that repair aims to restore effective exit, re-enable correction and appeal, minimize autonomy-reducing constraints, and re-open contestability. [n.23] [n.185] It does not aim to maximize performance, preserve institutional authority, or punish designers or operators. Repair is the restoration of legitimacy, not the improvement of outcomes. It is defined structurally rather than morally.

Redesign is what becomes obligatory when repair within the existing architecture is insufficient. [n.37] [n.81] [n.129] It is triggered when coercion is embedded structurally or when time-binding or lock-in prevent meaningful correction. Redesign is not an admission of failure; it is a standing response to structural constraint.

While they are separate, both repair and redesign can be triggered when standing gates fail persistently, multiple standing gates collapse at once, or emergency measures have altered system behavior beyond temporary scope. These triggers are identified by their net output as it couples to autonomy and risk rather than the operational mechanisms of the technology itself.

The constraints for repair in these systems are the same as the STC-5 gates but couple directly to the repair instances in this case and are consequently not categorized after this point as perpetual system failure. They are instead categorized as repair failure when the standing tests fail within the repair process itself. [n.24] [n.185] This is necessary as a distinction because it becomes a key signal for when redesign is justified.

The alternatives gate is particularly important as failing the gate of alternatives is a direct indicator to pivot to redesign. [n.79] [n.81] Systems which have met the prior three gates but cannot afford for alternatives to themselves or alternate fixes are inherently supposing a system which is coercive by means of limitation to formal choice rather than autonomous choice. Where repair is incapable of identifying alternatives to the structural failure or cannot provide for alternatives to the structure, redesign is required.

Design Principles for Legitimate Redesign

Redesign of technological systems must be oriented toward minimal autonomy reduction, modularity rather than monoliths, reversibility over performance, and contestability over automation. [n.23] [n.24] [n.118] These commitments are design elements that preserve standing and comply with NRPP, ALRP, and MOMA constraints. While performance and automation are not “off the table” in these respects, they cannot dominate over elements which preserve standing in pluralist communities.

Legitimate redesign avoids hard dependencies, credential monopolies, path dependency without consent and irreversible data accumulation. This is a principle called anti-lock-in design. [n.192] [n.81] [n.129] It preserves exit paths and helps validate that choice is not merely formal but is an act of agency.

As a measure of avoiding direct domination or coercion from the technological systems, redesign must always retain a human-override capacity [n.130] [n.140], assign responsibility for intervention, and prevent diffusion of accountability into “the system.” When technology systems run with none of these safety valves and accountability measures, technocratic authoritarianism is given pathways to emerge. Likewise, these substrates being mediums of other agency can provide concealment of wrongs from other domains when established in this format. Repair that is legitimate does not afford this.

STC-5 as Design-Level Testing

Since the design choices prior to deployment are considered acts in themselves, this framework triggers STC-5 prior to that deployment as well. In technological domains, it functions as design auditing and not simply a post-hoc justification test. This is because technological coercion often is formed at design level rather than later in the process.

Waiting for harm is structurally too late to prevent domination. Therefore, STC-5 must be applied ex ante. Post-hoc evaluations do not address scale, persistence, or irreversibility of the actions that were already taken. In fact, some failures cannot be corrected after launch.

In terms of design, this can take the form of stakeholder modeling, auditability, testability, design plurality, reversibility and migration paths, and minimal-intrusion architecture. Design can anticipate justification. When it does, it may afford for appeal, exit, and correction.

Failures to take these steps structurally mandates redesign when lock-in is created without alternatives or where there is persistent multi-gate collapse of the STC-5 criteria. It’s important to distinguish in this domain that testing is not optimization, review is not approval, and safety does not create de facto legitimacy. These principles likewise apply to repair and redesign but are not without limitations.

Limits on Repair and Redesign

Repair is not punishment. [n.185] [n.24] It does not justify retroactive sanctions, blame substitution, or moral scapegoating. Technology causing standing collapse does not imply culpability itself. While actors may have culpability of their actions by design or usage, the technology itself may likewise cause compounding errors when systems interact which were outside of the scope of knowledge of those agents. This is particularly common with patch updates as coding for extensive tools is so robust and large that the sum of potential outcomes for patches can extend beyond the reach of realistic foreseeability by designers, developers, or users.

Furthermore, repair is not optimization. [n.23] [n.118] Performance improvement without autonomy restoration is not repair. Stability without exit is still domination. For the same reasons, repair must not import emergency logic. Anti-precedent logic remains in force whether redesign or repair is taking place so that the future state of technological systems does not inherit the same autonomy-reducing qualities.

When repair is refused or deferred, failure to repair escalates standing against system operators. It legitimates external intervention and converts coordination systems into domination structures. Consequently, unrepaired systems can become technological IEWs that require redesign even without identifiable culpability. [n.185] [n.118]

Caselets

Algorithmic Eligibility

System Description
Algorithmic eligibility systems are used to determine access to benefits, credit, housing, healthcare, employment, or public services. [n.30] [n.49] [n.125] These systems typically aggregate historical data, proxy variables, and model outputs to produce eligibility determinations at scale, often with minimal human review.

StandingRelevant Couplings Activated
Algorithmic eligibility couples mediation (what counts as eligible), automation (decisions without deliberation), opacity (noninterpretable models), and scale (nonparochial impact). Because eligibility frequently gates essentials, these systems directly couple to autonomy and survival thresholds.

Standing Gate Failures

RiskInheritance & Validation: Applicants inherit misclassification risk without meaningful validation channels. Risk is often diffuse and asymmetric, while model designers and operators remain insulated.

Public Coupling of Evidence: Nonparochial evidence is difficult to access due to proprietary models or insufficient explanations.

Exit & Correction: Appeals, if present, are slow or ineffective; refusal or reapplication may be functionally nonviable.

Emergency or Escalation Dynamics
Eligibility errors can cascade rapidly—interrupting housing, healthcare, or income—creating timesensitive harm that compresses correction windows and escalates standing concerns.

Repair and Redesign Implications
Legitimate repair requires auditability, contestable outputs, reversible determinations, and human override for autonomyimpacting decisions. Redesign may require alternative access pathways during review, documented error bounds, and riskbearer validation mechanisms to prevent downstream harm.

AI Decision Support in Institutions

System Description
AI decision support tools assist institutions by recommending actions, prioritizing cases, flagging risks, or guiding resource allocation. [n.28] [n.15] [n.45] While nominally advisory, these systems frequently shape outcomes due to automation bias and operational reliance.

StandingRelevant Couplings Activated
These systems couple information/decision mediation (prediction substituting for justification), opacity (model complexity), and diffusion of accountability (decisions attributed to “the system”). Scale amplifies errors across populations.

Standing Gate Failures

Public Coupling of Evidence: Outputs are treated as authoritative without independent contestation or reproducible evaluation.

Proportionality (NRPP): Advisory outputs escalate into binding actions without graduated response.

Alternatives Considered: Human judgment is displaced rather than supplemented; nonautomated alternatives are not meaningfully considered.

Emergency or Escalation Dynamics
In crisis contexts, time pressure encourages reliance on AI outputs as necessary or inevitable, bypassing review and increasing the risk of unjustified coercion.

Repair and Redesign Implications
Repair requires clear boundaries of decision authority, mandatory human review for autonomyimpacting actions, documented model limitations, and rollback capability. Redesign should ensure AI augments rather than replaces judgment and preserves contestability under time pressure.

Infrastructure LockIn

System Description
Largescale technical infrastructures—such as cloud platforms, identity systems, payment rails, energy grids, or data standards—coordinate essential functions across societies. Their design choices often persist for decades. [n.81] [n.24] [n.129]

StandingRelevant Couplings Activated
Infrastructure lockin couples timebinding (irreversible commitments), exit collapse (high switching costs), and futureagent coercion (binding those who cannot consent). Scale and dependency intensify these effects.

Standing Gate Failures

Exit & OffRamps: Migration becomes economically or functionally infeasible; alternatives are treated as impractical.

Alternatives Considered: Path dependency is framed as necessity rather than a design choice subject to standing evaluation.

Emergency or Escalation Dynamics
Infrastructure crises are often addressed with emergency fixes that entrench dependency further, normalizing provisional controls and shrinking future exit options.

Repair and Redesign Implications
Legitimate redesign emphasizes modularity, interoperability, and migration paths. Antilockin commitments and sunset provisions are required to restore exit and prevent futureagent coercion.

Platform Ban and Demonetization

System Description
Digital platforms impose account bans, content restrictions, or demonetization through automated or semiautomated enforcement systems. These actions can affect speech, livelihood, and participation at scale. [n.116] [L.30] [L.29] [L.31] [L.32]

StandingRelevant Couplings Activated
Platform enforcement couples automation (penalties without deliberation), opacity (unclear standards), scale (nonparochial impact), and exit collapse (lack of viable alternatives).

Standing Gate Failures

Proportionality (NRPP): Binary bans replace graduated responses; penalties are often irreversible.

Public Coupling of Evidence: Reasons for enforcement are undisclosed or vague, preventing contestation.

Exit & Correction: Appeals are ineffective; alternative platforms do not restore equivalent participation or income.

Emergency or Escalation Dynamics
Rapid enforcement is justified by urgency or safety concerns, normalizing permanent exclusions and bypassing review.

Repair and Redesign Implications
Repair requires transparent standards, graduated sanctions, effective appeal mechanisms, and temporary rather than permanent exclusions. Redesign should restore contestability and preserve exit where livelihood or civic participation is at stake.

Coupling Without Adjudication

In all of these cases the engine applies in the same order: coupling occurs, relevance is generated, autonomy is impacted, and then standing is assumed rather than earned. Technology regularly produces standing effects before standing can be evaluated. These public adjudications do not happen because the rapid coupling and relevance of technology outpaces it even before intention or governance enter.

As discussed near the beginning of this chapter, this is a interdependent coupling that happens at rapid pace because the processing speed of technology itself far outpaces that of adjudication. This is not a consequence that is inherently attributable to designers, though this does not make them immune to coercive design attribution where they have this influence prior to public coupling. What is diagnosed here is a temporal mismatch between the emergence of technology and the relative capacity to adjudicate its impact to autonomy.

Consider technology such as “deep fakes.” The temporal mismatch occurred because this technology emerged quickly and thus became relatively inexpensive and widely accessible to consumer applications, open models, or easy pipelines. This emerged significantly faster than authentication at scale, evidentiary standards for them, trusted attribution, platform enforcement, or even public literacy.

Deep fake technology couples to the public through identity, reputation, trust, and evidentiary perception. It creates a representative interdependent coupling of media to the perception without the non-parochial evidence to validate it. The public cannot opt out of this once the coupling has propagated but also cannot validate it by means of public non-parochial evidence until those tools exist.

Standing for such technology is not established because there are no clear risk validations, no NRPP bound remedies, no off-ramps once virality begins, and no agreed operations for provenance, authenticity, or rapid contestation. Adjudication in this case arrives much later than can prevent coercive effects such as job loss or reputational damage.

Technology Without Automated Domination

Synthesis

This framework establishes that technology is standing-relevant mediation, not neutral tooling. Coercion arises structurally via design, automation, opacity, lock-in, and time-binding. Standing gates apply in an unchanged manner but are triggered differently.

The usage of caselets demonstrates that standing failures in technology are typically multi-gate failures. They show how emergency logic frequently can mask legitimacy collapse and that repair and redesign are structural obligations and not merely optional reforms. Technology itself cannot justify coercion whether via efficiency, necessity, or inevitability. It does not substitute legitimacy with prediction alone and cannot collapse exit, correction or proportionality without losing standing.

Why Technology Cannot Self-Legitimate

Innovation is not an excuse for standing failure, and it does not justify harm. Market adoption is not the same thing as consent and expertise cannot substitute standing. Such cases are directly related to exit foreclosure, risk inheritance, and autonomy constraints.

While technological systems may emerge within society prior to the capacity to adjudicate the usage or engagement of it, this does not inherently designate those systems as legitimate. Where technology scales constraint externally through automation, infrastructure, and design, identity scales constraint internally through recognition, role expectation, and selfinterpretation

At this stage, what distinguishes the power of technology is not that it can issue commands but that it can render alternatives increasingly unintelligible. Mediation becoming infrastructure and automation being defaulted makes constraint necessary. Technology operationalizes and normalizes the summary dispensing of authority through persistence, scale, and opacity. Standing doesn’t collapse from technology being malicious. It collapses because outputs impact autonomy even as justification evaporates. Erosion of viable exit, correction, and contestation with no pinpointed moment of decision creates an environment of domination that slowly chokes legitimacy in secrecy.

Technology in society accelerates coupling to a point that it is not simply impacting society in the sense of public standing but can reshape human agency, identity, and trust directly. Having established how technological systems mediate standing, coercion, emergency response and repair, the analysis must now turn to how that reshaping impacts identity and psychology individually and in society. The next chapter examines how the framework and structure that is built impact psychology and identity where pluralism and private warrant often collide.

Structural Warning

The analyses that follow shift attention from externally imposed constraints to those that persist through internalization, inheritance, time-binding and scale. In these domains, domination may endure without active coercion, and harm may emerge without identifiable malice, intent, or centralized authority.

This transition does not relax the framework’s constraints. On the contrary, the absence of intent does not mitigate standing failures, nor does structural inheritance excuse illegitimacy. Where harms arise from accumulated decisions, inherited systems, or pathdependent constraints, responsibility may be diffuse or absent even as autonomy is meaningfully reduced. Readers should therefore resist two common errors. The first is moralization: the assumption that identifying structural harm requires identifying culpable agents. The second is fatalism: the inference that inherited constraint forecloses repair. Neither follows.

The framework remains oriented toward authorization, exit, proportionality, and repair. Yet in these domains, repair may require redesign rather than reversal, acknowledgment rather than punishment, and forwardlooking safeguards rather than retrospective judgment. Some outcomes may be tragic even when no alternative standing could be established.

The chapters that follow address these conditions directly. They do not resolve them. They specify how legitimacy erodes, how domination persists without command, and how responsibility must be reunderstood when constraint outlives choice.

Communicative Drift Under Acceleration

A brief video clip of a political figure is uploaded to a platform with key contextual cues removed. Viewers who encounter only the edited version reconstruct relevance from incomplete information, generating autonomyimpact on the official’s perceived intentions. As the clip spreads faster than clarifications or corrections can reach the same audience, answerability collapses; those affected inherit mis-framed risks they cannot meaningfully exit. Even after the full context is restored, the mis-coupling persists because the correction loop cannot match the velocity of the initial spread. This produces a structural wrong without culpability: standing erodes through communicative acceleration rather than deception or malice. The vignette illustrates how technologically mediated coupling destabilizes legitimacy when uptake and correction operate on mismatched timescales.

Part III – Internalization, Scale & Inheritance: Across Minds and Societies

X — About Identity and Psychology

Purpose: This section examines how the coupling-standing-legitimacy engine operates with the identity and psychology domain and how misidentification of coupling produces characteristic failures of standing in this domain. It sets out to reframe identity beyond merely essence but as a culmination of inherent couplings which, in turn, serve to furnish collectives with the capacity to bring interests into the collective from the individuals.

Orientation

What This Chapter Is and Is Not

This chapter functions to translate the toolset to the domain of identity and psychology. In this framework identity is not only an internal essence. [n.194] [n.54] [n.159] It likewise exists as a standing-relevant interface between individual assertion and social recognition. External coordination systems such as technology and politics carry psychological impact and coordination impact to pluralist social collectives. [n.28] [n.130] [n.118] [n.159] [n.160]

This chapter is not an establishment of social policy or psychological evaluation. It shows how identity categories function as PFAs that can assign roles, structure expectations, enable or block participation, and mediate legitimacy. [n.22] [n.61] [n.185]

It does not adjudicate which identities are “true” but examines how identity claims acquire or fail to acquire standing in pluralist social systems. It evaluates those failures and offers paths to remediation. [n.1] [n.40] [n.41] [n.44] [n.17]

This chapter is not a biological theory of sex and does not deny any lived experience of any individuals. The personal stories of individuals carry their own inherent meaning and are not afforded any more or less value by this framework. [n.83] [n.84] It is an explicit misreading of this work to assert that it either validates or invalidates specific personal identities. Those identities stand on their own merit as we will discover in this chapter.

This chapter does not diagnose psychological disorders. It is not a replacement for clinical frameworks or seeking help when it is needed. Where distress arises from individual pathology, remediation belongs to clinical disciplines, not pluralist frameworks. The analysis here concerns when identity-relevant distress is structurally produced or amplified by social arrangements such that questions of standing, legitimacy, and repair arise beyond the individual. [n.83] [n.84] [n.60] [n.25] [n.129]

Not all distress is socially induced, and not all social distress creates standing. [n.21] Identity harm does not inherently justify constraint, but this is measured against the risk-inheritance and standing to coerce to avoid domination. [n.13] This is not advocacy for identity harm but is a measure by which to determine where such actions may gain justification or authority in pluralist settings. If someone “identifies” as an authority and uses that to dominate others, forms of identity harm against that may be justified where such harm is limited to removing illegitimate authority and restoring autonomy, but not to punishment, humiliation, or retaliation. [n.23] [n.63] [n.18] [n.90] [n.118] [n.25] Such cases then are likewise constrained to measures which return autonomy.

This is not a moral judgment of those identities or a psychiatric classification. This chapter does not prescribe policy either. [n.47] [n.26] [n.127] What it does is serve to translate the established toolset into a domain that notoriously has difficulty in coordinating among pluralist groups. This framework does not deny phenomenological accounts of lived experience; it evaluates how such experiences acquire standing in pluralist coordination.

Why This Chapter Matters

This chapter has specific implications to the treatment of the LGBTQIA+ community. While it does not give prescriptions for interaction itself, it will demonstrate the failure signals. A careful reader will be able to likewise identify where existing policies and prescriptions have been insufficient for these identities within many pluralist groups.

This chapter translates the standing engine and toolset into the domain of identity and psychology where coercion is often informal, and enforcement is often social rather than legal. [n.118] [n.25] [n.24] In these cases, legitimacy failures are often experienced as personal harm. While that personal harm is not something this framework supposes to handle, the collective impact of whole segments of a pluralist community experiencing this validates this as a domain which belongs to this framework.

Expectations

Readers should expect this chapter to treat psychology and identity structurally rather than therapeutically. This chapter does not function as clinical psychology, self-help, or personality theory. Psychological phenomena are analyzed by this framework as sites of coupling, vectors of standing, and interfaces between autonomy and structure.

Inner experience is not private insulation from legitimacy analysis. [n.14] [n.15] [n.98] Subjectivity does not exempt systems from standing evaluation. Identity in this sense will be treated as coupled rather than chosen or given.

Identity in this chapter is not assumed to be either purely self-authored or purely imposed. It is assumed to have authority by default as will be established in the chapter. [n.159] [n.160] [n.54] It is examined as a coordination surface and standing-relevant interface, not just a “feeling.”

Identity in this chapter is a stabilized coupling across perception, recognition, and constraint. [n.44] [n.194] This chapter consequently rejects both essentialist identity and voluntarist identity simultaneously. [n.16] [n.126] It instead views it likewise structurally.

Readers can expect discomfort where moral language loses explanatory power. Feelings of harm, offense, alienation, and distress are not dismissed. They are, however, treated as insufficient to establish standing, justify coercion, or explain legitimacy failure on their own. This chapter will distinguish psychological harm from autonomy impact and standing failure. While they often correlate, they are not identical.

In this chapter, the individual is neither the ultimate authority nor ultimate victim. It does not center individual experience as sovereign or reduce individuals to mere system outputs. It treats individuals as bearers of autonomy, participants in pluralist constraint systems, and nodes of coupling. Subjective experience is evidence, not adjudication by itself. [n.49] [n.15] [n.164]

The author expects that the reader is willing to hold inner experience and structural constraint in the same analytic frame. They will need to resist reducing psychological distress to moral entitlement or personal failure to get the most from this chapter. Readers will be expected to accept that identity can be harmed without wrongdoing, distress can exist without illegitimacy, and that legitimacy can fail without subjective distress.

This chapter assumes that the reader can distinguish between explanation and justification. It presumes an understanding of the differences between empathy and legitimacy and recognition as apart from standing. Readers should be able to tolerate analysis where no party is morally blameworthy but repair is required anyway.

Readers in this chapter will need to be able to track multi-level causation including individual psychology, social identity, and institutional coupling. This chapter should not be read as a denial of psychological harm or a call to suppress identity claims. It is not a validation of subjective veto power or a retreat to technocratic or behavioral reductionism. Psychology is not used here to override moral or political claims. It likewise does not subordinate them but shows where legitimacy fails or survives when subjectivity is the site of impact.

Psychological terms are often emotionally saturated, socially weaponized, or morally loaded. [n.118] [L.8] Without translations, standing may collapse into sentiment, coercion hides behind experience, and legitimacy debates become impossible. Since psychological language is already normatively overdetermined, the chapter must first translate it into structural terms that preserve autonomy without granting subjective sovereignty.

Translations

This section does not introduce new tools. [n.68] [n.69] It specifies how the existing standing engine and tools manifest in the identity and psychology domain. As with “About Technology” these are not re-derivations of the tools themselves or individualized interpretations of them. It is a recognizing of the unique coupling that arises from this domain rather than from the engine and tools themselves. It is the observation that these unique couplings emerge from the domains themselves that enables the tools and engine to have the cross-domain attribute that it has.

Translation Table:

Domain goal: Not to settle metaphysics, but to specify conditions for warrant, standing, agency, and constraint under pluralism.

PFA (Perceptual Frame Agreement): The operative lens (individual or collective) that determines what counts as relevant, evidential, actionable, and intelligible.

Internalized PFA (IPFA): The collective of perceptions within the consciousness of an agent which provides validation of their personal warrant.

Coupling: When a claim, perception, or concept enters a frame such that it shapes prediction, valuation, deliberation, or action.

Failed coupling: Uptake that does not alter prediction/action/selfrelation—i.e., does not become relevant within any operative frame.

Decoupling: Separating a claim from the conditions that warranted it (e.g., treating a structural claim as metaphysical, or vice versa).

Relevance: Significance arises only where coupling changes agency, choicespace, deliberation, or coordination.

Private warrant: Reasons that justify belief/action for the agent given their history, capacities, and PFA—without authority over others.

Public warrant: Reasons assessable and rerunnable under shared operations; supports coordination beyond private standpoint.

Standing: The legitimacy of a claim to bind action, allocate roles, constrain others, or trigger enforcement.

Internalized Standing (IS): The legitimacy of an internal claim that an agent makes of oneself to bind action, allocate roles, constrain themselves, or trigger enforcement.

Standing ≠ truth: A claim may be true yet lack standing to coerce; a claim may be widely accepted yet fail standing.

Standing ≠ sincerity: Sincerity creates personal warrant, not automatic public authority.

Metaphysical bracketing: The framework remains agnostic about “what reality is” while still governing how claims may bind others.

Existence vs relevance: “Exists” is not the same as “matters for coordination”; existence claims have value only where they couple to action/prediction.

Reasons vs causes: Causes explain events; reasons justify action within a frame. A causal story alone does not produce standing.

Agency (structural): Selfauthorship under viable alternatives, revision, and nonpunitive refusal—not merely intention or movement.

Autonomy: Capacity for selfauthorship across time and contexts; depends on alternatives, reversibility, and exit.

Autonomy constraint: Any structure (internal or external) that forecloses revision/refusal/exit, collapsing selfauthorship into compliance.

Exit (epistemic): Ability to revise beliefs without catastrophic cost (identity loss, expulsion, coercive penalty).

Exit (practical): Ability to refuse participation without losing survival thresholds or facing punitive collapse.

Foreclosed exit: “No real alternative” conditions that convert coordination pressure into coercion.

Coercion (epistemic): Forcing belief/acceptance by threat, exclusion, or mandatory certainty rather than shared operations.

Coercion (social): Enforced role/recognition norms that foreclose refusal or impose penalties beyond coordination necessity.

ERL (Epistemic Responsibility Ladder): Evidence burden scales with autonomy impact: lowstakes → trust/testimony; highstakes → rerunnable operations.

STC5 (Standing to Coerce): Coercion is legitimate only when riskbearers validate, evidence is nonparochial, alternatives considered, offramps exist, and proportionality holds.

NRPP: Even when intervention is justified, prescription must be least autonomyreducing, targeted, and reversible.

Riskinheritance: Who bears the costs of error, enforcement, or constraint—especially future selves and nonconsenting parties.

Riskbearer validation: Those who inherit the risk carry privileged standing to demand evidence, alternatives, and limits.

Peer disagreement: Qualified disagreement increases burden; it does not grant authority. Coercive standing is suspended until discriminating operations exist.

Testimony (default): Indispensable for lowrisk coordination; tightens as autonomyimpact and irreversibility rise.

Belief vs address: Internal belief is noncoercible; public coordination norms may be constrained where misrecognition forecloses autonomy.

Category error (philosophy domain): Treating a structural claim as metaphysical (or vice versa), or substituting private criteria while claiming public evaluation.

Operational capture: When power, fear, loyalty, or status substitutes for shared operations, producing false “public” warrant.

Repair: Restores agency, exit, and correction pathways; not necessarily moral agreement or metaphysical consensus.

Correction: Behavioral compliance without restoring agency or revisability (often a domination signal).

IEW: Harm arising from structural conditions without individual malicious intent.

[n.24] [n.25] [n.29] [n.68] [n.69]

Identity and psychology expose the individual-scale operation of the same engine while operating in a different medium. Technology exposed the cross-domain scaling and identity exposes micro-scale enforcement. These translations examine how identity and psychology, while individualistic, still relate to the pluralist collective itself.

Moral Identity & Self Worth

Philosophy of Mind

What this framework defines as a “mind” is a functional structure and not a substance in itself. [n.1] [n.66] [n.41] It does not consider it a metaphysical entity, container of representations, or a reducible physical object. Instead, this framework treats the mind as a structured accumulation of perceptual coupling that has the capacity to generate relevance, expectation, and action. The mind is not what it perceives, it is the pattern that persists across perceptions.

The mind in this framework is then a product of perceptual history. Each agent’s PFA is shaped by past perceptual exposure, trauma, salience, habituation, learned affordances, and reinforcement or correction. These histories have the capacity to generate expectations, confidence gradients, and sensitivity to blind spots. Consequently, combined with variances in perceptual uptake, two agents who share a capacity for uptake may experience the same event but generate different internal warrants.

Internal PFAs become relevance filters for the individual. They determine what registers as relevant to them, what counts as evidence to them, and what feels actionable to them. They are internally coherent, historically grounded, and not chosen freely in most cases. Consequently, perception is never neutral, even when sincere. [n.41] [n.59] [n.83] These Internalized PFAs do not inherently possess internalized standing to bind action or constrain future selves without likewise passing standing to coerce evaluations. [n.53]

While these internalized PFAs do generate personal warrant and validity, they are not transferrable inherently. A personal warrant is a reason that justifies belief or action for that agent. When a request is being made to acknowledge this to other agents, what can be reasonably accommodated is the acknowledgement of the validity of that warrant but not the sharing of it implicitly.

Personal warrant arises from internal validation, lived experience, and consistency with a PFA. Importantly, while they do create validity for the agent, they do not inherently create standing over others. [n.49] [n.15] Internalized validity does not create a standing to coerce. This works bidirectionally so that others likewise have no standing to coerce simply via dismissal of lived experience.

This account is truly compatible with many theories of mind including physicalist, phenomenological, emergentist, or agnostic accounts. The framework is concerned with effects themselves, not essences. Standing is established on impact and coupling, not metaphysical truth. Thus, this framework does not need to answer if the mind is physical, consciousness is fundamental, or if perception tracks reality.

It only needs the fact of differential perceptual uptake, existence of persistent internal structure, and non-identity of PFAs across agents. Mind matters for this framework because it shapes relevance, not because it settles ontology. Minds generate valid personal warrants through historically structured perception, but no internal mental state—however sincere—can generate public standing or coercive authority without shared operations and reproducibility.

PFAs vs Personal Warrant

The STC-5 standard in this framework applies to that of the collective group and that of the PFA itself; However, despite not creating validity among the PFA of the pluralist collective, the individual warrant is itself comprised of a collective of PFAs for the individual. The perceptual frame of the individual itself is not static and does not maintain the same scale or outcomes over time, yet recollection of previous perceptual frames for the individual persists. [n.1] [n.16] [n.41]

What we assign as a personal warrant then is really the evaluation of those changing perceptual frames for the individual comprised as a singular PFA that belongs to the individual self. This is the mechanism by which personal warrant generates candidates for Internalized Standing, through which autonomy and agency may be legitimately exercised over action. [n.22] [n.53] [n.155] It is the means by which we can assert that personal warrant is valid in itself. It is comprised of internalized PFA evaluation that is subject to the same level of internalized testing.

Personal STC-5 for Personal PFAs

STC-5 constraints are structurally embedded to internal normative constraints evaluated under Internalized Standing but scoped to that of the individual. [n.21] [n.37] [n.145] They emerge inherently from the individual and can be recognized through statements of what an individual “wants” or “desires.” When an agent speaks to this effect, what they are speaking to is the collected evaluation of those perceptions as an isolated PFA of their own which is validated over the temporal history of their own experience. [n.53] [n.82] [n.156]

Individuals naturally initiate risk validation by considering the risks to themselves and recognizing the potential harms to themselves. Failure of this capacity happens when there is a lack of capacity or when individuals temporally delay the consideration of these risks. Likewise, the individual evaluates the evidence which is available to them to make these evaluations. Where they are suspicious of the validity of this evidence, the non-parochial qualifier likewise enters the evaluation where one might demand “proof” or supporting evidence in addition to the original evidence. Such failures of evidence include purely emotional reaction which considers no evidence or a lack of re-runnable evidence being available to the individual. [n.14] [n.15] [n.98]

This framework does not presume that all individuals necessarily adhere to the individual principles of least autonomy-reducing means or that they are done with reciprocal nature. Instead, it identifies that when individuals do not abide these concepts and attempt coupling to a collective pluralist society a natural conflict emerges. [n.47] [n.127] [n.25]

Totalizing identity claims about what someone can never do or what they are incapable of fail by default. [n.64] [n.53] [n.145] This framework demands self-fairness in this respect just as it does to the collective. How could plural fairness be maintained if the individuals who comprise the collective are incapable or refuse to acknowledge what is fair to the individuals from the start?

While internal coercion does happen and is often conflated with motivation, this does not justify such actions. [n.19] [n.155] [n.25] We recognize these coercions without justification when we assert colloquialisms like, “you need to be fair to yourself.” Treating self-coercion as the first solution or immediate identity collapse instead of considering alternatives are key signals of failure of this gate. Individuals must consider non-binding and non-identity-level options like changing environment, partial commitment, reversible experiment, or temporal buffering to maintain that validity. [n.23] [n.24] [n.68]

Mind and Responsibility

Perceptual history mitigates moral blame because Internalized PFAs (IPFAs) are historically conditioned. Agents do not freely choose their relevance filters. [n.4] [n.59] [n.60] Consequently, error does not imply malice inherently and disagreement does not intrinsically imply bad faith. This is not to say that such elements may not or do not exist to the individual but that they are not implicitly a result of the IPFA or perceptual history of the agent.

Responsibility does enter and arise when agents are presented with correction, alternatives become accessible, or persistence forecloses other’s autonomy. Responsibility is not about having a mind—it is about what one does once relevance is challenged. Where an agent lacks the capacity or access to alternative means from their established IPFA or perceptual history, they act upon that history. This does not make their actions inherently beyond the scope of correction, yet actions which pursue those ends are constrained just the same.

As it concerns the individual, from where would they conjure alternative actions or thoughts of consequence where no perception of them had previously existed to some degree? Do not children require the experience of heat prior to the understanding of what a burn is? Is there any culpability for children then who touch a red-hot stovetop having never experienced this type of heat before? Certainly not.

This is emergent as an internalized IEW within the IPFA of that individual. Internalized IEWs are then a mechanism by which the agent has capacity to engage and expand this PFA. [n.14] [n.15] [n.68] We colloquially call this expansion of the IPFA “learning” and it is not limited to the form of internalized IEWs. Nonetheless, the expansion of a IPFA inherently supposes in its very meaning that new perceptions are being added to the sum volume for the individual, whether by externalized volition or internalized and regardless of whether internalized IEWs emerge.

This framework retains from Descartes the distinction between the perceiver, perception, and object but rejects representational certainty as grounding public truth. Likewise, for Sartre it retains non-self-grounding consciousness and perception as a mode of existence but rejects phenomenology as ontological proof. These retentions serve to justify structure rather than metaphysics and that structure itself is what gives validation to internalized PFAs. [n.95] [n.66]

Agency and Action

When referring to actions, this framework considers action as structured self-authorship. It is not merely a bodily movement, realization of intent, or causal chain from belief to desire. It is an authorized intervention to the world. [n.155] It occurs within a field of alternatives and under conditions where refusal, revision, and exit are viable. Action presupposes authorship and authorship presupposes alternatives. [n.4] [n.19] [n.22] [n.53]

This framework rejects the idea that identifying causes or tracing intention for behaviors is sufficient to explain agency. Where Davidson says that actions are events caused in the right way by beliefs or desires, this framework asserts that causal explanation does not establish standing, authorship, or responsibility as there are no inherent couplings between desire and action. [n.53] [n.4] [n.157] Many people have desires which they likewise do not act upon even when they believe them to be “right.” Causes explain to us what happened and agency gives explanation for who can be held to account for action and why.

This framework deliberately avoids metaphysical theories of will, libertarian free choice, and inner decision points as ultimate grounds. They are internal volitional states that are not publicly legible by default. They do not scale to pluralist legitimacy without further coupling and validation that are external to them so they cannot ground coercive standing. This is not a denial of volition.
