Scientific reliability, on this account, reflects successful coordination rather than metaphysical authority, and no increase in predictive power alone licenses a transition from epistemic success to coercive standing.

Knowledge and science are not inherently authoritative. [n.11] [n.12] Instead, they earn relevance by compressing uncertainty and enabling coordination under risk. They earn standing by validating risk-bearers, considering alternatives, and providing meaningful exit. Claims become relevant by justifying mandates, removing options, or reallocating harm.

This is in alignment with capacity-indexed autonomy as well as STC-5, ERL, and risk inheritance principles. Claims having justification which is beyond the capacity of those that they suppose to mandate without reasonable pathways to acquire that capacity are inherently a level of coercion. Where this evidence is presented in alignment with STC-5, the intentional gatekeeping of capacity to understand then becomes a violation of capacity-indexed autonomy and thus fails the non-parochial attribute for such evidence as it relates to the PFA of the public.

By these principles in action, it becomes not only necessary for non-parochial evidence to be presented to the public PFA for evaluation but the means by which to gain capacity for understanding such evidence must likewise be presented. This is an implicit structural necessity to avoid domination and becomes a premise for why gatekeeping knowledge or science is an inherent autonomy violation. One cannot be supposed to have full agency and autonomy in respect to things which lie beyond their capacity to understand or engage.

Gatekeeping in this domain often takes place in a cross-domain method such as markets pricing secondary education beyond the reach of many or areas being ecologically devastated to a degree that education becomes secondary to survival. [n.116] [n.94] Wherever learning opportunities for knowledge or science are kept beyond the reach of an agent, a level of capacity-indexed autonomy is being infringed. As discussed in previous chapters about identity and psychology, this is not limited to what is deemed as “neurotypical” or “able bodied.” This is a structural implication of non-dominant society such that, any capacity which is limited or intentionally gatekept while the means to avoid such limitations exist within that pluralist society, these acts or lack of action are a form structural coercion. [n.136] [n.25]

Science as a Standing-Relevant Coordination System

The result of this structural outcome is that science and knowledge become an infrastructure rather than a command. Science stabilizes expectations across time and institutions accumulate authority through memory. [n.172] [n.177] Without periodic revalidation, time-binding turns into epistemic inertia.

This system then carries the same requirements as all time-bound systems. Ceiling vs prescription principles apply to how remediation and correction are implemented. [n.23] [n.13] Compositional coupling does not absolve the requirement to meet STC-5 constraints such as NRPP.

Canonization of literature where review and audits are no longer allowed or required then carries an inherent risk of coercion and potential dominance. [n.185] [n.143] [n.207] Precedence, though containing a level of warrant in itself due to repeated and retestable outcomes, does not inherently have the standing to coerce without periodic evaluations of the current standing for itself. Failure in this respect is to temporally bind future agents without the presence of temporally relevant non-parochial evidence and transforms precedent into domination.

Proxy Standing in Science and Knowledge

While capacity-indexed autonomy applies in this domain, not every case is one where public will have the capacity even when granted the access to the knowledge itself. Science in these cases does not have blanket authority, yet the use of proxies who advocate for the standing of those who lack capacity remains. [n.29] [n.188] This is not optionally ideal for the framework, but a structural necessity presented by inherent variable capacities for uptake.

In this domain some common examples include biosecurity, medical trials, or classified research. They may operate with tiered disclosure, proxy standing of sample groups to validate risk-bearers and publish their methods and constraints publicly. In such cases, proxies must be authorized by the risk-bearers and likewise be replaceable. This is already standard testing format for clinical trials via consent forms for those who bear the risks of those trials as well as having alternates that can replace those who partake in the trials.

Likewise, these proxy standing instances must also be met with sunset clauses and be publicly published whenever possible. Where a subject of a study consents, this cannot be seen as perpetual or even feasibly given perpetually from the agent as the outcomes of perpetuity cannot be fully known to the agent or agents. Benefit for these proxy standings are not sufficient to justify the autonomy-reduction of perpetually imposing such standing upon them.

Epistemic Considerations

Epistemic Standing versus Epistemic Correctness

Standing and “truth” as relative to a PFA are not equivalent. Standing is evaluated ex ante but correctness in this sense is evaluated ex post. [n.207] Standing is about permission at the time of action, not validation after outcomes are known.

Even perfectly accurate predictions or life-saving outcomes do not retroactively create standing. They likewise do not even if they avoid catastrophe. The idea that something working is inherent justification for it does not account for circumstances beyond the control of action. [n.59] [n.53] The model aligning with an outcome does not inherently confer that the mandate was correct. This is an Argumentum ad Hujus Factum and is likewise fallacious. [n.11] [n.12]

Truth is not the same thing as permission and falsehood does not immediately create illegitimacy. [n.5] [n.54] The wedge between the two is temporal, not ideological. In such cases the concern is not about whether the claim is true in itself, but who bears the costs and how that truth is decided anyway.

If authorities impose action while error costs fall on others and alternatives are foreclosed, standing collapses regardless of the accuracy. The risk-bearers remain independently coupled to outcomes over which they have no autonomy or agency. Correctness for a PFA does not neutralize asymmetric risk just as incorrectness for a PFA does not automatically void guidance.

These are inherent violations of ALRP because risk is imposed on agents who did not authorize the coupling and oftentimes exit is foreclosed or correction is unavailable. Whether they were right or not does not matter if the people bearing the risk had no standing role in authorizing or exiting the coupling. This is a diagnostic of standing failure structurally and not an ethical viewpoint.

Likewise, with the Maxim of Mutual Autonomy interpersonally incorrect claims can still compress uncertainty, coordinate action, and guide provisional behavior but this maxim prevents obligation inflation permanence, and enforcement escalation. Knowledge that does not align with the PFA of the group as “correct” can guide action without ever acquiring standing to bind or coerce. This is likewise a diagnostic.

ALRP in this sense governs who bears the risk and MOMA governs how much may be demanded. “Truth” as a reflection of perceptual frame agreement does not govern either of them. Instead of asking if something is true, this structure demands to know who authorized coupling and who bears risks. IF those are not the same agent, correctness cannot supply standing.

Instead of asking what science requires us to do, this structure demands to know the maximum obligation that a coupling can legitimately impose. This prevents guidance from becoming mandate, warning from becoming exclusion, and prediction from becoming enforcement. The ceiling and prescription difference in this case is likewise limited by ceiling vs prescription principles.

Standing in this framework is evaluated based on the coupling and not based on outcomes so that later correctness cannot repair earlier standing failures. Even across temporal inheritances these couplings must be considered at the time of their coupling and not retroactively as the temporal constraints often foreclose alternatives and exits. Success does not reverse-authorize coercion structurally.

Neither having information nor being skeptical of it is structurally valid in this framework for coercion. While one is handedly a more natural pathway to reasonable and justified coercion as one has capacity to produce non-parochial evidence, this does not inherently grant authority for coercion. They both fail to inherit such standing structurally for the same reason.

Epistemic Injustice and Testimonial Asymmetry

Epistemic systems do not all contain symmetrical power, influence, or capacities. Standing collapse in epistemic systems often tracks discrepancies in social power as well as a compounded risk inheritance. [n.49] [n.165] [n.164] Oftentimes this can lead to testimonial exclusion and a subversive use of relational identity-defining coupling where expertise and roles are levied as standing itself rather than justifying such claims through non-parochial evidence.

This is further evidence of the need for a cross-domain measurement form which can evaluate these epistemic systems independent of their power, influence, or capacity. Such evaluative measures decouple testimonial asymmetry from subversive simulated couplings and recouple the non-parochial evidence to the PFA of the collective. This then becomes a direct measure for epistemic injustice not only between epistemic systems but across domains as well. Consequently, expertise in this framework is a claim that demands structural validation, not formal validation.

Expertise, Dependency, and Capacity-Indexed Autonomy

Even when standing is earned, expertise itself is not an epistemic superiority. It is an asymmetric dependency creation. Expertise does not coerce by knowing but by becoming irreplaceable. [n.22] [n.116] [n.118] [n.206] Rationally, if everyone had the same level of knowledge of the subject matter and the same capacity, then nobody is an “expert” any more than another. In this frame, “expert” then is a relational identity-defining coupling that is not itself inheriting of standing to coerce.

Standing failures emerge when agents cannot act without experts, cannot contest experts, or cannot exit expert-mediated systems. Expertise changes the dependency topology of a system structurally. Where systems themselves become wholly dependent upon experts for autonomy, dependency becomes coercive. Dependency in this case is the hidden coupling.

Dependency can become coercive even in situations where epistemic processes are flawless. A system can be transparent, accurate, peer-reviewed, corrigible and still be illegitimate by virtue of creating non-substitutable dependencies. [n.206] In this case, that non-substitutable dependency itself is what collapses autonomy. Ironically, even epistemic institutions are not required to justify rejection, they are structurally constrained such that those rejections must not function as coercive authority by foreclosing exit, imposing penalty, or allocating asymmetric risk without standing. Cross-domain gatekeeping on the whole is prevalent regardless of institutional scope.

Capacity-indexed autonomy, while still operationally the same principle and unchanged, operates as a negative test in this domain. It constrains when dependency substitution is allowed at all. It does not ask whether experts should decide. It asks whether dependency on experts has become unavoidable by foreclosing on alternatives or exit.

CIA is violated when capacity is not merely absent but withheld or gatekept. The framework does not require agents to become experts but explicitly frames gatekept capacity as a violation of autonomy. Likewise, it is violated when dependency is engineered rather than unavoidable or pathways to capacity restoration are blocked. What emerges from this evaluation are two variant forms of epistemic dependency, legitimate and illegitimate.

Legitimate epistemic dependency is temporary, substitutable, capacity-building, and accompanied by pathways to independence. It includes things like training, scaffolding, open methods, and teach-back mechanisms. Such dependency maintains legitimacy by virtue of providing off-ramps, alternatives, and viable exit.

Illegitimate dependency is permanent, non-substitutable, opaque, and reinforced by cost, time or credential barriers. This is not something that any domain is immune from as even in philosophical and systems theory this form of dependency commonly emerges via credential barriers. The problem here is not that people rely on that expertise but that this reliance becomes inescapable.

Consequently, gatekeeping is not simply exclusion from knowledge but also enforced dependency without alternate paths. A system violates CIA when it renders understanding structurally inaccessible while making dependence mandatory. Consequently, credential inflation, education barriers, and opaque models are not epistemic failures but dependency traps. In such cases, proxy standing often is a temporary dependency management tool and not a delegation of authority. Proxy standing is legitimate only when it shortens the distance to autonomy. [n.29] [n.188] It must not become entrenched, irreplaceable, increasingly dependent, or perpetual.

Commercialization – Funding Capture as Epistemic Coupling

Funding measures, corporate research incentives, and IP regimes function as coupling mechanisms to institutions in the domain of knowledge and science. [n.81] [n.125] [n.87] While this coupling is not an inherent flaw, it does produce constraints to avoid forms of illegitimate dependency and operational capture. Such methods may be necessary for output but are nonetheless grounds where coercion and domination may emerge.

When funding or resources necessary to produce epistemic claims are stifled, the formal autonomy of the domain itself is stifled. Since what epistemic domains produce is the outputs necessary for autonomy and capacity to increase, stifling them is structurally a form of mass coercion and potentially domination. This may emerge structurally, however, coupled with intent, this becomes a level of autonomy infringement which is extraordinarily destructive to pluralist society.

Such destructive ends, whether intentional or not, operate by compressing ERL, accelerating standing substitution, and biasing model selection. As we will see later in this chapter, this is not unknown territory but is a recurring and predictable precursor for violence. It presents inherent risk and, when intent and self-interest couple with a capacity to dominate these resources, violent acts predictably follow. In such cases, whoever inherits that risk is compounded.

Risk Inheritance, Evidence, and Exit

Risk Inheritance in Scientific Decision-Making

Risk inheritance is not about error. It’s about pre-allocation of harm before consent or exit. [n.21] [n.36] [n.129] Scientific decisions do not merely predict outcomes, they distribute exposure. Consequently, scientific coordination oftentimes assigns harm in advance, often invisibly and without room for autonomy or consent from pluralist society.

Risk is inherited when agents are coupled to outcomes they did not authorized. In these cases, harm is frequently assigned through infrastructure, policy, or constraint. As a result, correction happens after exposure and not before.

Risk inheritance is a temporal structural property of pluralist society, not a moral value. Prediction does not wait for consent and enforcement does not wait for correction. Modeling does not inherit validation simply by existing. At the moment a claim is operationalized, risk has already been assigned even if the outcomes are not yet known.

Even when those models are correct, risk inheritance persists. Some harms cannot be returned once imposed and some costs are borne privately while benefits are public. Some agents likewise cannot recover from what others may deem as temporary exposure. This leads to an asymmetrical distribution and potential for irreversibility. In these cases, ALRP is violated at the moment of imposition, not the outcome or resolution. Non-parochial evidence serves in these cases as a coordination constraint.

Non-Parochial Evidence and Public Contestability

Evidence does not authorize action. It coordinates how action may be coordinated. What evidence suggests alone does not warrant action alone even in the legal sense. We have recognized the injustice at least as far back as the Magna Carta.

Evidence is not merely something to be believed. It is something that must remain answerable while consequences unfold. Evidence itself fails structurally when it cannot be contested until after harm occurs, it becomes frozen or embedded in infrastructure, or when it is technically accessible or practically unreachable. [n.206] While this is load bearing for the domains of knowledge and science, arguably a case could be made for the legal structure this implies.

Evidence is a live coupling rather than a static input. Evidence must travel with action and be contestable during enforcement or it becomes retrospective justification. Contestability itself is not binary. It degrades under scale, speed, and dependency.

Contestability bears the load of time pressure, institutional opacity, economic precarity, and time pressure. Even while formal access exists in some cases, practical contestation does not. Such cases are not bad faith inherently but are structural overload. Exit then in these systems is the ability to refuse binding consequences without catastrophic loss. It is not disbelief.

Epistemic Exit and the Limits of Compulsory Belief

Epistemic exit fails when belief remains voluntary, but consequences do not. In a strictly legal sense this might emerge as appeal existing but only after harm is done to someone rather than giving a reasonable legal defense. It can likewise emerge outside of that sense when dissent is permitted but livelihood is not or when belief is optional, but compliance is mandatory.

Exit is structurally a coordination safety valve. It regards consequences, not opinions. Exit must exist before enforcement. [n.24] [n.26] [n.127] Using the legal example again this is understood when citizens are defaulted as innocent until proven guilty and off-ramps of appeal exist for them even after the fact. Exit in these cases and others is the precondition for proportionality.

When risk is inherited without authorization, evidence becomes retrospective, and exit collapses under dependency, coordination no longer operates through justification. It operates through compulsion. At that point, proportionality and alternatives are no longer preferences but the last remaining structural constraints before domination.

NRPP and Alternatives

NRPP and Scientific Enforcement

Knowledge systems, including scientific institutions, function as standing-generative systems and not truth-issuers. Their outputs can become coercive only when institutionalized rather than discovered. The question then becomes for pluralist society when these claims are used to limit autonomy, what constraints apply to this. We need to then derive why necessity claims are not epistemic facts but standing claims. NRPP applies to scientific enforcement exactly as it does to moral, political, and linguistic coercion. Any scientific intervention that limits autonomy must be the least autonomy-reducing means compatible with neutralizing validated harm. [n.23] [n.13] [n.25] [n.24]

Consequently, the formal application of NRPP in the knowledge and science domain implies that they must be protective rather than punitive. They must target validated harm rather than dissent and minimize autonomy reduction in scope, duration, and intensity. Evidence in these cases may justify a maximum ceiling of intervention but policy must select a narrower prescription. Failure to distinguish between the two is a standing failure rather than an epistemic one.

Typical violations that emerge of these principles in this domain are treating a ceiling as a mandate or escalating enforcement when compliance fails rather than reassessing coupling. Locking provisional measures into permanent structure is likewise common and becomes a violation of future autonomy by virtue of the temporal value of the provisional measure applying outside of its coupling. This makes this measure irrelevant to future agents without added validation of future coupling.

Alternatives, Uncertainty, and the Illusion of Necessity

Alternatives are not optional under pluralism. They are a structural necessity to it. They are required by the principles of NRPP, STC-5, and ALRP simultaneously within this framework. An alternative in this sense is any materially viable path that reduces autonomy less, preserves exit, and allows correction or future revision.

Claims that there are “no alternatives” fail structurally because they collapse ceiling into prescription and foreclose exit and correction. [n.93] [n.79] [n.169] They convert coordination into domination. Consequently, so long as the ceiling and prescription values are not equivalent, the promise of alternatives inherently exists as interdependently coupled to the difference between the two. This is the synthesis and causation for the ceiling vs prescription principle. Without alternatives, autonomy cannot be said to be anything more than formal.

This does not mean that failure cannot happen or that “no alternatives” is an impossibility. Structural emergences of no discrepancy between a ceiling and a prescription do happen. This is the synthesis and causation for the emergence of IEWs. This is structurally how they are generated within the framework and is not a moral evaluation of them.

Alternatives are generative of pluralist groups. They are not merely a safety valve but become an engine of innovation inherently. As public capacity increases, so does innovation and likewise does standing for coercion contracts. As a result, knowledge groups and scientific institutions must actively support capacity development structurally. This is also not a moral evaluation but a structural inevitability of these principles.

If these institutions claim authority to restrict autonomy, they likewise inherently accept reciprocal constraints by virtue of the maxim of mutual autonomy (MOMA). Refusal to permit alternatives is a refusal of mutual autonomy itself. This is reflected in over-reliance on singular models, suppression of parallel research, or funding structures that enforce epistemic monocultures.

Uncertainty is not a defect. It is endemic of science and knowledge claims, and pluralism assumes this uncertainty as a baseline. Treating uncertainty as justification for authority expansion or confusing urgency for necessity are both errors. This is not to say that such uncertainty is universal. Instead, as autonomy impact rises, tolerance for uncertainty falls.

This is reflective of the epistemic risk ladder. Lower autonomy impacts require lower evidentiary burden. Higher impact in this framework inherently demands higher burdens of justification. Diagnostics of misuse are available through actions such as using emergency rhetoric to skip ERL rungs or shortcuts such as “trust the science.”

Necessity, as such, is an illusion structurally. [n.79] [n.91] Claims that enforcement is unavoidable and absence of alternatives presented as epistemic fact contribute to this illusion. This illusion is manufactured through a compression of the ERL, exclusion of dissenting models, and framing disagreement as irrational or immoral. When communication in this domain becomes coercive or degrades autonomy by foreclosing deliberation, SHT-3 constraints likewise apply. [L.8] [n.26] [L.9]

Enforcement, Drift, and Humility

Knowledge and science in this framework are not defanged, however. Instead, STC-5 explicitly applies under uncertainty for the explicit purpose of enabling enforcement of these necessary tools for pluralism. Uncertainty in these cases raises the burden to justify coercion rather than lowering it. Precaution does not license maximal intervention.

As STC-5 applies, risk inheritance is identified, public evidence is disclosed with uncertainties acknowledged, NRPP sizing is enforced, alternatives are demonstrated, and off-ramps are specified. Where this domain is capable of passing these evaluations and tests, it follows that enforcement has been justified so that knowledge and science claims may still serve the best interests of the pluralist collective as they originally set out to do.

Even so, emergency measures cannot justify permanent authority. This is in alignment with the anti-precedent laundering principle. Common drift patterns include provisional models becoming dogma or temporary mandates becoming default infrastructure. In alignment with ALRP, the more autonomy that this domain restricts, the more its own authority contracts.

Alternatives, though structurally necessary, are also a structural acknowledgement of fallibility. They are protection against epistemic capture. Emergent coupling guarantees blind spots but the establishment of PFAs can help mitigate them. Consequently, alternatives preserve exit, maintain corrigibility, and prevent domination without denying coordination. This is not to say that failure cannot emerge systemically or that success is guaranteed. IEWs and failure emerge and repair, redesign, and forward legitimacy become relevant when these occur.

Failure, IEWs, and Repair

Institutional Failure Modes

Failure modes in this domain typically emerge in recurring patterns even when epistemic practices remain correct. Such cases are distinguished and separate from the concepts of corruption, bad faith, or error. Let us call these the Institutional Failure Modes (IFMs). They are as follows:

Failure Mode A – Standing Substitution By Procedure

Standing substitution by procedure is a form of operational capture. It emerges when scientific procedures such as modeling, peer review, or consensus statements begin to function as if they themselves confer standing. This is a bypass of the STC-5 criteria.

This mode of failure engages compositional coupling which becomes interdependent while being unacknowledged. It is a compression of the ERL where higher rungs on the ladder are activated prior to their criteria which allows them. It is a substitution of standing and a collapse of contestability.

Standing substitution by procedure has distinct diagnostic indicators as well. Appealing to authority instead of justification, disagreement framed as non-epistemic risk, or automation of enforcement from epistemic outputs are all indicators of this failure mode. It is often accompanied by claims that “the process was followed” as justification for such coercion.

This constitutes failure because procedure is not equivalent to standing. Correctness is not equal to permission. Methodological rigor, even as it applies to this framework, does not license autonomy reduction.

Failure Mode B – Dependency Capture

Dependency capture is a violation of capacity-indexed autonomy. When epistemic dependency becomes non-substitutable, epistemic authority becomes coercive. This is true even without secrecy or error. It collapses options for exit which is interdependently coupled to autonomy such that it produces an inherent reduction of autonomy itself.

This can emerge when expertise is used as relational identities and proxy standing is misused. It can be diagnosed with indicators like no visible pathways to capacity acquisition existing. Credential inflation without teach-back, dependency presented as unavoidable rather than temporary, or opaque models required for compliance are further diagnostic signals of this mode of failure.

Legitimate dependency is always temporary, capacity-building, and substitutable. Dependency on the whole is structurally emergent as interdependently coupled with the concept of alternatives and variability itself such that where alternatives exist and temporal values allow, variables which become dependent predictably emerge. In spite of this, illegitimate dependency takes form when it becomes permanent, opaque, and enforced.

Failure Mode C – Time-Binding Drift & Canonization

Epistemic authority becomes illegitimate when time-binding transforms precedent into standing without revalidation. [n.185] [n.183] Standing and relevance are not immutable once established because there is no universal perspective frame just as there is not preferred inertial frame in physics. The variability of these frames necessarily implies that the relationships between them that produces relevance and standing likewise is variable.

Furthermore, even if the perceptual frames themselves remain static, the agents which gain them do not. As demonstrated from the concept of the IPFAs, even internal perception does not remain static. Perception for the individual changes over time by virtue of motion itself.

The agent moving necessarily places it into another relative frame so that these frames are hyper-sensitive. Still though, this is the synthesis for why standing requires revalidation.

Since perceptual frames are constantly being shifted for agents whether by the moving of the frames or the agents themselves, the corresponding interactions via coupling and relevance likewise changes. Those coupling and relevance changes inherently have an upstream impact to standing. Thus, as time-binding progresses for agents, couplings and relevance changes. Holding a precedent as relevant when the validations of that standing have not been verified is a simulated coupling or an imposed coercion.

This is the laundering of precedent and is a violation of the anti-precedent laundering principle. It is a violation of the ALRP across temporal inheritance and compresses ceiling vs prescription where statements like “this has always been the standard” can emerge as coercion and potential domination. Consequently, canonized literature is not insulated from audit in this framework. Sunset logic is mandatory and provisional measures may not become infrastructure.

Failure Mode D – Risk Externalization Without Authorization

Epistemic coordination fails structurally when risk inheritance is imposed without standing, regardless of its accuracy. Likewise, proxy standing for risk bearers cannot occur without the consent of such risk bearers or the standing structurally demanded of those proxies as with temporal binding. Standing and correctness are not equivalent.

Risk inheritance cannot be simply passed off onto others, nor can it be assumed without structural justifications in this framework. Deflecting the risk from yourself without the impact landing to another may be a preventive measure for an agent but, where this implies an inherited risk for others it becomes coercive. Likewise, taking up standing to evaluate risk which has not been structurally or autonomously given to you creates the capacity to determine autonomous outcome without consent, producing a reduction of autonomy for agents who did not have agency in the matter.

These errors form out of mismatches of the ERL where rungs are assumed without the criteria required to engage them. They are violations of the ALRP structurally, not as a moral rendering. These failures are indicated diagnostically when harms are allocated before consent. They are observable when exit is available only after harm is caused, justification is retrofitted post-outcome, or benefits are public, but costs are made private.

These modes are not always inclusive of intent or culpability. Systemic epistemic harm can emerge without culpable agents. When such cases emerge as IEWs, punishment is often structurally inappropriate.

Independently Emergent Wrongs (IEWs) in Knowledge Systems

Epistemic IEWs emerge when practices are followed correctly, outcomes align with dominant PFA expectations, but autonomy collapse or harm emerges structurally anyway. This is a structurally collapsing of ceiling to the level of prescription where the alignment forecloses alternatives and has capacity to foreclose exit as well. It is a coupling drift by virtue of this where various other types of coupling drift into interdependent coupling such that the outcomes are inherently tied to the events or actions themselves.

Many of these cases imply collective risk inheritance. In the field of science these patterns typically emerge in similar formats. Model monoculture can suppress alternatives. Optimization toward success metrics over legitimacy and emergency rhetoric normalizing coercion are not uncommon either. Infrastructure lock-in many times forecloses exit. No blame attribution is structurally appropriate in these cases. [n.20] [n.60] They are structural failures, not agent failures.

CPS-7 routes IEWs away from punishment in these cases. [n.8] [n.9] [n.10] Wrongs may exist but responsibility in many of these situations is either absent or diffuse. Capacity is not isolated in these cases but distributed across the whole of the system. What the CPS-7 standard demands in these cases is acknowledgement through expressive blame, repair through redesign and safeguards, and institutional correction that is non-punitive. Where there is no culpability that is backed by non-parochial evidence, retributive punishment and moralized enforcement are structurally impermissible in this framework.

Repair, Redesign, and Scientific Legitimacy Recovery

How then can we restore legitimacy in epistemic domains without abandoning epistemics and science? Repair is not an abandonment of those epistemic domains. It is a restoration of agency in alignment with SRC-3. Repair is defined as a restoration of public epistemic agency, contestability, exit pathways, and capacity acquisition. [n.9] [n.26]

This is in alignment with capacity-indexed autonomy and the maxim of mutual autonomy so that methods which are reparative become constrictive rather than destructive and produce coordination rather than domination. Redesign and correction are not equivalent in this setting. Correction is an immediate safety neutralization that deploys STC-5 to reduce harm. Redesign is oriented toward long-term legitimacy recovery so that the two are compositionally coupled. This avoids treating emergency correction as a permanent design.

Resultingly, repair strategies demand a certain quality of components themselves. Methods must be capable of being reopened, transparency must be restored, capacity must have scaffolding, alternative models must have funding, and off-ramps and sunset clauses must exist. These are structurally necessary to the maintenance of repair itself not becoming a means of coercion or domination. Without them, any actor could simply pivot reparative processes to stake out a dominant claim in a field when the opportunity within a PFA emerges for them.

Scientific Emergency and Anti-Precedence

Emergency as ERL Escalation, Not Authority Inflation

Emergencies in this structure are always an ERL escalation and not an inflation of authority. Structurally, higher ERL rungs demand higher justificatory burden. This is in alignment with STC-5 principles and the NRPP. It prevents precedent laundering simply due to temporal values.

As a result, “necessity” is not epistemic. Claims of no alternatives diagnostically instead signal that ceiling has collapsed into prescription, exit is foreclosed, or that coordination has become domination. While these are variant outcomes, such claims apply to these structural diagnostics. When attributing blame and culpability to these outcomes, the cross-domain application of this toolset then shifts gears to the standards we have created in the STC-5, ALRP, NRPP, ERL, MOMA, and other tools for the exact purpose of determining if these outcomes require any form of attributive blame.

CPS-7 then determines the correct path to remediation predicated on the impact of those outcomes themselves so that remediation itself does not become a form of domination. In some cases, where there is no culpability and tragedy is unavoidable, tragic acceptance becomes structurally inevitable. [n.37] [n.59] Authority must not be laundered retroactively in these cases. To do so is likewise a form of domination but compounds the already irreversible tragic outcome.

From Knowledge to Force (Why Science Precedes War)

Knowledge claims, because of their capacity to align PFAs, are commonly and routinely weaponized. Epistemic claims are pre-authorization infrastructure. [n.91] [n.92] [n.183] They often frame necessity, allocate blame, or compress alternatives before action can be taken at all. They often precede violence in the first place.

ERL claims and existential rhetoric carry structural risks of justifying the bypassing standing because of urgency. Some examples of this include total war, irreversibility framing, and civilizational survival. Such claims have immense gravity as they relate to pluralist society and the collective PFA. They are interdependently coupled to the PFA of a collective where the validation of authority of those who make epistemic claims can produce highly volatile affective output. Many times, these affective outputs inform actions whether justified or not.

Where force is present, CPS-7 constraints apply to curb these outcomes. Many times, repair is foreclosed in these cases and correction may apply. Forgiveness is a private act here such that it may be done from the PFA of the collective but this conceptually insufficient to restore autonomy or establish the UCE for the PFA itself. Instead, where correction does emerge to secure such qualities, punishment is strictly order-bound so that correction does not become a form of domination as has become inherent to many prison systems globally.

Caselets

Sample

Limits of Scientific Authority

This framework is neither anti-science nor pro-relativism. Epistemic claims cannot structurally self-authorize coercion or collapse alternatives in the name of “correctness.” [n.45] [n.25] They cannot allocate risk without authorization within this framework.

Nonetheless, such claims remain essential for uncertainty compression, risk visibility, coordination scaffolding, and capacity building. Thus, they are not dispensable from society or pluralist communities and yet are likewise no “final authority” in any respect. They are structurally essential to the concept of pluralist society such that they are interdependently coupled to this framework as well.

Consequently, the limitations this framework imposes are merely recognitions of the lack of final authority of such domains and are not depowering of those domains themselves. While this has implications for self-legitimation and domination, it does not conclude that prior works in these domains is without justification or that further work in them is not likewise justified. To assert so from this framework would inherently be a violation by this framework of the temporal time-binding values it presupposes.

Why Science Cannot Self-Legitimate

Science and epistemic claims participate in the formation and generation of relevance. They inform coordination but do not supply standing. Standing emerges only through authorization, exit, proportionality, and mutual autonomy. Consequently, any domain, including knowledge and science, is structurally excluded from self-legitimation.

This likewise includes this very framework in that it does not gain validation simply because of its own merit. It does not require authority because it is not asserting an imperative of what society “ought” to do itself. It is establishing the boundary conditions for pluralist non-dominant society as emergent coupling from that society itself so that this is not produced as an authoritative claim that such pluralism “must” or is “right” to exist but that it simply stops existing based on these conditions.

Where epistemic claims of any kind are used to justify violence, however, CPS-7 collapse into coercive regimes, standing becomes decisive, and failures can become catastrophic. What has become visible in this section is that epistemic claims of all varieties become a threshold of power which are commonly used in other domains as justifications for final authority. As we discovered in earlier chapters, appeals to final authority from humanity predictably produce domination and coercion. Whether this is structurally necessary or not this framework leaves for other works to explore. Nonetheless, the pattern of predictability emerges.

These justifications have routinely been used as simulated couplings to action where capacity to differentiate them has been impeded and thus domination has been allowed to endure. This pattern is structurally evident in the world history of war, violence, and collective harm. Where one claim to final authority clashes with another, regardless of their cross-domain incompatibility, these incompatible measures of domains very commonly reduce to human actions of violence that are simulated to be coupled to a final authority of sorts whether epistemic, philosophical, or commonly theological.

From the collected PFA of the world on the whole, what has been fundamentally missing from these evaluations is a cross-domain tool that rejects such claims to final authority while preserving coordination. This framework cannot presume itself to be the authority which serves to solve such problems as this would likewise be a claim to final authority and would be intrinsically defeating.

Instead, this framework emerges as the boundary conditions to which such structures and derives a set of tools that, should the collected PFA of a group authorize via their adoption of them, remain inside of those boundaries. At most, one may hope that such adoption could contribute to the reduction of the frequency of war. The validated claim, however, remains narrower: reducing the structural incentives for violence and collective harm if adopted. [n.25] [n.37] [n.60] The next chapter seeks to evaluate those topics.

XIII — About Conflict, Violence, Collective Harm, and War

Purpose: This section examines how the coupling–standing–legitimacy engine operates within the scale of violence, collective war, and harm, and how misidentification of dominant coupling produces characteristic failures of standing across scale. This chapter uses the same coupling engine and toolset of the framework in the domain of violent conflict, with scale acting as the dominating variable. This chapter does not promise any emotional resolution. It instead offers analysis of structural failures and evaluates what happens to pluralist society as they compound and conflicts escalate.

Orientation

What This Chapter Is and Is Not

Thus far, scale has been noted in this framework as having pivotal impact [n.68] [n.69] [n.129], but it has not been the central focus. This chapter serves as the escalatory hinge of the work. No new tools are introduced here. Instead, the chapter analyzes escalation pathways across increasing scale.

Conflicts of varying scale are not different kinds of moral objects. [n.11] [n.12] [n.56] They are the same structural problem under increasing coordination pressure. Each step represents a failure to absorb that pressure without coercion. [n.25] War is not an exemption to ordinary legitimacy constraints. [n.23] [n.22] It is the point at which all prior failures have become irreversible.

The arc of these failures begins with conflict, where local coordination strains. [n.24] [n.33] When violence erupts, interpersonal resolution breaks down. [n.13] As this becomes collective harm, institutional incapacity emerges. When no institution remains capable of surmounting these failures, systemic coordination has collapsed with no internal repair path. [n.185] [n.187] This is war.

As we will see later in this chapter, war is not limited merely to internalized structures of a single culture but is routinely classified by the scale of institution which endures it. When a single political institution (such as a nation) experiences this internally, we label this as “civil” war. At the point this scales internationally, this is levied as war. As the scale impacts the PFA of the world collectively, we label these retroactively as “world” wars (though many conflicts of that scale have existed prior to this label and are often represented by the outcome of “empires” historically).

This chapter is not a delineation of moral categories, and it does not justify or moralize conflicts at any scope. [n.11] [n.12] It analyzes conflict, violence, collective harm, and war as states of coordination pressure. It does not judge wars. It shows how legitimacy collapses before wars occur. [n.26] [n.185]

Standing constraints do not relax under threat. [n.22] [n.23] [n.90] Epistemic correctness does not generate permission. Tragedy does not imply legitimacy. [n.5] [n.15] [n.98] [n.59] What follows is not a theory of just war. It does not offer moral evaluations of historical conflicts, a catalog of atrocities, or a policy proposal. It offers no defense or critique of specific military actions.

The framework does not evaluate wars, justify force, or introduce new standards of legitimacy. It examines how legitimacy fails prior to war, as coordination pressures exceed the capacity of existing response structures. What follows is a map of coordination pressure across scale and a demonstration of structural collapse before overt violence. The task of this chapter is not to settle how wars should be remembered but to show why, structurally, no actor remains entitled to claim legitimacy once war begins.

Expectations

Readers of this chapter should not expect moral verdicts about particular wars. It will not make comparative judgments of justification, necessity, or blame. Historical case studies will not be offered as exemplars or counterexamples. Prescriptions for prevention, intervention, or post-war reconstruction will not be provided. Comfort, closure, and reconciliation will not be afforded. Repair will appear only after war, and not within it, because war structurally forecloses repair.

All such expectations presuppose that legitimacy remains available within war. That is structurally incompatible with this framework. Readers should not expect this to resolve disputes about which wars were justified, which actors culpable, or which outcomes were preferred. [n.47] [n.26] This framework rejects that war is at all legitimate. The only remainder is what and how society picks up the pieces after.

What readers can expect in this chapter is that the framework will give an analysis of escalation rather than intention. It will focus on structural conditions rather than psychology. This chapter pays attention to coordination pressure, not moral reasoning. It will offer an account of how constraints narrow and fail across scale. It will shift agent-level responsibility to system-level responsibility. [n.60] [n.60]

This chapter treats war as a state of coordination failure, not an outcome of an event. [n.68] [n.69] [n.129] What follows is an analysis of escalation pathways rather than moral categories. It does not focus on why violence is chosen but on how coordination structures fail to absorb pressure without coercion as scale increases.

In this chapter, escalation is structural rather than purely intentional (though it may be coupled to and interact with intent). Escalation does not require bad faith, irrationality, or malice implicitly. [n.69] It emerges from misaligned incentives, collapsed exit, inherited risk, and coordination under scarcity. [n.24] [n.129] [n.68] Escalation is treated in this chapter as a structural phenomenon that arises when coordination pressures exceed the capacity of available response structures. [n.61]

Likewise, as scale increases, stakes rise, urgency increases, and harm diffuses. In spite of these changes, this framework does not relax standing constraint, tragedy does not license violation, and epistemic certainty does not authorize coercion. Increased scale intensifies pressure and urgency but does not create new permissions. Scale in this framework is a test of legitimacy, not a source of exemption. [n.22] [n.23]

Readers should expect that this chapter is not offered as justification. Structural explanation does not provide excuse, authorization, or redemption. [n.20] [n.59] Explanatory volumes for an occurrence do not claim that such occurrences “should” have happened or that it was unavoidable in any legitimating sense. [n.14] This framework draws a distinct line between intelligibility and permission. This chapter is operating entirely on the side of intelligibility.

Readers should expect that this chapter will be demanding in ways that are not solved by moral clarity. Discomfort, grief, anger, and urgency are not treated here as evidence of legitimacy or grounds for escalation. Affective responses are neither dismissed nor elevated to justificatory status. [n.56] [n.40] This framework demands that they remain analytically separable from claims about standing, authority and permission.

The author expects that readers will resist translating diagnosis as endorsement or searching for villains and heroes in this chapter. Readers will need to be able to separate permission from necessity and moral defense from structural explanations. They will be expected to attend to the things that disappear as escalation proceeds: the contraction of exit, the diffusion of risk, the shift from addressable wrongs to inherited conditions, and the replacement of coordination with force. [n.68]

The central analytic task of this chapter is to track the progressive loss of legitimate options, not the escalation of moral claims. Readers should expect that responsibility in this chapter is treated asymmetrically across scale. Individual agency, intent, and culpability do not disappear, but they no longer exhaust what is at stake and at some scales do not satisfy the PFA of the collective as justification or non-parochial evidence.

As coordination fails, responsibility increasingly attaches to structures, institutions, and inherited conditions rather than discrete acts. [n.60] [n.62] [n.20] The reader will be expected to follow this shift without attempting to restore legitimacy by re-centering individual attention once structural collapse emerges. [n.61] This chapter therefore asks something specific of the reader: not agreement, not approval, and not resolution – discipline. [n.33] [n.54] The discipline to let legitimacy fail where it fails and let tragedy remain without conversion to permission. The discipline to continue analysis after moral language has reached its limit.

Translations

The following translation table does not re-derive or change the definitions of any of the tools or terms. Instead, it maps how each of these resources interacts in this domain and specifies terms used in this chapter that are domain specific. The core concepts of each of the tools, the engine, and other resources remains static in this chapter while the application is predicated on how events or actions in the domain interact. The usage of them is, as with any domain, dependent upon relevance to the domain they interact in. [n.14] [n.15]

Translation Table

Conflict: A coordination strain at the interpersonal or local scale where exit and repair remain structurally possible.

Violence: An autonomyreducing intervention that forecloses interpersonal resolution and signals failure of repair at the interpersonal or group scale.

Collective Harm: Harm emerging from institutional incapacity, grouplevel action, or systemic misalignment, where risk diffuses and repair becomes increasingly inaccessible.

War: Total coordination collapse. All prior failures have become irreversible; no institution retains the capacity to restore repair or exit. War is not a distinct moral object but the terminal state of failed standing at scale. [n.26] [n.22] [n.185]

Escalation: Structural intensification of coordination pressure driven by misaligned incentives, exit collapse, inherited risk, and scarcity—not moral will or necessary intent. [n.24] [n.36]

Standing Collapse: The failure of legitimate authority such that no actor retains the structural entitlement to bind others through coercive force. [n.22] [n.26]

Exit Collapse: The point at which refusal, withdrawal, or dissent is no longer viable without catastrophic cost; signals domination and disappearance of repair. [n.24]

Risk Inheritance: Expansion of exposure to harm across unwilling or unrepresented agents and groups; becomes unbounded as scale increases. [n.129] [n.178] [n.179] [n.180]

Procedural Capture: Institutional forms persist but correction is foreclosed; institutions no longer couple to public standing, producing legitimacy failure at scale. [n.28] [n.30] [n.205]

Independently Emergent Wrong (IEW): A structural wrong arising from systemic conditions rather than individual intent; increases as escalation diffuses agency. [n.60] [n.62]

STC5 (Standing to Coerce Test): The fivegate test for legitimate coercion. War corresponds to the condition in which all relevant gates have failed and coercion is entirely detached from standing.

NRPP (NonRetributive Proportionality Principle): The requirement that any coercive action be the least autonomyreducing means that neutralizes validated harm; commonly abandoned as coordination collapses.

Ceiling vs. Prescription: The distinction between the maximum justified response and the narrower action warranted. Under war conditions, these distinctions collapse as constraints erode. [n.23] [n.13]

Operational Inertia: Institutional continuation after capacity has failed; governance persists in form without function, accelerating legitimacy collapse. [n.205] [n.30]

Proxy Standing: Delegated or surrogate validation on behalf of riskbearers (noncombatants, the displaced, future generations). Proxy standing becomes fragile or impossible as escalation widens exposure. [n.29]

Global Commons: Shared risk environments—ecological, economic, informational—where war impacts agents beyond local actors and forecloses global exit. [n.178] [n.179] [n.180] [n.36] [n.51]

Repair: Restoration of agency or autonomy; in war, repair is structurally foreclosed and can only be reestablished after violence ends.

Punishment: A culpabilitybased response whose relevance diminishes as harm and responsibility diffuse and structural rather than agentisolated harms dominate. [n.8] [n.18]

Blame: Attribution of responsibility; becomes indeterminate as escalation produces structural rather than discrete agentlevel wrongs. [n.4] [n.6]

Tragic Acceptance: The condition where every available option produces autonomyimpairing harm. War forces tragic acceptance without conferring legitimacy. [n.59] [n.5]

Coordination Pressure: Appears repeatedly in the chapter and is a driver of escalation.

Scarcity: A recurrent coupling condition in escalation and conflict.

Harm Diffusion: Critical in distinguishing interpersonal harm from collective harm or war.

Force (as distinct from coercion): War is the domain where force becomes the dominant coordination mechanism.

Domination: War is the maximal form of domination; including the translation sharpens this.

Collapse of Repair: This is a major structural inflection point in the chapter and deserves explicit translation.

Irreversibility: War introduces irreversibility, which is different from ordinary coordination error. [n.68] [n.129]

Capacity Collapse (Institutional Failure): Already implied, but explicit translation clarifies how this differs from procedural capture. [n.185] [n.187]

Global Exit (or Collapse of Global Exit): Especially relevant for world-scale conflicts or global coordination systems.

Necessity (Structural, Not Moral): Since the chapter repeatedly contrasts structural necessity with moral permission, this translation improves clarity.

These translations clarify how the framework’s structural vocabulary applies within the domain of war, violence, and collective harm. With these translations in place, the next section evaluated how conflict, violence, collective harm, and war emerge as progressively intensified coordination failures, each marking the loss of legitimate options before irreversibility takes hold.

Evaluation of Conflict Scales

Conflict

Conflict itself is not a form of failure. [n.33] [n.24] In its most pure sense, conflict emerges as simply a disagreement where the motivations of two agents are aligned in such a way that they create competitive pressure. This is not inherently a flaw in plural cooperation spaces. [n.47] [n.26] It is instead a phenomenon that emerges due to the very structure of varying perceptual frames and agreements made among them. [n.1] [n.40] [n.41]

Consequently, conflict itself can arise at any particular scale of those communities. [n.24] [n.33] It may be between two sole agents or even between two global groups. At the onset of conflict there is no coercion implied. Standing is intact and exit remains available. [n.13] [n.22] [n.25]

Conflicts can happen in various scenarios like the workplace, governance, cultural norms, interpersonally, or even community groups. The early signals of a conflict are misalignment, ambiguous authority, and partial misperception. [n.40] [n.41] Disagreements often arise because of a priority setting, fairness perception, or coordination error, though this is not exhaustive of causalities. [n.24] [n.26]

Healthy conflict may involve remediation methods of these disagreements which are non-coercive and non-dominating. These might emerge as acceptance, negotiation, compromise, exit, sacrifice, or otherwise. [n.26] [n.33] Conflict becomes unhealthy when it introduces coercion or domination into the coupling disagreement. [n.25] [n.13]

When two entities attempt a coupling to the same entity within a PFA which cannot be shared, conflict naturally emerges. Where the coupling may be shared and outcome shared, no conflict exists. Conflict itself then becomes a competition of standing based on coupling. It is a contesting of the validity of the couplings that each agent has such that the outputs cannot be reasonably shared or mitigated purely by the structure alone. Thus, it falls to the agents themselves to mediate this conflict where structure allows via PFA, alternatives, and viable paths for exit, correction, or repair.

Conflict as Standing Contestation

Conflict is a typical condition in pluralist society where standing remains intact. It is not an inherent failure and is not inherently pathological. It signals differences in relevance, values, preferences, and practical constraints. Pluralism requires and implies conflict because the agents themselves have diverse couplings and priorities of those couplings as they find their IPFAs providing personal warrant and their groups sharing PFAs as well. [n.47] [n.141]

Conflict between the individual perceptual frame agreement (IPFA) and other IPFAs or perceptual frame agreements (PFAs) is not an invalidation of the warrant for each of the IPFAs. Personal warrant is not relevant to the PFA of a collective group unless aspects of the IPFA are shared among the PFA such that those aspects are, themselves, part of the PFA. This is the synthesis of public warrant among that PFA so that public warrant is comprised of private warrants that have come into agreement perceptually. This is not a moral value but an alignment of perceptual framing itself structurally by interdependent coupling. [n.1] [n.40] [n.41]

The dominant coupling type for conflicts is variant, but it always involves an element of coupling between two entities such that an agent may be in conflict with another agent, an animal, or even nature. [n.193] [n.194] Conflict itself in this structure arises because of those shared couplings. The error is local and context-specific where misalignment can often be addressed with correction, re-coordination, or clarification. [n.26] [n.205]

At this stage, standing is intact. No autonomy is impaired and no coercion has entered the situation. Conflict itself does not assume exit has collapsed, is punitive, harmful, or non-viable. Instead, it assumes that repair is available through communication, re-framing, mutual justification, or procedural correction. From the onset of conflict there are no structural obstacles to restoration. [n.185]

As a result, there are no needs for the STC-5 or NRPP evaluations because legitimacy claims are not currently invoked. As discussed in earlier chapters, compromise, negotiation, and other outlets for conflict resolution remain viable at this stage. Viability regards pathways that preserve non-domination for all risk-bearers and remain acceptable under the PFA of the relevant scale. [n.25]

Where such viable paths are refused, regardless of motivation, this becomes the first path to escalation. [n.24] [n.36] Where an agent or agents within a conflict agrees to a resolution path which may solve the conflict and enacts it, no escalation is required. Where absent, escalation is the only remaining option.

Legitimate Conflict vs Early Standing Drift

Since couplings at this stage are variant and competitive, standing evaluations become unstable and start to shift. [n.24] The boundary between healthy conflict and incipient standing instability arises when exit signals begin to become costly, socially punished, or strategically discouraged. [n.26] [n.169] It may emerge when one party begins implicitly treating their coupling as more authoritative or imposing expectations which exceed their standing. [n.22] [n.90]

At this stage, the conflict between the two couplings has begun to produce not only pressure but actions which begin to impact autonomy. Parties often appeal to group identities, social leverage, or procedural default rather than justification of standing. [n.26] [n.169] Some early signals of escalation include unilateral shifting of processes, suspicion or reactivity replacing correction, asymmetry in risk bearer evaluation, or informal exclusion. [n.185] [n.205] [n.185]

Standing drift marks the earliest stage at which legitimacy begins to destabilize. [n.26] [n.23] [n.22] These forms of standing drift are reversible but warns of pending collapse of standing in that they are common pathways to coercive or dominant actions and outcomes. This becomes the first place where legitimacy begins to erode not through force but through authority claims that are not backed by standing.

Whether this emerges between two agents, between an agent and an institution, an agent and the ecology, or otherwise, the point where one party begins either claiming or acting out of authority without justification for standing is the point where legitimacy begins to erode and cooperation begins to fail. [n.25] [n.13] This still does not reflect inherent violence but demonstrates the tension which is produced by the pressures of these conflicts.

Structural Failure of Alternatives

What emerges at this point is a structural loss of non-dominating alternatives.. This is a structural failure. [n.68] [n.69] While some of these conflicts may be manufactured by an agent or institution situationally, the failure remains structural. Intent behind the construction of the structural failure may be assigned as responsibility and blame, however this does not change the situational condition of structural failure. [n.62] [n.60]

For instance, where an institution forecloses alternative options that are non-dominating, such as a policy which is designed to create intergroup scarcity, this is a structural failure for alternatives. Whether the policy emerged in a culmination of acts or policies as an unforeseen consequence or was set in motion intentionally does not change the structural impact of such a policy. [n.68] [n.129] While such manufacturing of a policy may be met again with culpability, doing so does not resolve the structural problem created by the policy itself.

This distinction is significant because it points to the idea that such manufactured conflicts are not solved merely by isolating the causation of the conflict itself. Even if manufactured, the thing that was manufactured was a structural problem. [n.68] [n.69] The conflict is the outcome of a structural problem that pits two couplings against one another with no non-dominating alternatives which are viable or agreeable among agents.

Viable Pathways for Conflict Resolution

Whether a path is viable for non-domination is the criteria for these structural conflicts to be resolved, however, as it relates to the PFA of the pluralist collective, such paths likewise require the acceptance of that PFA in order for paths to maintain such status as viable. A path which requires an agent to accept it cannot be considered viable by definition when no agents who view it find it acceptable. [n.14] [n.26]

Consequently, paths which are unable to be accepted within a PFA at all do not qualify as “viable” for that PFA because there is no coupling between the path and the PFA itself. This is a symptom of a failed coupling which produces non-viable alternatives. [n.1] [n.40] As escalation of these conflicts occurs, re-evaluations of this “viability” take place based on the scale of the conflict itself as coupled interdependently to the community scale they impact. [n.68] [n.129]

Thus, when a conflict arises that two agents may not solve and the conflict escalates beyond them, the evaluation of viable resolution paths likewise extends beyond them. The validation for a new-scale pathway emerges only because the smaller scale has already collapsed. [n.24] [n.26] No involved parties at the lower scale found any path acceptable, and that absence of validation forces escalation.

Should justification and validation be found for a pathway to resolution which is viable relative to the new scale of PFA be found, this stands as the only remaining justification for standing. [n.22] [n.54] Consequently, the party or group from the new scale of PFA who proposes this pathway must likewise apply the STC-5 and NRPP constraints at this point such that their pathway does not itself become coercive or dominating. [n.23] [n.13] The structural boundary between conflict and violence is crossed the moment an action removes or constrains a party’s ability to refuse without punitive consequence. [n.25]

Violence

Escalating to a larger group within the PFA is not the only form of escalation, which is possible, however. When conflict takes alternative paths of escalation and instead pivots toward coercive action, this is the moment that exit begins to collapse locally. Structurally, this is what violence is within pluralist communities. Violence does not begin where harm begins; it begins where autonomy reduction replaces justification. [n.13] [n.23] [n.22] Violence itself is the narrowing of exit in action via autonomy-reducing force. [n.24]

Violence as Exit Narrowing

Even low-level violence such as shoving, threats, or property destruction narrows exit. In such cases, legitimacy questions arise for the first time because coercion emerges from the actions themselves. [n.13] [n.23] [n.25] What is taking place in such cases are actions from parties attempting to simulate authority of the coupling they hold by acting as if standing exists where validation of that coupling has not been established. An example would be a shove in a workplace dispute where the use of force is used to replace standing as justification.

In such cases, standing has been compromised. The violent actor is now under the justificatory burden of the STC-5 gates. Even partial satisfaction of the criteria in this case becomes fragile. Coercion breaks trust, damages shared agency and triggers defensive actions of personal warrant and coupling relevant to other parties. These factors can often make repair more difficult in these situations.

Violence itself is a signal that persuasion and coordination have failed. It becomes a method by which escalation accelerates. The particular danger at this point is that force has already entered the picture when violence exists because violence itself is an autonomy-reducing force. [n.25] Consequently, accelerated escalation is not only impacting conflict but likewise force is impacted by this escalation such that, without resolution to the conflict, more autonomy reduction emerges over time. [n.129] [n.68] Force does not dissipate; it persists as domination when standing tests fail. [n.25] [n.141]

Effects of Force in IPFA and PFA

Violence is not limited to interpersonal actions. It has impacts in internalized perceptual frame agreements (IPFAs) as well as the perceptual frame agreements (PFAs) of groups as well. These shifts are typically asymmetrical and increase pressure on all parties involved.

When force appears, internalized risk perception often escalates. Force becomes illegitimate precisely when it imposes an asymmetry that cannot be restored within the structural equilibrium condition. This is understood colloquially when someone says they “felt threatened.”

The framework treats perceived threat as a structural output of prior frames, not a moral license. The phenomenon they are speaking to is this internalized increase in the perception of potential harm. Such phenomenon arise when actions within the perceptual frame of an agent align with previous frames of their IPFA where harm was downstream of similar actions where individuals have capacity to correlate action to outcome.

This effect is not isolated to the IPFA of an individual but is likewise capable of belonging to a shared PFA where individual IPFAs within the group likewise share previous perceptions of acts of the same kind which correlate to outcomes of the same kind. Thus, many actors in a PFA may share unidentical previous frames which share these qualities and still arrive at the same perception of potential harm within the PFA of the group.

Reactions to these perceived potential harms (threats) are variant and have been catalogued in other fields as having modes of fight, flight, freeze, or fawn outputs. Force engages the IPFA where violence compresses the individual’s decision horizon. [n.1] [n.7] [n.41] This temporal factor often, but not always, makes performing STC-5 reasoning impossible within the time frame and agency often becomes reactive rather than deliberative.

Additionally, affective outcomes do not occur in isolation from these events. Affective priming is a structural outcome of all interactions between conscious beings whether neutral or otherwise. [n.1] [n.40] [n.41] Temporally sensitive affective outputs commonly are followed by cognitive narrowing causing the perception of exit plausibility to likewise decrease in many cases.

This framework does not categorize outputs of the IPFA as internal motivators; however, this remains an important distinction as the output actions themselves become contributive of the general effect of force on the IPFA and PFA. These actions, where not restorative or de-escalating of the situation, may provide no resistance or even support for the escalation of violence. [n.1] [n.41]

PFA-level responses are not about individual intent but about how groups coordinate around perceived harm. Agents individually and even in groups or institutions often react in these modes by virtue of a pattern shift from justificatory reasoning to protective reasoning. When this has happened at the scale of a PFA, institutions typically respond with signaling, panic, increased monitoring, and similar outputs. [n.69] [n.129] [n.30] Nonetheless, such asymmetry accelerates escalation.

Force necessarily changes how perception reorganizes around harm for a PFA. As the PFA itself loses stability, multiple interpretations emerge. [n.40] [n.41] Many times, they have no choice of whether to be engaged or not and may not be prepared. When violence enters the PFA, expectations shift priorities. Where survival is threatened, UCE becomes a primary motivator for PFAs rather than optimal conditions or proportionality. [n.68] [n.129]

Collective attention to these violent actions can modify or amply the events, which is the origin of interpretational differences. [n.32] [n.130] Collective attention is not merely observation; it is a coordination effect that shapes perceived urgency, legitimacy, and risk. Oftentimes PFAs attempt to adjudicate risk quickly in these cases. Nevertheless, the variation in interpretation and the varying perceptual frames themselves within the PFA causes this effort to fail by virtue of the same compression of decision horizons for them.

Where these violent actions emerge, the violent actor or actors have taken upon themselves actions of a coercive nature. Consequently, the STC-5 evaluations apply directly to the violent actors. Force is not a valid substitute for standing [n.22] [n.23]; however, it does not dissipate for failure of the standing test either. Instead, failure of the STC-5 in this case diagnoses who is committing an act which is invalid or incompatible with non-domination. As a result, blame and culpability may apply. [n.4] [n.6]

Fragmentation of Agency

Fragmentation is not a moral lapse but a structural increase in the number of actors who influence outcomes. [n.61] [n.62] [n.129] From the receiving end of violence, fragmentation occurs as a structural phenomenon. Violence splits the alignment between intention, action, and outcome. Agency becomes distributed across actors involuntarily and no one can maintain full control over consequences. [n.20]

These fragmentations can happen intrapersonally, interpersonally, or institutionally where individuals lose control of their own state, bystanders and opponents shape the event, or institutions react in different and conflicting ways. These fragmentations of agency at various levels decouple agency from autonomy so that capacity and action may be disconnected from understanding and intent. [n.61] [n.62]

We may recognize this intrapersonally when someone says they didn’t know what they were doing or didn’t mean for an outcome to happen. We recognize it interpersonally when groups notice that a situation “got out of hand” without an intent or understanding of how that happened. Many interpersonal fragmentations likewise result in reciprocal escalation. [n.68] [n.129] Institutions recognize fragmentation when they acknowledge overshoots or delayed reactions. [n.69] [n.205]

Where agency is fragmented more actors now influence outcomes. This is the mechanism by which outcomes may propagate beyond intention. Still, more actors creating more standing conflicts implies structurally that STC-burdens have increased. [n.22] [n.23] [n.25] Each new actor becomes a risk-bearer requiring inclusion in STC5 validation, exponentially increasing the justificatory load.

As the coupling increases between agents and this violence, conflict becomes plural and responsibility is diffused. [n.60] [n.62] This fragmentation of agency becomes the very thing that makes violence structurally uncontainable over time. [n.68] [n.129] Fragmentation does not remove agency; it redistributes it. [n.61] This fragmentation of agency marks the transition point at which coercion can momentarily satisfy parts of STC5 but cannot sustain justification as scale increases. [n.22] [n.23]

To call back to the Ship of Theseus from About Perception, agency fragmentation is the object-level analog of the ship being scattered so widely that the capability of the collective frame to stabilize it disintegrates. The ship in this case is not “one ship” anymore because the shared perceptual frame that recognized it is gone. [n.16] [n.203] In this case, agency is the ship. Whether that agency exists independently of the fragmented perception of it does not change the outcome that it is not relevant to the perception of the group. [n.203] [n.61] The PFA is incapable at this point to perceive the ship, or agency, as a collected perception.

War doesn’t shatter the “ship” in the sense of an object. It shatters the coordinating frame itself. The “parts” of agency – individual actions, institutional outputs, group behaviors – continue to exist. What is shattered is the capacity of a PFA to stabilize them into a unified agent. What persists is not a coherent actor but scattered fragments that no collective frame can integrate. [n.203] [n.16]

Partial STC-5 Satisfaction

Scale increases both the number of stakeholders and the number of potential failure points in justification. [n.22] [n.23] Where agents at this level meet some of the STC-5 criteria such as risk validation, alternatives, and non-parochial evidence, coercion may still be conditionally legitimate. Partial satisfaction in these cases is unstable. Correctness is often compromised and risk inheritance widens because of it. [n.15] [n.98] [n.129] Violence itself introduces a sense of urgency, fear, and misperception. [n.1] [n.7] [n.41]

What makes these evaluations partial is when evidence deteriorates, off-ramps shrink, alternatives become unclear, or risk-bearers expand. [n.15] [n.98] When these factors take place, complexity rises and institutional or group-level effects may emerge. Partial legitimacy is an inherently unstable state because it depends on conditions (correctness, alternatives, bounded risk) that degrade under escalation. [n.23] [n.22] As a result, STC-5 becomes harder to satisfy.

Increasing STC-5 Burden With Scale

Necessarily, as impact begins to escalate outside of the conflict itself, the conflict undergoes new evaluations of the STC-5 constraints corresponding to the new level of escalation and makes the original level more difficult to satisfy, as the conditions any one agent must achieve must now satisfy all involved parties. While group-level constraint may satisfy this higher burden more easily because of the influential authority of the group given by the power of their numbers, this does not inherently foreclose on individual capacity for such satisfaction. Escalation increases the justificatory burden at exactly the moment when groups are most likely to mistake coordination power for legitimate standing. [n.22] [n.23]

Thus, at any scale where a fully viable resolution emerges, the resolution which best satisfies STC-5, NRPP, ALRP, and CPS-7 constraints becomes the least coercive and the structurally preferred solution. [n.23] [n.13] While this does not imply that all groups select such options, when they intentionally elect other options in spite of these tests, coercion and domination emerge in the solution itself.

Resolving a problem by coercive and dominating solutions is not an absence of domination. [n.25] This is a key distinction. It is a common misconception that the resolution of conflict itself is not domination, but this does not consider what alternatives for resolution were also available (STC-5) and does not presume to have chosen the least autonomy-impacting solution (NRPP). In such cases, the original conflict is not resolved—it is merely replaced by a new, coercively imposed one.
