Once coercion becomes the mechanism of resolution, its use produces risk that cannot be limited to its origin, making domination a structural generator of collective harm. [n.129] [n.108] [n.25] [n.60]

Collective Harm

The Sharing of Violence

Risk Inheritance Exceeds Authorization

Violence has a propensity to become distributed, structural, and difficult to localize. [n.51] [n.60] Where escalation of violence occurs, oftentimes individuals or groups bear harm they never originally consented to. [n.129] Those who stand to face this harm are inherently risk bearers to the conflict. Where violence localizes autonomy-reducing force, collective harm emerges when those effects propagate beyond the originating parties.

Collective harm is the point at which risk inheritance no longer tracks the circle of those who had standing to authorize it. [n.51] [n.60] [n.129] Collective conflict emerges precisely at the point when symmetry among agents collapses and the system shifts into domination or reactive subjugation. Violence narrows exit for specific parties; collective harm narrows exit for entire systems. Collective harm becomes war only when institutions, groups, or domains adopt sustained force as a strategic posture rather than as structural residue.

As harm diffuses, bystanders, institutions, marginalized groups, and environments become exposed. When exit begins to collapse systemically, conflict becomes unsafe or impossible and harm spreads beyond local boundaries. In such cases, standing collapses because authorization cannot be validated. Nonparticipants cannot be included in risk validation and proxy standing fails.

When systems cannot manage or coordinate risk equitably in these situations, institutional legitimacy is eroded. This is the synthesis for how collective harm emerges. Where interpersonal coupling disputes shift in scale to institutional relevance and institutions are incapable of reaching resolution, the erosion becomes systemic. [n.26] [n.169]

As one illustration of a structural institution intended to stabilize interpersonal conflicts, institutions such as police forces are often instituted for the purposes of containment. [n.26] [n.30] Police offer a strong example in that they embody the concept of a PFA collectively granting warrant for an institution to contain such violence. Police are not an isolated or special case but offer an illustration of a general institutional problem that can emerge.

Police typically exist as a coercive force but presumably PFA consented measure to enforce the collective PFA measures for maintaining the autonomy of the PFA collective society itself. [n.26] More simply, police forces functioning to “protect and serve” the people, when actively engaged in those activities, form an institutional boundary for the PFA to mitigate smaller coupling disagreements within the PFA of a community.

This is not a claim that all police forces actively operate this way but is an example of how such institutions may function properly at this level. It is neither an endorsement nor condemnation of those forces but an accounting of their self-declared structural function to the community. [n.26] [n.185]

Where such forces are not successful and the harm exceeds even the warrant that such a PFA has given to those forces, collective harm becomes a domain-level transformation. It is the point where institutions themselves have likewise failed standing. This can manifest as spontaneous collective breakdowns, including mass unrest, institutional bypassing, or communities withdrawing standing from an institution even while remaining subject to its force. We see this even softly in quiet mistrust of such forces within a community PFA.

When institutional standing decays, their retained coercive capacities become unmoored from the PFA that once constrained them. [n.26] [n.185] This mismatch transforms institutions from boundary stabilizers into new sources of coercion. This is how such forces themselves may become coercive and dominant.

As institutions fail at various levels, the risk inheritance increases proportionally as an interdependent outcome of NRPP principles – a sort of “negative” value of NRPP (the structural inverse of leastharm constraint) that emerges when NRPP is not abided in these cases. [n.108] [n.129] It is the imposition of involuntary risk inheritance as an outcome of this negative value. Risk inheritance itself emerges as the antithesis of non-retributive proportionality by virtue of either proportionality being violated or actions becoming retributive.

Disproportionate actions and retribution are, by definition, unstable actions because they cannot maintain bounded harm. Unstable actions presuppose a level of risk. [n.108] [n.129] The consequence of this is that parties who previously were not involved may be placed at risk such as neighbors, surrounding districts, economic networks, or even ecological systems. [n.41] [n.1]

Unbounded Risk Inheritance

When risk is forced into neighboring regions, non-combatant groups, economic networks, or ecological systems, this is a structural event. This structural event often happens faster than justification can track as unconsidered action is inherently faster than considered action and justification is itself a considered action. [n.1] [n.41] As violence escalates without consideration it then necessarily in places outpaces justification. [n.69] [n.129]

As this violence escalates risk is interdependently coupled with it such that those who are in proximity to it within the same PFA inherit the risk of violence where such violence emerges. Initial attempts to curb this escalation of violence is often met by institutions which are appointed by the PFA of the collective itself. This is not infallible as practice, however. By design, institutions which are formed to slow or curb unconsidered action must engage in considered action as a remedy or simply further accelerate unconsidered action.

Thus, if the institution intended to slow these unconsidered actions of violence likewise is not considering their actions, this only serves as a further accelerant to the violent acts themselves. The consequence of this demand for the purpose of such institutions is the same temporal deficit that they face amid violent acts. Resultingly, unconsidered actions of violence accelerate faster than institutional response as an output. [n.51] [n.26] [n.60] This is a coordination mechanic and not a psychological output.

As violence accelerates faster than institutions can respond, risk then necessarily propagates faster than institutional control as an output of risk being coupled interdependently to violence. Risk propagation that exceeds such control offers no consent to newly exposed parties, no representation, and no possibility of opting out. [n.51] [n.26] [n.60] In these situations, even good-faith institutions cannot represent all affected parties.

As a result of this process, risk becomes no longer bounded by identity, geography, affiliation, or initial involvement. [n.129] [n.178] [n.180] The risk is only bounded by those who stand to endure the harm that the violence itself propagates, whether aware of such harm or not. Authorization at this stage becomes structurally impossible. Risk inheritance being unbounded is the first irreversible widening of harm and is the threshold where collective harm becomes unavoidable.

Responsibility Escalation

Responsibility for collective harm becomes structurally impossible to localize or fulfill at scale. [n.62] [n.20] [n.60] Responsibility escalates because harm pathways at scale expand faster than causal control can track. A decision by a single actor may produce cascading consequences and circumstantial complexities may further compound structural IEWs in such a way that the general escalation to collective harm is not solely the output of that single actor.

Likewise, acts of harm may not occur in isolation. Violent circumstances often contain several actors who escalate the violence and thus the risk inherent to the circumstance collectively. Groups cannot be held responsible for things which are outside of their control such as unforeseeable consequences or IEWs that compound to their actions.

While their culpability for their individual actions and the understood downstream impacts of them to the PFA may be attributable as blame, the line for attribution stops there. Institutions cannot be expected to resolve problems they cannot access or do not have resources to mitigate. Individuals cannot be blamed for outcomes shaped by systemic forces.

This does not absolve personal accountability for the portion of autonomy infringed by individual agents, institutions, or groups in such situations. [n.62] [n.60] ALRP and MOMA constraints still apply to each of their scales respectively corresponding to the foreseeability from the PFA of the collective that evaluates these events. What the PFA determines as reasonably foreseeable for agents in that circumstance becomes the causal footprint of those agents.

Structural footprints are responsibilities that structure itself attributes to agents irrespective of their actions. [n.62] [n.60] They are the outflow of the structure compounding one actor’s causal footprint with either other causal footprints or structural IEWs. The mismatch of causal and structural footprints increases coordination pressure itself.

As more structural responsibility emerges as culpability for these problems, the pressure to coordinate and resolve these structural issues likewise escalates. As scale increases in this case, the system eventually demands accountability that no individual actor can satisfy. [n.62] [n.20] [n.60]

Failure at Scale

Correctness Failure at Scale

As established in previous chapters, correctness does not imply standing or legitimacy itself. Structurally, at scale, correctness fails inherently. Even when correctness is established at the origin point of the conflict, misinformation and misperception likewise scale with the conflict. Actors no longer share epistemic grounding of their PFA in these cases. [n.98] [n.40]

The epistemic non-parochial data serves in such functions to align the PFAs. Standing would be warranted to the coupling which aligns with the non-parochial evidence as it passes STC-5 standards. The escalation of the conflict itself therefore implies that such epistemic non-parochial evidence is already either misaligned or misperceived. At large scales, the “whole picture” can become opaque to any agent or institution. [n.15] [n.98] [n.68]

Mass complex systems, such as coding for programs, often create information asymmetry themselves and this likewise expands with the escalation of the conflict. Systems themselves may make this data opaque or obscure in a way where no agent can possibly align with or perceive the information as it applies to the PFA. As a result, conflicting interpretations or perceptions of this opaque data only further produces such disagreements. [n.15] [n.98]

Even without this interference of complex systems, if both agents had already aligned with and perceived correctly a set of non-parochial evidence, then the coupling disagreement would have already been resolved by the PFA alignment of the parties involved. Consequently, correctness failure for a PFA which is present at the onset of these coupling disagreements likewise escalates so that, at large scales, correctness loses relevance to the conflict itself. [n.98] [n.15] [n.203] Whether initiated structurally from the complexity of a system or initiated by the parties themselves, correctness in this framework is an alignment with a PFA. [n.15] [n.40] It is by definition excluded from scale while disagreement persists.

Correctness, or alignment to a PFA even at large scale is not a guarantee that resolution of a conflict will occur. Conflict may persist out of affective or retributive reasons or by those who prefer domination over pluralist coordination. Agreement on the PFA alone does not resolve conflict because once conflict erupts, such conflicts themselves often produce affective outputs or come into conflict with the desires of a party even though they agree with the PFA. [n.203] [n.40] Affective causes and desires for change for self-interest from the IPFA of agents or PFAs of groups and institutions are likewise strong motivators for action. The variance of perceptual frames inherently produces variant outcomes with respect to motivations as well, rendering correctness alone as unreliable as a motivator for resolution at scale. [n.5] [n.59] [n.98]

This removes correctness as a solution structurally by virtue of structural opacity, personal variance of perception, and even as a sole motivator at scale. Correctness at scale often is structurally impossible due to that scale and even when it can be reached, it is not reliable as a motivator at such scales. Not all of these failure types are terminal, however. Once correctness failure has destabilized PFA alignment, institutional failure becomes the dominant variable determining whether escalation remains reversible. [n.187]

Terminal and Recoverable Institutional Failure

Institutions are coordination technologies that are meant to stabilize PFA alignment. Their role is to validate standing, manage risk, provide correction, and maintain legitimate coupling. When those functions break or decouple, institutions fail.

Failure for institutions may be recoverable or terminal. Recoverable failures emerge when coupling is stressed rather than severed. Harm is reversible and standing can be evaluated. Correctness may be damaged but not completely destroyed for the PFA. Exit remains available and risk remains bounded. Terminal failure lacks all of those qualities, which are the qualities that enable recovery. [n.185] [n.89] [n.187]

Where failure starts as recoverable, error occurs. As misalignment grows, correction pathways shrink. This creates a scaled complexity as risk inheritance expands. At the point that PFA and institutions desynchronize, the risk of terminality appears. [n.185] [n.26] If no recovery is available, coercion may replace justification.

When this happens, standing and correctness both collapse and institutions become dominating rather than coordinating. [n.26] [n.89] [n.187] This domination is the emergence of terminal institutional failure. The point at which an institution’s failure cannot be reversed using their own tools, authority, or procedures is the “irreversibility threshold” for that institution. [n.185]

Recoverable failure exhibits localized breakdown where a specific procedure or action fails but the institution retains correction capacity, information intake, functional coupling with the PFA of the collective society, legitimacy repair pathways, and correctable misalignment. They are marked by procedural error, misapplication of rules, mistaken enforcement, misinterpretation of evidence, temporary loss of public trust, poor communication, or faulty internal coupling.

Recoverable failure might look like a court misapplying law but correcting through appeal or a regulatory agency withdrawing a flawed policy that was issued. [n.185] [n.89] Terminal failure looks more like a police force that becomes a generator of coercion rather than containment or a court that is procedurally captured and cannot correct itself.

Structurally in these cases recoverability still exists because the institution still receives feedback from risk-bearers. [n.187] It still has correction pathways, so exit has not collapsed. As a result, it can still satisfy STC-5 at the next cycle and has not produced unbounded risk inheritance. The structural indicators that institutional failure is recoverable are when re-coupling is possible, standing can be restored, risk inheritance remains bounded, IEWs have not yet emerged, and public warrant remains structurally accessible.

Terminal institutional failure no longer satisfies the structural conditions for legitimacy. It cannot restore standing or coordinate without coercion. Terminal institutional failure takes on very common indicators.

Procedural capture is where processes persist but no longer generate correction. Operational inertia is when an institution continues acting while decoupled from a PFA. Decoupled authority is where coercion replaces justification. These are all signals of terminal institutional failure. Likewise, opacity of information, exit collapse, correctness collapse, risk inheritance explosion, or misalignment beyond correction are signs that the failure is terminal.

Terminality does not regard intent. It is a mechanical output of the structure. [n.187] [n.185] Once correctness collapse and standing collapse align, institutions cannot validate risk bearers or generate credible evidence. Consequently, they may not restore legitimacy, maintain bounded harm, or restore correction loops. Terminal institutional failure creates a saturated environment where harms propagate independently of agency. This is where Independently Emergent Wrongs begin to dominate system behavior. Once IEWs emerge, they signal that failure is structural and has now reached system-level.

IEWs at Scale

Independently emergent wrongs (IEWs), by definition, arise structurally rather than individually. They occur when the system architecture itself generates wrongs. Consequently, it cannot emerge that individual causes or failures produce IEWs in isolation. [n.68] [n.169] While IEWs may emerge structurally from small errors between PFAs as a structural output of variance and error, what is culpable to a single agent or institution cannot by definition be an IEW.

When they emerge structurally, no actor is fully responsible but the responsibility fragments across agents. In spite of there being no agent or institution in these cases which is “blameworthy” this does not modify the output of the structural failure. [n.56] [n.12] [n.11] Thus, IEWs still demand repair. While punishment is not fitting for a structural failure that is not coupled with culpability, repair demands redesign of the structure itself so that the structure itself does not give rise to further conflicts.

IEWs create chronic instability. This instability accelerates collapse and is a common place where traditional moral systems fail. [n.68] [n.129] [n.169] [n.56] [n.12] [n.11] Where no shared justification remains, epistemic and moral ambiguity expand, oftentimes to a point where they not only fail but become unusable – giving way to a complete system collapse. [n.49] [n.98] Collapse here is not an absence of operation. It is the collapse of plural cooperation.

The Tipping Point

Structural Irreversibility in Operation

Systems where structural domination has become irreversible experience exit narrowing systematically. [n.49] The function of ceiling vs prescription is to establish a gap. If the ceiling of returnable action which is non-domination is set by the maxim of mutual autonomy and the prescription to restore autonomy and social order is set by NRPP, the gap between the two is necessarily the window for alternatives when a prescription fails.

Alternatives have collapsed as the prescription for remedy has fully reached the ceiling set by autonomous action. There is no more room for non-domination as the only escalation path remaining is beyond what is needed for social order and autonomy restoration. The only remaining viability is domination. [n.68] [n.129] [n.98]

Institutions at this point can no longer stabilize actions and standing can no longer be validated. As a result, force now moves faster than any agent’s deliberation. This irreversibility exists prior to any formal war. It is caused by the compounding of IEWs, correctness opacity, risk propagation outrunning institutional response, and institutional misalignment or paralysis.

The causal chain begins with conflict escalation. When local corrections fail, systemic feedback loops accelerate. As IEWs accumulate faster than repair mechanisms, standing collapses across domains. When standing has collapsed, options narrow until none remain that avoid widespread harm. This is the stage where structural irreversibility is reached. [n.20] [n.60] [n.68]

This irreversibility is not a matter of intent or malice, though it may be a part of the process. It does not matter whether the leaders “choose” war at this point. It is a mechanical, emergent property of coupled systems under stress that have failed cooperation. All non-domination options have collapsed. Return to the state that existed prior to this irreversibility is no longer possible. Once irreversibility takes shape, procedural capture has evolved along with it.

From Procedural Capture to Systemic Collapse

Operational inertia happens when institutions still run but produce no legitimate outcomes. The procedures exist and decision outputs happen, but correction is foreclosed, data no longer tracks public relevance, and outputs are no longer coupled to risk-bearers. Procedural capture is the first power and force isolation step in system collapse.

As operational inertia carries procedure forward and these procedures capture the structure of pluralist society, corrigibility and correction is lost. These institutions have nobody left to answer to. [n.26] [n.185] Standing actively decouples from their procedures as the PFA is no longer in consideration. Institutions are not, however, without force. They continue to produce force without justification as is the static outcome of procedures that had once benefitted society.

The very coercive nature which was once afforded to such institutions for the benefit of the PFA collectively becomes “cannibalistic” in a sense that it now is the very mechanism which enforces procedures that no longer track relevance to the PFA or their autonomy. When institutions endorse the production of force without justification or standing, system-wide collapse has begun. [n.187] [n.89]

This mirrors patterns of decoupled speech and decoupled political authority but on a larger scale. With no corrections on processes, captured procedures require no active input from anyone to continue generating IEWs. [n.205] [n.169] The operational inertia alone continues propagating them in acceleration as systems render validity irrelevant.

The public cannot appeal, evidence cannot be validated, and correction cannot enter. For example, a court or administrative body “follows the rules” but all internal avenues of correction for those bodies are sealed. Perpetuating systemic failures are active IEWs that are accelerating the system-wide collapse of the non-dominant legitimacy of these bodies.

Total Collapse

Correctness collapse destroys the possibility of non-coercive resolution at scale. IEWs dissolve causal clarity, remove avenues of accountability, and make repair structurally impossible. They are not causes in themselves but multipliers and accelerators of conflict as it escalates in pursuit of collapse. When the structure of pluralist cooperation has collapsed and failed to resolve conflicts, regardless of cause, while no justification remains to validate standing, domination is the remainder. [n.26] [n.22] War emerges.

Nobody “chooses” the war at this point. All options for non-domination has collapsed. War has arrived as a result. [n.91] [n.92] This can frequently look like institutional lag, competing perceptions, contradictory incentives or a lack of shared epistemic grounding. Nonetheless, where there is no more capacity for alternatives to domination then, by process of elimination alone, domination is all that remains. War is the emergence of a dominant group with no exit or alternatives available within what would otherwise be non-dominating cooperative pluralist society.

War

Separating Collective Harm From War

The Collapse of Repair

War is the terminal state where correction, standing, and repair are no longer structurally possible. Collective harm still allows bounded risk inheritance, partial alternatives, residual repair and some standing claims. War begins when even these remnants collapse.

War exists where coercion is the only remaining mode of coordination. Exit no longer exists and all non-dominating options are structurally foreclosed. All previous standing collapses converge across domains. War is an emergent condition, not a chosen event. War is domination as the default operational logic. [n.25] [n.91] It emerges as a structural state, not a declared one.

Consequently, repair cannot occur in war. [n.185] There is no shared PFA with those dominating. [n.26] [n.24] There is no corrigibility for them. There is no functioning institutions. IEWs and malicious acts dominate from institutions of power. Coercion in this state has replaced ever other form of cooperation.

Restoration of standing, correction, exit, and autonomy are all forms of repair. They no longer are possible in this state. It is systemic decoherence. No domain retains correction loops and standing has no institutional mechanism for reintegration for the PFA of the collective. Repair is not possible during war; it can only begin after war has ended.

The Evaporation of Agency and Proxies

War dissolves the capacity of any agent or institution to act coherently. Agency collapses at every level whether individual, group, or institutional. [n.60] [n.59] [n.20] With no scale of agency left, proxy standing no longer is possible. No one in this case can restore standing, coordinate alternatives, or validate risk.

When war emerges, intrapersonal breakdowns accompany it. IPFA collapses into reactive and fear-driven survival logic. Decision horizons close and justification becomes impossible. Interpersonal group dynamics become uncontrolled. Escalation cascades without deliberate choice.

Institutions break down and are no longer capable of correction. [n.69] [n.169] They cannot receive input or act with relevance. Standing cannot be expressed because representation requires stability and war eliminates stability.

Agency requires stable PFAs, correctability, available alternatives, and coherent risk evaluation. All of these disappear in war. Consequently, agency dissolves structurally, not psychologically. Blame, justification, and standing lose their structural foundations.

When causal chains are opaque, blame cannot be attributed and becomes impossible. Standing becomes impossible because no risk-bearer can validate coercion. With no standing possible, STC-5 cannot be satisfied, and justification is likewise rendered impossible. [n.129] [n.108]

IEWs and systemic feedback loops mean no discrete agent “causes” the outcomes. A leader ordering a military attack isn’t “causing” the chaos on the battlefield just as the enemy on the field doesn’t have “standing” that can be evaluated before action. Justification has collapsed altogether. [n.26]

There is no non-parochial evidence, no alternatives, no off-ramps, and no ability to restrict risk inheritance. Standing requires public warrant. War eliminates any shared epistemic environment for warrant. Risk bearers cannot be consulted, and structures cannot validate or align PFA.

Political leaders sending in military to enact acts of violence is not inherently war because these actions have not universally collapsed standing in such a state. [n.185] [n.69] Though the actions of one institution in such cases may be the catalyst for a war, once it has begun, the war itself does not hold any opportunities for any standing to be met until the war is over.

Blame assumes a link between an act and outcome. Justification assumes correctness relative to a PFA. Standing assumes inclusivity of risk bearers. War breaks all of these. Accountability for any actions of an agent or institution which were catalysts for the war cannot be found until war has finished and these structures can be mended or rebuilt. [n.185] [n.30] While war is actively happening, there is no risk ladder to evaluate.

ERL in Terminal State

During war, the Epistemic Risk Ladder (ERL) no longer functions. In order to function it requires visibility, reproducibility, and accessible evidence. None of these conditions exist in a stabilized form during war. Therefore, the ERL collapses completely.

Evidence in these cases cannot be made non-parochial. Information remains local, biased, or incomplete. [n.15] [n.98] Consequently, verification becomes impossible, rendering institutions incapable of validating testimony. When every agent receives incompatible feedback, there is no capacity for PFA or even IPFA alignment. Cross-group communication gets destroyed by the lack of ability to compare evidence. [L.25] [L.5] As a result, risk cannot be calibrated.

ERL assumes corrective pathways, standing, and evidentiary hierarchy. War eliminates or collapses all of those. With the ERL fully collapsed, no group can meaningfully evaluate risk or alternatives and irreversibility takes hold.

The Irreversibility of Conflict

What happens when irreversibility takes hold has been visible, but why does this conflict become impossible to reverse from within? Irreversibility is mechanical, not volitional. It results from structural saturation rather than intention.

When all alternatives have collapsed, no non-dominating options remain. When every operation produces harm, NRPP ceiling has been breached. [n.22] [n.23] [n.25] [n.108] When Path-dependency is locked, choices now worsen conditions. [n.68] [n.24] When IEWs overtake repair capacity, structural wrongs grow faster than correction can fix them. The product of these events is a formed equilibrium of dominance. Escalation becomes unavoidable.

Irreversibility in this sense means returning to previous conditions is no longer possible. [n.68] [n.129] There are no internal mechanisms for recoupling. No capacity for repair remains. Intent does not rescue legitimacy at scale because structural collapse overrides deliberative agency. [n.59] [n.54] [n.203]

Intent becomes a variable within the system rather than a privileged determinant. Structural collapse produces stable patterns even when agent intentions vary. [n.69] [n.68] [n.129] Thus, it is not “too chaotic” to analyze. With irreversibility established, what remains is to describe the structure of war itself.

The Characteristics of War

Structural Characteristics

War is characterized by several distinct features. Standing has totally collapsed. Exit has totally collapsed. Coercion emerges with no justification. Institutionless force emerges. Risk inheritance is unbounded. IEWs proliferate. Correction loops evaporate. Repair and stabilization mechanisms disappear.

Without exit, amid operational inertia, force becomes the predominant method by which domination operates. [n.24] [n.185] [n.89] Force decouples from standing and instead is coupled to domination itself, causing IEWs to propagate systematically. With domination and force being the governing cooperation methods, risk spreads without limit. Institutions act without jurisdiction or consent. Moral evaluation in this environment is not only nonsensical, but it becomes non-functional.

Moral Language and Value Systems Rendered Inept

Moral language tools have no function in war. Moral categories presuppose that alternatives, proportionality, intelligible blame, and corrigible action. [n.56] [n.5] [n.18] None of these survive in war settings. Without correctability, moral language cannot track outcomes. Without alternatives, blame cannot differentiate action. Without standing, terms like “ought” lose structural grounding.

What is “valued” in a war setting ceases to have relevance to any sort of PFA because the agency of that PFA has already been shattered. [n.49] [n.56] Nobody is capable of surviving the conditions while actively attempting to view the whole ship. There is no shared evaluative frame and alternative pathways are absent. [n.12]

STC-5, NRPP, and CPS-7 Under Force

With moral language and value systems inept to do their work, legitimacy tests fail entirely. Each tool within the set becomes impossible to satisfy. War operates outside of all constraint frameworks. This is understood with colloquialisms like “all is fair in love and war.”

With no evidence, alternatives, off-ramps, or risk control, STC-5 cannot be satisfied. Harm cannot be routed via CPS-7 predictably without these conditions. Since domination emerges as the primary form of coordination, there is no least-harm pathway. All actions exceed the minimum harm threshold in war. [n.23] [n.13]

There can be no stable assignment of causal footprints. There can be no institutional routing. Domains for validation are erased so that no agent is capable of demonstrating alignment to any of these validation tools. Legitimacy architecture cannot function rationally under total collapse. What remains is an experienced necessity.

Necessity and Ceiling Collapse

Perceived necessity does not generate legitimacy. Necessity is a structural pressure, not a justification. NRPP ceilings determine whether necessity is legitimate but, as just discussed, NRPP validation is not possible in war. [n.23] [n.13] When the ceiling collapses, necessity only indicates domination.

This structural necessity that feeds domination is not equivalent to a legitimate necessity. Agents are under compulsion, not discretion. NRPP cannot be met so actions become domination by definition. Alternatives are gone. Consequently, war amplifies experienced necessity but destroys permissive necessity. [n.22] [n.18] As such, structural necessity governs action inside war, but legitimacy can only be rebuilt after war ends.

How It Ends and Re-Entry

Wars do not resolve. They end through exhaustion of domination pathways. Ending war requires force exhaustion, collapse of dominant actors, external constraint, or systemic unsustainability. These are notably true of wars that end whether it regards surrender or the intervention of outside nations or allied forces.

Repair does not exist during war. [n.51] What is required for re-entry is a new legitimacy infrastructure. New PFA formation and reconstruction of institutions must take priority. Post-conflict reconstruction is an application of the Restorative Standing principle: repair requires restoring the baseline autonomy of impacted agents before any further claim can acquire legitimacy. This restores standing and the rebuilding of correction loops. As these loops correct and standing is validated, a reflexive reduction in IEWs emerges.

Re-entry is a structural reset, not a repair. [n.185] [n.187] It does not undo the autonomy that was taken. It does not return that which was lost. It does not heal that which was broken. It is purely a reset, and war produces inherited harm that must be addressed by new legitimacy machinery.

This is not limited to a physical sense of infrastructure but regards the rebuilding of the shared perceptions which form the collective PFA. [n.40] [n.16] This moment for re-entry is especially sensitive to coercion and corruption. [n.185] [n.26] After all, if a community plants an apple seed, an apple tree grows. Early-stage reconstruction reproduces whatever structural logic is present at inception. [n.68] [n.51] A coercive foundation yields coercive outcomes; a non-dominating foundation yields non-dominating outcomes. If what is planted in this re-entry phase is corrupt, coercive, or dominating, what grows from that will continue to escalate those same mechanics structurally.

This sensitivity in infancy of re-entry is not purely restricted to the PFA or institution which is reforming itself. After all, the planet itself forms a giant ecosystem and network. Where one hand hurts the other, the pain reaches us all, metaphorically speaking. Since global systems are interdependently coupled, local failures propagate outward as structural stressors for all connected domains.

Global harm structures display the same instability that arises whenever symmetry is violated at scale; the impossibility of equal standing across populations explains the collapse of blame and punitive logic. Humanity as a species and as a member of the global community is interdependently coupled to this environment such that these sensitive conditions of any of our subgroups has coupled impact to our whole group. [n.178] [n.179] [n.180]

As referenced in About Morality, though culpability may not be attributed to all of these external nations or groups, the structural obligation to safeguard this re-entry is present so that the community of humanity and the world at large shares diffused responsibility for this. [n.60] [n.20] This is not the responsibility of one person but of the human species such that the fragmented agency, when recollected, forms humanity itself into the ship of Theseus. [n.177] [n.172] [n.203]

Re-entry requires re-stabilizing a collective PFA. In this sense, post-war humanity resembles the Ship of Theseus: a collective identity reconstructed through coordinated uptake rather than any intrinsic continuity. We are the ship when we view the ship collectively. Once re-entry begins, the question shifts to whether pluralism can stabilize itself at scale without repeating systemic collapse.

A Structural Horizon

Everything in Parts I–III has been concerned with the structure of pluralist coordination as it exists:
in perception, identity, culture, institutions, and conflict.
But structures survive only insofar as they remain stable under forces that unfold across scales no single agent, institution, or generation controls.

Pluralism is not threatened only by internal contradiction; it is threatened by ecological limits, geopolitical pressures, asymmetric dependency, technological acceleration, inherited failures, and the long arc of time itself.
Across these horizons, coordination becomes planetary, not local; intergenerational, not immediate; reconstructive, not merely diagnostic.

Where Parts I–III reveal how standing collapses,
Part IV asks whether standing can be rebuilt in a world where the conditions of endurance span cultures, borders, and centuries. The framework must now be extended across the broadest horizon at which its constraints still apply.
This is not an expansion of authority, but an expansion of consequence. Pluralism endures only if the structures that sustain it can survive the future that arrives.

Institutional Correction-Lag and Fragility

A scientific advisory body releases a preliminary guideline during an unfolding crisis, acting on limited early data. When updated findings emerge, a revised advisory is issued—but the correction spreads far more slowly than the initial announcement. Citizens who relied on the early message now operate under outdated assumptions, while the institution continues to wield authority without having fully restored standing. The mismatch produces frustration, not because anyone acted irresponsibly, but because coupling and correction operate on different timescales. As reliance drifts and trust erodes, the institution inherits a structural IEW: harm emerges from temporal misalignment rather than culpable action. Legitimacy falters because authority persists despite an unrepaired standing gap, illustrating how institutional fragility arises even in goodfaith systems when correction cannot keep pace with uptake.

Part IV – Reconstruction: Global Pluralism and the Long Arc of Time

XIV – Global Concerns

Purpose: This chapter examines how the coupling → relevance → autonomy → standing → legitimacy → repair engine behaves at planetary scale, where crossborder interdependence, asymmetric exposure, and incompatible perceptual frames generate structural disagreement, borderless coercion, and global Independently Emergent Wrongs (IEWs). It analyzes why standing and punitive logics collapse internationally, how dominantcoupling misidentification amplifies global crises across ecological, economic, technological, and political domains, and why time and longhorizon commitments become the primary remaining coordination mechanisms. This chapter prepares the ground for reconstruction by showing that current global structures cannot sustain nondomination under conditions of deep pluralism and systemic interdependence.

Orientation

What This Chapter Is and Is Not

This chapter examines the structural engine that has been developed throughout this work and how it behaves when applied to planetary-scale coordination problems. At the global level, the same constraints continue to govern coordination, but with amplified pressures and without any of the shared operational scaffolding that made legitimate constraint possible at smaller scales.

Where earlier chapters analyzed discrete domains such as perception, morality, language, and politics, this chapter evaluates the global arena where no single domain can be isolated and where crossdomain failures are the norm. It explores how the engine functions when relevance cannot be localized, when exposure is asymmetric across states and populations, and when global IEWs proliferate due to mismatched coupling, strategic decoupling, and the absence of rerunnable global operations.

Global concerns are therefore treated not as moral disagreements or clashes of ideology. They are situated as structural expressions of misidentified couplings, asymmetric exposure, and the absence of any rerunnable global operations. Where Rawls and Habermas structurally fail to scale their frameworks across all domains, the reason is far simpler than their systems allow: global problems require crossdomain engines, not domainspecific solutions.

Even Fraser’s threedimensional model of redistribution, recognition, and representation presupposes communicative accessibility, institutional availability, and discursive standing. None are structurally possible at planetary scale without globally operational scaffolding, where relevance cannot be stabilized without coupling agreement and no global procedures can be rerun. Held assumes global institutions can hold standing constant; Benhabib relies on discourse and reciprocity; Beitz requires equality conditions that presuppose shared operations; Pogge diagnoses harms without modeling structural failure modes. Young comes closest in spirit, but her framework remains diagnostic and lacks domain portability.

The engine developed in this work precedes domains and is interdependently coupled to plurality itself. It has already been shown to be both crossdomain and scalar, supplying a unifying architecture capable of modeling failures that cut across perception, politics, morality, and global interdependence. This chapter establishes the full scope of that architecture and addresses a deeper problem: the absence of a general structural grammar for crossdomain global coordination.

This chapter is not a foreign policy analysis, geopolitical argument, or proposal for global governance. It does not endorse cosmopolitanism or worldstate models. It does not assess which actors behave “rightly” or “wrongly.” Instead, it evaluates why global coordination fails structurally — independent of intentions, ideologies, or moral judgments — and why nondomination collapses at planetary scale under conditions of deep pluralism.

Expectations

Readers should expect this chapter to show that global coordination does not merely replicate national or institutional coordination at a larger scale. It operates under fundamentally different structural conditions. This is the very reason why a structural engine which precedes domains is necessary. The engine cannot simply be applied across domains by fiat. For any solution to apply globally it logically must apply to all forms of plurality, thereby demanding the same level of portability in application and an engine which is predicated on the structural form of plurality itself.

Conditions at planetary scale function fundamentally differently. Scale discontinuity at the global level emerges because the shared couplings that establish the engine and toolset themselves often do not establish at this scale. Tools like STC-5, NRPP, ALRP, CIA, and the originating axioms apply at this level. They simply do not have a structural mechanism to be instantiated. This is structurally the largest remaining gap between global chaos and global autonomy.

Many nations do not share non-parochial evidence with one another. Global capacity-indexed autonomy requires global systems of cooperation that do not exist because capacity-indexing presupposes shared operational footing and public rerunnability. This does not imply such structures are impossible—only that they do not presently exist.

Without any such mechanisms at the global scale, coupling becomes involuntary, asymmetric, and overwhelmingly mediated through ecological, economic, technological, and informational systems. Relevance becomes global even where contact, consent, or intention are absent. Autonomy impact becomes unavoidable across borders and time.

At global scale, the Precedence Rule becomes unavoidable: terminal and base autonomy claims structurally outrank derivative agency and preference, regardless of institutional or geopolitical authority. Cumulative load magnifies asymmetries at this scale. Small shocks aggregate into systemic failures when population-level autonomy is already strained.

It is impossible to structurally generate standing globally because no global scaffolding exists to satisfy the requirements for non-domination. Thus, legitimacy collapses not because actors are malicious but because legitimacy criteria cannot be met. Without any legitimacy validation, IEWs become the dominant form of global harm as established in the last chapter's analysis of structural harms. No collective entity, geopolitical or institutional, can claim standing over the Level 1 or Level 2 autonomy of affected populations—derivative standing is bounded even at planetary scale.

At such scale, punitive logic fails because responsibility and culpability cannot be meaningfully attributed at that scale. One way to see the impossibility of proportionate global attribution is to consider a case where our intuitions are the clearest. To illustrate the scalar mismatch, consider the principal architects and perpetrators of the Third Reich.

What punitive logic could meaningfully attribute the proper amount of responsibility and culpability for the volume of autonomy and agency which was taken by those events? Are the lives of a few thousand men enough to repay millions of lifetimes of lost agency and autonomy?

No. Instead, repair globally becomes temporal and structural rather than interpersonal. This is not a moral comparison but a structural demonstration of why punitive logic cannot scale to planetary harms. Just as time has implications for individuals and cultures, it likewise impacts the whole world. Time becomes the dominant coupling mechanism capable of coordinating across generations and dulling the harms created by contemporary wrongs. Readers should not expect this chapter to solve global crises but to diagnose why they emerge.

Translations

Global analysis requires translating familiar geopolitical categories into the vocabulary of coupling, autonomy, standing, and legitimacy. Terms used in this table are not re-derived but represent the translation of the same core engine and tools. Normative terms and value systems have already been demonstrated in the last chapter to be insufficient for structural modeling at global scale. What follows is a structural translation table of geopolitical concepts as generated by this structural framework.

Translation Table

Global actor: any system (state, coalition, platform, market, infrastructure, or ecological process) whose couplings generate relevance and autonomy impact for populations beyond its own operational boundaries.

Global coupling: involuntary or emergent crossborder linkage where the actions or failures of one system impose relevance on others regardless of intention or awareness.

Interdependence: structural conditions in which decoupling is impossible because multiple systems share compositional, ecological, technological, or informational couplings that continuously regenerate relevance.

Asymmetric exposure: a condition in which one population bears autonomyimpacting consequences produced by another population’s couplings, without reciprocal influence or control.

Crossborder autonomy impact: any autonomy loss generated by a system’s operations that is borne by populations who are not participants in the originating system of coupling.

Scale discontinuity: the breakdown of domainspecific coordination tools when applied to planetary scale, where relevance surpasses institutional, normative, or jurisdictional boundaries.

Global standing: the structural requirement that an action affecting multiple populations must be validated by all riskbearers under nondomination conditions; at planetary scale this condition cannot be satisfied because no rerunnable mechanism exists to generate such standing.

Standing collapse: the structural impossibility of creating shared operational footing at planetary scale, resulting in the absence of any legitimate grounds for global constraint.

Global legitimacy: the hypothetical condition in which global actions satisfy nondomination across all exposed populations; structurally unattainable because no global system of rerunnability, standing generation, or shared operations exists.

Global coercion: any crossborder autonomy impact occurring without legitimate standing, produced through misidentified or involuntary coupling rather than intentional domination.

Planetary IEW: an Independently Emergent Wrong arising from globalscale couplings where no actor, collective, or institution possesses the agency or rerunnability necessary to prevent or repair the harm.

Systemic drift: largescale misalignment where global systems continue producing relevance and harm patterns that no actor can recalibrate because no system has sufficient coupling authority across domains.

Structural displacement: separation between decisionmakers and those bearing the autonomy impact, such that exposure and relevance are generated without operational proximity or shared standing.

Global relevance: the condition in which any local action produces nonlocal relevance because global couplings transmit its consequences across domains and borders.

Cascade coupling: multilayer propagation of relevance where effects generated in one domain (ecology, finance, information, technology) activate secondary and tertiary couplings globally.

Decoupling attempt: an effort by an actor to reduce exposure or relevance while continuing to benefit from global couplings; structurally unstable because couplings regenerate through surrounding systems.

Proxy standing: the appearance of legitimacy obtained through actors who do not bear the actual exposure, used to simulate validation that cannot be structurally generated.

Distributed agency: global fragmentation of control where no actor retains enough operational authority to prevent IEWs or maintain nondomination across systems.

Exposure inheritance: the transmission of global-scale relevance and risk to populations or generations who had no participatory role in originating decisions, arising from temporal coupling.

Temporal coupling: the use of time as the primary rerunnable coordination mechanism available at planetary scale, where repair occurs across generations rather than through institutional correction.

Planetary nondomination: the structural ideal in which global operations do not impose arbitrary constraints; shown in this work to be unattainable given current global couplings and the lack of operational scaffolding required for legitimate constraint, rerunnability, and standing generation.

With these terms translated for the framework, the topics that warrant global concern enter the frame structurally rather than through value systems or normative statements. As a result, the engine and toolset becomes free to address these issues structurally for any groups who consent to cooperative pluralist society. What follows is the application of these tools. These applications are not intended to be exhaustive but provide a launchpad for others.

Global Pluralism & Disagreement

What Makes Global Disagreement Structurally Distinct

Global systems lack accountability mechanisms. Meaningful exit from global constraints is structurally unavailable. Consequently, corrigibility across states without any final arbiter has yet to hold. Non-domination due to extreme power asymmetries regularly emerges.

At the global level, coupling is weak, uneven, and often adversarial. Relevance can be distorted by distance, propaganda, incompatible interpretive environments, or even time. Nonetheless, resource inequality amplifies autonomy impact to isolated groups tremendously. Standing and legitimacy become ambiguous and are often either laundered or contested. Global repair mechanisms are extremely limited.

Weak coupling produces reduced shared context. Without a shared context, relevance is distorted. This distortion produces incompatible world-models. When autonomy-impact is amplified across unequal resource baselines, asymmetrical risk burdens emerge. When standing has discontinuities inherent to distorted relevance, no shared legitimacy is possible. Without a repair infrastructure, irreversible drift becomes inevitable.

Non-transitive global alliances, unilateral power projection, and powerful states becoming asymmetry-impervious all contribute to axiomatic violations at this scale. At global scale, the lack of structure itself becomes one of the biggest challenges. Global pluralism represents pluralism in its most fragile form.

If asymmetry becomes globally irreversible, meaningful coordination becomes impossible — a form of global structural “heat death.” In thermodynamic form, global society occupies a lowfreeenergy state: . Autonomy potential is low, conflict pressure is high, and standing entropy is minimal. In such a regime, even small injections of asymmetry (ΔHₛ > 0) destabilize the system, and legitimate coordination cannot form spontaneously (ΔGₛ > 0). This is why global pluralism is not merely normatively fragile, but structurally near-critical.

This analysis does not aim to design or justify global governance. That, it leaves to those who are more suited for global institutional design. Instead, it identifies structural constraints that any globalscale coordination would be bound by and shows why most attempts historically violate them.

Pluralism at Planetary Scale

Global pluralism operates in an environment where the constraints defined earlier — partial orders, standing equivalence, and repair operators — cannot be satisfied due to the absence of shared coupling and diverging relevance structures. Global institutions emerge as attempts to resolve this structural inefficiency. Nonetheless, they are given derivative standing rather than primary standing. They often overreach — as persistent critiques of Bretton Woods institutions demonstrate. Institutions at this level cannot legitimately override level one or two autonomy of populations.

Many times, the resources to do so are constrained out of a fear of the power that giving such institutions may imply. Many of these institutions have historically relied on appeals to a higher authority, which has already been demonstrated in this framework to be inherently destructive of pluralist society when attributed to the acts of humanity. Pluralism at planetary scale demands a system that is structured such that it is not granted authority from any final authority but instead by the constraints of those who establish it.

Global decisions often impact mortality, sustenance, shelter, economic stability, preferences, and needs. Minor changes in these policies for wealthy institutions often lead to catastrophic impact for fragile ones. At global scale, pluralism exists in its most fragile form: maximum coupling weakness, maximum relevance distortion, and minimal repair capacity. These are not reflections of “more pluralism” but a reflection of pluralism through severe exposure asymmetry.

Historically, global systems have been grounded in architectures that generate, rather than mitigate, asymmetry. Domination is thus not a failure of implementation but a structural inevitability under existing arrangements. Nothing in this framework implies that a global structure ought to be built; the argument is only that if any system claims global legitimacy, it must satisfy these boundary conditions — and no known system has.

Why Peace Cannot Be Imposed

Peace itself presupposes that exit, corrigibility, and non-domination are present. Imposing peace violates all of those concepts as supported by research on imposed peace failures. External imposition induces a monotonic fragility, giving way to resistance and, ultimately, insurgency. Imposed peace isn’t a moral failure. It fails structurally.

This is not a treatise on international intervention. Instead, it is a statement to the structural bounds of any international interventions such that where domination or imposition of peace itself is not inherently peace. Beyond simply the intrinsic contradiction, structurally it produces insurgency. Imposing peace is not only a self-contradiction but becomes corrosive in itself.

As discussed when considering knowledge and science, capacity-indexed autonomy presumes that such interventions, to retain the maximal autonomy and arrive at peace, necessarily must carry structurally sound methods of capacity expansion. These methods of expanding capacity for autonomy within those cultures are likewise constrained by the principles of STC-5, NRPP, ALRP, and CPS-7.

Other solutions are, of course, possible. Nevertheless, where these boundary conditions are violated, what is produced is inherently not cooperation. It is domination even at a minute scale. As this framework has shown, however, such tiny fragments of domination uncorrected invariably grow. This replication is provided by the accelerants of escalation and ultimately is the explanation for why global conflicts have yet to be resolved even structurally.

They cannot be resolved structurally without a framework which can resolve them. This framework is not the establishment of any such structure. Rather, this work is setting the foundation of boundary conditions which any system must achieve in order to sustain such global level autonomy. They are no more or less than that of the individual perceptual frame agreements, regardless of borders.

Global Coercion Beyond Borders

Modern Warfare and Structural Coercion

Borders and nations themselves are product of derivative standing. They are not primary. Thus, nations cannot have primary standing over populations in other nations. This is supported by modern political theory on coercion across borders.

Borders themselves presume a level of differential coupling. Cross-border contexts lack shared interpretive baselines. Relevance structures diverge because world-models, languages, history, propaganda, and institutional scaffolds differ. In these cases, weak coupling leading to distorted relevance produces incompatible threat assessments.

Furthermore, there is no shared international repair infrastructure that is global. No supranational institution can enforce repair, so violations accumulate and instability is guaranteed. With no standing equivalence conditions across borders, the equivalence requirement that defines legitimacy breaks. As a result, drift into asymmetry is unbounded.

Without global mechanisms to correct asymmetry, it grows monotonically. Cross-border coercion guarantees directionality in these cases. When one nation has “greater” standing than another, instability increases inherent to the global pluralist society.

Cross-border domination creates a drift to instability and ultimately collapses feedback. It is an irreversible energy addition to the system where war injects asymmetry into the system causing rerunnability to be lost in the process. No mechanism exists to reduce this kind of asymmetry internationally.

Transnational coercion is inherently asymmetry. It imposes that one nation (A) is greater than the other (B) by virtue of force. Causality aside, this is the implication of such force as used to artificially simulate legitimacy and standing. As many have noted “history is written by the winners.” This doesn’t presume they had standing to be the winners.

Cross-border coercion leaves no rerunnability, repair, shared coupling, standing equivalence, or symmetry. It becomes purely asymmetric. One side determines the terms of interaction. The other side often cannot reciprocate. Standing is entirely stolen rather than granted. Impacted population has no exit. The influencing state is asymmetry-impervious in many cases (they cannot be reciprocally harmed on equal terms).

Repair is not possible because there is no shared accountability or interpretation. The system in this case enters monotonic fragility. As mentioned, peace requires symmetry, repair, non-domination, and exit. War violates all four of them. It is a base level autonomy violation and terminal agency violation.

Deriving Standing Across Borders

Symmetry requires shared relevance and shared repair. Institutions derive standing from the consent of the governed and standing is indexed to autonomy-impact in the affected population. Thus, nations cannot have primary standing over populations of other nations.

They cannot override foreign populations because they do not share perceptual coupling with that population. The corrigibility constraints are variable among several of them. International conflicts cannot satisfy rerunnability or perform repair due to the lack of structure. As a result, they cannot assess autonomy-impact accurately or assign standing equivalence.

This is supported by modern political theory, but this work also derives standing mathematically. It takes a common intuition of political theory but evaluates it from the standpoint of a structural framework. In such light, this becomes a structural inevitability rather than simply theory.

Coercion Without Borders

Even without warfare, cross-border coercion is still asymmetry injection into a structurally fragile global environment. Coercion without physical force still produces asymmetry. The lack of shared criteria for producing the criteria for symmetry does not simply disappear because force is not accompanying the coercion.

Even without military action, global coercion amplifies the Hierarchy of Impact violations. Sanctions and blockades can just as well impact mortality, medical shortages, famine pressures, collapse of autonomy to shelter and necessary resources, and a loss of agency. Arguably, these fall hardest on civilians rather than governing officials in these cases.

Non-military coercion in a weak-coupling order has low relevance fidelity and high propaganda distortion. There are incompatible world-models and no corrective feedback. Non-military coercion in these cases is not episodic aggression but structural violence.

Relevance distortions globally enable various forms of cross-border coercion: sanctioning, supply-chain weaponization, and information warfare. Sanctioning states treat their internal relevance structure as globally valid. They assert that something is a “threat” so it must be one.

This is a distortion because, across borders, targets’ perceptual frames are incompatible. Threat assessment cannot be standardized, and interpretive baselines do not match. This produces the distortion of relevance in the form of a mismatch. It functionally guarantees asymmetry escalation.

Supply-chain weaponization is an autonomy-impact amplifier. Baseline autonomy and even livelihood can be impacted by choke points, export bans, commodity dependency, currency leverage, and shipping lanes. These outcomes do not require military involvement.

Information warfare can form into relevance-sabotage. Digital influence campaigns often target credibility structures, perceptual coupling, or interpretive scaffolding. This produces world-model divergence, standing confusion, and legitimacy collapse. All the while, not a single shot was fired.

Coercion though, is a form of structural violence. Structural violence is a cumulative effect of asymmetry, drift, lack of repair, and autonomy-impact degradation. This is in alignment with standing conditions, partial order theory, instability metrics, and perceptual coupling.

Non-military coercion is structural violence because it injects asymmetry without battle. It destroys autonomy infrastructures and magnifies standing discontinuities. It often eliminates exit, removes repair options, and generates irreversible drift. The weaker the target, the greater the proportional harm as a structural condition rather than normatively. International coercion amplifies asymmetry.

Proxy Standing and Dependency

Proxy standing internationally as it relates to conflict is a laundering of standing. A proxy actor exercises force by claiming derivative standing that it does not possess and cannot inherit. Thus, proxy conflict is not merely “third-party” conflict. It is standing fraud.

Proxies act on borrowed standing but then act as if it is primary. They override the autonomy of populations they do not represent and produce asymmetry without responsibility. Where conflicts produce terminal agency harms, they do not stand as risk bearers.

International conflict proxies cannot share coupling. External sponsors do not share the perceptual frame of the population affected. A is not B. As a result, there is no way to derive standing for them. Standing must derive from the governed population. Proxies rarely have obligations for repair or even provide pathways for it.

Standing laundering is the structural analogue of money laundering. To launder money, the source of funds is obscured so that accountability is severed, rendering harm untraceable. Standing laundering obscures the source of legitimacy so that standing is severed, making autonomy changes untraceable. Where the population does not authorize a proxy, standing is counterfeit.

In proxy conflict, proxies are dependent on sponsors. This creates artificial incentives, relevance distortion, constrained autonomy, and unrepresented action. Sponsors can become dependent on plausible deniability. This gives motivation for systematic laundering, asymmetry shielding, elimination of accountability, and expansion of conflict through ambiguity. Dependency isn’t a side effect to these cases. It’s the structural engine of proxy war.

A coercive action at institution or state level is only legitimate if standing is derived from the population impacted. Relevance must be shared, rerunnability possible, repair feasible, and autonomy-impact accountable. Proxy war satisfies none of these. Consequently, proxy wars are structurally illegitimate. Proxy conflict becomes a monotonic asymmetry amplifier, satisfying exactly the drift dynamics outlined in the Second Law. It is merely one global issue among many.

Global Cross-Domain IEWs and Crises

Why Cross-Domain Failures Become Global IEWs

Cross-domain issues are a structural misalignment where coupling spans multiple domains simultaneously. Many international political problems are also economical or ecological. Technological and information conflicts across borders have historically become tools of war. At global scale, coupling is involuntary and asymmetric.

Without the instantiation of STC-5 to validate, NRPP to measure reciprocity, public rerunnability to collectivize a PFA, and no standing equivalency, IEWs become the default mode of failure at global scale. While actors and institutions may contribute to global harms, because standing cannot be generated globally, all global harms become IEWs, not culpable wrongs. Thus far, no single actor or institutions has functionally harmed the whole planet in such a way that is distinctly attributable as blame.

Global IEWs are a failure of the standing engine. They arise whenever coupling exists but standing cannot form and autonomy-impact is real. Repair frequently cannot be assigned. The lack of structure at the global scale forces IEWs because attribution and capacity-indexing cannot be applied across borders as a result.

Attempts at such structure have not been absent in the past of human history. They simply have failed to adhere to the principles that can sustain such structure. The primary mode that was discussed early on in this work is that of a final authority. Many cultures and nations have leaned on final authority as a structured mechanism to enforce such attribution and capacity-indexing. Those systems fail because, as discussed in the About Deity chapter, humans appealing to a final authority inevitably produces domination.

Personal motivations aside, these approaches attack the problem from entirely the wrong angle. When a pipe is leaking we don’t try to command the water, we fix the pipe. What is broken is the global pipe. The leaks are structural flaws. No amount of telling the water what it “ought” to do makes the water stop leaking even if you forcibly smack the water with all your might.

These leaks are the metaphor for the appearance of global IEWs as multi-domain drift. The Derived law of Asymmetric Fragility appears at this scale as a reflection of them. Drift accumulates because asymmetries cannot be corrected. Cumulative load becomes irreversible. Many global cross-domain issues and crises contribute to this drift.

Global Cross-Domain Issues

Cross-domain issues at the global scale are prolific in that they emerge as nearly the only type of IEW that can emerge at such a scale. What application of global policy does not also involve technology, epistemology, identity, ecology, economy, or otherwise? If such siloed global conflicts exist, they have not been considered to the extent that their weight demands, as they would represent an extremely isolated variant of global problem.

Attempting to catalogue every global crossdomain issue would be inexhaustible. Instead, it is more functional to group them into recurring crossdomain typologies. This isn’t an exhaustive accounting yet will suffice to group many of the global cross-domain issues that emerge.

Ecological-Economic-Political Entanglement

From the standpoint of resources, the exchange of them intrinsically gives way to the economic domain as this is what economics primarily regards. Where these must be controlled in a way that is sustainable, policy is placed to secure them, crossing domains into politics. Thus, it becomes that most ecological issues at all become both economic and political.

Climate IEWs at the global scale constitute a level of ecological harm. This harm gives rise to the threat of economic collapse which threatens to destabilize whole political systems. With no global STC-5 entity to validate coercive climate interventions, repair of this global IEW becomes futile. No global structures exist to facilitate the phases of the capacity-autonomy gradient or to address how it is indexed across nations.

While other forms of this entanglement exist in the form of previously discussed ecological issues such as the Great Barrier Reef or the deforestation in Africa, what they display is a collective typology of cross-domain IEW at global scale. Ecological problems at the global scale invariably get entangled in various scales of economics and politics. This is because economics and politics are mediums by which we manage global ecology, among other things.

Technological-Political-Identity Coupling

Many technological platforms have achieved international, cross-border influence. These platforms do not have a centralized form of governance, however. Nonetheless, this can lead to political destabilization. Consider Nepal, where political transitions became tightly coupled to platform dynamics. Platformmediated identity and speech structures amplified political volatility despite no centralized governance.

When such technology couples to both politics and identity, epistemic pollution becomes global because the epistemic risk ladder cannot be applied. Identity shocks propagate across digital networks without global repair mechanisms. While some may see the events in Nepal as particularly justified, this does not preclude negative impacts.

Just as well, alt-right pockets of the political and technological spaces have formed identity coupling and demonstrated in modern times the severe risk of this particular cross-domain and cross-border IEW. These formations qualify as identity-coupling drift under the framework because their linguistic and symbolic content cannot be evaluated with SHT3 or ERL at global scale. Since no global STC5 procedure can size, validate, or constrain the autonomy-impact of these identity signals, they become structural vectors of crossborder IEWs. They do not gain their influence from ideological content alone but from structural asymmetries in technological amplification, identity vulnerability, and the absence of global repair pathways.

Actors in many nations have taken these pockets of coupling in these domains and correlated them to personal identity as a mechanism to coerce a sort of “national identity” and yet, this can hardly be attributed to those actors alone. After all, with no audience for them, such actors would fall into obscurity. Nonetheless, these couplings are a breeding ground for global IEWs. Both of these cases illustrate a shared structural dynamic: whenever identity or political relevance crosses borders through technology without global rerunnability, ERL, or shared PFA, the standing engine collapses. Without STC5 to validate coercive or autonomy-impacting influence, these cases do not register as culpable wrongdoing but as global IEWs driven by cross-domain coupling.

Resource-Migration-Conflict Cascade

Resource scarcity produces cross-domain IEWs intrinsically. Harm is real and there is not always a blame-worthy party. Migration crises arise from level 1 and level 2 autonomy failures across borders. Receiving nations inherit risk without validated coupling or standing-preserving mechanisms.

Consider clean water scarcity in sections of Africa. Where the resource is scarce, infrastructure has failed via contamination, and migration is forced, this issue touches many domains and crosses national borders. No individual actor is fully culpable for this outcome, and no global repair mechanism exists yet to solve this crisis.

These are failures of capacity-indexed autonomy, risk, inheritance, and standing. Water scarcity emerges from structural factors, not because of “bad actors.” This is a direct example of where resources and migration cascade into potential conflict.

Another example is the rare-earth minerals crisis. Rare-earth metals sit at the crossroads of technology, economics, and geopolitics. When a single nation or cluster of nations restricts access it produces a global asymmetry injection and forces drift in the technology and economy domains. There is no global repair infrastructure.

It becomes an IEW because no global STC-5 mechanism within our structure sizes or validates autonomy-impact at that scale. No single actor is fully culpable for the global harm this causes. Supply chains are forcibly redesigned without validation. Migration, job displacement, and sector destabilization follow. These two cases are direct examples of how resource-migration-conflict cascades emerge as a type of global cross-domain IEW. They both contribute to a type of method by which the global standing engine collapses and ultimately makes rerunnability and accountability impossible at that scale.

The examples were chosen to highlight the two variant methods of this type of issue in that it can both be active as with the rare earth metals and passive as with clean water. A final and highly consequential category of global crossdomain IEW arises through financial abstraction layers, where risk propagates through economic structures faster than any repair mechanism can be instantiated

Financial System Coupling & Asymmetric Risk Inheritance

Global financial shocks create risk inheritance without standing. Derivative standing cannot be invoked globally and sovereign debt functions as coercion without STC-5. Financial IEWs consequently propagate through abstraction layers like derivatives or currency dominance.

One of the most historically significant examples of this was the Great Depression. What started as a financial system crisis eventually developed into a global financial collapse and worldwide systemic problem. Those outside of the original ignition point for this problem were risk inheritors who did not have any global structure by which to mitigate their own risk.

Likewise consider the Venezuelan hyperinflation cascade. Currency collapsed creating international debt exposure. Consequently, Venezuela became dependent in imported resources and external price shocks. This is indicative of multi-domain harm and international risk inheritance which does not have a global mechanism for repair.

Both of these cases demonstrate the bidirectionality of this type of international cross-domain IEW. They likewise demonstrate that such issues may have an origin point for a nation but, just as with crises like COVID, their international and global IEW impact is generated by an absence of structure. Without any structural forms to resist, mitigate, moderate, or otherwise repair such IEWs, they proliferate spontaneously and expand necessarily.

Cross-Domain Standing Laundering

Cross-domain standing laundering is when an actor uses legitimacy borrowed in one domain to assert coercive authority in another domain without standing. This might be when political authority is used to justify ecological exploitation or when scientific legitimacy is used to justify moral or political mandates. These actions exploit the authority of standing from one domain as legitimacy in another and are a structural category error.

With no global standing operator, such domain laundering cannot be globally corrected. While there are structural pathways via institutions, shared goals, alliances, and global systems, standing laundering often becomes the default mode of global decision-making. We can see this when environmental rhetoric becomes economic leverage or when scientific authority becomes political enforcement.

Standing laundering cannot be corrected at a global scale for the same reasons that IEWs cannot. Rerunnability collapses and no public coupling exists at that scale because no structures exist which can enforce them. ALRP and NRPP constraints cannot be applied, thus laundering becomes unstoppable drift. Standing laundering is a global-scale structural IEW because the standing engine cannot function across domains under asymmetric coupling.

Infrastructure as a Weapon

Global infrastructure such as energy grids, shipping lanes, fiber networks, satellites, and semiconductors act as the material instantiation of global coupling itself. No nation can refuse coupling to climate systems, maritime trade, financial networks supply chains, or even internet backbones. Exit is impossible in such cases. Autonomy is non-optional and, as such, coercion becomes intrinsic to the infrastructure itself.
