Infrastructure, or lack thereof, produces standing without having standing itself. Ecological choke points imply control over autonomy-impact. Semiconductor bottlenecks create economic fragility as leverage. Satellite networks create epistemic dependence which functions as perceptual capture.

All of these count as illegitimate coercion because STC-5 cannot be satisfied. NRPP cannot be sized and ALRP is violated structurally. Autonomy cannot be capacity-indexed or graded, and risk inheritance is asymmetric.

Such infrastructures can produce IEWs because no actor is solely culpable in many cases. Harm is always autonomy-impairing, attribution fails, and repair cannot be assigned. Thus, infrastructure harm is a paradigmatic IEW under global conditions.

Infrastructure is frequently weaponized via standing laundering on the global scale. Economic concerns are transformed into political authority. Political authority is enforced via technology. Scientific development is often used as justification for surveillance and military force is commonly used for resource control. Each of these instances is a case of standing laundering that forms into a global scale IEW.

At global scale, most conflicts are villainless because attribution, capacity-indexing, and standing cannot be instantiated across borders. Harm is real, autonomy-impact is profound, but no actor satisfies the structural conditions for culpability. The global domain produces IEWS not because the world is benign but because standing cannot form at planetary scale without sufficient structural scaffolding.

Villainless Conflict & Culpability

Why Global Conflict Lacks Villains

Since no standing operator exists at the global scale, capacityindexing cannot be instantiated. Without capacityindexing, the structural conditions for culpability collapse: autonomyimpact can be real, but standing cannot be assigned. Therefore, no actor can satisfy the necessary conditions for culpability established earlier. The global domain therefore collapses into structural conflict without blame – villainless conflict.

Every global conflict is autonomy-impairing, but no agent has the full cognitive reach of global consequences. Likewise, no nation has the capacity to avoid inherited global couplings such as resource entanglement, supply chains, or climate. No actor can foresee all cross-domain interactions. Therefore, wrongness exists as structural autonomy-impact, but culpability cannot attach because no agent can satisfy the standing, attribution, or capacityindexing conditions required for structural responsibility.

This is reflective of previous chapters in that wrongness is not always attributable as blame and structural wrongness does not always manifest as culpable. This is the synthesis for why global conflicts are inherently IEWs. They structurally manifest as IEWs because the global domain lacks the scaffolding required for rerunnability, validated autonomy-impact, or reciprocal standing. They do so because the scaffolding for them to exist otherwise does not yet exist.

Furthermore, such IEWs are amplified by unbounded drift, loss of standing equivalence, an absence of shared PFAs, and mismatched threat assessment. This situates global conflict as the limit case for IEWs. They account for maximum harm, minimum attribution, and zero coherent repair. This is how and why it is villainless.

War Without Villains

Some variations of war contain structural conditions that make even war villainless. War requires asymmetric exposure, coercive impact, collapsed exit and repair, and standing asymmetry. While war often presents as directionally asymmetric, globalscale conditions still prevent capacityindexing, validated risk inheritance, standing to coerce, and autonomy-preserving alternatives. War directionally assigns agency and force, but globalscale conditions prevent the structural prerequisites for culpability—risk inheritance cannot be validated, standing cannot be derived, and autonomypreserving alternatives cannot be evaluated.

Therefore, any nation which doesn’t pose risk inheritance to the whole of the globe cannot be deemed as a global villain. As conditioned at the opening of this chapter, this is the specific case that the global community sparingly has distributed for scales of war that impact the whole planet. It is the criteria for being labeled as a “world war” as compared to a scaled conflict.

No nation can possibly meet the structural criteria for justified coercion at global scale. Thus, global-scale conflict inherits the same structural signatures as global IEWs: unvalidated risk inheritance, collapsed standing, asymmetric drift, and the absence of any global repair engine. War is not just morally illegitimate; it is structurally illegitimate. Standing becomes impossible, rather than merely unearned. War without constraint invariably inflates to this level. Historically this has been met with coercive force by allied groups in opposing directions. This has, to date, not been an effective measure to stem such growth of conflict.

Rather, the same structural pattern is visible historically. Even for the Roman, Alexandrian, and Ottoman empires, each period operated only at the highest available scale of coupling for their era. In those eras, these empires represented the maximum scope of involuntary interdependence across regions.

They likewise exercised derivative authority without standing and generated cross-domain IEWs before the modern vocabulary existed. They were villainless at the global scale not because of their benevolence but because standing could not form and cumulative load and drift were inevitable. These same principles, ironically, were the very source of their downfall. This analysis is not a moral evaluation of ancient empires. Rather, it identifies them as early instances of largescale coupling where standing could not be instantiated due to the structural limits of the era.

In the modern era, world wars represent the updated form of this scalar failure: asymmetry, misaligned standing, crossdomain drift, and structural illegitimacy at a global level. Multiple nations typically ally themselves in the face of what promises to become a global threat if unchecked. What some have deemed as fixable by “remembering” or “not forgetting” alone is a far deeper problem. The belief that remembering alone could prevent recurrence misunderstands the structural inevitability produced by the absence of global scaffolding.

Intent at the global scale is structurally irrelevant. The coupling network is too large to foresee consequences. Despite ambition, none of the aforementioned efforts at global domination have proven to be either successful or sustaining.

Conflicts most commonly emerge from dependencies where nations act under scarcity, which is a scale conflict. Cascading IEWs create war as a structurally emergent phenomenon, not as a direct result of villainous actors, though they may exist in other scopes. Global conflict can generate culpable acts at smaller scopes, but not global culpability itself

Why Blame Logic Breaks

First and foremost, it is pivotal to situate our own understanding of these conflicts within multiple scopes because the conflicts themselves exist at multiple scopes. Consider the events of the second world war. The actions were not global alone. Each scale of act is rightfully addressed at the corresponding scope.

When this framework speaks to the lack of culpability and blame it is not speaking of smaller scales than the global frame or PFA. This does not presuppose that no level of culpability exists. Such evaluations of actions are handled structurally from the scale which has the capacity to do so.

To return to the example of the second world war, the evaluation from the national standpoint was justified just as it was internationally within Europe and via cross-continental establishments who came together in the Charter of the International Military Tribunal to address such considerations at this scale. From this charter and others, we have seen new levels of attributive blame emerge in the designation of “crimes against humanity” as coined at Nuremburg. Even so, this label did not hold institutions collectively responsible but defines this term as measured by context, knowledge, enumerated acts as independent of designated war.

Still, even with these prosecutions, the act of war itself was not attributed to individuals as global blame; they were tried only for specific acts within the conflict. The structural phenomenon of war remained decoupled from individual culpability. Instead, the outcomes of even these heinous actions are decoupled from the actions themselves. Though some were tried under this new category of crime, many of these harms went wholly unaddressed. This lack of clear action and outcome pairing violates the structural requirements for culpability.

Thus, in this example the agents independently can be responsible for their actions where structural scaffolding exists to hold them to such account, however, nations behave more like collectives under structural pressure than like moral agents. Consequently, collective blame logic fails at planetary level. The collective itself cannot bear blame because it cannot satisfy the conditions for collective agency.

Punishment presupposes a responsible agent, culpable wrong, viable alternatives, restorative pathways, and proportionate autonomy loss. None of these can be instantiated globally. Thus, punitive logic collapses accordingly where such collectives cannot meet these criteria. No collective can satisfy the standing to impose it and no individual actor has the structural position required for unilateral global punishment.

Instead, even such charters that have existed are formed to address the impact at the scales which currently have scaffolding. Arguably, it could be contended that such tribunals become coercive in the opposite direction. In fact, among many of the precursors to the second world war was the imposition of the Treaty of Versailles, which was itself imposed as a global solution without any measures to safeguard for boundary conditions.

Tribunals called to address the outcomes of such situations are not inherently a structural scaffolding themselves. They lack the level of oversight and capacity to regularly address such global IEWs but likewise have historically not adhered to these minimum structural requirements for pluralist cooperation. One could argue that the Treaty of Versailles itself was a violation of ALRP and NRPP principles by virtue of a lack of STC-5 evaluation.

The failure of blame logic at global scale is not moral relativism. It is a structural inevitability where this scale of structural scaffolding is absent. The next question becomes: If blame and punishment cannot function globally, what does repair mean at this scale?

Punitive Failure & Repair

CPS-7 and the Collapse of Punitive Logic

Punishment often feels intuitive but fails structurally at global scale. Human moral intuitions evolved in small-scale, symmetric groups. Punishment itself feels like accountability because it has immediate perceptual coupling. It mimics restoration in simple interpersonal cases and it functions as a symbolic reversal of harm.

Institutions, however, are not standing mechanisms. Punishment itself collapses because it is not rerunnable and destroys the symmetry that is required for legitimacy. It fails ALRP and violates NRPP by exceeding the least-restrictive means. While it passes psychological tests in many ways, it does not pass structural evaluation.

When punitive logic is evaluated past local symmetry, moral intuitions often fail over disagreement or misalignment of moral valuations. The very nature of these valuations presuming a level of standing itself is the structural flaw they endure. Moral valuations as such must first pass a structural standing evaluation such that the moral values themselves may first be aligned.

Consequently, this is where CPS-7 emerges as a structural evolution. Punishment assumes a one-way autonomy reduction to restore order. Structurally this appears as:

Punishment is thus an asymmetry injection rather than repair. Systems built on punitive logic accumulate structural “heat” (Hₛ), drift, and standing discontinuity. Punishment therefore increases entropy rather than reducing it. Consequently, punishment cannot create equilibrium. It only creates more “heat” or friction.

CPS-7 stands in this open space to reroute harm to standing and consequence. It evaluates risk inheritance, validation, public coupling, NRPP sizing, alternative testing, off-ramps, and reversibility. Thus, it serves as a mechanism that can ensure correction where needed, repair where possible, containment where unavoidable, and the maintenance of non-domination which is structurally necessary to cooperative pluralist society.

This is not softer – it is structurally rigorous where punishment is systemic structural destruction. It is not “leniency” in any sense. It is precision. Justice does not emerge from affective satisfaction that punishment can produce. Instead, it produces reciprocal domination and instability of the system itself. This conclusion echoes insights from Nietzsche, Foucault, Jacobs, and Braithwaite, but renders them explicit as structural conditions rather than moral, psychological, or sociological observations.

Why Punishment Fails at Scale

Punishment at scale magnifies asymmetry. At small scales it is perceived to “work” because there is a high volume of coupling, shared context, ability for symmetrical reversal, and rerunnable social roles. At large scale, coupling is weak, relevance drifts, standing becomes uneven, and capacity varies. Punishment at large scale amplifies asymmetry exponentially, as observed in the evaluation of the Treaty of Versailles earlier. In terms of the comparison to the field of thermodynamics, punishment is equivalent to an injection of enthalpy.

Punishment at scale merely transforms into structural violence. At scale, it reduces autonomy without restoring symmetry. It accumulates fragility, produces standing discontinuities, and propagates IEWs. Punitive institutions essentially become entropy factories:

This is why large political, legal, and carceral systems break. Systems that are built on punishment invariably drift into domination not because of intent or moral value. They are structurally predisposed to do so by their asymmetry.

Consequently, such systems cannot satisfy STC-5 criteria. Punishment is thus structurally unfit for pluralist societies. It almost always fails and inevitably produces an asymmetric output that, left unchecked, produces domination.

CPS-7 as Routing, Not Absolution

The methods proposed in this framework do not function as excuses for offenders. CPS-7 is not indulgence or “letting people off easy.” This framework is not anti-justice. Quite the opposite. It is corrective routing based on structural necessity rather than moral softness. This method is not absolution.

CPS-7 routes consequences through structural precision. First it determines if harm is validated rather than merely asserted. Next it determines what standing exists to coerce such correction. Then, it determines the right modality of response among correction, repair, containment, reparation, or exit/boundaries. Punishment is not a category of consequence in CPS-7 because it cannot satisfy the structural requirements of cooperative pluralist societies. It is an algorithm, not a doctrine.

CPS-7 functionally removes the criteria of “desert” as a structural category. As established in About Morality, this sense of punishment only serves as the upper bound or the ceiling of prescription. To resort to the ceiling as the default of punishment is to inherently remove opportunity for alternatives and to consequently produce domination as a result. Structural systems must route consequences causally rather than morally as a mechanical output of the structure itself.

Repair, Tragedy, and Limits

Repair is not universal. Some harms cannot be repaired such as death. Repair only operates when standing is symmetrical enough, relevance is stable, autonomy can be restored, and perceptual coupling is possible. Where repair is not possible, systems must shift toward containment, compensation, structural redesign, and tragic acceptance.

Culpability and blame do not intrinsically contain reparative values. Consequently, they fault and remedy are not equivalent. Furthermore, IEWs may emerge where harm is likewise irreparable, leaving no viable space for repair.

In cases where there is no viable repair, tragedy often emerges. Tragedy is a structural category, not a moral one. Tragic cases arise when autonomy-impact cannot be reversed, capacity is insufficient, options are over constrained, or all solutions produce loss.

Tragedy is not the same thing as failure. It is the point where CPS-7 solutions have exhausted their capacity to route outcomes. By default, since these methods account for non-dominating routes, the remaining options become tragic acceptance or a turn to domination and abandonment of cooperation itself.

Repair cannot become retribution. Many practices supposing to be reparative smuggle in punishment. Repair is a future-facing restoration where as punishment is a past-facing revenge. This can be seen in the following representations.

Repair:

Punishment:

Repair operates in the lowentropy regime: it decreases asymmetry, reduces structural heat, and moves the system toward a lower freeenergy state. Punishment does the opposite. Punishment injects structural heat, raises systemic entropy, and increases the freeenergy cost of future cooperation. Repair is reversible and worklike — it restores rerunnability and preserves information. Punishment is irreversible and heatlike — it destroys symmetry, eliminates rerunnability, and forces the system onto a higherentropy trajectory.

Where repair lowers activation thresholds and enables equilibrium recovery, punishment increases activation barriers and drives drift. Thus, repair is a thermodynamic descent toward stability; punishment is a thermodynamic ascent into disorder.

Repair vs Reversal

Reversal is not possible for most harms. Reversal presupposes a return of the system to the pre-harm state but the inherent variability of perceptual frames likewise presumes this to be increasingly improbable over time. Reversal is rare because harm often impacts autonomy conditions, not objects. Social systems have memory and consequences often propagate irreversibly.

Reversal often creates the illusion of “fixing.” Repair instead accepts the asymmetry and restores functional equivalence rather than historical restoration. Where reversal is metaphysical, repair is structural. It works by reducing systemic entropy.

Reversal attempts to “undo” the event, but repair stabilizes future trajectory. Repair is about correction of that trajectory as it is oriented toward sustainability rather than payback. Repair aims for continued coordination and restored autonomy. Where reversal aims to undo the impacts of time and create perfect symmetry, repair aims to minimize drift and preserve pluralist viability via the maintenance of autonomy, sustainability, and non-domination.

Where Do We Go From Here?

The Current Structural Position

There is currently no structural scaffolding to support global standing, capacity-indexing across borders, rerunnability, public coupling, mitigating irreversible drift, or avoiding involuntary cross-domain entanglement. The engine posed in this framework still applies but planetary-scale conditions do not instantiate it.

Therefore, we currently stand in a structural configuration defined by maximum coupling, minimum legitimacy, high fragile gradients, accumulated irreversible exposure, and standing laundering across domains. We currently occupy a structural position where repair alone cannot function, and reconstruction remains as the only viable path at planetary scale.

Since reversal is a return to prior autonomy conditions, it is impossible globally. Consequences globally propagate beyond any repair operator and IEWs cannot be reversed. Their consequences persist and propagate.

Repair restores equivalence through directed action but, globally, repair is currently temporal rather than interpersonal. Repair currently takes the form of long-horizon processes like policy, governance, memory, and institutions. At global scale, only temporal repair exists.

No actor can repair the autonomy-impact they themselves did not cause at global scale. Though reconstruction often times may appear as if they are a reparation of autonomy-impact, they are instead a variant construction of replacement rather than a return or repair of the original state.

As a metaphoric illustration, reconstructing a broken pencil is not effectively returning the pencil to its pre-violated state. It is to restore functionality in spite of its retained alternate state. Thus, reconstruction may take on a level of repair but does not reverse damage done.

Why Reconstruction is the Only Remaining Option

Reconstruction, though not a reversal of damage, remains as the most viable path to the maintenance of symmetry absent structural scaffolding to support the boundary conditions that sustain it. Repair itself is a restoring of symmetry within a shared frame where reform merely imposes internal corrections within existing structures. Where no reasonable structural scaffolding exists, reform cannot reasonably perform repair as the system itself produces asymmetry.

At global scale, reform is too small. Repair is insufficient to restore autonomy and reversal is impossible. As a result, reconstruction then remains as the only path that is structurally viable for cooperative pluralist society. This is not presumptive that a structural scaffolding at the global scale cannot exist. It is an assertion that, without such a system, this is what remains.

With reconstruction as the remaining path, it is not without requirements to maintain structural viability. Reconstruction requires perceptual infrastructure via shared operations, transparent signal channels, and anti-capture mechanisms. New standing-generating scaffolding and risk-bearer validation across scales is minimally required for symmetry and non-domination without implying final authority.

Global couplings must be interdependent rather than coercive and multi-domain coordination engines become structurally necessary to maintain them. Domains necessarily require boundary insertion to prevent laundering of standing. Economic reconstruction implies re-index incentives to autonomy preservation and mitigating level 1 and 2 autonomy exposure correspondingly. Technological design at a global level demands coupling safeguards and epistemic pollution reduction.

Taken together, the global-scale analyses in this chapter identify the structural boundary conditions of pluralist coordination. At planetary scale, standing cannot instantiate, capacity-indexing cannot be validated, relevance drifts across domains, and punitive logic collapses into entropy and domination. Global harms become Independently Emergent Wrongs, where neither culpability nor interpersonal repair can function, and where tragedy is produced not by malice but by structural conditions that exceed the reach of any agent.

In such an environment, legitimacy must migrate from spatial mechanisms of standing to temporal mechanisms of memory, inheritance, and intergenerational commitment. Reconstruction emerges only as one expression of this broader structural horizon: the effort to build the scaffolding that future agents will need for symmetry, rerunnability, and non-domination at scales where these conditions cannot yet exist. This chapter therefore marks the outer limit of what current pluralist systems can sustain—and the beginning of the question of how endurance, legitimacy, and autonomy can be preserved across scales and across time.

Repair presumes an existing stable structure, but reconstruction builds the structure necessary for future repair. Without reconstruction, the system remains in irreversible drift in spite of repair attempts. Reconstruction is the structural equivalent of laying tracks for future symmetry-restoring operations.

Reconstruction conceptually requires a level of temporal depth as it applies to intergenerational repair. Standing can be expanded across time even when it cannot extend across borders. Memory becomes the repair operator over time for IEWs such that history is a coupling medium for future autonomy preservation. Legacy is then the interdependent structure by which pluralist endurance is scaffolded.

When repair fails within a system, time becomes the only remaining medium of repair. When standing cannot be generated in space, it must be generated across time. Reconstruction happens through memory, inheritance, historical recognition, and future-facing commitments. Absent global standing, the only stable repair operator left is time. That is where we go from here.

XV — ABOUT TIME, MEMORY, HISTORY, AND LEGACY

Purpose: This chapter examines how pluralist societies coordinate across time by storing, transmitting, and contesting relevance through memory, history, and legacy. It evaluates how the coupling–standing–legitimacy engine behaves when actors, harms, and narratives persist beyond their originating agents, and it identifies the structural conditions under which temporal claims may legitimately bind the present. The chapter diagnoses characteristic temporal pathologies—mythic authority, nostalgia governance, erasure, inherited domination—and derives criteria for reparative standing, intergenerational legitimacy, and autonomy-preserving legacy. Time is treated not as a metaphysical medium but as a coordination infrastructure: the storage layer through which asymmetry, repair, and rerunnability propagate across generations.

Orientation

What this Chapter Is and Is Not

Time is not simply a background dimension. It is the medium in which coordination becomes durable. It is where asymmetries persist and where standing decays or amplifies. This chapter provides a structural account of how time functions as a coordination infrastructure. It examines how standing behaves across temporal distance, especially when harmed agents, responsible agents, or risk-bearers are no longer present.

This chapter will show how dominant coupling in temporal domains is frequently misidentified and analyzes the temporal triad of memory, history, and legacy as three stages of stored coupling, each with their own failure modes. It explains how repair scales across temporal asymmetry using the frameworks repair tools. This chapter derives structural criteria for legitimate versus illegitimate appeals to the past and demonstrates how legacy can become domination if not constrained by symmetric standing and autonomy preservation.

The central insight is that time is the final structural test of the entire engine. This chapter addresses the coordination of agents who are temporally separated. It is not a theory of metaphysical time or a moral narrative about historical justice. It will not make a political theory of nationalism or heritage policy nor will it make a historical argument about which interpretations are correct.

Instead, it treats time as a structural medium in which legitimacy, standing, autonomy, and repair must still satisfy the very same constraints as every other domain but under more difficult conditions. There will not be a historiographical survey of philosophy of history or moral adjudication of past actors or civilizations. This is not a genealogical or cultural critique of specific traditions. It evaluates the temporal impact of relevant agents not being present to validate, refuse, correct, or contest.

Expectations

Readers should expect in this chapter a structural analysis of temporal impact and not a narrative history. They can anticipate to encounter conceptual discomfort where many societies treat their past as sacred, but structural legitimacy demands corrigibility, rerunnability, and answerability even for inherited narratives. All the same tools used in other chapters will be applied to temporal disputes.

Likewise, it can be expected that time will behave like a public institution and not a descriptive archive. Precision over moral language, national identity, and tradition often appear here and this chapter will translate them into structural terms rather than moralized conclusions. Readers can expect that memory will be demonstrated as a stored coupling that can generate asymmetry and will be shown to be non-neutral.

The author expects readers to be willing to understand that memory, history, and legacy are not “cultural decorations” but structural determinants of standing, constraint, and repair. They will need to be able to separate legacy as a normative claim that attempts to bind the present on behalf of the absent. Since this framework is evaluating structure as apart from value, readers will be expected to hold the two separate even in the face of inheritance and legacy.

Translations

As Einstein demonstrated in general and special relativity, time and space are interdependently coupled features of a single geometric structure—spacetime. Just as physics developed new terminology to avoid smuggling in prerelativistic assumptions, temporal terms in philosophy require structural translation to prevent the importation of cultural, moral, or identityladen presuppositions.

Terms such as memory, tradition, legacy, heritage, and history carry centuries of metaphysical weight, national identity claims, and moral sediment. If incorporated uncritically, they distort standing evaluations, inflate identity-based relevance, and disguise domination as continuity.

Thus, this chapter provides a explicit translation discipline:
Each term must be interpreted functionally, according to its role in the structural engine.
Each term must be stripped of moralized, nationalist, genealogical, or traditional authority.
Each term must be grounded in the logic of coupling → relevance → autonomyimpact → standing → legitimacy → repair.

Memory seems to imply accuracy or authenticity, but structurally it is simply stored coupling, which can drift.
History seems to imply truth, but structurally it is a public, institutionalized mechanism of standing allocation.
Legacy seems to imply entitlement, but structurally it is a teleological coupling attempting to bind the future.
Tradition seems to imply continuity, but structurally it is identitydefining coupling, not standing.
Heritage seems to imply reverence or ownership, but structurally it is a standing claim requiring validation.

These translations prevent historical narratives from laundering legitimacy, manufacturing standing, or simulating authority. They free the structural evaluation from cultural assumptions and ground temporal analysis in the same procedural rigor applied across all prior chapters.

Translation Table

Memory: The storage of relevance and coupling within individual or collective frames, vulnerable to drift, bias, and asymmetry accumulation.

History: Institutionalized, public-facing memory that claims standing; a shared repository of narratives that shapes coordination and confers or withdraws legitimacy.

Legacy: A teleological coupling that attempts to bind the future by projecting obligations, values, or identity forward in time; requires standing constraints to avoid domination.

Tradition: A relational identity-defining coupling that stabilizes group continuity; not intrinsically standing-generating without STC5 validation.

Heritage: A socially asserted claim of historical identity treated as property; structurally a standing claim that must satisfy autonomy constraints to avoid domination.

Ancestry: A genealogical coupling used to infer relevance or authority; structurally inert unless tied to autonomy-impact and validated standing.

Commemoration: A public salience practice that amplifies memory into shared relevance; has no coercive standing unless autonomy-impact is demonstrated.

Narrative: A linguistic-coupling structure that organizes memory into meaning; not evidence without reproducible coupling.

Temporal Standing: The structural capacity of a past event or agent to impose relevance or constraint upon present agents via validated impact, not via identity claims.

Inherited Claim: Any obligation attributed to descendants on behalf of ancestors; requires STC5 and NRPP to avoid illegitimate domination.

Historical Harm: An autonomy-impact pattern stored across time whose effects persist even when the original agents are gone; may constitute an IEW (Independently Emergent Wrong).

Structural Residue: A lasting asymmetry embedded in institutions or collective memory; a target for Temporal Repair Protocols.

Myth: A narrative coupling treated as dominant without validation; structurally a form of semantic capture over history.

Nostalgia: A backward-oriented teleological coupling that constructs idealized past states to justify present constraint.

Erasure: Decoupling of stored coupling; removal of memory that forecloses correction and collapses standing.

Institutional Memory: Compositional coupling stored within institutional practices; can entrench asymmetry if uncorrected.

Generational Drift: The gradual transformation of stored coupling across time; source of misalignment between relevance and standing.

Intergenerational Risk Inheritance: The transfer of exposure or harm across generations; requires CIA (capacityindexed autonomy) to determine standing.

Temporal Repair: A directed repair operation (Derivative Law of Directed Repair) applied to historical asymmetry; targets restoration of symmetric standing.

Legacy Domination: A failure mode where legacy is used to constrain present autonomy without satisfying standing or relevance criteria.

AutonomyPreserving Legacy: Future-oriented narrative that respects CIA and ALRP; supports future autonomy rather than constraining it.

Temporal Asymmetry: Any condition in which stored coupling privileges one group across time; requires repair to restore rerunnability.

Historical Validation: Public, non-parochial procedures (cross-check, agreed operations) used to evaluate historical claims for standing.

Temporal Decoupling: Loss or degradation of stored coupling that impairs repair, relevance, or standing evaluation.

Founding Narrative: A teleological and identity-defining coupling used to justify present governance; not intrinsically authoritative without structural validation.

Continuity Claim: Assertion that past practices bind the present; requires standing via autonomy-impact, not tradition alone.

Inherited Burden: A claim that descendants inherit guilt, duty, or obligation; must be bounded by NRPP and CIA or collapses into domination.

Posthumous Standing: The structural problem of whether the dead retain standing; resolved by evaluating impact on the living, not metaphysical authority.

Generational Exit: The structural right of a generation to decouple from inherited narratives or obligations when standing is illegitimate.

Temporal Equity: A standing and repair principle ensuring that asymmetry is not passed forward without justified standing.

Time as Coordination Infrastructure

Why Time is a Coordination Problem

Time becomes a coordination problem when the conditions for standing must persist beyond the agents who generated them, creating both a mechanism for asymmetry and rerunnability. As a result, time becomes problematic whenever relevance, standing, and autonomy-impact must persist without the agents who generated them. Coordination requires persistence, but persistence often is accompanied by loss.

The core of these losses stems from the perceptual frame variance as discussed in About Perception and the semantic drift discussed in About Language and Communication. Memory itself is a type of “storage” substrate for the experiences of these frames. It likewise becomes its own form of frame-like perception. Thus, memory inherits both perceptual variance (IPFA/PFA) and semantic variance, making it a fundamentally unstable substrate. When internalized, the frames decay over time to the individual such that the resolution of details and specifics to the individual likewise are less vivid. Memories fade over time. As previously demonstrated with unstable concepts like asymmetry and domination, memory as a system itself cannot function as the primary driver of legitimacy within pluralist groups for the same reason. Asymmetrical structures are inherently less stable and prone to failure.

Since memory itself is not a stable substrate, it produces a temporal asymmetry. Temporal asymmetry is asymmetry that persists after the original agents exit the system. As a result of this asymmetry, standing decays, amplifies, or transforms across time. Where standing had previously evaluated between co-present agents, the harmed agent or agent causing harm may not be present. Institutions which store these standings likewise can drift over time from the interpretations of their own procedures and systems because institutional memory is a compositional coupling rather than a fixed archive. Thus, standing must be reconstructed rather than assumed.

STC-5, NRPP, and the Hierarchy of Impact provide the necessary tools to do so because time introduces “absent factors” into coordination. Since standing cannot be read off presence, it must be reconstructed. Whether political, economic, cultural, identity related, or global, each standing claim is structurally precarious in those domains from the absent to the present. These tools, however, are not storage systems and are not held in isolation but are portable through time as well.

Domains change over time by their very nature of belonging to perceptual frames in one way or another. Given this instability, we require a temporal anchor that does not drift. Only structural operators with reproducible criteria can persist through time. Therefore, measurement—not memory—is the only structure capable of persisting symmetrically through time. Memory and history inherently produce drift whereas measurement is routinely stable. What can be measured over time is agreed operations, reproducibility, and auditability rather than the positions of those claimants within frames themselves.

Thus, any cross-domain engine which seeks to maintain relevance over time must be comprised of measurements which can be taken in principle over time to the same extent. This is a structural necessity created by not only the variance of domains but the impact of perception upon them as a function of time. As a result, the method by which such measurements are taken may change but the principle of measurements needed over time cannot do so without the engine itself falling subject to coercion.

Stored coupling which does fall subject to coercion can dominate future autonomy. Legacy and heritage behave like teleological constraints on future agents. Without capacity-indexed autonomy (CIA), legacy becomes domination. Without the Autonomy Limiting Reflex Principle (ALRP), legacy assigns obligations illegitimately.

For instance, consider a community which borrowed money to dig a well and wrote a charter that obligates everyone in the community to maintain this debt in the future. The founding generation operates under necessity but say a current generation has the capacity to provide its own water structure. What began as necessity becomes coercive when projected across generations without further standing evaluations, off-ramps, or exit viability. While the debt may need to be contractually satisfied, the perpetuity of the contract being demanded over time as legacy is a violation of CIA principles.

Contracts may bind legally even when they cannot bind structurally. Legal obligation does not automatically satisfy structural legitimacy. The inherited water debt is an IEW as the contract for the legacy water system no longer holds standing to bind current agents.

Stored coupling retains salience but loses context, making it easy to mistake for present relevance. Temporal pathologies arise when stored coupling is mistaken for live coupling. Identity coupling gets mistaken for autonomy-impact coupling, or identity laundering. Narrative coupling is often mistaken for truth. Ritual coupling gets mistaken for legitimacy. Repair of such mistakes is inherently temporal.

Repair cannot be instantaneous; Temporal repair must be proportional to temporal accumulation as a reflection of NRPP. It must address accumulated asymmetry. This is in accordance with the Derivative Law of Directed repair and correlates to the nature by which independently emergent wrongs (IEWs) emerge. Thus, to check rerunnability we must ask if the system can restart under symmetric constraints. Consequently, time is the double-edged sword which validates the success or failure of rerunnability and gives way to memory, history, and legacy.

The Temporal Triad (Memory, History, Legacy)

Memory

Memory constitutes the first, most lossy, and most fragile layer of the triad. Memory is stored coupling at the frame level and is subject to drift. While memory itself is the holder of the IPFA such that it holds the stored previous frames of the user and gives value to personal warrant, it does not inherently attribute this warrant to the public. It generates internal salience and personal standing but does not create public standing outside of externalized coupling.

Memory is often vulnerable to distortion, motivated retention, selection by identity or affect, compression, and integrity. Thus, memory is to time what perception is to space, a salience filter. It operates functionally to both create the IPFA from the collected perceptions but also as a system which is not inherently impervious to error. It is often encoded with tools that are subject to perception itself, such as narrative, and thus even to the individual may hold variance.

This instability deepens once memory becomes encoded in narrative, paving the ground for semantic capture. Memory narrative is necessarily variant as the perceptual frames which it is comprised of and is a form of compositional coupling. Internal frames are compositionally coupled, and memory is the name we give to the working volume of those couplings. Consequently, concepts like morality take shape from memories and who is seen as harmed and identity boundaries are likewise formed.

Memory does not generate STC-5 conditions by itself because standing requires public accessibility, not private salience. It is evidence, but not an authority itself. This is not only true in examples of eyewitness testimony being varied as discussed in About Perception but holds true even for IPFAs as our perceptions of memories often change or take on new meanings as new additions to the IPFA grant the agent new perspectives of old memories. Where perceptions filter the present, memory filters the past.

Memory is not an immutably perfect storage system. It is a “lossy compression” that is prone to faults intrinsically. Thus, it experiences data decay far faster than even its technological counterparts. It is subject to being falsified, selective, erased, or even inflated or deflated based on affective input at the time of generation.

History

History is memory that has been externalized and standardized. It is a form of institutionalized memory, is public-facing, and often claims standing authority because it creates shared coupling that institutions issue as standing-generation. It is often held by institutions such as education, government, and media. History being stored and propagated by these institutions is the very cause for our sense of value for those institutions and likewise our purpose in holding them to strict standards for the maintenance of those memories.

As the adage goes “history is written by the winners” but ultimately this too is a form of domination over the collective memory of a people group itself. Winner-written history is not incorrect because of bias but because it allocates standing without validation. The adage may be more accurately updated to say, “History is written by the institutions that prevail, but standing is upheld by repeatable evaluation and measurement.” All such history-writing institutions hold no less burden than that of the autonomy of all the people who are impacted by their recording of such memories. In the face of such burden, the standards for conduct and procedure are then necessarily high purely set in accordance with NRPP and ALRP.

Where politics often establishes founding documents, national narratives, and precedent, culture often creates rituals of remembrance, holidays, and collective ceremonies. As shown in About Politics and About Economics, within such political domains, economic systems are inherited in the form of capital, harm, and debt and conflict is passed down via histories of grievance, violence, and victimization. Where such events impact populations, narrative construction of history itself creates a form of semantic normalization. In terms of global history, this takes on the form of colonialism, migration, and resource extraction.

Many times, historical values fail via mythic authority, scapegoat history, progress teleology, nostalgia governance, or even institutional amnesia. History is validated by cross-checking mechanisms and capacity-indexing for descendants. STC-5 evaluations thus ask who has valid standing to make such claims over time and whose autonomy is violated by such claims. Institutional memory cannot be simply presumed legitimate, as a result.

Legacy

Legacy is the most structurally dangerous form of stored coupling because it seeks to bind the future without the future’s participation. Legacy arises when history becomes prescriptive rather than descriptive or analytic – when memory institutionalized as history is projected forward as obligation. It is a structurally future-facing form of teleological coupling of history and value continuity. It is a blend of teleological and identity-defining coupling that attempts to bind future agents through identity and culture obligations, inheritance structures, land claims, governance rules, or moral debts. Legacy often attributes a purpose or value to historicity itself as a mechanism to bypass standing and legitimacy evaluation.

Where morality steps in with moral debts over time, NRPP constrains them and demands fairness to descendants via CIA. Economic structural advantages emerge through wealth inheritance while ALRP constrains this to not strip others of autonomy via the preservation of exit viability and repair options. Politics creates constitutional legacy that often gives way to founding mythologies. Such mythologies often produce IEWs in the form of obligations over tradition, inherited enmity or vengeance narratives, or even genealogical meaning-making.

Repair for these harms can likewise remain as a purpose or legacy over time. As purpose and function emerge in how pluralist society values these structural outputs, repair and rerunnability become structurally paramount to that legacy. It asks of these values whether they allow restarts or not.

Where legacy does not allow restarts or repair, domination emerges. Legacy that cannot be rerun under symmetric conditions collapses structurally. Burden is inherited, governance is often frozen, and anti-exit constraints emerge structurally. While history itself is not always coupled teleologically with purpose or value as given by individuals, where such components are coupled, identity and even autonomy can be captured over time.  As such, legacy emerges as a common direct pathway to domination over time.

Philosophy of History and Memory

Philosophy has a tradition of handling history and memory that is varied over the scope of the domain. Halbwachs speaks to collective memory, Ricoeur to narrative identity, Nietzsche to monumental/antiquarian/critical history, Foucault & Derrida to archives and power, and Benjamin to the progress myth. All of these forms in this framework represent various modes of coupling whether teleological, interdependent, emergent, or otherwise. These thinkers illustrate the range of tools societies use to stabilize or shape temporal coupling. They show the many ways memory and history have been approached, all of which can be reframed as structural couplings within this system.

Their concerns illuminate the conceptual landscape but this framework diverges by not focusing on attempting to interpret meaning or determine moral evaluation. It doesn’t aim at a narrative coherence or hermeneutics. Instead, this framework focuses on standing, legitimacy, autonomy-impact, repair, drift, and rerunnability. By doing so, the framework is able to avoid the limitations inherent to moral and narrative categories because structural tests eliminate mythic authority, identity laundering, reverence-based claims, and ancestor-based coercion.

This is not an invalidation of the fields of moral evaluation or hermeneutics. Instead, it is a reframing of what those fields apply to. Where many of them presume standing or legitimacy from the onset, this framework pre-empts them by determining when those conditions exist in the first place. Thus, while it outperforms many of those categories in terms of outcome, it is not an invalidation of their work. It is instead a re-framing that liberates those categories from the common pitfalls and recursive debates which they have fallen recursively into for many years.

Cross-Domain Integration

Time is where every prior domain’s coupling is revealed for what it is – durable, unstable, or dominant. Each of them contains a form of stored coupling. Time is where these storages reveal their fragility. It exposes the deepest failures because it is where drift accumulates.

Since every prior domain interacts with stored coupling, temporal analysis becomes the point where the entire system’s coherence is tested. Perception drift is a parallel to memorial drift in that salience selection often leads to memory selection. Where language allows narrative to create coupling semantically, history is a form of institutionalized narrative. As such, myths emerge as a form of historical semantic capture.

When morality leads to responsibility across time, NRPP demands that no such inheritance of punitive outcomes endures. Standing must be reconstructed over time. Harms may persist independently of the original wrongdoer, but it is structurally incompatible with pluralist cooperation to assign this debt to future agents.

Even though politics establishes legacy through constitutions and institutional memory through precedent, legitimacy must be temporally validated. Legacy systems in this domain and others technologically constrain future choices as technological systems often store drift, error, and bias intrinsically. Markets store asymmetry through technology and debt, making economic coercion inherently temporal.

Such instrumental couplings over time shape our identities through tradition, heritage and ancestry. Culture is often ritualized as memory and conflicts become historical enmity over time. As a result, global concerns often transform into intergenerational harm. Thus, temporal coordination is the backbone of global justice and stability. Failures of temporal coordination produce the most durable forms of domination — expressed through what we can now identify as dominant temporal coupling.

Dominant Temporal Coupling

The Mechanism

All forms of coupling have a temporal value. Thus, all types of coupling can be temporally dominant. Dominant Temporal Coupling is not a newly introduced type of coupling itself but regards the coupled attribute of domination as an outcome of that temporal factor to the prevailing type of coupling for a given domain or event.

A temporal coupling becomes Dominant Temporal Coupling (DTC) when stored coupling performs the majority of standinggenerating or autonomyimpacting work that would ordinarily be distributed across present capacities and conditions such that present agents, conditions, or capacities become secondary or overridden. Stored coupling emerges when institutional, contractual, cultural, or commitment-based constraints persist across time. This modifier to coupling can emerge from either past states or intergenerationally. Coordination under plurality requires accountability, corrigibility, and non-domination.

DTC forecloses future corrigibility and is a violation of the Axiom of Interaction & Coordination. Since one party’s temporal projection overrides a future agent’s standing, rerunnability becomes non-viable as a violation of the Axiom of Symmetry. Furthermore, DTC treats institutions or present selves as possessing standing over future selves without the means to validate the legitimacy of such standing. This is a violation of the Axiom of Derivative Standing.

DTC as a modification of other couplings compounds them by creating a conditional coupling where future agents are treated as subordinate components of a present actor’s intent. It often emerges as a misused form of teleological coupling that has been misidentified as legitimate because the future agent cannot revise or advise but is no less bound by this established coupling. This temporal asymmetry increases fragility as future feedback is suppressed, in line with the Derivative Law of Asymmetric Fragility.

When future agents inherit fixed obligations, it is impossible to retain rerunnability. This effectively establishes the asymmetry as A>B where A is the present agent and B is the future agent. If constraints are frozen at a given time and inherently limit future autonomy, the present agent structurally limits their own justificatory space by virtue of the ALRP. In alignment with the CAGP, capacity is indexed in phase A such that constraints applied become illegitimate by phase C without revalidating the constraints against rerunnable tests with non-parochial evidence.

The outcomes of Dominant Temporal Coupling emerge as linked to the Hierarchy of Impact as well. DTC often loads level one and two risks on future agents while present agents enjoy level three and four benefits. This violates the standing priority rule where levels one and two take priority over lower levels as demonstrated earlier.

Even small long-term constraints accumulate into high-impact consequences for future agents, as recognized by the Law of Cumulative Load. DTC increases “heat” of the system by enforcing non-revisable commitments. The heat represents increased systemic volatility resulting from reduced symmetry and suppressed feedback loops. The system drifts toward instability as a byproduct.

The Structural Mistake

Temporal conditions necessarily cannot be static. Time situates each frame such that any change across time — even under stationary conditions — alters the frame. Consequently, temporal conditions vary necessarily as frames themselves necessarily also vary.

Treating temporal conditions as static is the core mistake that leads to domination. It violates the Axiom of Interaction & Coordination because it assumes future coordination conditions identical to the present. Furthermore, it violates the Axiom of Symmetry because it assumes A and B are equal across time without allowing future agent re-expression.

It is the condition of present agents treating teleological coupling as if it were interdependent coupling. This misclassifies future conditions as compositional parts of a static system. This is an asymmetrical action which causes asymmetrical fragility to increase as it suppresses future agents. It is a trigger for the Directed Repair law. Repair must reduce asymmetry, but this structural mistake prevents this.

This mistake is often difficult to detect because perceptual frames themselves also drift. Present self overweights current relevance and future harms are perceptually discounted frequently. Present and future selves lack frame overlap to establish a PFA, making the action of the present self illegitimate. It creates a propagandistic framing directed inwardly as a form of self-capture. Future agents’ autonomy is reinterpreted through present-tense values, which is a form of asymmetry itself.

This structural mistake hides the transfer of risk to future selves. Risk cannot be imposed on agents without validation and future selves cannot validate. Risk inheritance without validation is structurally equivalent to moral hazard. While there is capacity for each individual to stake “risks” against their future agency, where these risks strip the individual of their UCE, it becomes destructive. UCE cannot be voluntarily surrendered if such surrender undermines the structural prerequisites for future autonomous agency. Ultimately, if all participants in a pluralist society operate with this method, pluralist societies cease to exist as they risk the conditions of the collective.

This is a genesis for how “gambling” becomes a coercive trap that agents place against themselves when it becomes “addiction.” It also establishes that some forms of future obligations that do not consider cumulative load such as “predatory loans” are themselves violations of the future selves of other agents. Addiction is a form of dominant temporal coupling against the future self and predatory loans are the same thing imposed by institutions. Consequently, in this framework all such actions are unjustified forms of coercion and lead to domination.

Derivative standing faces temporal consequences as well. Institutions that overclaim stability leads to claims of standing over future agents’ level one and two protections, such as shelter or means to feed themselves being a cost taken by the institution. By limiting future agents’ autonomy, present agents structurally limit the legitimacy of their own autonomy claims even when accepting this structural condition from an institution as the institutions themselves create the structural flaw itself in many cases. This happens as a consequence of the ALRP such that to reduce someone else’s relevant autonomy conditions is to reduce the justificatory set available to you because results must be universally defensible.

Where asymmetry is created, directed repair stands to contract. It requires acknowledging temporal misalignment and reinstating revision pathways. Dominant Temporal Coupling (DTC) cannot be solved by instant repair. Widespread temporal domination erodes pluralism as established by the Axiom of Interaction & Coordination. Only longitudinal standing maintenance can ensure symmetry over time. Standing over Time (SOT) must operate as a longitudinal measurement system, capable of tracking and recalibrating standing as agents, risks, and conditions evolve.

The Axiom of Symmetry applies across all temporal segments, not just present-time agents. As such SOT becomes necessary to define rerunnability, corrigibility, revision rights, and standing distribution over time for all such agents. Since standing must be preserved over time in order for these structural necessities to maintain viability, the criteria which provides standing likewise need to be maintained.

Diagnostic: How Dominant Coupling is Misidentified in Temporal Space

The Axiom of Symmetry checks whether future agents have symmetric rerun rights as a measure to test misidentification. It detects when temporal coordination turns into temporal domination. Likewise, when applying agree-operation analogues one may ask if the future agent can inspect, revise, or audit constraints. If they cannot, this is dominant temporal coupling misidentified as coordination.

To pre-test for standing over time we can evaluate if the present agent arrogates higher standing than the future agent. By comparing impact levels now versus later, and by applying the capacity-indexed autonomy gradient, domination can be identified. Assuming that agents will remain in Phase A of the gradient is a temporal misidentification just as awarding less standing to future agents who inherit more risk is.

A false positive may emerge when present constraint looks like domination but includes sunset clauses, revision mechanisms, and off-ramps. NRPP exists to review if revision exists such that constraint may be legitimate. Likewise, a false negative may emerge in the form of future constraints appearing voluntary but hiding irreversible outcomes. Using the Cumulative Load Law to identify when small present burdens begin to snowball into high future harm can help avoid these inadvertent mistakes. Where they cannot, IEWs may emerge where autonomy is impaired without culpability.

Consequently, the set of tools still operates over time to mitigate these misidentifications. Standing tests may take place where future stakeholders are identified. When they cannot validate, standing fails. Symmetry checks can compare present to future agents for rerunnability. Capacity-Indexed Autonomy can be forecast such that future capacity is not awarded less autonomy than present assumption. Risk inheritance may be evaluated by considering future agents facing level one or level two risks for harm. If the future cannot revise, dominant temporal coupling inherently creates structural opacity by virtue of varying frames and unpredictability among them.

Diagnostic results show that standing cannot be evaluated at a single time slice. Standing must be temporalized. Standing over time (SOT) defines how standing is preserved across increasing capacity, shifting risk, changing frames, and emerging conditions. Measurements may degrade over time, but the process of measurement is among the only things that do not. Thus, only measurement systems like SOT resolve misidentification because it embeds rerunnability, revision, and capacity alignment over time.

Standing Over Time

The Standing Problem of Absence

Temporal absence itself is a form of structural asymmetry. Future agents cannot answer, contest, revise, or refuse claims made in their name. Since they cannot participate in the justificatory process, nothing in the present can legitimately bind them without a built-in path for revision once they arrive. Absence of future agents creates a standing vacuum where no one is present to authorize, refuse, or redirect the claims made on their behalf.

Future agents always have stakes, even if they cannot appear to voice them. Treating them as if they have no standing because they are absent is structurally indistinguishable from domination. Agents who cannot authorize or contest decisions cannot have standing. Any claims which assert standing over future agents without corrigibility and proxy are then, by definition, dominating.

Temporal absence collapses symmetry because the Axiom of Symmetry requires rerunnability of all relevant agents, including those not yet present or those who do not have capacity. Absence amplifies asymmetric fragility because feedback cannot be received from the temporally displaced or those with lower capacities. The Axiom of Pluralistic Inclusion implies that future agents cannot be treated as a “null” value because standing cannot be withdrawn across temporal frames without violating autonomy.

Temporal drift in this sense becomes perceptual and structural decoupling. Future frames inherit constraints but not the perceptual or justificatory frame from which they were authored. This is the temporal analogue of perceptual frame misalignment. In this case, the misalignment is guaranteed by time rather than variance. Claims projected into the future cannot rely on present parochial perception. The requirement for non-parochial evidence binds temporally as much as synchronically. Absence forces evidence to be structurally incomplete, intensifying demand for corrigibility.

Types of Temporal Standing Claims

Temporal standing claims are not all identical. While the variations of them are numerous and this is not an exhaustive accounting of them, what emerges are several structural types. Beginning with the most obvious of them, consider Self-Binding Temporal Standing Claims.

Self-binding appears legitimate because the same identity persists. Agents often couple the confidence they have in a given moment to the choice in such a way that this binding appears legitimate at face value. Capacity and context however do not persist in the same way that identity and self-binding do. Capacity-Indexed Autonomy as a principle reveals phase-transition asymmetry. A constraint authored in phase A may violate autonomy in Phase C.

In terms of capacity indexing, it is the agent themself imposing constraints via phase A that correspond to later phases. Intergenerational Projection Standing Claims are claims that bind the not-yet-born. These claims are a violation of the Axiom of Derivative Standing because they assign derivative standing without successor inclusion. The hierarchy of impact exposes the asymmetry risk. Level one and level two burdens drift forward while level three and four benefits concentrate backward temporally.

While agents and externalized agents from them fail to address the standing of an agent or agents over time, Institutional Continuity Claims function in the opposite fashion. They occur when institutions assume their derivative standing persists unchanged over time. Continuity is not the same as legitimacy, however. Under ALRP, institutional claims contract over time as accumulated constraints narrow the justificatory space. Compositional coupling becomes unstable across temporal drift. Without revision pathways and rerunnable standing evaluations structure erodes. If the pathways lag behind inherited constraints, the same result occurs.

Many times, what is inherited by future generations are constraints to ecological systems and resources. Resource and Ecological Legacy Claims often create long-term risk inheritance. This framework treats irreversible or cumulative harms as structural standing failures rather than environmental errors. Temporal externalities cannot be validated by future agents. Therefore, they trigger constraints under the ADS, AoS, MOMA, and ALRP simultaneously. NRPP constraints to these decisions apply not only for the formal autonomy of the systems themselves but for future agents that rely upon them.

Even when these situations become emergencies, emergencies themselves introduce asymmetry due to temporal delay of correction. Emergency Deferment and Temporal Ratchet Claims trigger the Directed Repair Law, demanding a contraction of asymmetry. Any non-sunsetting temporal projection is structurally suspect. As discussed in previous chapters, emergencies accelerate the necessity for STC-5 and NRPP evaluation rather than relaxing them for this exact purpose.

STC-5, NRPP, ALRP & CIA Over Time

STC-5 is inherently a temporal constraint. The requirements do not direct actions. They articulate the structural limits within which temporal projection remains legitimate. Actions of all kinds have an implicit temporal value already as demonstrated in Minkowski space, where all objects have an X, Y, Z, and time variable.

All actions, even of a single object, are then reflected by the variance in the time vector of these objects such that any action at all is time bound. Thus, even what has been discussed in previous chapters truly already represents temporal values. What changes here is the separation created by time as a construct that inherently separates agents. Over time, each gate of the STC-5 becomes more restrictive because fewer risk-bearers can participate in validation.

Where STC-5 constraints apply NRPP is a limit on autonomy compression. Since all of them are inherently temporal, all NRPP evaluations limit temporal autonomy compression relative to the scale of time in consideration. It forbids imposing autonomy-reducing constraints beyond the minimally necessary level. Over temporal distance, necessity becomes epistemically weaker, thus the structural ceiling narrows.

Even though necessity becomes weaker epistemically over time, the ALRP remains as a reflexive temporal limitation even if NRPP is distorted by inability to identify necessity. When present agents restrict future agents, ALRP reflect the restriction back onto the present justificatory space. Temporal domination reduces present legitimacy because the Maxim of Mutual Autonomy extends across temporal identity as well.

Where such autonomy is extended across temporal values, capacity indexing and phases drift as well. Capacity phases shift not only within individuals but across generations. Claims authored under low-capacity conditions (phase A) cannot bind high-capacity agents (phase C) without violating the Axiom of Symmetry.

To maintain such symmetry over time, rerunnability must remain. When rerunnability fails or becomes structurally impossible, constraints extend into conditions where relevant agents cannot replicate the justificatory frame. This is the temporal analogue of a failed experiment under controlled conditions. Rerunnability conceptually carries implicit temporal value as the very definition of it presumes non-simultaneity.

Structural Admissibility Conditions

Standing remains admissible over time only if temporal arrangements preserve the possibility of revision under altered conditions. Corrigibility is not a “procedure” but a structural necessity to maintain the Axiom of Symmetry across time. Corrigibility is structurally necessary across frames.

Likewise, drift can break any single link in the chain and thus standing dissolves over time. The full core engine of coupling, relevance, autonomy-impact, and standing must remain functional over time in order for relevance and standing to remain admissible. Likewise, temporal commitments that cannot be exited or recalibrated become domination by structural necessity.

Non-domination across temporal distance implies that the Axiom of Interaction & Coordination forbids coordination that forecloses future refusal. Since opacity increases over time due to memory loss, institutional, and context collapse, legibility becomes a structural requirement rather than a procedure. Without it, derivative standing collapses.

When standing collapses, irreversibility is the temporal form of coercive non-exit. Any constraint that cannot be reversed as conditions drift becomes structurally inadmissible. This applies just as well to the Law of Cumulative Load in that it becomes stricter across time because accumulation is an inherent feature of temporal systems. Even low-impact present actions can convert into high-impact future harms.

Stability must be structurally afforded without future lock-in. Stability is required for coordination but lock-in generates domination. Admissibility lies directly between volatility and irreversibility. In the face of such volatility, stable structural patterns of failure emerge temporally.

Canonical Temporal Failure modes

Mythic Authority

Mythic Authority is a temporal failure mode marked by the elevation of historical figures, founding narratives, or civilizational myths to a status that overrides current standing, contestation, or corrigibility. It creates distorted relational-identity defining coupling where past agents gain unilateral influence over present risk-bearers. This is a violation of the Axiom of Symmetry because the past can bind the present, but the present cannot rerun the past.

Mythic narratives generate asymmetric relevance weights that dominate all present alternatives because mystic relevance is non-rerunnable and therefore structurally untestable. It typically fails the relevance evaluation because mythic salience is not equivalent to structural necessity. To determine that necessity, NRPP evaluations can be made of mythic invocations to establish their connection to present actors.

As Jason Stanley highlights in “How Fascism works” this is a key temporal failure mode in the implementation of fascist regimes as they harken to what he calls a “mythic past” as a tactic to gain power and divide societies. This tactic creates standing without accountability and is a violation of the Axiom of Derivative standing because present risk-bearers cannot modify or contest the narrative.

After evaluating for the STC-5 constraints, Mythic Authority violates nearly every single boundary condition for pluralist collective cooperation. It furthermore violates the Law of Cumulative Load by allowing past dogma to accumulate coercively. Repair then requires demythologizing relevance weights, restoring corrigibility, and applying directed repair to reassign standing to present agents.

Nostalgia Governance

Many people often confuse Nostalgia Governance with Mythic authority because they both end to share an active coupling to the past and often involve modern invocations of past events. Nostalgia Governance, however, is created when governing runs by idealized or selective pasts. This is often combined with Mythic Authority in such a way that what is mythicized is the idealized or selective path itself as a form of creating that idealization.

This often takes on rhetorical forms of expressing a need to “return to tradition” or “restore what was lost.” When nothing truly was lost, this becomes a hybrid of Nostalgia Governance that is fed by Mythic Authority. Nostalgia typically forms an affective form of relational-identity defining coupling rather than a structurally relevant one. It is an emergent coupling type that couples to the affective traits of individuals as a method of coercion. Affectation, as discussed in earlier chapters, is not however a standing-bearing category. Affective salience cannot substitute for structural relevance, as demonstrated in earlier chapters.

Nostalgia often masks structural exclusion and ultimately violates the Axiom of Symmetry because it elevates past standing over the standing of present or future risk-bearers. Without a re-evaluation of standing, SOT shows that this standing decays over time and produces the emergent asymmetry. This is a violation of the Axiom of Pluralistic Inclusion when new groups, identities, or needs are excluded in the name of past norms.

Nostalgia fails when alternatives are blocked, evidence is reliant upon selective memory and is unverifiable, or when there are no off-ramps. Thus, repairs are necessary for Nostalgic Governance. They involve temporal relevance recalibrations and sunset clauses.

Presentism and Erasure

Though the past cannot hold immutable authority of the present, this does not predispose the past to having no value or contribution for standing. Instead, forgetting, suppressing, or rewriting past harms to avoid repair obligations or responsibility is another temporal failure mode called Presentism or Erasure. It is a temporal decoupling failure affecting compositional coupling that refuses to inherit history as a part of standing. This is a violation of derivative standing since descendants of harmed agents cannot claim repair that has been inherited.

Erasure reduced the relevance of past harms to zero, making harm-repair structurally impossible. Likewise, new harms in the form of IEWs or even intentional harm may be produced as autonomy impacts of Presentism/Erasure. This fails STC-5 evaluations because not all risk-bearers are being accounted for when the history of those who had once been considered is forgotten in future evaluations. It produces a structural asymmetry by virtue of severing the present form any sort of inherited risk that is necessarily implicit.

This is evidenced in examples of groups which seek to minimize or rewrite the harms that have come to the black community in the USA, the Jewish populations in Germany, and elsewhere over time. Directed repair always flows forward from the events and suppressing or rewriting the harms that happened constitutes a violation of the STC-5 standard for non-parochial evidence as it intrinsically taints evidence itself where the PFA is only capable of performing such alignments based on this recorded history. Simply put, risk-inheritance is inherently temporal and cannot be nullified by merely forgetting.

Scapegoat History

Scapegoat History is a mode of temporal failure that attributes responsibility for present asymmetries to constructed or powerless past groups. It is a fabricated teleological coupling projected backward in time. Scapegoat History is comprised of a decoupling of present non-parochial evidence and a simulated temporal teleological coupling. Scapegoating generates a false relevance past making past “others” become permanent containers for present responsibility.

Scapegoat History blocks directed repair because responsibility is temporally displaced. It violates STC-5 because risk-bearer validation is impossible. It makes off-ramps structurally impossibly and is thus a violation of the Law of Cumulative Load.

Responsibility and culpability displacement creates asymmetry which inherently produces fragility in accordance with asymmetric fragility. Repair of this failure mode involves the reassignment of responsibility by operating STC-5 evaluations again and abiding ALRP and NRPP constraints. This establishes current coupling to existing evidence within the PFA as an alignment of that PFA to the current standing that is represented by it.

Destiny/Progress Teleology

Justifying present harms by appealing to an inevitable future is a temporal failure mode as well. Destiny/Progress Teleology commonly makes use of rhetoric like the “arc of history” or a “necessary sacrifice” when the ultimatum did not initially exist. It is coupling dynamic that prioritizes future agents over present agents and violates symmetry. It binds the future to the present such that it cannot be rerun. Examples include justifying current harm as necessary for imagined “future flourishing” or “inevitable progress.”

Teleological narratives generate illusory relevance such as saying “this must happen for a destined outcome.” When future autonomy is invoked to reduce present autonomy, however, this violates Capacity-Indexed Autonomy in that it inherently stifles a motion from one phase of the gradient to another without a justification. Instead, it supplants the justification with a supposition of a future autonomy that hasn’t been validated through STC-5.

When applying the NRPP, teleological temporal claims generally fail by neither being least restrictive nor proportional to the level of harm being done. Since, alternate futures exists in the form of Sartre’s possibilities, such alternate futures collapse and thus collapse exit and autonomy with it. The justificatory standards for such actions via STC-5 are then proportionally maximized as Destiny/Progress Teleology oftentimes defers repair indefinitely.

Institutional Amnesia

Institutional Amnesia is the decay of memory inside institutions leading to repeated harms, loss of correction capacity, and structural drift. Institutional memory is intrinsically a compositional coupling. This is a reflection of the instability of memory itself as a structural pillar. Amnesia within that coupling represents a collapse or decoupling happening structurally. It removes the informational inputs required for STC-5 Evaluations.

Institutional Amnesia blocks rerunnability and prevents asymmetry correction because past harms cannot be brought forward for repair.
